stories.headline: Exercise changed fat in mice before weight loss

sources.title: Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice (ScienceDaily)
Strength training causes fat cells to shrink even before weight loss (Agência FAPESP)
Strength Training Shrinks Fat Cells in Just 7 Days, Study Finds (Newsweek)

chunks.text: Many people {{work out}} because they want to {{burn off}} [[body fat]]. When the [[scale]] does not change, some think their training is not helping. A new study in mice suggests that some helpful changes can {{kick in}} before any [[weight loss]] {{shows up}}. Scientists at a state university in Brazil published the study in the [[journal]] Life Sciences. [[News outlets]] reported the results in September and October 2026.

verbs.correct: To exercise to stay fit
verbs.wrong: To weigh yourself often
verbs.why: I work out at the gym before work. My sister works out three times a week. Many people work out because they want to lose body fat.

verbs.correct: To lose fat by exercising
verbs.wrong: To eat food with less fat
verbs.why: A long walk burns off some extra fat. Daily swimming burns off extra weight quickly. Many people exercise because they want to burn off body fat.

verbs.correct: To start to have an effect
verbs.wrong: To be checked by scientists
verbs.why: Most pain pills kick in after about twenty minutes. New tax rules often kick in at the start of the year. The study suggests that some helpful changes from exercise can kick in before weight loss.

verbs.correct: To become easy to see
verbs.wrong: To be written in a report
verbs.why: Small cracks often show up only on a second X-ray. Bruises show up a day after a fall. In the mice, helpful changes came before any weight loss showed up.

chunks.text: The researchers {{set up}} an experiment with male mice. Some mice ate a [[high-fat diet]] until they were [[obese]]. One group of obese mice stayed [[inactive]]. Another group did seven sessions of [[strength training]]. In each session, the mice climbed a small [[staircase]] 20 times with weights attached to their tails. Both groups kept eating the same food. The team wanted to {{find out}} what exercise does to fat before weight loss begins.

verbs.correct: To plan and prepare a test
verbs.wrong: To repeat an old test
verbs.why: Science classes set up simple tests with plants. Doctors set up studies with hundreds of patients. The researchers set up an experiment with male mice.

verbs.correct: To discover facts by testing
verbs.wrong: To share results with others
verbs.why: Doctors find out the cause of most fevers with a blood test. Mechanics find out what is wrong by testing the engine. The team wanted to find out what exercise does to fat before weight loss.

chunks.text: After the seven sessions, the trained mice weighed about the same as the inactive mice. However, they had less fat around their [[intestines]], and their [[fat cells]] were smaller. In people, similar fat is found deep inside the [[belly]], near important [[organs]]. It is considered more [[harmful]] than fat under the skin. Obesity had [[disrupted]] the system that {{breaks down}} stored fat for energy. The training seemed to {{turn on}} parts of that system again.

verbs.correct: To make fat usable as energy
verbs.wrong: To move fat to the skin
verbs.why: When you exercise, your body breaks down fat for fuel. The body breaks down stored fat when it needs more energy. Obesity had disrupted the system that breaks down stored fat in the mice.

verbs.correct: To make something start working
verbs.wrong: To measure how something works
verbs.why: Exercise turns on certain genes in the body. Cold weather turns on the body's system for making heat. The training seemed to turn on parts of the fat-breaking system again.

chunks.text: The researchers {{point out}} that the results are still [[experimental]]. They do not mean that seven days of training will do the same for people. The study used only male mice and one kind of fat. A doctor who was not [[involved]] told a U.S. magazine that mice are very different from humans. The team now plans to {{look into}} longer training [[periods]] and fat around the heart. One author said beginners should {{keep at}} it, even when the scale does not change.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To repeat a fact many times
verbs.why: Teachers often point out that the test is on Monday. Doctors point out that some pills are not safe for children. The researchers point out that the results are still experimental.

verbs.correct: To study something carefully
verbs.wrong: To describe a past study
verbs.why: The police look into the cause of every fire. A good manager looks into problems quickly. The team now plans to look into longer training periods and fat around the heart.

verbs.correct: To continue trying hard
verbs.wrong: To train in a group
verbs.why: Good students keep at it when a language gets hard. Musicians keep at their practice for years. One author said beginners should keep at it.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in Brazil found that a week of strength training changed fat in obese mice whose weight stayed the same. Their fat cells shrank, but it is unclear if people would see this too.
mainIdea.why: The trained mice weighed about the same but had smaller fat cells. The researchers point out that the results may not be the same for people.

mainIdea.s: Brazilian scientists showed that seven workouts made the fat cells of overweight mice smaller. They say this proves that people will get the same benefit after only a week of lifting weights.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers point out that the results are still experimental. They do not say people will get the same results in seven days.

mainIdea.s: A new survey finds that many adults stop going to the gym within three months of joining. Most of the people who quit say that work and family leave them too little free time for exercise.
mainIdea.why: This is about a study in mice. Seven sessions of strength training seemed to turn on the system that breaks down stored fat.

tf.s: Some changes from exercise kicked in before any weight loss.
tf.why: The trained mice had less fat around their intestines and smaller fat cells, but they weighed about the same.

tf.s: The mice that worked out lost a lot of weight in one week.
tf.why: After the seven sessions, the trained mice weighed about the same as the inactive mice.

tf.s: The researchers did their study with people at a gym.
tf.why: They set up an experiment with male mice, and they point out that the results are still experimental.

tf.s: The trained mice had smaller fat cells than the inactive mice.
tf.why: After they worked out, the trained mice also had less fat around their intestines.

tf.s: Training seemed to help part of the fat-burning system work again.
tf.why: Obesity had disrupted the system that breaks down stored fat, and training seemed to turn on parts of it again.

tf.s: The researchers say people will surely get the same results.
tf.why: They point out that the results are still experimental and may not be the same for people.

stories.headline: China's economy grows faster than expected

sources.title: China's economy grows 4.5 percent in Q3, beating forecasts (Al Jazeera)
China economy: Growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness (BBC News)
China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates (CNBC)

chunks.text: New official [[figures]] that {{came out}} on Monday, October 19, 2026, show that China's [[economic growth]] has {{picked up}}. The economy grew 4.5 percent from July to September, compared with the same months in 2025. That was slightly better than most experts expected. Growth had {{slowed down}} to 4.3 percent from April to June, the weakest rate in three years. The government's [[target]] for 2026 is 4.5 to 5 percent.

verbs.correct: To be made public
verbs.wrong: To be checked again
verbs.why: Exam results come out in the middle of August. A new report on jobs comes out every month. China's new growth figures came out on Monday, October 19, 2026.

verbs.correct: To become stronger or faster
verbs.wrong: To be counted in a new way
verbs.why: Sales usually pick up in December. The wind picks up in the afternoon. China's economic growth picked up from July to September.

verbs.correct: To grow more slowly
verbs.wrong: To be reported late
verbs.why: Growth often slows down as a country gets richer. Home sales slow down in the winter months. China's growth slowed down to 4.3 percent from April to June.

chunks.text: Exports were the main reason for the growth. Chinese factories have {{cashed in on}} a global [[boom]] in artificial intelligence. There is strong [[demand]] for computer chips and other parts for AI [[data centers]]. Production of batteries and [[industrial robots]] grew by more than 29 percent. These strong sales abroad have {{made up for}} weak spending at home. Experts expect China's [[trade surplus]] to beat last year's record of 1.2 trillion dollars.

verbs.correct: To make money from a good chance
verbs.wrong: To lend money to new companies
verbs.why: Hotels cash in on big sports events in their city. Ice cream shops cash in on hot summer days. Chinese factories have cashed in on a global boom in artificial intelligence.

verbs.correct: To balance a weak part with a strong one
verbs.wrong: To hide a weak part from buyers
verbs.why: Good online sales make up for a slow month in the store. A busy summer makes up for a quiet winter at the beach hotel. Strong sales abroad have made up for weak spending at home in China.

chunks.text: Spending at home is much weaker. Many shoppers in China are still {{holding back}}. [[Retail sales]] rose only 1.1 percent in September. An economist said worries about trade have {{put many families off}} spending. Slow [[wage growth]] and high [[youth unemployment]] also hurt. The biggest problem is the [[property market]]. China has struggled for years to {{shake off}} a [[housing slump]]. Property [[investment]] fell by more than 20 percent in the first nine months of 2026.

verbs.correct: To be careful about spending money
verbs.wrong: To buy things mostly online
verbs.why: Many families hold back when prices are high. Shoppers hold back when they worry about their jobs. Many shoppers in China are still holding back.

verbs.correct: To make someone not want to do something
verbs.wrong: To make prices higher for someone
verbs.why: High prices put many people off buying a new car. Long lines put customers off the new restaurant. Worries about trade have put many Chinese families off spending.

verbs.correct: To get free of a problem
verbs.wrong: To blame others for a problem
verbs.why: Some towns never shake off the loss of a big factory. It takes years to shake off a bad reputation. China has struggled for years to shake off a housing slump.

chunks.text: The government {{stepped up}} its support in late September. It offered lower [[interest rates]] to some businesses and [[subsidies]] for home buyers. Some [[trading partners]], including the U.S. and the European Union, are {{pushing back}} against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods. One economist expects China to {{keep up}} its faster pace for the rest of 2026. A finance professor at Stanford University said a slow, controlled [[slowdown]] is the best the government can hope for.

verbs.correct: To give more of something
verbs.wrong: To explain a plan again
verbs.why: Police step up patrols on busy weekends. The city steps up its help for poor families in winter. China's government stepped up its support for the economy in late September.

verbs.correct: To show you do not accept something
verbs.wrong: To sell goods at a lower price
verbs.why: Workers push back against longer hours. Parents often push back against new school rules. Some trading partners are pushing back against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

verbs.correct: To continue at the same level
verbs.wrong: To change the target for growth
verbs.why: Good runners keep up the same speed for the whole race. Our team needs to keep up this level of work. One economist expects China to keep up its faster pace for the rest of 2026.

vocab.def: To be made public
ex: The test scores come out next Friday.
The election results came out late at night.
The truth about the deal came out a year later.

vocab.def: To become stronger or faster

vocab.def: To grow more slowly
ex: Car sales slowed down after prices went higher.
Growth in online sales has slowed down.
Sales growth slows down when prices rise.

vocab.def: To make money from a good chance
ex: Toy stores cash in on the weeks before Christmas.
Many companies tried to cash in on the new trend.
Local farmers cashed in on the demand for fresh fruit.

vocab.def: To balance a weak part with a strong one
ex: Her hard work made up for her lack of experience.

vocab.def: To be careful about spending money

It took the city ten years to shake off its money problems.

vocab.def: To give more of something

wordDefs.def: Official numbers that show how much of something there is
ex: The latest sales figures look good for the store.
Can you check these figures before the meeting?
The figures show that more people are moving to the city.

wordDefs.def: An increase in how much a country produces and earns
ex: New jobs are a sign of economic growth.
The president promised strong economic growth.

wordDefs.def: A number or result that you plan to reach
ex: Our sales target for this month is 50 cars.
The school met its target for new students.

wordDefs.def: A time when something grows very fast and makes a lot of money

wordDefs.def: Machines that do work in factories, like building cars

wordDefs.def: When a country sells more to other countries than it buys from them

wordDefs.def: The money people spend in stores and online shops

wordDefs.def: The number of young people who want a job but cannot find one
ex: Youth unemployment is a big problem in many cities.

wordDefs.def: The buying and selling of houses, apartments and land
ex: The property market in our city is very busy.

ex: Many builders lost money in the housing slump.

wordDefs.def: The extra money you pay a bank when you borrow money
ex: Low interest rates make it cheaper to buy a car.

wordDefs.def: Money that a government gives to help pay for something
ex: Farmers get subsidies to grow certain crops.

Some students get subsidies for their bus rides.

wordDefs.def: Countries that buy from and sell to each other
ex: Canada and Mexico are important trading partners of the U.S.
The two trading partners signed a new deal.
Japan is one of Australia's biggest trading partners.

wordDefs.def: A time when something becomes slower or less active
ex: The factory cut hours during the slowdown.

mainIdea.s: China's economy grew a bit faster than experts expected from July to September, mostly thanks to strong sales of tech goods abroad. Spending by families and the housing market are still weak.
mainIdea.why: Growth picked up to 4.5 percent because exports were strong. At home, many shoppers are still holding back and the housing slump goes on.

mainIdea.s: Chinese shoppers have started buying far more in stores, and this lifted the economy to its best result in years. Because of that, factories now sell fewer chips and robots to other countries.
mainIdea.why: Close, but it was the other way around. Strong sales abroad made up for weak spending at home, where many shoppers are still holding back.

mainIdea.s: Beijing has announced a plan to build thousands of new factories in poor rural areas of the country. Officials say the project will create millions of jobs for young workers over ten years.
mainIdea.why: The real news is about new growth figures that came out on October 19. Exports helped the economy, while spending at home stayed weak.

tf.s: China's economic growth picked up between July and September.
tf.why: The economy grew 4.5 percent in those months, up from 4.3 percent from April to June.

tf.s: Strong spending at home made up for weak exports.
tf.why: It was the other way around. Strong sales abroad made up for weak spending at home.

tf.s: Chinese factories have cashed in on a global boom in artificial intelligence.
tf.why: There is strong demand for computer chips and other parts for AI data centers.

tf.s: Shoppers in China are now spending freely again.
tf.why: Many shoppers are still holding back, and worries about trade have put many families off spending.

tf.s: Some trading partners are happy to buy more cheap Chinese goods.
tf.why: Some trading partners, including the U.S. and the European Union, are pushing back against large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

tf.s: China is still struggling to shake off a long housing slump.
tf.why: China has tried for years to shake off the slump, and property investment fell by more than 20 percent.

stories.headline: Storm Adam floods towns on Spain's east coast

sources.title: Four dead as torrential rain batters eastern Spain (Al Jazeera)
At least five killed and thousands evacuated as Storm Adam batters eastern Spain (Euronews)
Pedro Sanchez to visit Valencia village left 'upside down' by deadly Storm Adam as 280 were rescued by helicopter and 2,100 evacuated (The Olive Press)

chunks.text: Storm Adam caused [[severe flooding]] in eastern Spain in October 2026. Heavy rain {{set in}} on Saturday, October 17. Some towns in the Valencia and Alicante areas got more than 600 millimeters of rain, or about 24 inches, in 24 hours. Rivers [[overflowed]], and many streets were [[under water]]. The floods {{washed cars away}} and {{cut off}} several towns. News reports on October 20 counted at least four deaths. Some reports counted five.

verbs.correct: To begin and seem likely to last
verbs.wrong: To fall only in a small area
verbs.why: Cold weather sets in early in the mountains. In some places, the rainy season sets in each June. Heavy rain set in on Saturday, October 17, along Spain's eastern coast.

verbs.correct: To move something with the force of water
verbs.wrong: To fill something with river water
verbs.why: Heavy rain often washes the soil away on this hill. A big wave sometimes washes small boats away. The floods washed cars away in several towns.

verbs.correct: To make a place impossible to reach
verbs.wrong: To send help to a place by air
verbs.why: Deep snow cuts off our village every winter. Floods often cut off farms near the river. The floods cut off several towns in eastern Spain.

chunks.text: Emergency services {{carried out}} about 500 rescues in the Valencia region, a government official said. In one [[coastal town]], helicopters lifted about 280 people to safety, many from [[rooftops]]. In Alicante province, rescuers {{pulled 13 people out}} of their cars after a tunnel flooded. The government also {{brought in}} its [[military emergency unit]]. More than 2,100 people were [[evacuated]]. A [[public shelter]] in the [[hardest-hit]] town {{took in}} about 400 people overnight.

verbs.correct: To do a planned task or job
verbs.wrong: To count the number of people
verbs.why: Firefighters carry out safety checks every month. The team carries out a test before each trip. Emergency services carried out about 500 rescues in the Valencia region.

verbs.correct: To remove someone from a place
verbs.wrong: To check that someone is not hurt
verbs.why: Lifeguards pull swimmers out of strong waves. Firefighters sometimes pull drivers out of crashed cars. Rescuers pulled 13 people out of their cars after a tunnel flooded.

verbs.correct: To ask a group to come and help
verbs.wrong: To give a group new orders
verbs.why: The city brings in extra workers after big storms. Schools bring in experts when there is a serious problem. The national government brought in its military emergency unit.

verbs.correct: To give people a place to stay
verbs.wrong: To move people to a safer town
verbs.why: The church takes in families who lose their homes. Animal shelters take in lost dogs. A public shelter took in about 400 people overnight.

chunks.text: On Monday, October 19, officials told people in about 145 towns to {{stay in}}. They asked people to avoid travel and move to [[upper floors]]. The regional government {{sent out}} [[emergency alerts]] to cell phones over the weekend and on Monday. The alerts told people to {{stay away}} from rivers and to move to [[higher ground]]. Classes were [[canceled]] for more than 100,000 students. By Monday afternoon, most of the [[restrictions]] had ended.

verbs.correct: To remain inside your home
verbs.wrong: To keep your doors locked
verbs.why: We stay in on cold, rainy nights. Many people stay in when the roads are icy. Officials told people in about 145 towns to stay in on October 19.

verbs.correct: To deliver a message to many people
verbs.wrong: To check a message for mistakes
verbs.why: The school sends out a text when classes are canceled. The city sends out warnings before a big storm. The regional government sent out emergency alerts to cell phones.

verbs.correct: To not go near something
verbs.wrong: To keep watching something
verbs.why: Doctors tell sick people to stay away from crowds. Good swimmers stay away from the rocks. The alerts told people to stay away from rivers.

chunks.text: The floods {{brought back}} [[painful memories]] of October 2024. Back then, floods killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region. Officials faced [[criticism]] for late phone warnings. The rain began to {{die down}} on Tuesday, October 20. Spain's prime minister planned to visit the flooded coast that day. The national weather agency kept warnings in place for nine [[provinces]]. It asked people in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands to {{watch out for}} more heavy rain.

verbs.correct: To make you remember something
verbs.wrong: To make you angry about something
verbs.why: This song brings back happy memories of my childhood. Old photos bring back memories of our first home. The floods brought back painful memories of the deadly floods in October 2024.

verbs.correct: To slowly become less strong
verbs.wrong: To suddenly change direction
verbs.why: The wind usually dies down at night. The noise dies down when the teacher arrives. The rain began to die down on Tuesday, October 20.

mainIdea.s: Storm Adam brought extreme rain to eastern Spain, flooding towns and killing at least four people. Officials sent early phone alerts, unlike in 2024, and warnings moved north to Catalonia.

mainIdea.s: Heavy rain from Storm Adam flooded Spain's eastern coast and killed several people. Many residents were angry because the phone warnings reached them only after the water had risen.

stories.headline: Designers debate whether social media killed taste

sources.title: Is Taste Dead? We Asked 4 of London's Most Exciting Creatives to Unpack Our Obsession With the 'Hyper-Curated' (Livingetc)
'Filterworld' explores how social media algorithms 'flatten' our culture (NPR, Fresh Air)
Beige mania: the color defining the interiors of the TikTok Generation (Domus)

chunks.text: Some people say social media has killed personal [[taste]]. The organizers of a London [[art fair]] {{put on}} a [[panel]] on October 15, 2026, to debate that question. A writer for a British design magazine led it. She said people shape their style around [[algorithms]]. Feeds and [[targeted ads]] tell them what to like and buy. Shoppers can {{look up}} an outfit straight from an [[influencer]]'s photo. Critics worry that homes and clothes {{end up}} looking alike.

verbs.correct: To organize an event for people
verbs.wrong: To pay to visit an art show
verbs.why: Our school puts on a play every spring. The library puts on a free talk about local history every month. The organizers of a London art fair put on a panel to debate whether social media has killed taste.

verbs.correct: To find something on the internet
verbs.wrong: To save a photo to your phone
verbs.why: Shoppers look up store hours online. Music fans look up a song after they hear it on the radio. Shoppers can look up an outfit straight from an influencer's photo.

verbs.correct: To reach a result you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To be designed by the same company
verbs.why: Drivers who take a wrong turn often end up in the next town. Many art students end up working in banks. Critics worry that homes and clothes end up looking alike.

chunks.text: Critics say the [[sameness]] is easy to see in homes. In October 2025, an Italian design magazine searched [[vacation rentals]] in Paris. Room after room was sand, ivory or cream. It said beige was {{taking over}} from gray as the [[safe choice]]. People like beige because it does not [[offend]] anyone and seems to {{fit in}} anywhere. The same colors {{show up}} in furniture [[catalogs]]. The magazine warned that beige could become a [[formula]] that algorithms reward.

verbs.correct: To become the most common one
verbs.wrong: To be mixed with another color
verbs.why: In many homes, streaming services take over from cable TV. Each new phone model quickly takes over from the old one. An Italian design magazine said beige was taking over from gray in homes.

verbs.correct: To look right with everything else
verbs.wrong: To cost less than other colors
verbs.why: The old lamp fits in well with the new furniture. A bright red sofa would not fit in with the rest of this quiet room. People like beige because it seems to fit in anywhere.

verbs.correct: To appear in a place
verbs.wrong: To be painted by hand
verbs.why: Her name shows up in many old newspapers. That same song shows up on every radio station this summer. The same beige colors show up in furniture catalogs.

chunks.text: A writer for The New Yorker made a similar argument in a 2024 book. He told a radio show that feeds guess what each person will click on. They offer things that are not too surprising or [[challenging]]. But he also said the internet has {{opened up}} culture. Anyone can {{put out}} their art or music. In the past, magazine editors and [[record company]] bosses could {{shut out}} artists who did not match their taste.

verbs.correct: To make something available to all
verbs.wrong: To make something cost more
verbs.why: New train lines open up the coast to day visitors. Free online classes open up college courses to many people. The New Yorker writer said the internet has opened up culture.

verbs.correct: To share your work with the public
verbs.wrong: To sell your work to a magazine
verbs.why: Popular bands put out a new album every few years. She puts out a short video every week. Anyone can now put out their art or music on the internet.

verbs.correct: To not let someone take part
verbs.wrong: To give someone bad advice
verbs.why: Private clubs shut out anyone who cannot pay the high fee. Many tech companies shut out older workers. In the past, editors and record company bosses could shut out artists who did not match their taste.

chunks.text: Not everyone thinks taste is dead. A designer on the London panel said people {{build up}} taste slowly, through travel and making mistakes. You can buy beautiful furniture, he said, but not a [[point of view]]. A home with [[secondhand]] objects and pieces {{handed down}} in a family can feel special, because each one has a story. The writer {{came away}} from the panel feeling [[hopeful]] that taste is still alive.

verbs.correct: To develop something slowly
verbs.wrong: To prove something to others
verbs.why: Cooks build up skill over many years. Wine fans build up their knowledge one bottle at a time. A designer said people build up taste slowly, through travel and making mistakes.

verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: Fathers often hand down their watches to their sons. Mothers hand down old family recipes to their daughters. A home full of pieces handed down in a family can feel special, because each one has a story.

mainIdea.s: Designers and writers are debating whether online feeds have made homes and clothes look the same. Critics point to beige rooms everywhere, but others say personal taste can still grow.
mainIdea.why: Critics say algorithms push everyone toward the same safe look. Others say people build up their own taste slowly, so it is not dead.

mainIdea.s: A panel of London experts agreed that algorithms have completely destroyed personal style. They said the only answer is for people to delete their apps and stop shopping online.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the panel did not agree that taste is dead. The writer who led it came away from the panel hopeful that taste is still alive.

mainIdea.s: A new survey finds that most young adults now paint their homes in bright, bold colors. Furniture stores report that sales of beige sofas have fallen sharply over the last two years.
mainIdea.why: There is no survey about bold colors. This is a debate about whether social media has made homes and clothes end up looking alike.

tf.s: An art fair's organizers put on a panel to debate whether taste is dead.

stories.headline: Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs

chunks.text: On October 14, 2026, Netflix told its staff that it will {{lay off}} about 1,000 workers. That is around 6 percent of its [[workforce]]. It is the company's biggest round of [[job cuts]] since 2022. The news first {{came out}} in The Wall Street Journal. The company's two [[co-chief executives]] explained the cuts in a [[memo]] to staff. Most of the cuts will hit the product, technology, legal and [[human resources]] teams.

verbs.correct: To stop employing workers
verbs.wrong: To train workers for new roles
verbs.why: Factories lay off workers when sales drop. Some companies lay off staff every winter. Netflix told its staff that it will lay off about 1,000 workers.

verbs.correct: To become known to the public
verbs.wrong: To be sent only to managers
verbs.why: The truth about a secret plan often comes out in the end. Bad news comes out fast in a small town. The news about the Netflix job cuts first came out in The Wall Street Journal.

chunks.text: "Decisions like these are never easy," the two leaders wrote. They said business is strong. Thanks to new members {{signing up}} and higher prices, Netflix's profit has grown in 2026. But the leaders said the company must be [[disciplined]] about where it puts its people and money. Netflix plans to {{go on}} investing [[heavily]] to improve its service. In 2022, it cut about 450 jobs after losing [[subscribers]] for the first time in over a decade.

[[Competition]] is growing too. Free [[platforms]] such as YouTube and TikTok keep {{drawing in}} viewers.

chunks.text: On Monday, October 19, 2026, people in the Canadian province of Alberta voted in a [[referendum]]. They were asked whether to stay in Canada or start a [[legal process]] that could lead to a second vote on {{breaking away}}. Early results on October 20 showed about three in four voters chose to stay. About one in four [[backed]] the path toward separation. Delays at about 100 [[polling stations]] {{held up}} the results by more than two hours.

verbs.wrong: To hold a vote on the same question
verbs.why: Some regions want to break away from their country. Some islands want to break away and become their own country. Voters were asked about a second vote on breaking away from Canada.

verbs.correct: To make something happen later

chunks.text: Alberta is rich in oil. Many separatists there are angry with Canada's [[federal government]] in Ottawa. They say its [[environmental policies]] have hurt the province's [[oil industry]]. A citizens' group collected about 300,000 [[signatures]] asking for a vote on separation. A judge {{threw out}} that [[petition]], saying it had failed to [[consult]] Indigenous First Nations. Alberta's [[premier]], who opposes separation, {{went ahead with}} a [[nonbinding]] vote anyway.

verbs.correct: To refuse to accept a request

chunks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who {{grew up}} in Alberta, said Albertans had made "a clear choice." The premier said the result showed [[widespread]] support for staying in Canada. Before the vote, Carney and other national leaders {{spoke out}} against separation. Elon Musk, a well-known supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump, wrote online that Alberta should separate. The Associated Press reported that Trump's [[trade war]] and [[threats]] to make Canada a U.S. state helped Carney {{win over}} voters in Alberta.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think

verbs.correct: To make people support you

chunks.text: [[Separatist]] leaders say they will not {{back down}}. One leader called the vote a [[first step]] and said the movement would {{carry on}}. He had hoped for 30 percent of the vote. The early results {{fell short of}} that number. At one separatist event in Edmonton, people {{packed up}} and went home. Some separatists now want to {{push the premier out}} as leader of her party. [[Official results]] could take days to {{come in}}.

verbs.correct: To accept defeat and stop trying

verbs.why: My brother never backs down in an argument. The workers don't back down until they get a fair deal. Separatist leaders say they will not back down after the vote.

chunks.text: On October 12, 2026, a car bomb {{went off}} at a [[toll booth]] on a highway in southwestern Colombia. The army said at least three [[civilians]] were injured. The [[blast]] destroyed the toll booth and damaged nearby homes. Officials {{shut down}} part of the highway. The army blamed a group led by former members of Colombia's largest [[rebel]] army. These fighters did not {{go along with}} the 2016 [[peace deal]].

chunks.text: Colombia's president [[condemned]] the attack on social media. He said attacks on [[infrastructure]] hurt truck drivers and everyone who needs to travel. He took office in August 2026, and his government has {{called off}} peace talks with the country's [[remaining]] rebel groups. He has promised to {{crack down}} on these groups, which he says he will treat as [[terrorists]]. Some groups have {{hit back}} by {{stepping up}} attacks on the military.

verbs.why: Cities step up police patrols downtown during the holidays. Airports step up security before Thanksgiving. Some rebel groups have been stepping up attacks on the military.

chunks.text: The bombing came during a [[wave of violence]] in the region. On October 9, the army said the same group killed a soldier in a [[clash]]. The next day, a drone attack killed another soldier. The army said a different rebel group {{carried out}} that attack. In September, the army {{sent in}} troops to a Caribbean city after a drug gang burned vehicles. The president has also {{set up}} a [[task force]] to stop a group from stealing fuel from a [[pipeline]].

chunks.text: The president's policies are a big change. The previous government spent four years trying to [[negotiate]] with rebel groups. In 2016, about 14,000 fighters {{laid down}} their weapons after the peace deal. But the deal left some [[rural areas]] without strong government control. Smaller armed groups have tried to {{take over}} land the old rebel army once held. They fight for control of gold mines and [[drug routes]], and they [[demand]] money from local businesses.

stories.headline: Fragrance-free and unscented are not the same

sources.title: Fragrances in Cosmetics (U.S. Food and Drug Administration)
How can I find eczema friendly products? (American Academy of Dermatology)
U.S. FDA Sets November 2026 Timeline for Formaldehyde Ban and Fragrance Allergen Rule (ChemLinked)
What is the difference between "Unscented" and "Fragrance-free" products? (McGill University Office for Science and Society)

chunks.text: Shoppers who want to avoid [[fragrance]] may {{watch out for}} two words on a label: "fragrance-free" and "unscented." These words do not mean the same thing. The American Academy of Dermatology says parents of children with [[eczema]] should {{pick out}} fragrance-free products, not unscented ones. Labels may also change. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration plans a rule on fragrance [[allergens]].

verbs.correct: To try to notice something
verbs.wrong: To print words on a bottle
verbs.why: I always watch out for sugar on food labels. She watches out for sales at her favorite store. Shoppers who want to avoid fragrance may watch out for two words on a label.

verbs.correct: To choose something from a group
verbs.wrong: To decide the price of something
verbs.why: Most shoppers pick out their own fruit at the market. Many parents pick out safe soaps for babies. The academy says parents should pick out fragrance-free products for children with eczema.

chunks.text: Fragrance in [[cosmetics]] is a mix of many natural and [[man-made]] chemicals. The agency says some of them may cause [[allergic reactions]] in some people. Children with eczema have very [[sensitive skin]], and many products can {{set off}} the problem. Their skin may {{break out}} a few hours or even days after a product is used. This can make the cause hard to find. The academy tells parents to {{cut out}} scented shampoo and [[laundry detergent]].

verbs.correct: To cause something to start
verbs.wrong: To name something on a label
verbs.why: Pollen often sets off sneezing in spring. Cheap perfume sets off headaches for some people. Many products can set off eczema in children with very sensitive skin.

verbs.correct: To suddenly get spots or a rash
verbs.wrong: To be listed as an ingredient
verbs.why: My skin breaks out when I feel stressed. Many teenagers break out before a big event. A child's skin may break out a few hours or even days after a product is used.

verbs.correct: To stop using something
verbs.wrong: To wash something with soap
verbs.why: Many people cut out sugar to lose weight. Some families cut out soda for a whole year. The academy tells parents of children with eczema to cut out scented shampoo and laundry detergent.

chunks.text: A fragrance-free product should {{leave out}} every ingredient added for its smell. An [[unscented]] product may still contain fragrance. The agency says some makers add just enough to {{cover up}} the [[unpleasant]] smell of other ingredients. A science office at a Canadian university gives an example. If [[lavender]] is hidden in an unscented product, a person who is allergic to it may not {{find out}} that it is there. A fragrance-free product can still smell a little. An oil that softens skin may {{give off}} this light smell.

verbs.correct: To not include something
verbs.wrong: To stack something on a shelf
verbs.why: A good cook leaves out the onions for picky eaters. Short news stories often leave out small details. A fragrance-free product should leave out every ingredient added for its smell.

verbs.correct: To hide something so it is not noticed
verbs.wrong: To list something on the package
verbs.why: A scented candle covers up the smell of cooking fish. Air fresheners only cover up bad smells. Some makers add just enough fragrance to cover up the unpleasant smell of other ingredients.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To make a soap smell stronger
verbs.why: Many travelers find out about late flights by text. Shoppers find out store hours on the website. A person who is allergic to lavender may not find out that it is hidden in an unscented product.

verbs.correct: To produce a smell
verbs.wrong: To soften dry skin
verbs.why: Old fish gives off a strong smell. These flowers give off a sweet smell at night. In a fragrance-free product, an oil that softens skin may give off a light smell.

chunks.text: On U.S. [[ingredient lists]], a mix of many scent chemicals can {{show up}} as the single word "fragrance." The agency says the law does not force companies to share these [[trade secrets]]. A 2022 law told it to make a rule on fragrance allergens. chunks.text: On October 12, 2026, China announced [[sanctions]] against two ministers from Paraguay and Belize. Beijing {{singled out}} Paraguay's communications minister and Belize's foreign minister. The measures [[freeze]] any [[assets]] the two men hold in China. They also {{keep the ministers out}} of China, Hong Kong and Macau. The move came two days after Taiwan's [[national day]]. In a speech that day, Taiwan's president said the island would not {{give up}} its freedom.

verbs.wrong: To make someone pay a large fine

chunks.text: China sees Taiwan as part of its [[territory]]. Taiwan's government strongly rejects that view. The two sides have been ruled separately since a [[civil war]] in 1949. Paraguay and Belize are two of only 12 countries with [[formal ties]] with Taiwan. China has worked to {{win over}} these [[allies]]. In recent years, Nauru, Honduras and Nicaragua have {{cut off}} their ties with Taiwan. They now [[recognize]] the government in Beijing instead.

chunks.text: China's foreign ministry said the sanctions protect the country's [[sovereignty]]. A [[spokesperson]] called the two ministers [[pawns]] of Taiwan's leaders. She said they had spread false claims about Chinese [[cyberattacks]]. In July, Paraguay said cyberattacks linked to China's government had affected its state computer systems. China denied the [[accusations]]. The spokesperson said Taiwan's allies could {{miss out on}} chances to grow. News agencies say the sanctions are mostly [[symbolic]], since such ministers rarely travel to China.

verbs.correct: To lose a chance to get something good

chunks.text: Paraguay and Belize {{hit back}} at the sanctions. Paraguay's foreign ministry said they caused [[unnecessary friction]]. Paraguay's communications minister said his country would {{push ahead with}} its technology projects with Taiwan. He said Paraguay would even {{speed up}} the work. Belize said the measures would not change its [[foreign policy]]. It said it would {{stand by}} its minister. Taiwan's foreign ministry also {{spoke out}} against the sanctions. It said China had no right to [[interfere]] in Taiwan's ties with other countries.

stories.headline: People see AI as aware but not conscious

sources.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious (ScienceDaily)
When AI behaves like us, we still don't think it is conscious (LMU Munich)
AI Can Be Aware, But Humans Draw the Line at Consciousness, New Study Finds (The Debrief)

chunks.text: AI chatbots can talk, answer questions and help with work. To many users, they {{come across as}} almost human. Researchers at the University of Munich in Germany asked if people think these machines are [[conscious]]. They {{looked into}} the question in a study in the [[science journal]] Cognition. The university shared the results on October 2, 2026.

verbs.correct: To seem a certain way to others
verbs.wrong: To copy the voice of a person
verbs.why: He comes across as shy, but he is very funny. A short email often comes across as rude. To many users, AI chatbots come across as almost human.

verbs.correct: To study a question carefully
verbs.wrong: To ask people to join a study
verbs.why: Many researchers look into how people trust new technology. Police look into the cause of every big fire. Researchers in Munich looked into whether people think AI is conscious.

chunks.text: The team {{set up}} several experiments with nearly 1,100 people. Each person read short [[scenarios]] about a [[character]]. Some people read about an AI. Others read the same stories about a human instead. In one example, the character reacted to a sound. In another, it could {{pick up on}} someone's [[emotional state]]. People then [[rated]] how conscious and how [[aware]] each character was of its [[surroundings]].

verbs.correct: To plan and prepare something
verbs.wrong: To check the results of a test
verbs.why: Science teachers set up simple experiments for their students. Researchers often set up tests with hundreds of volunteers. The team set up several experiments with nearly 1,100 people.

verbs.correct: To notice something small
verbs.wrong: To hide your own feelings
verbs.why: Dogs often pick up on their owner's mood. Good teachers pick up on a student's worry quickly. In one story, the character could pick up on someone's emotional state.

chunks.text: In both versions, the AI and the human did exactly the same things. Nobody could {{tell them apart}} by their actions. When a human or AI character reacted more to the world around it, its scores {{went up}}. But on consciousness, people showed a [[clear gap]]. Even the most [[responsive]] AI {{fell behind}} the least responsive human. The researchers say people {{hold back}} from calling AI conscious, even when it acts like a human.

verbs.correct: To see the difference between two things
verbs.wrong: To say which of two you like better
verbs.why: The twins look so alike that their teachers rarely tell them apart. Bank workers tell real and fake money apart by touch. The AI and the human acted the same, so nobody could tell them apart by their actions.

verbs.correct: To become higher
verbs.wrong: To be counted twice
verbs.why: The price of eggs goes up every winter. Test scores usually go up after extra practice. When a character reacted more to the world around it, its scores went up.

verbs.correct: To get a lower score than another
verbs.wrong: To be tested by a different group
verbs.why: Students who miss class often fall behind in math. A team that loses its star often falls behind in the second half. Even the most responsive AI fell behind the least responsive human on consciousness.

verbs.correct: To choose not to do something
verbs.wrong: To change your answer at the end
verbs.why: Many people hold back from saying what they really think. Shy workers hold back in meetings because they fear sounding rude. People hold back from calling AI conscious, even when it acts like a human.

chunks.text: The word aware gave a different result. People [[judged]] awareness in much the same way for AI and humans, and the gap mostly {{went away}}. A [[philosopher]] on the team said people may {{end up}} using words about the mind for AI only because they [[lack]] better ones. Another [[senior author]] said companies and journalists often {{talk up}} AI. They describe it as having plans and even a [[conscience]]. He said [[word choice]] matters. The study does not try to {{figure out}} whether AI really is conscious.

chunks.text: Scientists are {{looking into}} why baby whales are {{dying off}} in large numbers in 2026. Since June 2026, dead southern right whale [[calves]] have been {{washing up}} on beaches around a peninsula in southern Argentina. The area is a major [[breeding ground]] for the [[species]]. [[Residents]] have reported hundreds of dead calves. Researchers have not given an official [[death toll]]. They say it will be clearer after the season ends in late November.

Every year, the whales return to the peninsula's [[sheltered waters]] to [[give birth]] and [[nurse]] their young. The 2026 count found nearly 400 calves, down from about 800 in 2025. The gulls {{go after}} whales that {{come up}} to breathe, and they eat bits of their skin. Adult whales have learned to keep their backs under the water. Calves have not, so they get [[wounds]]. Scientists think bacteria from the sea enter the calves through these wounds. Bacteria have already {{turned up}} in some [[tissue samples]].

chunks.text: Many [[advocates]] say governments {{stepped in}} too late on social media. This summer, Meta reached an $18 billion [[settlement]] with U.S. states and agreed to add stronger [[safeguards]]. Meta did not launch teen accounts on Instagram until 2024. AI companies are now {{rolling out}} similar tools, such as [[age checks]] for [[minors]]. OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August. They [[ban]] romantic chats.

verbs.correct: To make a new product available

chunks.text: Some experts are {{speaking out}} about the risks. A professor at the University of Chicago says society should not learn about harm only after it happens. A well-known psychologist worries about children's [[emotional attachments]] to chatbots. He also worries when people {{hand over}} their thinking to a bot. Others {{point out}} the [[benefits]]. A tech policy expert at Cornell says AI helps teens with [[tutoring]] and homework. So limits made for social media may not {{carry over}} to AI easily.

chunks.text: Congress has been slow to {{catch up}} with the technology. Some child safety bills on AI have passed Senate subcommittees with support from [[both parties]]. They still face a [[long road]]. On October 1, House members from both parties introduced a bill to stop chatbots from acting human with children. Only parents could {{turn off}} those protections. States are moving faster to {{look out for}} young users. On September 10, California's governor signed laws on [[companion chatbots]], including [[parental controls]] and [[safety audits]].

stories.headline: Europe grows tougher on trade with China

sources.title: EU sends envoy to Beijing as rising exports from China raise economic anxiety (Associated Press)
In Beijing, EU trade envoy says deficit with China 'unsustainable' (AFP, via 24 News HD)
EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure (Al Jazeera)
EU trade envoy eyes yawning goods deficit on first day of China visit (video, France 24)

chunks.text: On October 8, 2026, the European Union's trade chief {{sat down with}} China's [[commerce minister]] in Beijing for two days of talks. Europe's [[trade deficit]] with China is about 360 billion euros, or 410 billion dollars. The deficit keeps {{piling up}} by more than 1 billion dollars a day. The trade chief wants to {{bring down}} that number. Earlier in 2026, he gave Beijing an October [[deadline]] to show real results.

verbs.wrong: To send someone a list of demands
verbs.why: A good boss sits down with workers to discuss their pay. Tenants sit down with their landlord about repairs. The EU's trade chief sat down with China's commerce minister in Beijing on October 8, 2026.

verbs.correct: To grow bigger little by little
verbs.wrong: To be repaid in small amounts

verbs.correct: To make a number smaller

chunks.text: Chinese exports to the European Union rose 15.3 percent in the first eight months of 2026. European leaders say [[state subsidies]] help Chinese companies sell steel, batteries and [[solar panels]] cheaply. Chinese [[carmakers]] are {{taking on}} Europe's [[best-known]] brands. Many fear that European workers will {{lose out}}. The head of the European Commission calls this another "China shock." In the United States in the early 2000s, Chinese competition helped {{wipe out}} hundreds of thousands of [[factory jobs]].

verbs.correct: To make something disappear completely

chunks.text: On October 7, the European Parliament voted 454 to 86 for a [[resolution]] calling for a tougher China [[policy]]. In a letter, the leaders of France and Germany {{stepped up}} the pressure. They want a tool to {{push back}} quickly against countries that [[harm]] Europe's economy. But not every EU country will {{go along with}} [[tough measures]]. Spain has been friendlier toward China. Its prime minister has visited Beijing four times in three years.

chunks.text: China's commerce ministry warned France and Germany against [[protectionist]] steps. It said such steps would hurt others and help no one. Days before the talks, China opened a [[trade investigation]] into a European chemical. Europe asked China to {{cut back on}} its exports of [[hybrid cars]], but Beijing opposes such limits. The talks are meant to {{head off}} a [[trade war]]. Experts doubt the two sides will {{work out}} a [[broad deal]] in these talks.

mainIdea.s: Europe is getting tougher on trade because cheap Chinese goods threaten its factories and workers. Its trade chief held talks in Beijing as lawmakers and leaders asked for stronger tools.

mainIdea.s: Several big European carmakers have opened new electric car plants in China this year. They hope to win more buyers there, since car sales across Europe have been weak for a long time now.

stories.headline: Astronauts make fastest American trip to space station

sources.title: Historic SpaceX Crew-13 Launches to Space Station from Florida (AP, via WDTV)
SpaceX's Crew-13 reaches space station in record-fast trip as mission begins (FOX 35 Orlando)
SpaceX smashes US record as astronauts reach ISS in just 7 hours and 55 minutes (Interesting Engineering)
SpaceX Crew-13 docks with International Space Station after record-fast flight (video, WKMG News 6)

chunks.text: Four astronauts {{blasted off}} from Florida on Thursday morning, October 1, 2026. Their SpaceX capsule {{closed in on}} the International Space Station that evening. It {{linked up with}} the station 7 hours and 55 minutes after launch, a new US record. The launch had been {{pushed back}} three weeks to repair a [[leaking]] [[fuel system]]. There were [[thick clouds]] that morning, but the weather {{cleared up}} in time.

chunks.text: On October 6, 2026, a South African research institute wrote about a new [[investigation]] into Russian army recruiting. It was done by Code for Africa, an African group of [[investigators]]. They found 289 websites, [[social media profiles]] and other online tools. Many were {{set up}} in Russia and Belarus but [[hosted]] on Western computers. The recruiters mostly {{go after}} young men without [[steady work]] in Africa and other [[lower-income]] regions.

verbs.correct: To create something, such as a website
verbs.wrong: To keep something to use later
verbs.why: Many people set up small online stores from home. Scammers often set up fake websites in a few hours. Many of the recruiting websites were set up in Russia and Belarus.

verbs.correct: To choose someone as a target
verbs.wrong: To agree with someone's plan
verbs.why: Some phone scams go after older people. That company goes after college students with its ads. The recruiters mostly go after young men without steady work in Africa and other lower-income regions.

chunks.text: According to the investigators, the ads look like [[ordinary]] job offers. They promise construction work, jobs as [[security guards]], visa help or film roles. Some websites carry [[forged endorsements]], such as the logos of Western news outlets. Politico reported that one ad promised 15,000 dollars for {{signing up}} and 3,000 dollars a month. When people {{fill out}} the online forms, their [[personal details]] are sent to Russia.

verbs.correct: To agree to join the army
verbs.wrong: To end a message or a letter
verbs.why: Many young people sign up for the army after high school. Fewer students sign up for the military each year. One ad promised 15,000 dollars for signing up and 3,000 dollars a month.

verbs.correct: To write answers on a form
verbs.wrong: To do someone's job for a while
verbs.why: Patients fill out a form at the front desk. Most job seekers fill out many applications each week. When people fill out the online forms, their personal details are sent to Russia.

chunks.text: In a report on September 10, 2026, Amnesty International said Russia has recruited thousands of people from low-income countries. Many were promised [[civilian]] jobs or Russian [[citizenship]] but {{ended up}} on the [[front line]] in Ukraine. Amnesty spoke with 15 foreign [[prisoners of war]]. Only three said they knowingly signed a military contract. A South African truck driver applied for a driving job in Poland, his wife said. He {{found out}} in Moscow that he would become a soldier. Amnesty says these practices [[amount to]] [[human trafficking]] in many cases.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a place you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To visit a place for a short time
verbs.why: Travelers who take the wrong bus often end up downtown. Many art students end up working in banks. Many recruits were promised civilian jobs but ended up on the front line in Ukraine.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know

verbs.why: Most people find out about parties from friends. Workers often find out about job changes by email. The truck driver found out in Moscow that he would become a soldier.

chunks.text: Tech companies have {{taken down}} some of the content. Code for Africa's director said Meta has removed more than 300 [[ad campaigns]]. But new sites quickly {{pop up}}, the investigators say. Google [[disputed]] some of the findings and said it is {{looking into}} the report. The researchers say [[billing records]] could help {{track down}} the people behind the ads. Media reports suggest more than 3,000 Africans have {{gotten caught up in}} the war.

stories.headline: Argentina offers passports to wealthy foreigners

Argentina to sell citizenship to foreigners for US$350,000 to raise dollars (MercoPress)

chunks.text: On October 2, 2026, Argentina announced a plan to offer [[citizenship]] to wealthy foreigners. The country's economy minister {{laid out}} the plan at an investor event in Paris. Applicants could make a [[nonrefundable]] payment of 350,000 dollars to the national [[treasury]]. Or they could buy a new government [[bond]] worth 800,000 dollars and {{hold on to}} it for seven years. [[Applications]] are expected to open before the end of 2026.

verbs.why: Many families hold on to their houses when prices fall. My grandmother holds on to her gold coins for good luck. Bond buyers would have to hold on to the new bond for seven years.

chunks.text: The plan is meant to {{bring in}} [[foreign currency]]. Argentina's treasury must make nearly 25 billion dollars in foreign-currency [[debt payments]] in 2027. The government has {{held off}} on a return to international bond markets. So it is {{turning to}} other sources of money. Its advisers say the program could raise up to 2.5 billion dollars. Dollars matter to President Javier Milei, who plans to seek [[reelection]] in 2027.

stories.headline: Tom Cruise checks on a woman lost in her phone

sources.title: The cure for doomscrolling? Why Tom Cruise stopped a woman mid-scroll (The Guardian)
Tom Cruise surprises woman doomscrolling at work, viral video wins hearts online (WION)
Tom Cruise Surprises Woman While She's "Doomscrolling" In Viral Video (iHeart)

chunks.text: Tom Cruise has [[gone viral]] for a small [[act of kindness]]. Security camera [[footage]] shared online in late September 2026 shows him walking past the open door of a [[break room]] at a workplace. Inside, a woman sat with her back to the door, her head bent low over her phone. Her [[body language]] {{gave off}} signs of [[distress]]. Cruise {{picked up on}} those signs and stopped. He stepped inside and tapped her shoulder to check on her.

verbs.correct: To show a sign or feeling
verbs.wrong: To copy a sign or feeling
verbs.why: Some people give off confidence the moment they walk in. Tired eyes often give off signs of stress. From behind, the woman's body language gave off signs of distress.

verbs.correct: To notice something small
verbs.wrong: To treat someone unkindly
verbs.why: Kids pick up on small changes at home. Good teachers pick up on a nervous smile right away. Cruise picked up on the woman's posture and stopped.

chunks.text: It {{turned out}} nothing was wrong. The woman was only [[doomscrolling]], or reading negative posts online for a long time. When she saw who it was, she could only say, "Tom Cruise?" The tap on the shoulder made her {{snap out of}} it. The two shared a [[fist bump]], and he wished her a good night. Cruise {{came back}} for a photo after she had {{gotten over}} the [[shock]].

verbs.correct: To become clear at last
verbs.wrong: To be filmed by a fan's phone
verbs.why: It often turns out that the cheap option costs more. A quiet coworker often turns out to be very funny. It turned out that the woman was only doomscrolling.

verbs.correct: To suddenly stop a bad habit or mood
verbs.wrong: To feel very tired and sleepy
verbs.why: Most people snap out of a bad mood after a walk. Drivers snap out of a daydream when the light turns green. The tap on the shoulder made the woman snap out of her doomscrolling.

verbs.correct: To return later
verbs.wrong: To call a guard for help
verbs.why: The repairman comes back the next day with the right part. Shoppers often come back for a forgotten bag. Cruise came back later so the woman could take a photo with him.

verbs.correct: To feel normal again after a shock
verbs.wrong: To leave a place in a hurry
verbs.why: Most people get over the shock of a big bill in a few days. Kids get over a scary movie quickly. The woman had gotten over the shock by the time Cruise came back.

chunks.text: The woman later posted the footage on TikTok. "He literally tapped me on my shoulder, and I don't remember what he said," she wrote. "I was in complete shock." The clip quickly {{took off}} and {{ended up}} on X and other [[platforms]]. Many viewers [[praised]] Cruise for stopping. One person on X called him "just a kind man." A Guardian writer joked that doomscrolling can make anyone look deeply upset from behind.

verbs.correct: To become popular very quickly
verbs.wrong: To be saved on a work computer
verbs.why: Songs often take off after a famous singer shares them. New apps sometimes take off during the summer. The woman's clip took off on TikTok.

verbs.correct: To arrive somewhere at last
verbs.wrong: To invent a false story
verbs.why: Tourists often take the wrong bus and end up downtown. Letters with old addresses end up at a neighbor's house. The video ended up on X and other platforms.

chunks.text: Doomscrolling is not only a joke, though. Research has shown that it can increase [[anxiety]], [[depression]] and stress. It can also cause [[physical discomfort]]. The British government is {{looking into}} limits on apps that let people scroll without end. The video spread during a busy week for Cruise. His new film, Digger, is a [[dark comedy]] that {{came out}} in North America on October 2, 2026. It is his first movie in years that is not an action film.

verbs.correct: To study an idea carefully
verbs.wrong: To admire and respect someone
verbs.why: Many companies look into a four-day work week. Some towns look into free buses for everyone. The British government is looking into limits on apps that let people scroll without end.

stories.headline: California limits how employers use AI on workers

sources.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs laws to protect workers from AI risks (Associated Press, via ABC News)

California Lawmakers Try to Restrict 'Robo Bosses' (The Sacramento Bee, via Government Technology)

chunks.text: California's governor signed several new laws on Wednesday, September 30, 2026. They {{rein in}} how California employers use AI on workers. Under one law, companies cannot {{turn firing decisions over}} to a computer alone. Another law bans AI tools that read workers' feelings. A third says employers must give [[written notice]] before they {{lay off}} large groups of workers because of AI. It was his last day to sign or reject bills this year.

verbs.correct: To control or limit something
verbs.wrong: To pay a worker more money
verbs.why: New mayors often rein in city spending. Many parents rein in how much time kids spend online. California's new laws rein in how employers can use AI with their workers.

verbs.correct: To give control of something to another
verbs.wrong: To hide something from workers
verbs.why: Many owners turn their store over to their children when they retire. Police often turn difficult cases over to a special team. Under one law, California companies cannot turn firing decisions over to a computer alone.

verbs.correct: To stop employing workers
verbs.wrong: To print a new company rule
verbs.why: Factories lay off workers when sales fall. Many hotels lay off staff after a slow summer. Under a new California law, employers must give written notice before they lay off large groups of workers because of AI.

chunks.text: The law on feelings covers [[workplace surveillance]] tools. These include video and audio [[monitoring]], [[location tracking]] and time trackers. Employers cannot use these tools with AI to {{pick up on}} workers' emotions. Nor can they collect data on workers' [[brain activity]]. Companies can be [[fined]] up to $500 for each [[violation]]. The state's labor commissioner and public [[prosecutors]] can {{go after}} companies that break the rule. The governor asked lawmakers to {{clear up}} how far the law reaches.

verbs.correct: To notice something that is not obvious
verbs.wrong: To treat someone in an unkind way
verbs.why: Dogs pick up on their owner's mood. Good teachers pick up on a student's worry right away. Employers in California cannot use AI tools to pick up on workers' emotions.

verbs.wrong: To take orders from someone
verbs.why: Cities go after drivers who park in bus lanes. Banks go after customers who never pay their loans. Prosecutors in California can go after companies that use AI to read workers' feelings.

verbs.wrong: To make a rule last for more years
verbs.why: A good manager clears up confusion about the schedule quickly. A short email often clears up questions about a meeting time. The governor asked lawmakers to clear up how far the new law on feelings reaches.

chunks.text: Under the firing law, a human must {{go over}} decisions made with [[automated systems]]. Labor unions supported the bill. The head of the state's union federation said decisions about a worker's [[paycheck]] or [[livelihood]] need human oversight. The state senator who wrote it said businesses should not depend entirely on machines to fire workers. The California Chamber of Commerce {{pushed back}} against the bill. Groups for restaurants, stores and [[grocers]] also opposed it. They warned that employers could {{end up}} facing [[costly lawsuits]].

verbs.correct: To check something carefully

Instead, it reached a [[voluntary]] deal with the AI industry. He said states must {{step up}} without national leadership. His [[term]] ends in January, but he did not {{rule out}} [[special sessions]] of the legislature on AI.

chunks.text: On October 7, 2026, Myanmar's president arrived in Malaysia for a [[two-day visit]]. It was his first trip there since he became president in April. As [[army chief]], he led the military when it {{took over}} the country in 2021. That move started a [[civil war]]. Relations with the region {{broke down}} after that. Since April, his government has been {{reaching out}} to nearby countries to [[restore]] [[ties]].

chunks.text: Overnight from October 11 to October 12, 2026, hackers {{turned up}} the temperature in refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets across France. In some stores, the temperature {{went up}} to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit. The Paris [[prosecutor's office]] said the attack caused [[food losses]] and some fires. It called the attack "large-scale" and opened an [[investigation]].

chunks.text: Several of France's biggest [[grocery chains]] said they were hit. One chain said 80 of its supermarkets were affected. The owner of another chain said refrigerators in about 150 of its stores stayed at 50 degrees for six hours. It said staff {{threw away}} all the affected food to avoid [[health risks]]. The head of that chain said losses across France could {{add up to}} tens of millions of euros in a single day.

chunks.text: Police in New Delhi [[detained]] Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on October 7, 2026. It was the third time in two days. He and other opposition lawmakers were marching toward a [[protest site]] in the capital. On October 6, police {{broke up}} a march from parliament and {{let the lawmakers go}} soon after. Gandhi said the protesters {{showed up}} again [[without warning]]. They are {{calling for}} India's chief election commissioner to {{step down}}.

chunks.text: The protests are about a huge [[revision]] of India's [[voter lists]]. The Election Commission began {{carrying it out}} in one eastern state in 2025. It has since spread to most of the country's other states. According to the Associated Press, more than 130 million names have been {{taken off}} the lists. Millions of people have [[appealed]] the [[removals]]. About 969 million people were [[eligible]] to vote in India's 2024 election.

chunks.text: Opposition parties say many [[legitimate]] voters have been {{left out}}. They claim the changes [[unfairly]] removed more people who support the opposition. Some critics say [[minority groups]] have been hurt the most, especially Muslims. The opposition wants the revision stopped and the names {{put back}} on the lists. In September, an Indian newspaper reported that two of the commission's three members had [[objected]] at least 14 times to [[key decisions]].

It says it is {{cracking down on}} [[fake registrations]] while keeping eligible voters on the lists. India's Supreme Court has ordered the government and the commission to explain decisions linked to the revision. Another [[hearing]] was expected in mid-October.

stories.headline: People are talking less every year

sources.title: A quiet crisis? Study finds people are speaking far less (Ynet)
Are we talking less? A Q&A with psychologist Matthias Mehl (University of Arizona)
We're losing 338 spoken words every day (BBC Science Focus)
Are We Speaking Less Than Ever? (video, The Social CTV)

chunks.text: How many words do you say in a day? Fewer than your parents did, and far [[fewer]] than people twenty years ago. A new [[study]] in the [[journal]] Perspectives on Psychological Science found that the [[average]] person spoke about 16,000 words a day in the mid-2000s. As the years {{went by}}, people talked less and less. By 2019, the number had {{dropped off}} to about 12,000, a fall of nearly 28 percent. On average, people lost about 338 [[spoken words]] from their daily talk every year.

verbs.correct: To pass, one after another
verbs.wrong: To slow to a complete stop
verbs.why: Weeks go by, seasons go by, and whole decades go by faster than we expect. As the years went by, people simply said less and less.

verbs.correct: To become smaller over time
verbs.wrong: To be counted one by one
verbs.why: Ticket sales drop off after opening week, and visits drop off in winter. Daily spoken words dropped off from 16,000 to about 12,000.

chunks.text: The [[researchers]] did not {{set out}} to study [[silence]]. They combined 22 older studies from 2005 to 2019, covering about 2,200 [[volunteers]] aged 10 to 94 in the United States, Europe, and Australia. In those studies, people wore small [[recorders]] that captured short moments of sound during the day. Because the recordings were made for other research questions, nobody changed their [[behavior]]. Scientists are still trying to {{figure out}} what the numbers mean, but the [[pattern]] is clear, and it is strongest in people under 25.

verbs.correct: To begin with a clear goal
verbs.wrong: To publish results early
verbs.why: Explorers set out to cross oceans, and startups set out to change an industry. These researchers set out to study other topics and found the silence by accident.

verbs.correct: To find the reason for something
verbs.wrong: To doubt a new discovery
verbs.why: Mechanics figure out why engines fail, and parents figure out why a baby keeps waking up at night. Scientists are still working to figure out why we all talk less.

chunks.text: Where did the words go? Think about a normal day. We {{type out}} messages instead of calling. We {{check out}} at the store without a word to a [[cashier]]. We order food in an app and follow a map's quiet [[directions]] instead of asking a [[stranger]] for help. One by one, we have {{cut out}} the [[small conversations]] that once filled a day, and the [[habit]] of [[chatting]] with strangers is slowly {{dying out}}.

verbs.correct: To write a message with a keyboard
verbs.wrong: To read a long message twice
verbs.why: People type out long birthday wishes and type out complaints to airlines. We now type out words we once would have spoken.

verbs.correct: To pay and leave a store
verbs.wrong: To wait in a longer line
verbs.why: Shoppers check out at the machines near the door, and a customer with one item can check out in under a minute at the pharmacy. Millions now check out without a single word to anyone.

verbs.correct: To remove something from your life
verbs.wrong: To plan something for later
verbs.why: Doctors tell patients to cut out salt, and savers cut out small daily purchases. One by one, we have cut out the little chats that filled a day.

verbs.correct: To slowly disappear completely
verbs.wrong: To grow louder over time
verbs.why: Old customs die out, and languages die out when children stop learning them. The habit of chatting with strangers is slowly dying out.

chunks.text: Why does it matter? The scientists warn that people who talk less may {{miss out}} on [[connection]], at a time when many countries already worry about [[loneliness]]. A text message cannot copy the [[tone]], timing, and [[warmth]] of a voice. Some good [[advice]] is simple and free. {{Strike up}} a conversation while you wait [[in line]] for coffee. Call an old friend to {{catch up}}. In a world that is slowly going quiet, the healthiest thing you can do may be to {{speak up}}.

verbs.correct: To lose the chance to enjoy something
verbs.wrong: To arrive too early for a party
verbs.why: Late shoppers miss out on the best deals, and busy workers miss out on family dinners. People who talk less may miss out on real connection.

verbs.correct: To start a conversation naturally
verbs.wrong: To argue with a stranger
verbs.why: Travelers strike up conversations on trains, and neighbors strike up friendships over the fence. One easy step is to strike up a chat while you wait in line.

verbs.correct: To share news with a friend
verbs.wrong: To cancel plans at the last minute
verbs.why: Old classmates catch up over coffee, and cousins catch up at weddings. Calling a friend to catch up is one easy way to talk more.

verbs.correct: To talk instead of staying quiet
verbs.wrong: To practice a new language
verbs.why: Shy students learn to speak up in class, and workers speak up in meetings. In a quieter world, the healthiest choice may be to speak up.

chunks.text: Serbia will hold an early parliamentary election on October 25, 2026. It follows nearly two years of student protests. The protests began after a concrete [[canopy]] {{came down}} at a train station on November 1, 2024. The disaster killed 16 people in Serbia's second-largest city. Students {{rose up}} and blamed it on government [[negligence]] and corruption. They {{called for}} [[accountability]] and [[early elections]].

verbs.correct: To say that something must happen

chunks.text: Serbia's longtime leader {{stepped down}} as president on September 27, 2026. The [[constitution]] did not allow him to run for a [[third term]]. He now wants to return as prime minister. He {{kicked off}} his campaign at a [[rally]] in Belgrade on October 3, 2026. If his party wins a [[majority]] of seats, parliament is expected to choose him. He has said, without giving evidence, that the protest movement is backed by [[foreign agents]].

chunks.text: Over time, the protest movement {{turned into}} a [[nationwide]] political force. Its election group, the Student List, includes university professors, teachers and experts. Its candidates hope to {{stand up to}} the governing Serbian Progressive Party at the [[ballot box]]. That party has been in power for 14 years. It hopes to {{hold on to}} power. Analysts expect a [[tight race]]. They say the students could gain if many people {{turn out}} to vote.

chunks.text: A new [[dispute]] is about voters who live in other countries. Serbia has a large [[diaspora]], and at least 100,000 citizens have {{signed up}} to vote abroad. [[Polling places]] are usually {{set up}} in [[embassies]] and other offices. On October 5, 2026, the [[election commission]] tied overseas voting hours to Serbia's own time. Some voters in Australia would have to vote [[overnight]]. One commission member said this could {{shut out}} more than 26,000 people. The foreign minister {{pushed back}}. stories.headline: Republican candidates keep some distance from Trump

sources.title: Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds (Reuters, via Investing.com)
Voters favor Democrats on key issues but lack faith in either party to solve problems: AP-NORC poll (AP)
Republicans seek distance from Trump as US midterms loom (AFP, via The Standard)

chunks.text: On October 7, 2026, the news agency Reuters published a review of Republican candidates running for Congress. It found that candidates in 41 of 62 [[competitive races]] were {{backing away from}} President Donald Trump. Some have {{broken with}} him on at least one policy. Others have {{played down}} their [[ties]] to him. The vote on November 3 will decide which party controls Congress. The result could affect Trump's ability to {{carry out}} his [[agenda]].

verbs.wrong: To ask a leader to visit your state

verbs.correct: To publicly disagree with a leader

verbs.correct: To do what you have planned

chunks.text: Policy [[disagreements]] were the most common kind of split. They appeared in 23 of the 62 races, on issues such as [[beef imports]] and [[data centers]]. About a dozen candidates {{took down}} Trump's name, picture or [[endorsement]] from their websites. Most did this after winning their party's [[primary]]. Others {{stayed away from}} his events. Very few have {{spoken out against}} him directly. Most splits are over single issues, not his wider agenda.

verbs.correct: To choose not to attend something

verbs.correct: To criticize someone openly
verbs.wrong: To repeat someone's words in a speech

chunks.text: Reuters says keeping distance from the president is not new. Democratic candidates did the same in 2014 and 2022. A Reuters poll put Trump's [[approval rating]] at 32 percent, the lowest of his career. In that poll, Republicans {{fell behind}} Democrats among [[registered voters]], 37 percent to 44 percent. Campaign advisers privately told Reuters that candidates need this distance to {{win over}} [[independent voters]].

verbs.correct: To have less support than a rival

chunks.text: A Republican [[consultant]] {{summed up}} the challenge. She said candidates want [[credit]] for the government's successes without being tied too closely to the Trump [[brand]]. A White House spokesman {{stood by}} the president and called him the party's best messenger. An Associated Press poll in late September found that voters favor Democrats on the [[cost of living]], 38 percent to 27 percent. Few voters in that poll said either party can solve big problems. Republicans hope to {{hold on to}} control of Congress.

verbs.correct: To describe something briefly

verbs.why: A good movie review sums up the story in one sentence. Teachers often sum up the lesson at the end of class. A Republican consultant summed up the challenge that candidates face.

chunks.text: Brazil held the [[first round]] of its presidential election on October 4, 2026. Senator Bolsonaro {{came in}} first with about 47 percent of the vote. President Lula got about 45 percent. A candidate needs more than half the valid votes to win [[outright]]. Both men {{fell short of}} that [[mark]]. Lula will now {{take on}} Bolsonaro in a runoff on October 25. The result shows a country [[evenly split]] between two leaders.
