chunks.text: On October 9, 2026, President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to send diesel to American and [[world markets]]. Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons right away, he said. Larger [[shipments]] would follow, starting with 500,000 tons in November. Trump made the deal with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. The United States is {{turning to}} Russia for fuel. Trump says the deal will help {{bring down}} prices. The announcement comes before the [[midterm elections]] on November 3.

chunks.text: The deal is a [[sharp change]] in US policy. In September 2026, Trump signed a broad [[sanctions]] law. It was meant to {{clamp down on}} the energy money that funds Russia's war in Ukraine. Now Washington is {{backing away from}} the pressure it {{stepped up}} only weeks earlier. A [[temporary]] [[license]] from the Treasury Department lets Russian diesel reach world markets without [[penalties]]. The license [[expires]] in April 2027.

chunks.text: The Associated Press calls the deal an effort to fight high fuel prices. Diesel prices have {{gone up}} by almost 70 percent since February. The [[national average]] hit a [[record]] of $6.52 a gallon on September 22. Drivers who {{filled up}} on October 9 still paid an average of $6.23 a gallon. Russia was once a major [[exporter]] of diesel. It {{cut off}} exports in July after Ukrainian attacks on its [[refineries]] left too little fuel at home.

chunks.text: On October 9, 2026, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck a [[remote]] area of central Panama just before 1 p.m. [[local time]]. The U.S. Geological Survey first measured it at magnitude 8, then [[revised]] the number. The quake was [[shallow]], and people felt it as far away as Colombia. A magnitude 6.6 quake followed that afternoon. Office workers in Panama City {{cleared out}} of their buildings [[as a precaution]]. The shaking also {{set off}} [[tsunami warnings]], which were later lifted.

In Cali, [[search teams]] {{picked through}} the [[rubble]] of fallen buildings.

chunks.text: Medical tests are changing families too. A Columbia University study in New York offers free [[genome]] sequencing to newborns, a business news channel reported on August 10. Standard [[newborn screening]] checks for 30 to 50 diseases; the study checks for 450. In the first 4,000 babies, the test {{picked up}} [[serious conditions]] in just under 4 percent. One baby girl received a [[diagnosis]] of a [[fatal]] nerve disease at six months, years before [[symptoms]] would {{show up}}. Doctors started a [[treatment]] that may {{hold off}} the [[damage]].

chunks.text: Researchers now ask what these discoveries do to families. mainIdea.s: Home DNA kits are revealing unknown relatives to many Americans, while a hospital study finds rare diseases in babies before symptoms. Researchers now want to learn how such results change families.

mainIdea.s: Home DNA kits can now warn parents about rare diseases in their babies before any symptoms appear. Doctors say these cheap kits catch far more conditions than the screening done in hospitals.

mainIdea.s: A large DNA testing company has sold its customer database to a drug maker after going bankrupt. Millions of families now want to know what will happen to their private genetic information.

stories.headline: Older adults took more steps on days with younger family

sources.title: Intergenerational Engagement in Daily Life
The Journals of Gerontology: Series B
Oxford University Press academic journals

chunks.text: Many people {{slow down}} as they get older. A new study adds a detail. Researchers at Stanford University and Washington University in St. Louis {{carried out}} the study with 265 [[participants]], aged 23 to 92. On days when older adults spent more time with younger [[relatives]], they took more steps. They also reported more [[high-energy]] positive feelings, such as happiness, [[enthusiasm]] and excitement. The study was published in The Journals of Gerontology, Series B, on September 10, 2026.

verbs.correct: To become less active than before
verbs.wrong: To learn a new skill quickly
verbs.why: A busy lawyer slows down after retirement, and a puppy slows down once it is a few years old. Many people slow down as they get older, which is why the study looked at what older adults did each day.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To continue after a difficult time
verbs.why: A mechanic carries out repairs on a car, and a school carries out a fire drill twice a year. Researchers at two universities carried out the study with 265 participants aged 23 to 92.

chunks.text: Each person kept a [[daily diary]] for nine days. Each day, they {{filled in}} a short record of who they spent time with and how they felt. The researchers did not leave [[physical activity]] to memory. Instead, they {{kept track of}} it [[objectively]], through [[step count]] and the number of minutes each person spent sitting. The diaries and the movement data were then placed [[side by side]] to see whether the two moved together.

verbs.correct: To complete a form with information
verbs.wrong: To sign a paper to join a study
verbs.why: A traveler fills in a customs form at the airport, and a patient fills in a health history at the clinic. Each day, the participants filled in a short record of who they spent time with and how they felt.

verbs.correct: To record and follow something over time
verbs.wrong: To stay at the same level as others
verbs.why: A parent keeps track of a child's height on the kitchen wall, and a driver keeps track of fuel costs in a notebook. The researchers kept track of physical activity through step counts and minutes spent sitting.

chunks.text: Older adults were not the only ones who felt better. Across every age in the study, one part of the [[pattern]] {{held up}}. On days with more time with younger family members, people reported more calm positive feelings, such as [[contentment]] and [[relaxation]], as they {{wound down}} before bed. The same link did not {{show up}} for other company. Time spent with people who were not younger family members had no [[connection]] to step count or [[sitting time]].

verbs.correct: To stay true when tested
verbs.wrong: To keep something in a safe place
verbs.why: A weather forecast holds up if the rain arrives as promised, and an alibi holds up if the times match the facts. The calm feelings before bed held up across every age in the study, not only among older adults.

verbs.correct: To relax before going to sleep
verbs.wrong: To visit family for a short stay
verbs.why: Some people wind down with a warm bath, and others wind down by listening to a podcast in the dark. Participants reported more contentment and relaxation as they wound down on days with more time with younger family members.

verbs.correct: To appear or be seen
verbs.wrong: To display something proudly
verbs.why: A stain shows up on a white shirt, and a typing error shows up when you print the page. The link with step counts did not show up for time spent with people who were not younger family members.

chunks.text: It is important to {{point out}} that the study found a link, not a [[cause]]. Nine days of diaries do not {{add up to}} [[proof]]. The study cannot {{rule out}} other [[explanations]]. The results do not show that a visit {{cheers up}} an older person. They show only that family days and active days were often the same days. Even so, the pattern raises a question for [[future studies]]. What happens when the [[generations]] {{get together}}, or simply {{hang out}} at home?

verbs.correct: To tell people about a fact
verbs.wrong: To give something to each person
verbs.why: A guide points out that the museum is free on Sundays, and a friend points out that your shirt is on backwards. It is important to point out that the study found a link, not a cause.

verbs.correct: To combine to produce a result
verbs.wrong: To happen before an event
verbs.why: Three short walks add up to an hour of exercise, and a few missed classes add up to a low grade. Nine days of diaries do not add up to proof that family time causes anything.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To plan something in detail
verbs.why: A vet rules out a broken bone after an X-ray, and a coach rules out an injured player for the final. The study cannot rule out other explanations for why family days and active days often matched.

verbs.correct: To make someone feel happier
verbs.wrong: To live near a family member
verbs.why: A sunny morning cheers up the whole office, and a funny movie cheers up a friend after a bad week. The results do not show that a visit from a younger relative cheers up an older person.

verbs.correct: To meet with people socially
verbs.wrong: To reach the end of a hard time
verbs.why: Neighbors get together for a barbecue in July, and former coworkers get together once a year for lunch. The study raises the question of what happens when the generations get together.

verbs.correct: To spend relaxed time with someone
verbs.wrong: To wait for a short time
verbs.why: College friends hang out in the dorm on Friday nights, and cousins hang out by the pool all summer. Older adults took more steps on days when they spent time with, or simply hung out with, younger family members.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day diary study found that older adults took more steps and felt happier on days spent with younger family members. The study shows a link, not a cause.
mainIdea.why: Researchers tracked 265 people with diaries and objective activity measures, and older adults moved more and felt better on days with more time with younger relatives, though the study cannot rule out other explanations.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day diary study found that older adults took more steps and felt happier on days spent with anyone at all. Friends and neighbors had the same effect as family.
mainIdea.why: Close, but time spent with people who were not younger family members showed no connection to step count or sitting time.

mainIdea.s: A nine-day walking program helped older adults sleep better and feel calmer at night, according to a new study. The program is now being tested in several cities.
mainIdea.why: The study did not test a walking program at all; it tracked what people did and felt day by day and found a link between family time and activity.

tf.s: Time with people who were not younger relatives also showed up in the step data.

tf.s: The study found a link between family time and steps, not a cause.

stories.headline: FTC wants stores to reveal when data sets your price

sources.title: Personalized pricing: Why some pay more than others
FTC moves to make retailers disclose use of 'personalized pricing'
FTC Proposes Enforcement Policy Statement on Personalized Pricing (Skadden)
FTC targets online pricing based on shoppers' personal data (video, KHOU 11)

chunks.text: Two people can look at the same product online and see two different prices. This is called [[personalized pricing]]. [[Retailers]] use [[personal data]] to {{size up}} each shopper and estimate how much that person is [[willing]] to pay. If the system thinks you will {{pay up}}, it can {{mark up}} the price just for you. Another shopper may see a lower price for the same item. Most people never know, so they cannot {{opt out}}.

verbs.correct: To judge someone carefully before acting
verbs.wrong: To pack a customer's order for shipping
verbs.why: A boxer sizes up his opponent before the first punch, and a landlord sizes up a new tenant during the visit. Retailers size up each shopper with personal data to estimate how much that person will pay.

verbs.correct: To give money, even when you do not want to
verbs.wrong: To return money that someone lent you
verbs.why: A driver pays up when the parking fine arrives, and a tenant pays up when the landlord knocks for the rent. If the system thinks a shopper will pay up, it can raise the price for that person.

verbs.correct: To raise the price of something
verbs.wrong: To write a review of a product
verbs.why: A cafe marks up bottled water in summer, and a hotel marks up rooms during a big festival. Stores can mark up the price for a shopper who seems willing to pay more.

verbs.correct: To choose not to be part of something
verbs.wrong: To have no more of a product to sell
verbs.why: You can opt out of a company's marketing emails, and a student can opt out of the school trip. Most shoppers cannot opt out of personalized pricing because they never know it is happening.

chunks.text: The Federal Trade Commission wants that to change. On August 19, 2026, the [[agency]] {{put forward}} an [[enforcement]] [[policy statement]] on personalized pricing and asked the public to {{weigh in}}. The [[comment period]] ran until September 18. Under the [[proposal]], a company would have to tell shoppers when personal data is setting their individual price. A company that hides the [[practice]] could be breaking the law against unfair or [[deceptive]] practices. That would let the FTC {{crack down on}} stores that stay quiet.

verbs.correct: To suggest a plan for others to consider
verbs.wrong: To delay something until a later time
verbs.why: A coach puts forward a new training plan, and a neighbor puts forward an idea for the block party. In August 2026 the FTC put forward an enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing.

verbs.correct: To give your opinion on a topic
verbs.wrong: To make money from a situation
verbs.why: Parents weigh in on the new school schedule, and fans weigh in on a team's new logo. The FTC asked the public to weigh in, and the comment period ran until September 18.

verbs.correct: To start dealing strictly with a problem
verbs.wrong: To admit you were wrong and stop arguing
verbs.why: A city cracks down on illegal parking, and a school cracks down on cheating during exams. Under the proposal, the FTC could crack down on stores that hide the use of personal data in pricing.

chunks.text: The agency has been studying these tools [[for some time]]. In July 2024 the FTC ordered eight pricing-technology companies to {{hand over}} information about how their systems work. The study that followed was published in January 2025. It {{tracked down}} at least 250 [[clients]] of those eight companies, including [[grocery]] retailers. The software, [[in other words]], is not a rare [[experiment]]. It has reached the stores where many people buy their food.

verbs.correct: To give something to someone in charge
verbs.wrong: To share printed papers with a group
verbs.why: A driver hands over his license to the police officer, and a passenger hands over her passport at the border. In July 2024 the FTC ordered eight pricing-technology companies to hand over information about their systems.

verbs.correct: To find something after a careful search
verbs.wrong: To say no to an offer or a request
verbs.why: A librarian tracks down a rare book for a reader, and a mechanic tracks down the cause of a strange noise. The study published in January 2025 tracked down at least 250 clients of those eight companies.

chunks.text: What kind of data feeds these systems? The list is long: precise location, [[browser history]], shopping [[behavior]], [[demographics]] and [[credit history]]. Even your mouse movements can {{give away}} clues about you. Once the software has {{figured out}} your limit, the price follows. The proposal would not end the practice. If it takes effect, people will at least {{find out}} when their data is setting the price. Then they can decide whether to buy or {{walk away}}.

stories.headline: Flash-panning: romance that starts hot, ends in silence

sources.title: What is flash-panning? (News in Levels)
Flashpanning Is Yet Another Troubling Dating Trend Fueled By Commitment-Phobes (Glam)
New Dating Trend: Flashpanning (G105, iHeart)
Dating Games: 5 Signs of a 'Flashpanner' (video, Susan Winter)

chunks.text: Dating experts have a name for a [[romance]] that starts fast and ends in silence: [[flash-panning]]. The [[pattern]] begins like a movie. Two people meet and {{hit it off}} so well that they talk every night and see each other every day. There are gifts, dates, and big [[promises]]. One person is [[swept off their feet]] and {{falls for}} the other completely. The new [[couple]] even {{show off}} the romance online, where every photo looks like a [[perfect match]]. Then, within weeks, one partner vanishes, and the ending is [[cruel]].

verbs.correct: To like each other right away
verbs.wrong: To meet someone for the first time
verbs.why: Two strangers can hit it off at a party, and new coworkers sometimes hit it off on the very first day. This couple hit it off so well that they were talking every night and seeing each other daily.

verbs.correct: To begin to love someone
verbs.wrong: To wait for someone patiently
verbs.why: A neighbor can fall for the person who walks her dog every morning, and sometimes people fall for someone before they really know that person. One person falls for the other quickly, charmed by gifts, dates, and big promises before ordinary life begins.

verbs.correct: To display something proudly
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a planned meeting
verbs.why: Kids show off a new bike to friends, and travelers show off vacation photos online. This couple showed off their romance online, where every picture looked like a perfect match.

chunks.text: Then [[ordinary]] life {{comes along}}: work schedules, tired evenings, and small [[disagreements]]. For most couples, this is where the real work of love begins. For a flashpanner, it is the [[exit]]. The excitement {{wears off}}, and the flashpanner begins {{pulling away}}, answering less and less each day. Soon that partner disappears completely, without a fight and without an [[explanation]]. The person {{left behind}} keeps asking the same question: what did I do wrong?

verbs.correct: To arrive or appear
verbs.wrong: To find something by chance
verbs.why: A good opportunity can come along when you least expect it, and sometimes trouble comes along just as things feel settled. Here ordinary life comes along, with work schedules, tired evenings, and small disagreements.

verbs.correct: To slowly disappear over time
verbs.wrong: To make someone tired over time
verbs.why: The excitement of a new job can wear off after a few months, and the thrill of new shoes can wear off after one wear. For a flashpanner, the early excitement wears off the moment real life starts.

verbs.correct: To slowly become more distant
verbs.wrong: To succeed at something hard
verbs.why: A friend can pull away after moving to a new city, and a quiet student may pull away from the rest of the class over a long semester. The flashpanner starts pulling away by answering messages later and later each day.

verbs.correct: To go and not take someone with you
verbs.wrong: To carry someone a long way
verbs.why: A fast hiker can leave behind slower friends on a trail, and a school bus can leave behind a student who arrives one minute late. A flashpanner disappears completely and leaves the other person behind, confused and hurt.

chunks.text: Why do people do this? Relationship expert Susan Winter says flashpanners love the [[electric]] first weeks but cannot {{deal with}} boring Tuesdays and real [[compromise]]. Many never learned that small fights are a normal part of love, and the root cause is a fear of commitment. They will not {{open up}} about a problem; they simply vanish. The pattern is not new: a radio station website described it in 2019, and Winter explained it in 2023. It starts like [[love bombing]], with [[extreme]] attention and gifts, but the flashpanner leaves within weeks, and the romance usually ends in [[ghosting]].

verbs.correct: To handle a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To forget an old memory
verbs.why: Nurses deal with stress every shift, and parents deal with tantrums calmly. Flashpanners love the exciting first weeks but cannot deal with boring Tuesdays and the compromise real love needs.

verbs.correct: To talk about private feelings
verbs.wrong: To make a joke of something
verbs.why: Close friends open up about their fears late at night, and therapy helps some people open up for the first time. Flashpanners will not open up about a problem; instead of talking, they simply vanish.

chunks.text: The harm is real. After weeks of [[closeness]], the sudden silence is deeply painful. It is hard to {{get over}} someone who simply disappeared, and many people are left with less trust in dating. Experts say the best [[defense]] is to be honest about what you want and to take things slowly, with a little [[patience]]. So {{watch out for}} the [[warning signs]]: a [[flawless]] first week, gifts and big promises, and [[excitement]] that feels too strong too soon. Real love grows more slowly, and it survives boring Tuesdays.

verbs.correct: To feel better after something bad
verbs.wrong: To stop talking to someone on purpose
verbs.why: It takes time to get over a bad cold, and some people never fully get over their first heartbreak. It is hard to get over someone who disappeared without any explanation.

verbs.correct: To be careful about a danger
verbs.wrong: To choose quickly without thinking
verbs.why: Drivers watch out for ice on the road, and shoppers watch out for hidden fees on cheap deals. Experts say to watch out for a flawless first week, early gifts, and promises that feel too big too soon.

mainIdea.s: Flash-panning is a dating pattern where someone starts a romance with great energy and then disappears when ordinary life begins. Experts say daters should learn the signs.

stories.headline: Gen X creators are winning fans on TikTok

sources.title: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? (The Guardian)
This Gen Xer spent 28 years in a cubicle and never made more than $70,000. At 59, she made $500,000 in the creator economy (Fortune)
Overlooked and Under-Marketed: "Gen X" Emerges as Most Influential Global Consumer Cohort, According to NIQ and World Data Lab (NIQ)

chunks.text: On October 4, 2026, a British writer published an [[opinion column]] in the Guardian about her generation. She is 51 and part of Generation X, people born between 1965 and 1980. She said a [[marketing expert]] on TikTok had told viewers to stop {{sleeping on}} Gen X. In his view, Gen X has become a strong but [[underrated]] force online. She asked whether her [[peers]] could {{take over}} as the next big influencers.

verbs.correct: To fail to see how good someone is
verbs.wrong: To pay someone to post an ad
verbs.why: Critics often sleep on quiet movies with small budgets. Many fans sleep on a team's young goalie until she wins. A marketing expert on TikTok told viewers to stop sleeping on Gen X.

verbs.correct: To become the new leader
verbs.wrong: To leave a job for a new one
verbs.why: A new captain takes over when the old one retires. A young manager often takes over when her boss leaves. The writer asked whether her Gen X peers could take over as the next big influencers.

chunks.text: Gen X has a lot of [[buying power]]. A [[market research]] company reported in July 2025 that Gen X became the world's top-spending generation in 2021. Gen X women [[influence]] 70 to 80 percent of [[household]] buying decisions. According to the column, many young people now think Gen X is cool. But the writer says her generation is not known for {{showing off}}. Many of them are busy {{looking after}} [[aging parents]] and worried children.

verbs.correct: To try to make people admire you
verbs.wrong: To post the same video twice
verbs.why: Some people show off their new cars to everyone. A young player shows off instead of passing the ball. The writer says her generation is not known for showing off.

verbs.correct: To keep someone safe and well
verbs.wrong: To give someone a new name
verbs.why: I look after my sister's dog on the weekend. Nurses look after patients day and night. Many Gen Xers are busy looking after aging parents and worried children.

chunks.text: The column's main example is a food director at a large British [[store chain]]. She {{set up}} her TikTok account in May 2026. Her videos have {{racked up}} as many as 2 million [[views]], and nearly 250,000 people follow her. She {{talks viewers through}} new food products. In the writer's view, she {{comes across as}} calm and [[competent]]. Many fans {{look up to}} her. One wrote that they would follow her into war.

verbs.correct: To start a new account
verbs.wrong: To rate a post with stars
verbs.why: Most people set up a new email account in a few minutes. Parents often set up a bank account for their children. The food director set up her TikTok account in May 2026.

verbs.correct: To reach a large total
verbs.wrong: To guess a total wrongly
verbs.why: A strong team racks up ten wins in a row. Delivery drivers rack up a lot of miles on their cars. Her videos have racked up as many as 2 million views.

verbs.correct: To explain something step by step
verbs.wrong: To film a video in a store
verbs.why: A good teacher talks students through each math problem. A phone store clerk talks customers through the new app. In her videos, the food director talks viewers through new food products.

verbs.correct: To seem a certain way to others
verbs.wrong: To have a strong accent
verbs.why: He comes across as shy, but he is very funny. Nervous people often come across as unfriendly in interviews. In the writer's view, the food director comes across as calm and competent.

verbs.correct: To admire and respect someone
verbs.wrong: To guess someone's age
verbs.why: Many kids look up to their older brothers and sisters. Young players look up to the team's oldest star. Many fans look up to the food director, and one wrote that they would follow her into war.

chunks.text: In August, the business magazine Fortune described a 59-year-old former [[insurance]] worker who {{brought in}} about 500,000 dollars in 2025 from online videos and sales. She says fears about being too old should not {{hold people back}}. A marketing professor in Germany told the magazine that brands have a [[blind spot]] for age. The Guardian writer loves seeing [[capable]] people like the food director {{popping up}} online. She hopes more of her peers will be less [[modest]] and [[shine]].

verbs.correct: To earn an amount of money
verbs.wrong: To owe a friend money
verbs.why: My summer job brings in about 300 dollars a week. A school bake sale brings in money for new books. The former insurance worker brought in about 500,000 dollars in 2025.

verbs.correct: To stop someone's progress
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel younger
verbs.why: Fear of failure holds many people back. A fear of flying holds him back at work. She says fears about being too old should not hold people back.

verbs.correct: To appear suddenly
verbs.wrong: To lose followers quickly
verbs.why: Ads pop up on my phone all day. New coffee shops pop up all over town every year. The writer loves seeing capable people like the food director popping up online.

stories.headline: Many Americans plan homemade Halloween costumes

Survey Says: Halloween Shoppers Choose Creativity Over Costumes Off the Rack (Lynnwood Times)

chunks.text: Halloween falls on Saturday, October 31, and many Americans are already deciding what to {{dress up as}}. This year, many shoppers are skipping the [[costume aisle]]. Instead, they {{put together}} their own looks from [[thrift-store clothing]] and [[household objects]]. Some {{make do with}} whatever they already have at home. For many of them, the goal is a [[one-of-a-kind]] look that does not cost much.

chunks.text: Homemade costumes are not new on TikTok. Last October, a [[trend tracker]] from Vogue Business counted more than 22,000 posts under a tag for homemade costumes. According to the tracker, creators take [[thrifted finds]] and household materials and {{turn them into}} [[polished]] looks. They {{show off}} the whole process in [[sped-up]] videos. The trend is strongest around Halloween. It also continues all year, through fan conventions and festival fashion.

chunks.text: A survey released in late September shows the same [[shift]] among shoppers. It was [[commissioned]] by Goodwill, the thrift-store [[charity]], and asked 2,000 American adults who buy or make costumes. It found that 85 percent plan to use thrift shopping or homemade pieces this year. More than half {{turn to}} thrift stores to [[save money]]. And 44 percent go there to {{pick up}} [[materials]] for a homemade look. Seventy-one percent want pieces they can {{hold on to}} and use again after Halloween.

verbs.correct: To go to someone or somewhere for help

verbs.why: When I need advice, I turn to my older sister. Many families turn to food banks at the end of the month. In the survey, more than half of the shoppers turn to thrift stores to save money.

verbs.correct: To buy something cheaply

chunks.text: [[Store-bought]] costumes are still [[big business]]. The National Retail Federation expects Americans to {{shell out}} $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, up from $13.1 billion in 2025. That includes $4.4 billion on costumes. Fewer people now {{look up}} costume ideas online, 32 percent compared with 37 percent last year. Most still {{go for}} [[classic]] characters. About 4.8 million plan to be a witch and 4.2 million a vampire. A federation official said shoppers are paying close attention to prices this season.

stories.headline: Plague lab worker in Russia dies of pneumonia

sources.title: Russia reports a worker at a Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from an unknown cause and died (AP, via KTRE)
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation (NBC News)
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia; US monitoring case (Al Jazeera)
What to know about pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death (video, PBS NewsHour)

chunks.text: A worker at a plague [[research institute]] in eastern Russia has died, and Russian officials say the cause is unknown. The 28-year-old [[laboratory technician]] {{came down with}} [[pneumonia]] and died last week in a local hospital. [[Unconfirmed]] media reports said she may have had pneumonic plague. This rare form can be {{passed on}} from person to person. Her death has {{set off}} fears in Russia and abroad.

verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.wrong: To study a disease in a lab
verbs.why: Many kids come down with a cold after a long trip. Travelers often come down with the flu in winter. The 28-year-old laboratory technician came down with pneumonia and died last week.

verbs.correct: To spread a disease to another person
verbs.wrong: To be cured quickly with medicine
verbs.why: Sick workers often pass on colds to their coworkers. Kids at day care pass on colds all the time. Pneumonic plague is a rare form of plague that can be passed on from person to person.

verbs.correct: To cause a strong feeling
verbs.wrong: To delay the work of a lab
verbs.why: Bad news often sets off panic at the grocery store. A rude comment sets off anger online. The worker's death has set off fears in Russia and abroad.

chunks.text: The hospital was put under [[quarantine]] on Friday, October 2. It stopped {{taking in}} new patients. Its laboratory also stopped {{carrying out}} [[routine tests]]. About 200 people who may have had contact with her are under [[medical observation]], according to regional officials. Tests on her contacts {{turned up}} two cases of a [[common cold]] virus and two cases of the coronavirus. The director of a nearby [[aluminum plant]] told workers to wear masks.

verbs.correct: To accept people as patients
verbs.wrong: To hire new nurses and doctors
verbs.why: A busy emergency room takes in new patients all night. Small hospitals take in patients from nearby towns. The hospital in quarantine stopped taking in new patients.

verbs.correct: To do or complete a task
verbs.wrong: To lend equipment to others
verbs.why: Our team carries out a safety check every week. A nurse carries out a blood test in a few minutes. The hospital's laboratory stopped carrying out routine tests.

verbs.correct: To find something by checking
verbs.wrong: To cost the hospital a lot of money
verbs.why: A simple search often turns up old family photos. A home inspection sometimes turns up a problem with the wiring. Tests on the woman's contacts turned up two cases of a common cold virus and two cases of the coronavirus.

chunks.text: Russia's health agency has {{looked into}} the case. On Sunday, it said the woman had pneumonia of [[unknown origin]]. It said [[extensive]] testing found no germs linked to her work. The leader of a neighboring region said she died "maybe of the plague." He also said no disease had {{broken out}} in his region. A former head of the health agency said it was most likely not plague. A Kremlin spokesman {{played down}} the [[rumors]]. He told people to trust [[official statements]] instead.

verbs.correct: To study something to learn the facts
verbs.wrong: To give medicine to a patient
verbs.why: A good manager looks into every customer complaint. Police look into reports of missing money. Russia's health agency has looked into the case and found no germs linked to her work.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly and spread
verbs.wrong: To be named after a place
verbs.why: Fires sometimes break out in old factories. The flu often breaks out in nursing homes in winter. The leader of a neighboring region said no disease had broken out there.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To pretend you share an opinion
verbs.why: Coaches often play down a team's loss. Politicians often play down bad news before an election. A Kremlin spokesman played down the rumors and told people to trust official statements.

chunks.text: The World Health Organization said no cause of death has been officially confirmed. On Monday, the US secretary of state said the case was not a [[cause for alarm]]. He said the US is [[monitoring]] it closely. The State Department {{called on}} Russia to share [[accurate information]] quickly and openly. One British expert {{pointed out}} that plague still exists in many parts of the world. [[Antibiotics]] can treat it if it is caught early, experts say.

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone to do something
verbs.wrong: To cancel a planned meeting or trip
verbs.why: Teachers often call on the state to raise their pay. City leaders call on drivers to use less gas in summer. The State Department called on Russia to share accurate information quickly and openly.

stories.headline: Small brain area helps the body cope with cold

sources.title: USF Health researchers uncover a hidden brain region that helps regulate metabolism (EurekAlert!)
USF Health researchers uncover a hidden brain region that helps regulate metabolism (USF Health News)
A hypothalamic neuronal population coordinates metabolic adaptations to cold (Neuron, via PubMed)

chunks.text: When [[body temperature]] drops, two [[natural responses]] {{kick in}}. The body {{ramps up}} its energy use to produce heat. It also increases [[appetite]] to replace the [[fuel]] it used to stay warm. Scientists have known about these responses for decades. However, it was unclear exactly how the brain {{brings about}} both changes at the same time. A new study now offers some [[clues]].

verbs.correct: To start working or having an effect
verbs.wrong: To force someone to leave a place
verbs.why: Medicine often kicks in after about half an hour, and the air conditioning kicks in when a room gets too hot. When body temperature drops, two natural responses kick in to protect the body.

verbs.correct: To increase the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To bring something to an end
verbs.why: Factories ramp up production when demand grows, and stores ramp up hiring in December. When body temperature drops, the body ramps up its energy use to produce heat.

verbs.correct: To cause something to happen
verbs.wrong: To mention a subject for discussion
verbs.why: A new manager can bring about big changes, and regular exercise can bring about better sleep. Until now, it was unclear how the brain brings about both cold responses at the same time.

chunks.text: The study {{came out}} in the [[journal]] Neuron on September 25, 2026. It was led by scientists at the University of South Florida. Working with [[lab animals]], the team {{zeroed in on}} a small, [[little-studied]] area at the back of the [[hypothalamus]], deep in the brain. This area becomes [[highly active]] when body temperature falls. This is the first known job for this part of the brain.

verbs.correct: To be published
verbs.wrong: To find by chance
verbs.why: A new phone comes out every fall, and a popular novel can come out in many languages at once. This study came out in the journal Neuron on September 25, 2026.

verbs.correct: To give all your attention to one thing
verbs.wrong: To reduce an amount to nothing
verbs.why: A good doctor zeroes in on the cause of the pain, and police can zero in on one suspect. The team zeroed in on a small, little-studied area at the back of the hypothalamus.

chunks.text: To test its role, the researchers {{switched on}} the [[nerve cells]] in this area that respond to cold. The animals ate more food and burned more energy. Their body temperature rose, and [[brown fat]] made more heat. Because the animals used more energy, they were less likely to {{put on}} weight. Their [[blood sugar control]] also improved. When the team {{shut down}} these cells, the animals' normal reactions to cold became weaker.

verbs.correct: To make something start working
verbs.wrong: To attack someone without warning
verbs.why: You switch on a lamp when it gets dark, and a sensor can switch on the lights in a hallway. The researchers switched on nerve cells in the area that respond to cold, and the animals ate more.

verbs.correct: To gain body weight
verbs.wrong: To delay until later
verbs.why: Some people put on weight after they stop exercising, and many people put on a few pounds during a long vacation. The animals used more energy, so they were less likely to put on weight.

verbs.correct: To stop something from working
verbs.wrong: To keep someone from entering
verbs.why: Workers shut down the machines every night, and a storm can shut down a power plant. When the team shut down the cold-responding cells, the animals' normal reactions to cold became weaker.

chunks.text: The team also {{pinned down}} a protein that works as a [[cold sensor]] inside these cells. When the researchers blocked this protein, the animals ate more and {{warmed up}}. The team now hopes to {{come up with}} medicines that block it. Such drugs could one day help treat [[obesity]] and [[type 2 diabetes]]. Many [[current approaches]] focus on reducing appetite. The team's leader said new drugs might keep people healthy without dieting or [[cold exposure]].

verbs.correct: To identify something exactly
verbs.wrong: To blame someone for something
verbs.why: A mechanic can pin down the cause of a strange noise, and doctors try to pin down the source of a fever. The team pinned down a protein that works as a cold sensor inside the brain cells.

verbs.correct: To become warmer
verbs.wrong: To stay at the same level
verbs.why: Your hands warm up quickly near a fire, and a cold room warms up in the afternoon sun. When the researchers blocked the cold sensor protein, the animals ate more and warmed up.

verbs.correct: To develop a new idea or product
verbs.wrong: To become sick with an illness
verbs.why: Engineers try to come up with better batteries, and a drug company can come up with a new vaccine. The team hopes to come up with medicines that block the cold sensor protein.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found a small, little-studied brain area that helps the body handle cold by raising hunger and energy use. A protein inside it may lead to new obesity drugs.
mainIdea.why: The area becomes highly active in the cold, and a cold sensor protein in its cells could become a target for future medicines.

mainIdea.s: Scientists found that a tiny region deep in the brain makes animals hungrier when they get cold. Since the extra eating caused weight gain, they hope to find drugs that quiet it.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the animals burned more energy too, so they were less likely to gain weight. The team wants drugs that block the cold sensor protein.

mainIdea.s: A large survey found that people living in cold places eat more during winter than summer. Doctors believe this seasonal habit explains why many adults gain weight every year.
mainIdea.why: There was no survey of people. The study was done in lab animals and looked at a small brain area that responds to cold.

tf.why: It was published on September 25, 2026, and was led by scientists at the University of South Florida.

stories.headline: Aura points: the internet's new game of looking cool

sources.title: What is an 'Aura Battle'? Why is everyone suddenly 'Farming Aura' (Hola)
The boy behind the viral 'aura farming' boat racing dance (BBC)
What is 'aura farming'? Gen Z's viral obsession with looking cool (South China Morning Post)
What is an 'Aura Battle'? Young Mexicans turn confidence into a competition (video, Euronews Culture)

chunks.text: Some people just seem cool. They walk into a room and {{come across as}} [[effortlessly]] calm and [[relaxed]]. They {{give off}} an easy, quiet [[confidence]] without trying. On the internet, that [[quality]] has a name: [[aura]]. Teenagers everywhere talk about gaining and losing [[aura points]], [[imaginary]] [[scores]] for every cool or [[embarrassing]] moment in daily life. The idea borrows from [[gaming]] culture, and in 2026 it is everywhere.

verbs.correct: To seem a certain way to others
verbs.wrong: To change your opinion over time
verbs.why: A shy person can come across as unfriendly at first, and a nervous speaker can come across as more confident than he feels. On the internet, some people just come across as effortlessly cool without even trying.

verbs.correct: To produce a feeling or energy
verbs.wrong: To hide a strong emotion
verbs.why: A quiet library gives off a calm feeling on a rainy afternoon, and a coach who smiles before a big game gives off confidence that the whole team can feel. Teenagers describe this quality as aura, the feeling someone simply gives off in a room.

chunks.text: The trend exploded thanks to one boy. In 2025, a video went [[viral]]: an eleven-year-old from Indonesia was dancing calmly on the front [[tip]] of a long, narrow racing boat. His relaxed moves {{won over}} millions of viewers, and kids around the world {{look up to}} him as the king of cool. People joked that he had {{racked up}} more aura points than anyone alive. The joke created a new phrase, [[aura farming]], which even reached a famous dictionary's [[shortlist]] for word of the year.

verbs.correct: To gain someone's support or love
verbs.wrong: To recover a title you lost
verbs.why: A new teacher can win over a whole class within a week, and honest answers can win over even the toughest judges. The boy's calm dance moves won over millions of viewers around the world.

verbs.correct: To respect and admire someone
verbs.wrong: To protect a younger child
verbs.why: Young players look up to their team captain, and kids often look up to an older sibling or a coach. Kids around the world look up to this calm eleven-year-old as the king of cool.

verbs.correct: To collect a large number of points
verbs.wrong: To divide something into parts
verbs.why: A champion racks up win after win over a long season, and a frequent flyer racks up miles without even noticing. Fans joked that the boy had racked up more aura points than anyone alive.

chunks.text: The rules are simple but strict. When a skater {{pulls off}} a hard [[trick]] perfectly, his aura grows. If he {{messes up}} in front of everyone, the points vanish instantly. And there is a [[twist]]: visible effort is [[fatal]]. People who {{show off}} their new clothes and money usually lose aura, not gain it. True aura belongs to those who {{stand out}} without trying, or at least without letting anyone see the trying. Coolness, the internet has decided, must look [[accidental]].

verbs.correct: To succeed at something difficult
verbs.wrong: To practice something for hours
verbs.why: A skater can pull off a hard trick on the first try, and a team can pull off a surprise win against the odds. In this game, a skater who pulls off a hard trick perfectly watches his aura grow instantly.

verbs.correct: To make a big mistake
verbs.wrong: To win by a small amount
verbs.why: Everyone messes up a name at some point, and a nervous actor can mess up his lines on opening night. If a player messes up in front of everyone here, the aura points disappear right away.

verbs.correct: To display something proudly
verbs.wrong: To offer something for free
verbs.why: A proud driver shows off a new car around the block, and a student shows off a shiny new trophy at school. Here, people who show off their new clothes or money usually lose points instead of gaining them.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.wrong: To follow the group quietly
verbs.why: A bright red coat can stand out in a gray winter crowd, and a calm voice can stand out in a loud, noisy meeting. True aura belongs to people who stand out without even seeming to try.

chunks.text: In 2026, the game turned physical. Reports from Latin America described aura battles, in-person [[contests]] in parks and plazas where two players face each other and try to look cooler with every move. At some Mexican events, winners {{take home}} [[prizes]] of 3,000 pesos. Most fans just {{play along}} at home, rating their friends' aura after every party. Meanwhile, [[psychologists]] are not worried. Learning to [[play it cool]], they say, is an old teenage sport. Only the [[scoreboard]] is new.

verbs.correct: To win and keep a prize or money
verbs.wrong: To agree to fight an opponent
verbs.why: A lucky player can take home a new car from a game show, and the best baker takes home a blue ribbon at the fair. At some Mexican aura battles, winners take home prizes of 3,000 pesos.

verbs.correct: To join a game and act your part
verbs.wrong: To stop a game before the end
verbs.why: A parent might play along with a child's pretend game, and friends often play along when someone tells a silly story. Most fans simply play along at home, rating each other's aura after every party.

mainIdea.s: Young people online measure coolness with imaginary aura points, a trend borrowed from gaming that grew out of one viral boat video. In 2026 it created real contests.
mainIdea.why: The article explains aura points, the boy who made aura farming famous, and the aura battles held in Latin America in 2026.

mainIdea.s: Young people are earning real money by collecting coolness points inside a popular phone game. The app pays its calmest players about three thousand pesos every month.

stories.headline: Brazil votes for president and Congress on Sunday

sources.title: Brazil's 2026 Elections: Timeline and Fast Facts (AS/COA)
Lula and Bolsonaro's mudslinging heats up ahead of weekend vote (France 24)
Brazil vote approaches with Lula and Bolsonaro polling in close race (Reuters, via Investing.com)
Brazil heads to the polls for high-stakes election between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro (video, France 24)

chunks.text: Brazil holds a [[general election]] on Sunday, October 4, 2026. About 159 million people are [[eligible]] to vote. They will choose a president, state governors, all 513 members of the lower house of Congress and 54 of the 81 senators. Voting is [[compulsory]] for people aged 18 to 70. Those who do not {{show up}} have to pay a [[fine]]. Two of the 13 candidates for president have {{pulled ahead}} in the polls.

verbs.correct: To be present where you are expected
verbs.wrong: To leave the whole ballot empty
verbs.why: Some students never show up for early classes. A good plumber always shows up on time. In Brazil, voters aged 18 to 70 who do not show up on election day have to pay a fine.

verbs.correct: To become the race leader
verbs.wrong: To join another party
verbs.why: A strong team often pulls ahead in the second half. One runner usually pulls ahead after the first mile. Of the 13 candidates for president, two have pulled ahead in the polls.

chunks.text: President Lula, who is 80, is seeking a fourth [[term]]. He {{faces off}} against Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator and the son of a former president. Under his current government, inflation and [[unemployment]] have {{come down}}. He has promised a more generous [[welfare program]] and [[debt relief]] for families. He has also promised to {{crack down on}} [[online betting]].

verbs.correct: To compete directly against someone
verbs.wrong: To accept a hard truth about yourself
verbs.why: In most tournaments, the top two teams face off in the final. Rival candidates face off in a TV debate before each election. President Lula faces off against Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator.

verbs.correct: To become lower
verbs.wrong: To become a news topic
verbs.why: Gas prices often come down after the summer. A fever usually comes down after a good night's sleep. Inflation and unemployment have come down under Lula's current government.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To collect taxes from a business
verbs.why: The city cracks down on illegal parking near schools. Teachers crack down on cheating during final exams. Lula has promised to crack down on online betting.

chunks.text: Bolsonaro has made crime the center of his campaign. He has {{set out}} a plan to build five [[maximum-security prisons]] like those in El Salvador. Trade is another issue, because of US [[tariffs]] on Brazilian goods. His team says his ties with the Trump administration would protect Brazil. Lula says Brazil must {{stand up for}} its independence, including on trade with China. Both men are trying to {{win over}} voters who worry about crime, [[household debt]] and the [[cost of living]].

verbs.correct: To explain a plan clearly
verbs.wrong: To start a new organization
verbs.why: A new coach sets out her plan for the season. In most meetings, the manager sets out the main goals first. Bolsonaro has set out a plan to build five maximum-security prisons.

verbs.correct: To defend someone or something
verbs.wrong: To be a short name for something
verbs.why: She always stands up for her friends. Good union leaders stand up for workers' rights. Lula says Brazil must stand up for its independence, including on trade with China.

chunks.text: High school students in France are protesting about [[overcrowded]] classrooms and [[teacher shortages]]. The protests {{broke out}} at schools in the Paris region during the week of September 21, 2026. This week they {{spilled over}} into other parts of the country, including Marseille, Strasbourg and Rennes. On Friday, October 2, about 400 of France's 3,700 high schools were {{shut down}}.

verbs.wrong: To be stopped by police

chunks.text: Students say 35 of them {{squeeze into}} a single classroom, without enough chairs for everyone. They are {{calling for}} more [[substitute teachers]], better buildings and more money for schools. Some also object to their [[class schedules]], to rooms that get too hot, and to a short [[lunch break]]. The government's draft 2027 budget raises [[education spending]] by 1.7 percent, to 65.53 billion euros. That increase does not {{keep up with}} [[inflation]].

chunks.text: In some places the protests have [[turned violent]]. Police used [[tear gas]] in Strasbourg, and trash cans were set on fire in Rennes. On October 1, the interior minister said police had [[detained]] more than 400 people, many of them [[minors]]. He said nothing [[excuses]] violence. The education minister said about 170 students and at least 65 school staff have been hurt. Officials are {{looking into}} [[claims]] of police violence. The education minister planned to {{sit down with}} unions, parents and student groups on Friday.

chunks.text: The school protests come during a wider fight over [[public sector]] pay. On September 29, teachers, health workers and firefighters {{walked out}} across France. Unions said 300,000 people {{turned out}}, while police counted about 30,000 in Paris. Workers want a 6 percent [[raise]]. The government plans to {{hold down}} [[base pay]] in 2027 to save 2 billion euros. It would be the fourth [[pay freeze]] [[in a row]]. Teachers' unions are now {{stepping up}} the pressure with another strike on Tuesday, October 6.

stories.headline: Paying students to sleep improves rest and grades

sources.title: Sleep payments: could they lead to better rest and better health? (The Guardian)
We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours and their grades quickly improved (The Conversation)
Incentives to sleep boost college students' grades, new study finds (University of Pittsburgh, via EurekAlert!)

chunks.text: A new study shows that paying college students to sleep can improve their sleep and their grades. [[Economists]] at the University of Pittsburgh {{handed out}} [[wearable sleep trackers]] to more than 1,100 [[undergraduates]]. The trackers [[recorded]] how long each student slept. For four weeks, 468 of the students earned about $5 for each night they slept at least seven hours. The study {{came out}} in July in the Journal of Political Economy. It drew [[widespread attention]] in September.

verbs.correct: To give something to every member of a group
verbs.wrong: To give control of something to another person
verbs.why: Teachers hand out tests at the start of class, and volunteers hand out water at a race. The economists handed out wearable sleep trackers to more than 1,100 students.

verbs.correct: To be published or made public
verbs.wrong: To find something by chance
verbs.why: A new report on sleep comes out every spring. Most new phones come out in the fall. The study came out in July in the Journal of Political Economy.

chunks.text: At the start, the students slept 6.6 hours a night on average. Half of them usually {{stayed up}} past 1 a.m. They {{fell short of}} seven hours on more than half of [[school nights]]. Many students did not know how little they slept. Two-thirds said they usually got seven hours. The trackers showed that only about a third of the students reached that [[target]] on at least three nights out of five.

verbs.correct: To not go to bed until late
verbs.wrong: To remain at home for the evening
verbs.why: Many kids stay up until midnight on New Year's Eve. Students often stay up late before a big exam. Before the study, half of the students usually stayed up past 1 a.m.

verbs.correct: To fail to reach a goal or amount
verbs.wrong: To use something when other plans fail
verbs.why: Many charities fall short of their fundraising goals. Runners sometimes fall short of their target time in hot weather. The students fell short of seven hours of sleep on more than half of school nights.

chunks.text: The paid students reached seven hours on 26 percent more nights than students who were not paid. They slept about 19 more minutes per school night. They also {{cut back on}} [[screen use]] late at night. The extra sleep {{paid off}} [[modestly]] in class. Their [[grade point average]], on a scale where an A equals 4, {{went up}} by about 0.08 points that [[semester]]. [[First-year students]] {{stood out}}, with the biggest [[gains]].

verbs.correct: To use or do less of something
verbs.wrong: To interrupt someone who is speaking
verbs.why: Many people cut back on sugar to lose weight, and families cut back on gas when prices rise. The paid students also cut back on screen use late at night.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result after effort
verbs.wrong: To make two people compete with each other
verbs.why: Hard practice usually pays off on game day. Careful saving pays off when you buy a home. The extra sleep paid off modestly in class, with slightly higher grades.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level

verbs.why: Rent often goes up every year. Gas prices usually go up in the summer. The paid students' grade point average went up by about 0.08 points that semester.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.wrong: To support someone in a hard time
verbs.why: A tall player stands out in a crowd, and a bright yellow car stands out in a parking lot. First-year students stood out in the study, with the biggest gains in sleep and grades.

chunks.text: After the payments ended, the students {{kept up}} part of the new [[habit]]. They still slept about eight minutes more per night for the next three to four weeks. Their grades stayed higher the next semester, but the effect {{wore off}} after that. [[Bedtime reminders]] without money had little effect. The hard part was {{following through}} [[night after night]]. The researchers say late-evening [[deadlines]] to {{turn in}} work can make it harder for students to sleep enough.

verbs.why: Few people keep up a new exercise routine for a whole year. Some people keep up a diet for only a week. After the payments ended, the students kept up part of the new habit, sleeping about eight extra minutes a night.

verbs.why: The effect of coffee wears off after a few hours, and the numb feeling from a dentist visit wears off by evening. The grade boost lasted into the next semester, but then it wore off.

verbs.why: Many people make big plans in January but rarely follow through. Good students follow through on their study plans every week. Nearly all the students wanted more sleep, but the hard part was following through night after night.

stories.headline: The world now has more seniors than young children

chunks.text: The world now has more people aged 65 and older than children aged 5 and younger, the U.S. Census Bureau said in a report that {{came out}} on August 31, 2026. Between 2020 and 2025, the [[share]] of older adults {{caught up with}} and passed the youngest children's share for the first time in [[recorded history]]. The report, by Census Bureau [[demographers]], {{pulls together}} population [[figures]] from every country.

verbs.correct: To be published
verbs.wrong: To be counted in a survey

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as
verbs.wrong: To be measured at the same time
verbs.why: A runner can catch up with the leader on the last lap, and a small company can catch up with a bigger rival. Between 2020 and 2025, the share of older adults caught up with the share of the youngest children and then passed it.

verbs.correct: To collect from many places
verbs.wrong: To compare over many years
verbs.why: A coach pulls together a team from three schools, and a reporter pulls together facts from many interviews. The report pulls together population figures from every country in the world.

chunks.text: Two things {{lie behind}} the change: people are living longer, and [[birth rates]] have {{gone down}}. In 2023, 71 percent of people lived in countries where women have 2.1 children or fewer [[on average]], the number needed to {{keep up}} a population. In 2013 it was 45 percent. China, India and Mexico are among them. The [[shift]] is {{speeding up}}: the world passed this "[[tipping point]]" much earlier than experts expected a [[decade]] ago, the report says.

verbs.correct: To be the cause of something
verbs.wrong: To be expected in the future
verbs.why: Money worries often lie behind a family argument, and a small mistake can lie behind a big accident. Two things lie behind the world's aging: longer lives and lower birth rates.

verbs.correct: To become lower
verbs.wrong: To continue for years
verbs.why: Gas prices go down in the winter, and a fever goes down after a day in bed. Birth rates have gone down in most of the world, so there are fewer young children.

verbs.correct: To hold at the same level
verbs.wrong: To stop something from growing
verbs.why: A shop has to keep up its stock in the busy season, and a runner tries to keep up her speed on the hills. Women need to have about 2.1 children on average to keep up a country's population.

verbs.correct: To happen faster than before
verbs.wrong: To reach its highest point
verbs.why: Traffic speeds up once you leave the city, and a computer speeds up after you delete old files. The shift toward an older world is speeding up, and it passed this tipping point much earlier than experts expected.

chunks.text: Japan is the oldest country, with 29.7 percent of its people aged 65 or older, but South Korea is expected to {{take over}} the [[top spot]] by 2060, at 41 percent. Europe is the oldest [[region]], yet Africa's older population is expected to {{shoot up}} by more than 300 percent, to 249 million by 2060, against 214 million in Europe. The United States, 48th oldest in 2025, is expected to {{end up}} 110th by 2060 as other countries age faster.

verbs.correct: To replace another at the top
verbs.wrong: To look like an older relative
verbs.why: A new champion takes over from the old one, and a younger manager can take over from her boss. South Korea is expected to take over the top spot from Japan as the world's oldest country by 2060.

verbs.correct: To rise very quickly
verbs.wrong: To try to reach a goal
verbs.why: Rents shoot up when a new factory opens, and a child's height can shoot up in a single summer. Africa's older population is expected to shoot up by more than 300 percent by 2060.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a position
verbs.wrong: To stop growing for good
verbs.why: A late bus can end up an hour behind schedule, and a weak team can end up last in the league. The United States is expected to end up 110th on the list of oldest countries by 2060.

chunks.text: The report {{points out}} that 73 percent of older Americans had two or more [[chronic conditions]] between 2016 and 2019. One expert who [[contributed]] to the report said old age could {{turn into}} an economic [[asset]] if countries [[invest]] in [[preventive health]] and let people {{stay on}} at work longer. By 2060 the world's older population is expected to reach nearly 2 billion, up from 852 million in 2025, and {{make up}} one in five people worldwide.

verbs.why: A coach points out that the team always plays better after a long rest, and a neighbor points out that the trash is collected a day late this week. The report points out that 73 percent of older Americans had two or more chronic conditions between 2016 and 2019.

chunks.text: Foreign patients fly to India for [[heart surgery]], new knees and cancer treatment. In 2025 the country {{took in}} about 507,000 medical visitors, an industry review reported in July 2026. India's tourism minister said on March 3, 2026, that the market should reach 13 billion dollars this year, up from 6 billion in 2022. A German public broadcaster asked on September 5, 2026, how India can {{hold on to}} its [[lead]] as rivals grow.

chunks.text: The main reason is price. A heart [[bypass]] can cost 150,000 dollars in the United States but only 4,500 to 8,000 in India. A [[knee replacement]] costs about a tenth of the American price, and the [[savings]] {{add up}} fast. India also {{stands out}} for quality. It has 44 hospitals with top international [[accreditation]], the most in Asia, and 1.3 million [[registered doctors]], many of whom speak English.

chunks.text: But India is {{falling behind}} its [[rivals]]. Thailand, which offers faster [[visas]], now {{brings in}} 2.5 million [[medical tourists]] a year, five times India's number. The [[conflict]] involving Iran, Israel and the United States has {{cut off}} many patients from the Middle East. [[Arrivals]] from that region fell 40 to 75 percent as [[airfares]] rose 25 percent, a March 30, 2026 report said. Arrivals from Bangladesh, the largest [[source country]], also {{dropped off}} after its government changed in August 2024.

chunks.text: One of the world's biggest makers of phone chips has [[unveiled]] a new chip for earbuds. chunks.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping began a three-day [[state visit]] to Washington on September 23, 2026. It is his first visit in 10 years and his third meeting with President Donald Trump in less than a year. Neither side expects major deals. Both leaders hope to {{smooth over}} tensions and steady [[fragile ties]]. Their countries have {{pulled back from}} last year's [[trade war]] and its very high [[tariffs]].

It accuses Chinese developers of {{tapping into}} American AI models to copy their abilities. Beijing {{pushes back}}, saying this practice, called [[distillation]], is widely used, including by American companies. It says Washington wants to [[monopolize]] the industry. stories.headline: Chimpanzees throw stones at the same trees for years

sources.title: Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade (ScienceDaily)
Why Do Male Chimpanzees Throw Rocks At the Same Trees for More Than a Decade? (AllAfrica, republishing The Conversation)
Chimpanzees Keep Throwing Stones at the Same Trees, Scientists Want To Know Why (SciTechDaily)

chunks.text: Male chimpanzees in West Africa have been throwing stones at the same trees for years, scientists say. The [[habit]] was reported in late August 2026 from a national park in the region, a savanna-woodland [[landscape]]. The males {{pick up}} stones and throw them at [[particular]] trees. They {{come back to}} the same spots, so [[piles]] of rocks have {{built up}} at the base. The throwing sites have been [[in active use]] for more than ten years.

verbs.correct: To lift something from the ground
verbs.wrong: To throw something far away
verbs.why: Kids pick up shells on the beach, and a gardener picks up fallen branches after a storm. Here the male chimps pick up stones from the ground and throw them at particular trees.

verbs.correct: To return to the same place
verbs.wrong: To find something by chance
verbs.why: Birds come back to the same nest every spring, and families come back to a favorite campsite each summer. These chimps come back to the same spots again and again, year after year.

verbs.correct: To grow bigger over time
verbs.wrong: To separate into small pieces
verbs.why: Dust builds up on a shelf nobody cleans, and snow builds up against a door overnight. Because the chimps keep throwing, piles of rocks have built up at the base of those trees.

chunks.text: The behavior {{stands out}} because it is so rare: only four chimpanzee groups in West Africa have been [[observed]] doing it. Researchers from the University of Victoria and local [[field assistants]] {{set out}} to learn why. The chimps are unhabituated, not used to humans, so the team could not watch them directly. Instead, they {{set up}} [[camera traps]] and audio recorders at the sites, scanned the rocks in 3D, and measured the trees. They also noted [[nests]] and [[feeding signs]] and slowly {{put together}} a picture of the behavior.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different from others
verbs.wrong: To represent an idea or a group
verbs.why: A red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one tall building stands out on a flat skyline. This behavior stands out because it has only been observed in four chimpanzee groups in all of West Africa.

verbs.correct: To begin a task with a clear goal
verbs.wrong: To keep something for later use
verbs.why: A hiker sets out to reach the top before noon, and a detective sets out to find the missing money. The research team set out to learn why the chimps throw stones at these trees.

verbs.correct: To put equipment in place for use
verbs.wrong: To make an alarm or camera start
verbs.why: Campers set up a tent before dark, and a band sets up its speakers before a show. Since the chimps are not used to humans, the team set up camera traps and audio recorders at the sites instead of watching in person.

verbs.correct: To create something from many parts
verbs.wrong: To delay something until later
verbs.why: A child puts together a puzzle piece by piece, and a reporter puts together a story from many small facts. The researchers put together a picture of the chimps' behavior from cameras, recordings, scans, and measurements.

chunks.text: The researchers have not {{figured out}} why. The throwing is part of a bigger [[display]]: the males also call loudly and drum on the tree's buttress roots. It may be a [[tradition]] {{passed down}} in these groups, or serve a symbolic [[purpose]], such as marking [[territory]]. Or the males may be {{showing off}} their [[status]]. The team cannot {{rule out}} any of these ideas, so the reason remains [[an open question]]. It is a rare case of stone use that is purely social, not to [[crack]] nuts or get food.

verbs.correct: To find the answer to a question
verbs.wrong: To watch for signs of danger
verbs.why: A mechanic figures out why a car will not start, and a student figures out a hard math problem. The researchers still have not figured out why the chimps throw stones at all.

verbs.correct: To teach a habit to the next generation
verbs.wrong: To choose not to include someone
verbs.why: Grandmothers pass down family recipes to their grandchildren. Small villages pass down old songs from one generation to the next. One theory is that the stone throwing is a tradition passed down within these particular chimp communities.

verbs.correct: To display skill to impress others
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place at a set time
verbs.why: A skater shows off a new trick in front of his friends, and a cook shows off her knife skills behind the counter. Another idea is that the males are showing off their skill or status to other chimps.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible

mainIdea.s: Male chimps in West Africa have thrown stones at the same trees for over ten years. Scientists studied the sites indirectly and still do not know why the chimps do it.
mainIdea.why: The same throwing sites have been in active use for more than ten years, the team studied them with camera traps and recorders, and the reason is still an open question.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in West Africa proved that male chimps throw rocks at trees to mark their territory. Camera traps at the sites recorded the behavior for more than a decade.
mainIdea.why: Close, but marking territory is only one of several theories. The researchers say they cannot rule out any of the ideas yet.

mainIdea.s: A new study found that chimps in a national park in West Africa crack nuts with stone hammers. The scientists say young animals learn the skill by watching their mothers.
mainIdea.why: These chimps use stones in a purely social way, not to crack nuts or get food. Nothing in the study is about young animals learning from their mothers.

tf.s: Scientists now know why the chimps throw the stones.
tf.why: Marking territory is only one theory. The researchers have not figured out why the chimps do it, and they cannot rule out any of the ideas yet.

tf.s: The team set up camera traps at the throwing sites.
tf.why: They also placed audio recorders, made 3D scans of the rocks, and measured the target trees.

tf.s: Stone throwing is common among chimps across Africa.
tf.why: The behavior stands out because it is so rare. It has been seen in only four chimp groups in West Africa.

tf.s: Mining could push the chimps out of the area.
tf.why: The area is under threat from bauxite mining exploration, and if mining begins it could push the chimps out of the landscape they have used for so long.

tf.s: The chimps are used to having people nearby.
tf.why: They are unhabituated, so the team set up cameras and recorders at the sites instead of watching the chimps directly.

tf.s: Piles of rocks have built up under the target trees.
tf.why: The chimps come back to the same spots again and again, and the sites have been in use for more than ten years.

chunks.text: World leaders {{came together}} in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly. The main debate {{kicked off}} on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. About 130 [[heads of state]] and government are expected to speak. The meeting takes place amid wars and [[bitter divisions]]. Russia's president is not attending. India's prime minister {{backed out}}. China's president sent a vice president instead.

chunks.text: The UN secretary-general opened the debate with his final speech. "Cracks have become [[canyons]]," he said. He {{set out}} four tests: war or peace, [[inequality]], climate change, and artificial intelligence. Wars are still {{going on}} in Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, and other places. The war in Ukraine is in its fifth year. Ukraine and its European [[allies]] are seeking more support. Russia has used its Security Council [[veto]] to block UN [[involvement]]. He also {{spoke out}} against machines making [[life-and-death decisions]].

chunks.text: The UN is also [[short of money]]. The United States paid $725 million of its [[dues]] this year, so it kept its vote in the Assembly. An expert at the International Crisis Group said money troubles forced the UN to {{cut back on}} [[peacekeeping]] and [[humanitarian aid]]. [[Supply chain]] problems are {{pushing up}} [[living costs]]. They are also {{slowing down}} growth. The secretary-general said [[cooperation]] is more necessary than ever to {{deal with}} the world's biggest threats.

chunks.text: The secretary-general's second five-year [[term]] ends on December 31. The Security Council has held three [[straw polls]] but has not {{settled on}} anyone to {{take over}} from him. By tradition, the next leader is expected to come from Latin America. A former president of Chile {{dropped out}} over the weekend, leaving seven [[candidates]]. No woman has ever held the job, and many countries want that to change. The United States says the next leader must get the UN "back to basics."

chunks.text: Gamescom, the world's largest [[trade fair]] for video games, {{wrapped up}} in Cologne, Germany, on Sunday, August 30. Organizers said 368,000 visitors from 131 countries {{turned out}} over the week, up from 357,000 in 2025. The number of international visitors hit a record, and 72 percent of the 1,743 [[exhibitors]] came from outside Germany, another record. For the first time, all 233,000 square meters of [[floor space]] {{sold out}}.

chunks.text: The debate over whether AI could cause [[human extinction]] has {{flared up}} again. On September 8, a researcher at Anthropic quit. He wrote online that top labs were racing toward [[self-improving]] systems and "gambling with our lives." His posts drew 153 million views in 36 hours. A senior [[safety researcher]] there {{backed him up}}. He put the [[odds]] of AI killing all humans above 10 percent within a [[decade]].

verbs.correct: To suddenly become active again
verbs.wrong: To be settled by a formal vote
verbs.why: Old arguments flare up at every family dinner. Tempers often flare up at long, tense meetings. The debate over AI and human extinction flared up again after a researcher quit Anthropic.

verbs.correct: To support what someone has said
verbs.wrong: To replace someone in a job
verbs.why: A good manager backs up her team in difficult meetings. Loyal friends back you up when others disagree with you. A senior safety researcher backed up the researcher who quit, saying AI really could kill all humans.

chunks.text: The industry calls this number the "probability of doom." [[Estimates]] vary widely. The head of one leading lab puts the chance of disaster at 10 to 25 percent. One AI scientist {{points out}} that any such number is a [[wild guess]]. A 2025 [[survey]] of 272 experts {{came up with}} 21.5 percent. In 2023, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind {{put out}} a statement. It said this risk should be treated like [[pandemics]] and [[nuclear war]].

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To refuse to answer a question
verbs.why: A good teacher points out mistakes in every essay. He often points out that the store closes early on Sundays. One AI scientist points out that any such number is really a wild guess.

verbs.correct: To produce an answer or figure
verbs.wrong: To reach agreement with others
verbs.why: Good teams come up with cheaper plans. A chef comes up with a new dessert every month. A 2025 survey of 272 experts came up with a risk figure of 21.5 percent.

verbs.correct: To publish something for the public
verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan at the last minute
verbs.why: The company puts out a short press release after every big deal. The city puts out a weather warning every summer. In 2023, the heads of three major labs put out a statement comparing AI risk to pandemics and nuclear war.

chunks.text: If AI builders believe this, why do they {{carry on}}? An academic news site gave three answers on September 11. Some leaders believe the [[benefits]] will {{make up for}} the risks. Some say you cannot make AI safe without building it first. And many fear that if one lab {{slows down}}, a [[rival]] will {{catch up}} and win. In July, 1,300 lab employees signed an [[open letter]] asking the US government to help {{hold back}} the [[pace]] of development.

verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.wrong: To move work to a new place
verbs.why: Workers carry on despite the rain. She carries on studying even after a long day at work. Critics ask why the labs carry on building AI if they believe it could end humanity.

verbs.correct: To be enough to balance something bad
verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: A big bonus makes up for the long hours. Good weather makes up for the high prices at the beach. Some AI leaders believe the benefits will make up for the risks.

verbs.correct: To move or work at a lower speed
verbs.wrong: To close a company for good
verbs.why: The train slows down before the station. Sales slow down every January. Many in the industry fear that if one lab slows down, a rival will simply win the race.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as a leader
verbs.wrong: To copy what another company makes
verbs.why: The second runner often catches up near the finish line. Small companies catch up fast when they copy good ideas. Labs fear a rival will catch up if they slow down.

verbs.correct: To stop something from moving fast
verbs.wrong: To keep a promise made earlier
verbs.why: The dam holds back the river in spring. High prices hold back sales of new phones. About 1,300 employees asked the US government to help hold back the pace of AI development.

chunks.text: On September 12, the head of Anthropic published an essay calling for a [[voluntary]] slowdown and [[independent auditors]]. Two days later, the US president {{pushed back}} against new AI rules. A rival chief executive called the plan "a [[cartel]] by any other name." A campaign for global AI "[[red lines]]" began at the United Nations in September 2025. It wants governments to {{sign off on}} an agreement by the end of 2026. That [[deadline]] is four months away.

verbs.correct: To oppose an idea or plan
verbs.wrong: To hand a job to someone else
verbs.why: Parents push back against longer school days. Staff push back when the boss cuts breaks. The US president pushed back against new AI rules two days after the Anthropic essay.
