mainIdea.s: A researcher's resignation from a top AI lab has renewed the argument over whether AI could end humanity. Labs admit the risk is real, but they say stopping alone would not work.
mainIdea.why: After the resignation, labs gave three reasons for continuing, while critics and a red lines campaign ask governments to act.

mainIdea.s: After a researcher quit, the leading AI labs agreed to pause all training until governments sign a global treaty. Rival companies quickly called the pause a cartel in disguise.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no lab paused training. The head of Anthropic called for a voluntary slowdown, and one rival attacked that plan.

mainIdea.s: The United Nations has adopted a binding treaty that bans AI from designing weapons or copying humans. Leading labs say they will follow the new rules starting next year.
mainIdea.why: No treaty exists yet. A campaign wants governments to sign off on an agreement by the end of 2026.

stories.headline: The US military says it must be ready to fight in space

America's troops must prepare now for warfare on moon, top general says (Stars and Stripes)

chunks.text: The US military says it must be ready to fight in space, even near the moon. On September 16, 2026, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff {{spelled out}} that view at a conference in Maryland. The [[joint force]], he said, must fight, [[endure]], and win "from the [[seabed]] to [[cislunar space]]," the region between Earth and the moon. He {{pointed out}} that future wars may not {{play out}} with safe [[rear areas]] or easy access to supplies.

verbs.correct: To explain something clearly and in detail
verbs.wrong: To send a message in secret code
verbs.why: A good contract spells out who handles repairs. Most teachers spell out the rules on the first day. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff spelled out his view on space at a conference in Maryland.

verbs.correct: To tell people about a fact they should notice
verbs.wrong: To refuse to answer a reporter's question

chunks.text: Two days earlier, the Air Force secretary {{brought up}} a new fact. He said the Space Force now has weapons in [[orbit]] that can defend US forces against [[hostile]] action. He {{held back}} the details and would not say whether the weapons could physically {{take out}} a target. He said the US has watched China and Russia {{build up}} space [[capabilities]] for more than ten years.

verbs.correct: To destroy or disable a target

verbs.why: A strong storm often takes out power lines. A single virus sometimes takes out a whole office network. The secretary would not say whether the weapons could physically take out a target.

verbs.wrong: To copy another country's plans exactly
verbs.why: Many countries build up their navies over many years. A good coach builds up a strong team slowly. The secretary said the US has watched China and Russia build up space capabilities for more than ten years.

chunks.text: The head of the Space Force's combat command {{laid out}} a [[growth plan]]. The service was {{set up}} in 2019, during Trump's first term. It plans to double its [[personnel]] to about 25,000 within five years. About two-thirds of them will {{carry out}} [[combat]] work. He said humanity is moving deeper into space, and China is active in parts of it. The US must {{keep up}} and be ready for [[operations]] near the moon.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, signed by 95 countries including the US, China, and Russia, {{rules out}} [[nuclear weapons]] in orbit and [[weapons tests]] on the moon. Asked about the [[treaty]], the Space Force general said the service would keep its operations safe and responsible. chunks.text: After the long night, the [[volunteers]] were {{split up}} into three groups. One group cycled at [[moderate to vigorous]] effort for 20 minutes. A second group took a 90-minute nap. The third group did neither. Right after, everyone tried to {{take in}} a set of images. Three days later, the researchers tested how well those memories had {{held up}}. The exercise and nap groups both scored about 22 percent better than the group that did nothing.

verbs.correct: To divide people into smaller groups
verbs.wrong: To put your name on a list to join

verbs.correct: To notice and remember what you see
verbs.wrong: To start a new hobby or activity

verbs.correct: To stay strong or good over time
verbs.wrong: To stop yourself from doing something
verbs.why: Cheap shoes rarely hold up through a whole winter, and a good friendship holds up even at a distance. Three days later, the researchers tested how well the memories had held up.

chunks.text: The two methods {{turned out}} to work in different ways. The study's lead author, a [[doctoral candidate]] in [[neurology]], {{pointed out}} that the nap let the brain [[recharge]]. The [[brain recordings]] showed that exercise made the brain use its [[resources]] more [[efficiently]], without adding [[fatigue]]. A hard ride might seem sure to {{wear down}} a tired body. Instead, the exercise group {{kept up with}} the nap group on the memory test. The senior author is a professor of [[physical therapy]] at McGill University.

verbs.correct: To be found to be true in the end
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: A cheap hotel sometimes turns out to be very clean. A quiet coworker often turns out to be very funny. The two methods turned out to work in different ways.

verbs.wrong: To decide something cannot happen
verbs.why: A guide points out the oldest building on the street, and a mechanic points out a worn tire before a long trip. The lead author pointed out that the nap let the brain recharge.

verbs.correct: To make someone weak and tired
verbs.wrong: To slowly stop having an effect
verbs.why: A long illness wears down even a strong person. Months of night shifts wear down many nurses. A hard ride might seem sure to wear down a tired body.

verbs.correct: To do as well as someone else
verbs.wrong: To stop someone from entering
verbs.why: A good young runner keeps up with the adults in a short race. Some new students keep up with the class from the first week. The exercise group kept up with the nap group on the memory test.

chunks.text: The findings matter for anyone who cannot {{catch up on}} sleep [[right away]]. Nurses, new parents, students and [[shift workers]] often {{go without}} a full night in bed. A short ride on a bike may help them {{bounce back}} until a real rest is possible. The study looked only at healthy young adults after a single [[sleepless]] night. Even so, moving your body for 20 minutes beats doing nothing at all.

verbs.correct: To do something you missed earlier
verbs.wrong: To become popular with many people
verbs.why: Students catch up on homework after a sick day, and travelers catch up on emails at the airport. Many people cannot catch up on sleep right away after a bad night.

verbs.correct: To live without something you need
verbs.wrong: To check something carefully
verbs.why: Campers sometimes go without a hot shower for a week, and a busy family may go without dinner together. Nurses and shift workers often go without a full night in bed.

verbs.correct: To feel well again after a hard time
verbs.wrong: To make someone remember the past
verbs.why: Most children bounce back quickly from a cold. Strong athletes bounce back after a painful loss. A short bike ride may help tired workers bounce back until real rest is possible.

stories.headline: Australia banned teen social media. Did it work?

sources.title: Most Australian teens still online three months after under-16 ban (Al Jazeera)
Australia's under-16 social media ban failing, study shows (Al Jazeera)
Why young people say the social media ban is not working (ABC News Australia)
Australia's social media ban is failing, new study suggests (video, CBS Boston)

chunks.text: In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to [[ban]] [[social media]] for everyone under 16. The law was [[designed]] to {{keep out}} young teenagers, closing the doors of TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat to young users. [[Platforms]] {{shut down}} about 4.7 million [[accounts]], and parents hoped their children would spend less time on [[screens]]. New [[data]] tells a different story: most under-16s are still online, and many use the apps just as often as before.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from entering
verbs.wrong: To watch someone carefully
verbs.why: Fences keep out wild animals, and passwords keep out strangers. The law was written to keep young teenagers out of the biggest apps.

verbs.correct: To close something completely
verbs.wrong: To sell to a bigger company
verbs.why: Factories shut down in a crisis, and websites shut down for repairs. The platforms shut down about 4.7 million underage accounts.

chunks.text: How do teenagers stay online? The country's [[internet regulator]] found that about half of the children who kept their accounts were never even asked to [[prove]] their age. Others simply {{signed up}} again with a false [[date of birth]], or used [[tricks]] to {{get around}} the [[age checks]]. Some fooled [[face scans]] with photos of older people. One teenager said a friend passed the scan using a printed photo of a famous singer. Still others {{switched over}} to smaller apps that the law does not cover.

verbs.correct: To join a service with your details
verbs.wrong: To pay a monthly service fee
verbs.why: People sign up for gym memberships, newsletters, and free trials. Many teens just signed up again with a false date of birth.

verbs.correct: To avoid a rule in a clever way
verbs.wrong: To read a rule very carefully
verbs.why: Drivers get around tolls by taking back roads, and kids get around bedtime rules by pretending to be asleep. Teens found many ways to get around the age checks.

verbs.correct: To change to a different service
verbs.wrong: To pay for a premium version
verbs.why: Families switch over to cheaper phone plans, and viewers switch over to another channel. Some teens switched over to apps the law does not cover.

chunks.text: The numbers are [[hard to argue with]]. Before the ban, 86 percent of Australian children under 16 used social media. Three months after it began, the [[figure]] was 81 percent, and daily use had [[barely]] moved, from about 60 percent to 58 percent. Many teenagers who left at first have {{come back}}, and news reports in August 2026 said most under-16s use the apps just as often as before the ban. Only a small number have truly {{given up}} their accounts. Kids who {{slip through}} the checks [[rarely]] get caught, because the platforms hardly ever {{follow up}}.

verbs.correct: To return after leaving
verbs.wrong: To warn a younger friend
verbs.why: Customers come back to a store they like, and birds come back every spring. Many teens who left the apps in December have quietly come back.

verbs.correct: To stop having something
verbs.wrong: To hide something from parents
verbs.why: People give up sugar, old habits, and gym memberships. Only a small number of teens have truly given up their accounts.

verbs.correct: To pass a check without being caught
verbs.wrong: To report a problem to a website
verbs.why: Small mistakes can slip through an inspection, and a broken part can slip through the final test at a factory. Kids who slip through the age checks rarely get caught, because platforms check very little.

verbs.correct: To check again after a first action
verbs.wrong: To block an account permanently
verbs.why: Doctors follow up with patients after surgery, and sellers follow up on unpaid bills. Kids who slip through the age checks rarely get caught, because the platforms hardly ever follow up.

chunks.text: The government is not ready to {{back down}}. [[Ministers]] point to the millions of closed accounts and say the law has changed how families talk about phones. [[Officials]] compare it to [[age limits]] on alcohol: nobody expects perfect [[compliance]], but the rule still matters. The regulator wants platforms to {{crack down}} with stronger age checks, and companies that fail to act may face heavy [[fines]]. Meanwhile, in living rooms across Australia, teenagers quietly {{log on}}, and the world watches an [[experiment]] that many other countries want to copy.

verbs.correct: To change your mind under pressure
verbs.wrong: To announce a bigger new plan
verbs.why: A boss can back down after workers protest, and a country can back down in a trade fight. Australia's government refuses to back down on the ban.

verbs.correct: To get tough on rule breaking
verbs.wrong: To ask users for their opinions
verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding, and schools crack down on cheating. The regulator wants platforms to crack down with stronger age checks.

verbs.correct: To enter an online account
verbs.wrong: To charge a phone overnight
verbs.why: Workers log on every morning, and students log on for online classes. Across Australia, teenagers quietly log on despite the ban.

mainIdea.s: Months after the world's first under-16 social media ban, most young Australians are still online and use the apps as often as before. The government wants stronger age checks.

stories.headline: The Gen Z stare: rude, honest, or just misunderstood?

sources.title: The Gen Z Pout and the Gen Z Stare are both a warning to CEOs (Fortune)
The 'Gen Z Stare' Is Real - Here's What's Underneath It at Work (Forbes)
Gen Z stare: Why young workers are giving blank looks and going viral (ABC News)
Millennials poke fun at Gen Z over so-called 'Gen Z stare' (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: Walk into a coffee shop and say hello to the young worker at the [[counter]]. Sometimes the answer is a long, silent [[pause]]: no smile, no [[nod]], just a [[blank look]]. The internet named this the [[Gen Z stare]]. The phrase took off online in 2025, and the look is everywhere, from cafes to job interviews. Some workers' faces simply {{freeze up}} for a second before they answer normally. But many older customers say the look {{comes off as}} rude, cold, or even [[hostile]].

verbs.correct: To suddenly be unable to react
verbs.wrong: To become angry very quickly
verbs.why: A nervous speaker can freeze up in front of a crowd, and a driver might freeze up when the car slides on ice. Some young workers' faces freeze up for a second before they answer a simple hello.

verbs.correct: To seem a certain way to people
verbs.wrong: To end earlier than planned
verbs.why: A short reply can come off as cold, and a joke can come off as mean if the timing is wrong. To many older customers, the blank Gen Z stare comes off as rude even when nothing rude is meant.

chunks.text: The stare {{comes up}} in every [[debate]] about the youngest [[generation]] at work. Older coworkers often read it one way: the kids are not listening, or they {{zone out}} from [[boredom]] halfway through a long meeting. Gen Z workers tell a different story. To them, the stare is a choice. They refuse to {{put on}} a [[fake smile]] for every stranger. False friendliness fools nobody, they say, because people {{pick up on}} it in seconds. Why [[perform]] excitement when calm [[honesty]] works fine?

verbs.correct: To be mentioned in a talk
verbs.wrong: To change your opinion slowly
verbs.why: A person's salary can come up at a job interview, and old arguments often come up again during family dinners. The Gen Z stare comes up in almost every debate about young workers at work.

verbs.correct: To stop paying attention
verbs.wrong: To leave a meeting quietly
verbs.why: Students zone out during a long lecture, and drivers can zone out on a boring highway. Older coworkers sometimes assume a blank look shows that a young worker has simply zoned out.

verbs.correct: To wear a false expression
verbs.wrong: To accept something annoying
verbs.why: An actor puts on a brave face for the camera, and a tired host might put on a cheerful voice for guests. Gen Z workers refuse to put on a fake smile just to please a stranger at the counter.

verbs.correct: To notice something not said directly
verbs.wrong: To treat one person unfairly
verbs.why: Kids pick up on tension between parents, and good waiters pick up on what customers need before being asked. Gen Z workers say people pick up on a fake smile within seconds, so they choose not to fake one.

chunks.text: Some researchers offer a gentler explanation. Gen Z was in high school or college when [[pandemic]] lockdowns hit, the years when people learn to talk face to face. Supporters argue a calm face, or even [[silence]], can {{get across}} more than words could: I am listening, and I am not performing. Many young workers {{brush off}} the [[complaints]] as no big deal. But the numbers matter. Gen Z is about 30 percent of the American [[workforce]], yet a 2024 survey found that six in ten companies had avoided hiring a young candidate over worries about [[professionalism]]. New [[graduates]] should take note.

verbs.correct: To make an idea understood
verbs.wrong: To have a friendly relationship
verbs.why: A good teacher can get across a hard idea in one clear sentence, and a smile can get across kindness without a single word. Supporters say a calm, honest face can get across more meaning than forced small talk.

verbs.correct: To treat something as unimportant
verbs.wrong: To improve a skill you had before
verbs.why: An athlete might brush off a small injury before a big game, and a manager can brush off customer feedback without checking it. Many young workers brush off complaints about their blank expression as no big deal.

chunks.text: So what is the answer? Work experts suggest patience on both sides. Bosses and [[managers]] get better results when they {{reach out}} to young [[staff]] with real questions instead of complaints, and when they explain why [[eye contact]] and [[small talk]] still matter in many jobs. The youngest workers may find that a tiny smile costs nothing. And in the end, maybe both sides should just {{lighten up}} and laugh about the whole thing: every generation was once the strange new kid at work, and every generation [[survived]] it.

verbs.correct: To try to connect with someone
verbs.wrong: To give someone a final warning
verbs.why: A school might reach out to worried parents, and an old friend can reach out after years of silence. Managers get better results when they reach out to young staff with real questions instead of complaints.

verbs.correct: To become less serious
verbs.wrong: To work harder than before
verbs.why: A stressed friend might need to lighten up before a big trip, and a strict boss could lighten up during the holidays. Experts suggest both sides just lighten up and laugh about the whole blank stare debate.

vocab.def: To suddenly be unable to react
ex: He froze up when the teacher called his name.

chunks.text: A [[regional]] train {{came off}} the rails in Normandy, in northern France, on Friday evening, September 11. The train had {{set out}} from Rouen and was traveling to Caen. It [[derailed]] near Cléon, in the Seine-Maritime area, at about 7:30 pm. There were 186 passengers [[on board]]. Forty-four people were hurt, roughly one passenger in four. One of them, an 18-year-old woman, was taken to the hospital in [[critical condition]]. The accident happened at the start of the weekend.

The [[public prosecutor]] in Rouen {{pointed out}} that the reason it was there is unknown and still has to be [[established]]. Investigators are {{looking into}} the [[possibility]] that someone put it there [[deliberately]]. They have not {{ruled out}} that idea, but nobody has [[confirmed]] it either. For now, the case remains open, and no cause has been announced.

Caneta inteligente e IA detectam Parkinson com 98% de precisão (Jornal Impresso Brasil / Gazeta Brasil)

chunks.text: Researchers in India say they have {{come up with}} a drawing test that can {{pick up}} signs of Parkinson's disease. It was published in the journal Discover Computing and reported on August 29, 2026. Parkinson's is a [[nerve disease]] that affects movement, and doctors often make a [[diagnosis]] only after clear [[symptoms]] {{show up}}. Handwriting changes can appear earlier, but they are often too [[subtle]] to see with the [[naked eye]].

verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem while doing research
verbs.why: Students come up with excuses for late homework, and cooks come up with new recipes from leftovers. Researchers in India came up with a drawing test that looks for signs of Parkinson's disease.

verbs.correct: To notice something hard to see
verbs.wrong: To confirm a doctor's diagnosis
verbs.why: A careful reader picks up a tiny spelling mistake on a menu, and a good teacher picks up the small signs that a student is lost. The drawing test can pick up signs of Parkinson's that are too subtle to see with the naked eye.

verbs.correct: To appear or become visible
verbs.wrong: To display something with pride
verbs.why: A stain shows up after a shirt dries, and roof problems show up in winter. Doctors often make a Parkinson's diagnosis only after clear symptoms show up, but handwriting changes can appear earlier.

chunks.text: Participants [[trace]] two patterns with a smart pen: a spiral and a meander, a [[zigzag]] line with sharp corners. The pen records the drawing plus [[pressure]], [[tilt]], and acceleration. The team {{broke the analysis down}} into two parts: computer models studied the images, and a separate model studied the pen's [[motion]] data. An algorithm then {{put the two results together}} to {{tell the two groups apart}}, people with Parkinson's and healthy people, using only their drawings.

verbs.correct: To divide something into smaller parts
verbs.wrong: To make an important discovery
verbs.why: A teacher can break a long word down into syllables, and a manager can break a big project down into weekly tasks. The team broke the analysis down into two parts: one model for the images and another for the pen motion data.

verbs.why: A child can put a puzzle together, and a coach can put together a team from new players. An algorithm put the two results together into one final answer for each drawing.

verbs.correct: To see the difference between two groups
verbs.wrong: To sort the results by patient age
verbs.why: It is hard to tell twins apart, and some people cannot tell a real photo apart from a fake one. The goal was to tell people with Parkinson's apart from healthy people using only their drawings.

chunks.text: The study was {{carried out}} with 66 participants: 31 with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people, a [[control group]] from an earlier study in Brazil. The system reached 98.95 percent [[accuracy]] on meander drawings and 97.74 percent on spirals. But a small study does not {{rule out}} mistakes in real life. The researchers called it a [[proof of concept]], not a [[clinically validated]] tool, and said it cannot {{stand in for}} a [[neurological evaluation]]. The results still need to {{hold up}} in larger, more [[diverse]] groups.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of work or research
verbs.wrong: To continue for a longer time
verbs.why: A hospital carries out a survey of its patients, and a mechanic carries out a full check of a car. The study was carried out with 66 participants: 31 with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people.

verbs.correct: To say that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To measure something very carefully
verbs.why: A doctor can rule out a broken bone after an X-ray, and a weather report cannot rule out rain. A strong result in a small study does not rule out mistakes in real life, the researchers warned.

verbs.correct: To take the place of a person or thing
verbs.wrong: To defend a person or an idea in public
verbs.why: A nurse can stand in for a doctor at a meeting, and a substitute teacher stands in for a sick one. The researchers said the drawing test cannot stand in for a neurological evaluation by a doctor.

verbs.correct: To stay true after more testing
verbs.wrong: To keep information secret
verbs.why: A guess about the weather may not hold up once the forecast comes in, and an excuse that sounds fine at first often does not hold up when parents check with the school. The results still need to hold up in larger and more diverse groups of people.

chunks.text: Still, the researchers are hopeful. If the results are {{backed up}} by further studies, a simple drawing task could support [[non-invasive]], low-cost [[screening]] that people could do [[remotely]], far from a hospital. The team plans to {{follow up}} with larger trials before anything can be {{rolled out}} in clinics. For now, the smart pen is a research tool, not a way to {{find out}} whether you have Parkinson's.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in India built a smart pen test that uses computer models to spot Parkinson's signs in drawings. They call it a proof of concept that still needs larger studies.
mainIdea.why: A smart pen records the drawings and the motion data, two computer models study them, and the researchers themselves say the results need to hold up in larger, more diverse groups.

mainIdea.s: A smart pen drawing test has been approved as a reliable way to diagnose Parkinson's disease. Clinics can now use it instead of a full neurological evaluation by a doctor.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers called the test a proof of concept, not a clinically validated tool, and it cannot stand in for a doctor's evaluation.

mainIdea.s: A university in India has developed a wearable wrist sensor that tracks tremors in Parkinson's patients at home. Doctors use the data to adjust medication between hospital visits.
mainIdea.why: The test uses a smart pen and drawings, not a wrist sensor, and there is nothing about adjusting medication.

tf.s: The spiral drawings gave the most accurate results.
tf.why: The meander drawings did slightly better, at 98.95 percent accuracy against 97.74 for the spirals.

tf.s: The study was carried out with just 66 participants.
tf.why: There were 31 people with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people, whose data came from an earlier study in Brazil.

tf.s: The researchers say the test can replace a doctor's evaluation.
tf.why: They said the opposite. It is a proof of concept and cannot stand in for a neurological evaluation.

tf.s: Separate computer models studied the images and the pen motion data.
tf.why: The team broke the analysis down into two parts, and an algorithm then put the two results together into one answer.

tf.s: The team plans to roll out the test in clinics before larger trials.
tf.why: Larger trials come first. Only after that could anything be rolled out in clinics.

tf.s: Doctors often make a diagnosis only after clear symptoms show up.
tf.why: Handwriting changes can appear earlier, but they are often too subtle to see with the naked eye.

Michigan town erupts over proposed AI data center as fight gets political (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: Across the United States, huge AI [[data centers]] are {{springing up}} near small towns, and many residents are {{pushing back}}. A Gallup poll {{carried out}} in March found that 71 percent of Americans oppose building a data center in their area. Almost half, 48 percent, are strongly against the idea. Only 27 percent are [[in favor]]. Opposition is strongest in the Midwest, at 76 percent, and weakest in the West, at 63 percent.

verbs.correct: To appear suddenly in many places
verbs.wrong: To start a company or organization
verbs.why: Coffee shops spring up on every corner of a busy street, and new apps spring up every month. The story says AI data centers are springing up near small towns across the United States.

verbs.correct: To resist or oppose a plan
verbs.wrong: To hire extra workers for a job
verbs.why: Employees push back when a manager wants weekend work, and parents push back against a longer school day. Many residents are pushing back against data centers in their towns.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To keep something for a later time
verbs.why: A mechanic carries out a full check of the car, and a school carries out a fire drill every year. Gallup carried out its poll in March and published it in May.

chunks.text: Why do so many people say no? Half of the [[opponents]] {{bring up}} resource use. Data centers {{eat up}} enormous amounts of electricity and water. Another 22 percent worry about [[quality of life]], and 20 percent fear the cost effects. Fifteen percent expect their own [[utility bills]] to {{go up}}. The [[supporters]] {{weigh up}} the same project differently. Two thirds of them say a data center would help the [[local economy]], and 55 percent expect new jobs.

verbs.correct: To mention a topic in a discussion
verbs.wrong: To cause something to happen
verbs.why: A student brings up a question at the end of class, and a friend brings up an old story at dinner. Half of the opponents bring up resource use when they explain their objections.

verbs.correct: To use a very large amount of something
verbs.wrong: To supply a town with water and power
verbs.why: Video calls eat up a phone's battery, and a long commute eats up two hours of the day. Data centers eat up enormous amounts of electricity and water.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher level or price
verbs.wrong: To check something carefully
verbs.why: Rent goes up every year in big cities, and the temperature goes up in the afternoon. Fifteen percent of opponents expect their own utility bills to go up.

verbs.correct: To think carefully before deciding
verbs.wrong: To make someone feel worried
verbs.why: A buyer weighs up two used cars before choosing, and a student weighs up a job offer against more study. Supporters weigh up the same project and see the local economy first.

chunks.text: The opposition has real effects. In 2025, local [[resistance]] delayed or canceled projects worth 156 billion dollars. In Indiana, one company {{gave up}} a 1.3 billion dollar project after the town council opposed it. In Virginia, a [[planning commission]] {{turned down}} a 12 billion dollar project with a [[unanimous]] vote. In Arizona, a [[developer]] {{pulled out}} of a 14 billion dollar plan after officials blocked a [[rezoning]]. In July alone, residents {{turned out}} for 142 protests across 42 states.

verbs.correct: To stop a plan and not try again
verbs.wrong: To hand something to many people
verbs.why: A runner gives up a race after an injury, and a family gives up the idea of moving abroad. One company gave up a 1.3 billion dollar project in Indiana after the town council opposed it.

verbs.correct: To refuse a request or an offer
verbs.wrong: To give control to someone else
verbs.why: A bank turns down a loan request, and a singer turns down an invitation to a festival. A planning commission in Virginia turned down a 12 billion dollar project.

verbs.correct: To leave a plan or an agreement
verbs.wrong: To attract money or new business
verbs.why: A sponsor pulls out of a tournament, and a buyer pulls out of a house deal at the last minute. In Arizona, a developer pulled out of a 14 billion dollar plan.

verbs.correct: To go somewhere to join an event
verbs.wrong: To refuse to let someone enter
verbs.why: Thousands of fans turn out for a parade, and neighbors turn out for a street cleanup. Residents turned out for 142 protests across 42 states in July.

chunks.text: Some state governments are now {{stepping in}}. On July 14, New York {{brought in}} the first [[statewide]] [[moratorium]]. It covers any [[facility]] that would use 50 [[megawatts]] or more. Texas announced its own pause on August 10. Maine's [[legislature]] passed a moratorium in April, but the state's governor [[vetoed]] it. The industry still promises jobs and [[tax revenue]]. Yet residents keep {{speaking out}}, and the fight is far from over.

chunks.text: Apple {{showed off}} its first [[folding phone]] on September 9, 2026. The [[device]] is called the iPhone Duo, and it opens like a small book. When it is {{folded up}}, the [[outer]] screen measures 5.4 inches. When the phone {{folds out}}, a larger 7.6-inch screen appears on the inside. The company {{laid out}} the prices and dates at the same event. The Duo [[starts at]] 1,999 dollars. Apple has never sold a folding phone before, so the Duo is a new [[category]] for the company.

The company says the phone {{holds up}} better [[over time]], keeping 35 percent more [[performance]] than the iPhone 17 Pro. [[Battery life]] depends on how the phone is used. On the front screen alone, it can play up to 31 hours of video before the battery {{runs out}}. When both screens are used [[equally]], that [[figure]] drops to 24 hours.

chunks.text: Twenty-five years have {{gone by}} since the attacks of September 11, 2001, in which 2,977 people were killed. On the [[anniversary]], families {{came together}} at the [[memorial plaza]] in New York City for the main [[ceremony]]. The plaza stands on the [[site]] of the [[former]] World Trade Center. Most of the people who died were killed there. The ceremony was not open to the [[general public]]. Only families, [[rescue workers]] and [[invited guests]] were {{let in}}.

The reading {{went on}} for several hours. When the name of their own [[relative]] {{came up}}, some families added a few words of their own. Every name was said [[aloud]]. For the families, the morning was a time to {{look back on}} the day they lost someone they loved.

chunks.text: Seven [[moments of silence]] marked the morning. The first came at 8:46, the minute the first plane [[struck]] the north tower. At 9:03 the plaza fell quiet a second time, for the moment the second plane struck the south tower. The third, at 9:37, was for the plane that struck the Pentagon. The south tower fell at 9:59. Then came 10:03, when a plane {{came down}} in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The sixth was for 10:28, when the north tower fell.

Ceremonies were also [[held]] at the Pentagon and at the Shanksville site. There, too, people came to remember. chunks.text: Gen Z spent summer 2026 "joymaxxing," says a [[research firm]] that studies young [[consumers]]. The word describes young people who {{set out}} to find more happiness in [[ordinary life]]. The firm's August 20 report says they {{cut back on}} [[screen time]], {{showed up}} at events [[in person]], and spent more time {{hanging out}} with friends face to face. Instead of recording every moment for social media, they chose to be [[present]].

verbs.correct: To begin with a clear goal
verbs.wrong: To save time for a purpose
verbs.why: A runner sets out to finish a marathon, and a small company sets out to win new customers. The research firm says young people set out this summer to find more happiness in ordinary life.

verbs.correct: To use less of something
verbs.wrong: To lose contact with someone
verbs.why: Many families cut back on eating out to save money. A city cuts back on water use in a dry summer. The report says Gen Z cut back on screen time and spent more time offline.

verbs.correct: To be present at an event
verbs.wrong: To try to impress other people
verbs.why: Only half the class shows up for the early lecture. The whole town shows up for the summer parade. According to the research firm, Gen Z showed up at events in person instead of only watching online.

verbs.correct: To spend relaxed time together
verbs.wrong: To wait for a short time
verbs.why: Teenagers hang out at the mall after school, and coworkers sometimes hang out at a cafe on Friday. The report says young people spent more of the summer hanging out with friends face to face.

chunks.text: The report {{fits in with}} other [[findings]] this year. A 2025 [[survey]] by a polling company found 47 percent of Americans under 30 were trying to reduce screen time. In a Talker Research survey from December 2025, 63 percent of Gen Z said they [[intentionally]] {{put away}} their phones, against 29 percent of [[baby boomers]]. Nearly half of teenagers tell Pew Research that social media has a mostly [[negative effect]] on them. The numbers {{add up to}} a clear pattern.

verbs.correct: To match other information
verbs.wrong: To give someone the details
verbs.why: The new evidence fits in with the witness's story. Her test results fit in with what the doctor expected. The youth research report fits in with other survey findings from this year.

verbs.correct: To stop using something for a while
verbs.wrong: To delay something until later
verbs.why: Children put away their toys before bed, and a teacher asks students to put away their books before a test. In one survey, 63 percent of Gen Z said they intentionally put away their phones.

verbs.correct: To combine to make a result
verbs.wrong: To include something as an extra
verbs.why: Small daily savings add up to a nice vacation, and a few late nights add up to a very tired week. Taken together, the survey numbers add up to a clear pattern of young people using their phones less.

chunks.text: Businesses have {{picked up on}} the change. A news site reported in April 2026 that restaurants and bars in at least 11 states now limit phones or [[reward]] customers who leave them alone. A bar in North Carolina locks phones in [[pouches]] for two hours, and one fast-food chain's restaurants {{hand out}} free ice cream to phone-free diners. The Offline Club, a group that {{puts on}} phone-free [[gatherings]], began in Amsterdam in 2021 and now runs events in 19 cities.

verbs.correct: To notice something new
verbs.wrong: To make a rule about something
verbs.why: A good teacher picks up on a student's confusion, and a store quickly picks up on what shoppers want. Businesses have picked up on the change and now offer phone-free dining.

verbs.correct: To give something to many people
verbs.wrong: To give control to another person
verbs.why: Volunteers hand out water at a race, and a teacher hands out the test papers. Some restaurants in a fast-food chain hand out free ice cream to customers who eat without their phones.

verbs.correct: To organize an event
verbs.wrong: To let someone stay overnight
verbs.why: The school puts on a play every spring, and the city puts on a fireworks show in July. The Offline Club puts on phone-free gatherings in 19 cities.

chunks.text: The trend {{grew out of}} years of worry about [[heavy]] phone use. A [[psychology professor]] at Georgetown University told a news site that interest in phone-free spaces has become "a huge thing." It does not mean {{giving up}} phones completely: The Offline Club has nearly 600,000 Instagram [[followers]]. But rather than wait for life to improve, the research firm says, Gen Z is choosing to {{slow down}} and enjoy what is [[within reach]].

chunks.text: The Korea University researcher who presented the study {{went through}} data from a national [[health survey]] of 40,727 South Korean adults from 2016 to 2023. Catch-up sleep was the difference between weekend and weekday [[sleep duration]]. Weekend catch-up sleep was linked to 6 percent lower odds of high blood pressure. The benefit {{went up}} to 6.9 percent among [[physically inactive]] adults. The [[ideal]] amount {{came to}} 1 hour 27 minutes, with 9 percent lower odds.

chunks.text: Blood pressure normally {{goes down}} during sleep, but too little sleep can reduce that [[nightly drop]], said a sleep scientist at the University of Utah. The researcher said a [[lack of sleep]] keeps the heart and [[blood vessels]] working harder, and weekend sleep may help the body [[recover]]. But she {{pointed out}} that more is not always better. People who slept more than four extra hours had a higher risk, because an [[irregular schedule]] may {{cancel out}} the benefit.

chunks.text: Experts still advise people to {{stick to}} a regular [[bedtime]] and [[wake-up time]]. The study is not a [[green light]] to {{cut back on}} exercise, the cardiologist said, but people need not feel [[guilty]] about sleeping late on weekends. mainIdea.s: A large South Korean study linked a moderate amount of extra weekend sleep to lower odds of high blood pressure. Sleeping more than four extra hours, however, was tied to a higher risk.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that the more extra sleep people got on weekends, the less likely they were to have high blood pressure. Experts now say a regular bedtime no longer matters for the heart.

mainIdea.s: A survey of shift workers found that people who sleep during the day have higher blood pressure than day workers. Doctors say night shifts should be limited to protect the heart of every worker.
mainIdea.why: The study looked at extra weekend sleep among adults in general, not at shift workers or daytime sleep.

stories.headline: UN votes for a map that shows Africa at its true size

chunks.text: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday, September 4, 2026, to encourage the world to {{move away from}} the [[traditional]] Mercator map. Togo {{put forward}} the [[resolution]] on behalf of the African Group, with the [[backing]] of the African Union. It {{went through}} with 164 votes [[in favor]]. The United States was the only country to vote against it, and six countries, including Ukraine and Serbia, [[abstained]].

chunks.text: The Mercator map {{dates back}} to 1569, when a Flemish [[mapmaker]] named Mercator designed it for sailors. On his map, a straight line matches a fixed [[compass direction]], so [[navigators]] could {{map out}} a course along one straight line. The price was size. The map {{blows up}} [[landmasses]] near the [[poles]], so Greenland {{comes across as}} roughly the same size as Africa, although Africa is about 14 times larger.

verbs.wrong: To be replaced by a newer version

verbs.wrong: To agree after some time
verbs.why: A quiet person can come across as unfriendly, and a short email can come across as rude. On the Mercator map, Greenland comes across as roughly the same size as Africa.

chunks.text: The Equal Earth [[projection]] is much newer. A former [[senior cartographer]] at the U.S. National Park Service {{came up with}} it in 2018 with two colleagues. It shows continents in their [[true proportions]], though shapes are slightly [[distorted]]. The resolution {{calls on}} governments, schools, international organizations and technology companies to use Equal Earth and similar maps when [[relative size]] matters. It is not [[binding]]. It does not ban Mercator and does not {{rule out}} its use for sea and air navigation.

verbs.why: A school can rule out phones during exams, and a landlord can rule out pets in an apartment. The resolution does not rule out the use of Mercator for sea and air navigation.

chunks.text: Togo's [[foreign minister]] said, "Maps shape our understanding of the world." The United States {{spoke out against}} the resolution, calling it part of an [[ideological]] project. Ukraine raised concerns about how [[occupied territory]] would appear, and the European Union said the vote had no [[bearing]] on borders. France said it would {{switch over to}} Equal Earth for its world maps. Africa No Filter, a campaign group, wants accurate maps {{rolled out}} in schools, textbooks and news organizations.

mainIdea.s: The UN General Assembly voted to encourage the Equal Earth map instead of the Mercator map, which makes Africa look much smaller than it is. The vote is a recommendation, not a ban.

chunks.text: A new AI system can {{pick up}} signs of a heart disease after seeing only about [[a dozen]] [[confirmed cases]], researchers at Scripps Research in California say. The study on the system {{came out}} in The Lancet Digital Health on September 1, 2026. To build it, the team {{put together}} more than 1.7 million [[electrocardiograms]], recordings of the heart's electrical activity, from more than 540,000 people, along with doctors' notes about each one.

verbs.why: A dog picks up a scent from far away. A good nurse often picks up a fever before the patient feels sick. The new AI system can pick up signs of a heart disease after seeing only about a dozen confirmed cases.

chunks.text: The system is a [[foundation model]], an AI that first learns general knowledge and is then [[adapted]] to many tasks. It learned which words in a doctor's note {{go with}} which patterns in a heart recording. The study's senior author said a [[clinician]] learns the same way: not from a million examples, but by understanding the heart first and then seeing a few cases. The model {{builds up}} a [[general picture]] before it {{zeroes in on}} one disease.

chunks.text: The researchers {{tried out}} the model on more than 800,000 heart recordings. It {{kept up with}} the best models while using about 91 percent less [[hand-labeled]] data on average. It detected [[heart attacks]] and two other heart conditions, and it beat other models at predicting an [[irregular heartbeat]] from recordings that looked normal. It also predicted who would develop [[kidney disease]] or type 2 diabetes within three years. The [[advantage]] {{fell away}} once many labeled examples were available.

mainIdea.s: Researchers built an AI model that learned from 1.7 million heart recordings and doctors' notes. It can now recognize a heart disease from about a dozen examples, which could help with rare diseases.

stories.headline: Study: most online creators earn less than you think

sources.title: A 67% Majority of Creators Earn Less Than $10,000 per Year, Study Finds (TheWrap)
CreatorIQ Study Reveals a Growing Authenticity Gap (CreatorIQ)
67% Of Creators Earn Under $10,000 A Year While Pay Still Favors Reach, Study Finds (NetInfluencer)

chunks.text: Being an online [[creator]] looks like a [[dream job]]. But a large study says the money is much smaller than most fans imagine. A 2026 report on the creator industry [[surveyed]] 5,095 creators in around 100 [[regions]]. Two thirds, or 67 percent, said their videos and posts {{bring in}} less than ten thousand dollars a year. Six in ten do not {{get by}} on online money alone, because it is not their main income. Many {{turn to}} other jobs to pay the [[bills]].

verbs.correct: To earn money for a person or business
verbs.wrong: To mention a subject in a video
verbs.why: A weekend market stall brings in a few hundred dollars, a spare room for rent brings in steady cash each month, and a good year brings in extra profit. In this study, two out of three creators said their videos and posts bring in less than ten thousand dollars a year.

verbs.correct: To survive with just enough money
verbs.wrong: To save money for the future
verbs.why: Families get by on one salary, students get by on canned soup, and retirees get by on a small pension. In this study, six out of ten creators do not get by on online money alone, because it is not their main income.

verbs.correct: To use something as a source of help
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer politely
verbs.why: People turn to friends for advice, turn to a lawyer for help, or turn to prayer in hard times. Many creators in this study turn to other jobs to pay their bills when online money is not enough.

chunks.text: The study also shows how hard the work is. Creators often spend years {{building up}} a [[following]] from zero. They must {{keep up with}} new [[trends]], new apps, and [[constant]] posting [[schedules]]. And with so many [[channels]] online, it is hard to {{stand out}} in a crowded [[feed]]. The report found that pay follows size: creators with more [[followers]] and views earn more, and comments and likes from fans matter less for pay than the size of the audience.

verbs.correct: To grow something slowly over time
verbs.wrong: To repair something old and broken
verbs.why: Runners build up strength week by week, savers build up a bank account, and companies build up a reputation over time. Creators in this study often spend years building up a following that started at zero.

verbs.correct: To stay current with changes
verbs.wrong: To watch something from far away
verbs.why: Workers keep up with new technology, drivers keep up with changing traffic rules, and fans keep up with the latest news. Creators in this study must keep up with new trends, new apps, and constant posting schedules.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.wrong: To represent an idea or a brand
verbs.why: A bright red coat can stand out in a crowd, and one strong answer can stand out on a job application. With so many channels online, it is hard for any single creator to stand out in a crowded feed.

chunks.text: So who actually makes money? Only a small group at the top. Almost every big name {{started out}} small, with few fans and years of low pay. The winners often {{cash in on}} their [[fame]] by selling their own products: about half of the creators in the study have [[launched]] their own [[brand]] or plan to start one. [[Top earners]] do most of their paid posts for companies on Instagram, with TikTok in second place. But many others {{give up}} and go back to [[full-time]] jobs when the money stays small.

verbs.correct: To begin a career or journey
verbs.wrong: To begin again after failing
verbs.why: Many chefs start out washing dishes, and many companies start out in a garage with little money. The study found that almost every famous creator started out small, with only a few fans and years of low pay.

verbs.correct: To make money from a success
verbs.wrong: To pay money to get more fans
verbs.why: Stores cash in on holiday shopping, and singers sometimes cash in on a hit song with a world tour. The most successful creators in this study cash in on their fame by launching their own brand of products.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To distribute things to a crowd
verbs.why: People give up on a diet after one bad week, and some students give up on a hard class too soon. Many creators in this study give up and return to full-time jobs once the money stays small.

chunks.text: The lesson is simple: treat creating like a slow business, not a [[lottery ticket]]. Successful creators earn from many places, like [[ads]], [[tips]], and product sales, and the small numbers {{add up}} month after month. For a [[patient]] few, the years of work finally {{pay off}} with a real [[career]]. The study found one more problem: 42 percent of creators say the posts companies pay for are not the posts their fans want to see. That can put their fans' [[trust]] at risk. Even in a dream job, nothing is free.

verbs.correct: To slowly become a large amount
verbs.wrong: To disappear little by little
verbs.why: Small daily coffee purchases add up fast, and minutes of daily practice add up to real skill over a year. For patient creators, small payments from ads, tips, and sales add up month after month into a real income.

verbs.correct: To bring success after hard work
verbs.wrong: To give money to many people
verbs.why: Years of studying can pay off on exam day, and early morning practice can pay off at the big game. The article says that for a patient few, years of effort finally pay off with a real, lasting career.

stories.headline: New York City bans AI tools for younger students

sources.title: AI banned for elementary and middle school students in NYC (AP News)
NYC to ban student AI tools in 2-K through 8th grade and limit classroom screen time (Chalkbeat)
Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation's Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools (NYC Mayor's Office)
New York, Los Angeles Restrict Student AI Use. Will Other Districts Follow? (Education Week)
Mamdani announces ban on AI for young students in NYC public schools (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: New York City's public schools will not let elementary and middle school students use generative AI tools this year. The mayor {{laid out}} the plan on September 2, 2026, eight days before students {{head back}} to class. The one-year [[moratorium]] covers all student-facing AI software from 2-K through eighth grade, nearly 600,000 students, which the mayor's office called the broadest ban in the country. It is also {{cracking down on}} [[AI companion apps]] in every grade.

verbs.correct: To explain a plan in detail
verbs.wrong: To end a worker's job
verbs.why: A coach lays out the game plan before the match, and a travel agent lays out the whole trip day by day. The city's mayor laid out the new AI plan for the schools on September 2, 2026.

verbs.correct: To return to a place
verbs.wrong: To stop a problem early
verbs.why: After lunch, the workers head back to the office, and the family heads back home when the beach gets too hot. New York City students head back to class on September 10, eight days after the announcement.

verbs.correct: To take strict action against something
verbs.wrong: To begin to fail under pressure
verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding drivers near schools. Many stores crack down on shoplifting before the holidays. New York City is cracking down on AI companion apps, which are now banned in every grade.

chunks.text: The city also wants younger students to {{cut down on}} [[screen time]], recommending a daily [[cap]] of 30 minutes on [[individual devices]] for grades three through five and 45 minutes for grades six through eight, and no individual devices before third grade. Officials will {{turn off}} AI features in about 38 [[education tools]] and {{phase out}} technology that is not [[essential]] to learning. Teachers may still use AI for [[lesson planning]], but not [[grading]].

verbs.correct: To use less of something
verbs.wrong: To remove something completely
verbs.why: Many people cut down on salt for their heart. Families cut down on driving when gas prices rise. The city wants younger students to cut down on screen time, with a recommended daily cap of 30 or 45 minutes.

verbs.correct: To make a feature stop working
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: Many people turn off phone notifications at night. Parents turn off automatic downloads on the family tablet. Officials will turn off the AI features in about 38 education tools the schools already use.

verbs.correct: To stop using something gradually
verbs.wrong: To test something before wide use
verbs.why: The airline phases out its oldest planes over ten years. Many stores phase out plastic bags slowly. The city will phase out any technology in its schools that is not essential to learning.

chunks.text: For high school, the city will {{roll out}} two 45-minute [[AI literacy]] classes a year for every high schooler, and up to 50,000 students can {{try out}} five approved AI programs under a teacher's [[supervision]]. Supporters {{weighed in}} quickly. New York's governor [[commended]] the plan, and the head of the teachers' union welcomed the screen-time limits. The mayor said children need teachers and human [[connection]] to learn.

verbs.correct: To introduce something new widely
verbs.wrong: To cancel a rule or decision
verbs.why: The bank rolls out a new app to all its customers. The city rolls out electric buses on a few routes each year. New York City will roll out two AI literacy classes a year for every high school student.

verbs.correct: To test something to see how it works
verbs.wrong: To ask for permission to use something
verbs.why: Shoppers try out several cameras before they buy one. Restaurants try out new dishes on a small menu first. Up to 50,000 high school students can try out five approved AI programs under a teacher's supervision.

verbs.correct: To give an opinion on an issue
verbs.wrong: To compare two choices carefully
verbs.why: Doctors often weigh in on new diets. Neighbors weigh in on plans for the local park. Supporters weighed in quickly, including the governor and the president of the teachers' union.

chunks.text: The union leader also {{pointed out}} [[gaps]]: many questions remain [[unanswered]], and schools must {{figure out}} [[after the fact]] whether their tools fit the rules. A children's advocacy group said one year is not enough time to [[evaluate]]. An education researcher warned that poorer students could {{miss out on}} technology wealthier families have. The mayor said he trusts teachers and principals to [[enforce]] the policy. A new [[coalition]] of students, parents and educators will {{look into}} the effects and publish [[recommendations]] by the end of the school year.

verbs.why: A tour guide points out the oldest building on the street. Good editors point out mistakes in a report. Critics pointed out gaps in the policy, such as how schools will enforce it.

chunks.text: On September 3, 2026, Argentine President Javier Milei {{stepped up}} his country's claim to the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, in a [[nationally televised address]]. He said he would {{speed up}} [[sanctions]] against companies working on the Sea Lion [[offshore]] oil project, about 220 kilometers north of the islands, and {{go after}} their [[suppliers]], [[shareholders]], and directors. He also promised extra funding for a [[naval base]] in the far south of Argentina.

verbs.correct: To increase the force of something
verbs.wrong: To leave a top political job
verbs.why: A city steps up security before a big game, and a store steps up its advertising before the holidays. On September 3, 2026, President Javier Milei stepped up Argentina's claim to the Falkland Islands in a nationally televised address.

verbs.correct: To make something happen faster
verbs.wrong: To put something to a vote
verbs.why: A new road speeds up the trip to the airport. A second cook speeds up service in a busy restaurant. Milei said he would speed up sanctions against companies working on the Sea Lion oil project.

verbs.correct: To try to punish or catch someone
verbs.wrong: To agree to support a plan
verbs.why: Police go after the people who plan a robbery, and a tax office goes after companies that hide income. Milei said Argentina would also go after the project's suppliers, shareholders, and directors.

chunks.text: Milei said he would send Congress a [[bill]] to {{crack down on}} [[unauthorized]] activity near the islands and {{shut out}} the companies involved from doing business in Argentina. "Argentina will not stand idly by," he said, calling any further advance there a threat to [[national security]]. A British company and an Israeli company, which run Sea Lion, plan to {{press ahead}} with drilling this year and {{pump out}} oil from 2028. The British firm's shares fell 6 percent, but both say their [[licenses]] are valid.

verbs.correct: To punish something more strictly
verbs.wrong: To surrender a claim to land
verbs.why: Many cities crack down on illegal parking downtown. Schools crack down on cheating during exams. Milei said he would send Congress a bill to crack down on unauthorized activity near the islands.

verbs.correct: To stop someone from taking part
verbs.wrong: To close a business for good
verbs.why: A club shuts out members who do not pay. Some countries shut out foreign banks from their markets. The bill would shut out the companies involved in the oil project from doing business in Argentina.

verbs.correct: To continue with a plan anyway
verbs.wrong: To ask strongly for something
verbs.why: A builder presses ahead with a project despite the rain, and a student presses ahead with her studies after a bad grade. The British and Israeli companies plan to press ahead with drilling this year.

verbs.correct: To produce large amounts of something
verbs.wrong: To ship oil to another country
verbs.why: A factory pumps out thousands of shoes a day. A busy studio pumps out a new song every week. The companies hope to pump out oil from the Sea Lion field from 2028.

chunks.text: Britain {{hit back}} quickly. Britain's [[defense secretary]] said the islands are British because the islanders choose to be British, and Britain's [[commitment]] to them is "absolute and unshakeable." Britain's foreign secretary said the islanders' right to [[self-determination]] is [[paramount]]. Britain {{backs up}} its position with a 2013 [[referendum]], when about 4,000 islanders voted [[overwhelmingly]] to remain a British [[overseas territory]]. The defense secretary {{played down}} the speech as "domestic politics in Argentina."

verbs.correct: To reply strongly to an attack
verbs.wrong: To reach an agreement quickly
verbs.why: A singer hits back at critics on social media, and a coach hits back when reporters question his team. Britain hit back quickly after Milei's address, saying the islands are British.

verbs.correct: To support with evidence
verbs.wrong: To hold a public vote on something
verbs.why: A lawyer backs up her case with documents, and a scientist backs up a claim with data. Britain backs up its position with a 2013 referendum in which about 4,000 islanders voted to stay British.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To pretend to agree with someone
verbs.why: A company plays down a small data leak, and a runner plays down an injury before a race. Britain's defense secretary played down Milei's speech, saying it reflected domestic politics in Argentina.

chunks.text: The dispute {{dates back}} decades. A 74-day war in 1982 killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British [[service members]], and three islanders. Milei also {{brought up}} U.S. President Donald Trump's comment on August 31 that he was reviewing the [[neutral]] U.S. position. [[Opposition lawmakers]] accused Milei of using the issue to {{shore up}} support before next year's election. Neither government has {{backed down}}, but Argentina has not announced any [[military operation]].

verbs.why: The old church dates back to the 1600s, and their friendship dates back to college. The dispute over the islands dates back decades, to the 1982 war and before.

chunks.text: A [[flash flood]] {{swept through}} Bright Angel Canyon, in Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, on Saturday, August 29, 2026. Up to an inch of rain fell in about 30 minutes. The water {{tore down}} nearly all the [[footbridges]] over Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch, a [[stopover]] for hikers and river [[rafters]]. Rain also fell on the [[burn scar]] of the Dragon Bravo Fire of July 2025, where bare ground {{speeds up}} [[runoff]].

stories.headline: Corals show El Niño is now 40 percent stronger

El Niños more intense over last 40 years than previous 1,000, according to U-M study (University of Michigan News)

chunks.text: El Niño is a natural [[climate pattern]] where part of the Pacific Ocean {{heats up}} every few years, changing weather worldwide. Researchers led by Julia Cole of the University of Michigan found that El Niño events of the last 40 years were about 40 percent stronger than in the [[preindustrial era]], and stronger than any in a [[record]] that {{goes back}} roughly 1,000 years. The study {{came out}} in the [[journal]] Science on August 27, 2026.

verbs.correct: To become warmer
verbs.wrong: To rise to the surface
verbs.why: A parked car heats up fast in the summer sun, and a kitchen heats up when the oven is on. El Niño happens when part of the Pacific Ocean heats up every few years, changing weather around the world.

verbs.correct: To reach far into the past
verbs.wrong: To check something carefully
verbs.why: A family's story can go back five generations, and some town records go back hundreds of years. The coral record in this study goes back roughly 1,000 years, and recent El Niño events are stronger than anything in it.

verbs.correct: To be published
verbs.wrong: To happen by chance
verbs.why: A new phone comes out every fall, and a popular book can come out in twenty languages. This study came out in the journal Science on August 27, 2026.

chunks.text: The team {{carried out}} a study of 13 Galápagos corals, including living corals and ancient [[boulders]]. Corals {{build up}} [[growth bands]] over time, like tree rings. They drilled [[cores]] and measured [[chemical signals]] in the skeleton that change with water temperature. From these they {{worked out}} [[sea-surface temperatures]] for the last 1,000 years. They then compared the results with [[climate models]] of natural causes, such as [[volcanic eruptions]] and changes in the sun, to {{rule out}} those explanations.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of research or work
verbs.wrong: To continue doing the same thing
verbs.why: A hospital can carry out a survey of its patients, and a mechanic carries out a full check of a car. The team carried out a study of 13 corals from the Galápagos Islands, including living corals and ancient coral boulders.

verbs.correct: To form slowly in layers over time
verbs.wrong: To be the parts that form a whole
verbs.why: Dust builds up on a shelf nobody cleans, and ice builds up on a plane's wings in cold weather. Corals build up growth bands over time, much like the rings of a tree.

verbs.correct: To calculate something from evidence
verbs.wrong: To describe results in a formal report
verbs.why: A detective works out who was in the room from a few clues, and a shopper works out the total before reaching the register. The researchers worked out sea-surface temperatures for the last 1,000 years from chemical signals in the coral skeletons.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not the cause
verbs.wrong: To choose one thing for special study
verbs.why: A doctor can rule out an infection with a simple test, and police rule out a suspect who was out of town. The team compared its results with climate models to rule out volcanic eruptions and changes in the sun as the cause.

chunks.text: In the 1,000-year record, the strongest recent events {{stand out}}. "This is such a clear story," Cole said. "The big El Niño events of the last 40 years are not normal in the context of the last thousand years." The rise in [[intensity]] {{lines up with}} global warming since the [[widespread]] use of [[fossil fuels]] began in the 1800s. Since natural causes cannot explain it, the change {{comes down to}} human-caused warming, they say. Several other universities took part.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different from the rest
verbs.wrong: To give the same result when tested again
verbs.why: A red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one great player stands out on a weak team. In the 1,000-year record, the strongest recent El Niño events stand out clearly.

verbs.correct: To match something closely
verbs.wrong: To be as good as expected
verbs.why: A witness's story should line up with the video, and a receipt should line up with what you actually bought. The rise in El Niño intensity lines up with the rise in global temperatures since fossil fuel use began in the 19th century.

verbs.correct: To have something as the real cause
verbs.wrong: To become sick with an illness
verbs.why: A close game often comes down to one last shot, and a hard choice usually comes down to money. With natural causes ruled out, the researchers say the change comes down to human-caused warming.

chunks.text: Stronger El Niño events can {{set off}} [[droughts]], floods, and [[wildfires]] worldwide. They are also linked to [[food insecurity]], damage to homes and roads, and conditions in which diseases such as cholera {{break out}}. They could also cause [[lasting shifts]] in major [[ecosystems]] such as the Amazon rainforest. Meanwhile, global temperatures are on a path that could {{end up}} 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.

verbs.why: A piece of burnt toast can set off a smoke alarm, and one rumor can set off a panic. Stronger El Niño events can set off droughts, floods, and wildfires in different parts of the world.

verbs.why: A fire can break out in an old kitchen, and a fight can break out at a crowded game. Strong El Niño events create conditions in which diseases such as cholera break out.

verbs.wrong: To stop rising and stay the same
verbs.why: A late train can end up an hour behind schedule, and a small loan can end up costing twice its size. Global average temperatures are on a path that could end up 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.

chunks.text: London Waterloo, one of Britain's busiest train stations, has {{taken on}} three team members with four legs. Since August 2026, three trained dogs have been [[on duty]] with the station's security team. South Western Railway (SWR) and Network Rail Wessex {{teamed up with}} Alpha Canine Specialists to {{bring in}} the dogs. Waterloo is {{trying out}} the idea in a three-month [[trial]], and officials say it is the first major British station with regular dog [[patrols]].

lines.text: Did you see that Waterloo station has {{taken on}} three dogs for its security team?
Dogs? On patrol in a train station? [[That's a first]].
It actually is. Officials say it's the first major station in Britain with regular dog patrols. The railway {{teamed up with}} a dog company to {{bring them in}}.
What kind of dogs are we talking about?
Two Cocker Spaniels and a Labrador. They {{stand out}} in a crowd, which is the whole point. Anyone looking for trouble can see the station is well protected.
And the passengers?
That's the other half. The dogs {{help out}} the security staff, and they {{look after}} passengers too. [[The best of both worlds]], really.
[[Don't tell me]] something happened there.
Nothing like that. The railway said it's not linked to any new threat. They're just {{trying it out}} for three months.
And after that?
The dogs retire. They're nine, ten and eleven years old, so they're {{winding down}}. Waterloo is their last job.
[[Going out on a high]], then. Anything else new at the station?

They've {{set up}} better cameras, and the staff wear bright vests so you can {{pick them out}} in a crowd. There's also an outreach worker who will {{reach out to}} young people and {{look out for}} anyone in trouble.
That's [[a lot on their plate]]. Can they {{keep up}} with all of it?
They've had the top safety score three years in a row, so I'd say yes.

stories.headline: Lionel Messi retires from Argentina's national team

Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina national team
Jorge Messi, the father of Lionel, dies at 68

chunks.text: Lionel Messi has {{hung up}} his boots for Argentina's [[national team]]. He announced his [[retirement]] on Monday, August 31, after 20 years. He wrote the letter on July 21, two days after Argentina lost the World Cup [[final]] to Spain, 1-0 in [[extra time]]. He {{held off}} on publishing it because his father and [[longtime agent]], Jorge Messi, was [[seriously ill]]. His father {{passed away}} on August 8 at age 68, after a long [[illness]]. Messi said his father's death made him "even more [[convinced]]" the decision was right.

verbs.correct: To retire from a sport
verbs.wrong: To score late in a game
verbs.why: A goalkeeper hangs up her gloves after 15 long seasons. Many boxers hang up their gloves after one last fight. Messi has hung up his boots for Argentina's national team after 20 years.

verbs.correct: To delay doing something
verbs.wrong: To keep a secret from family

verbs.correct: To die, said in a gentle way

chunks.text: Messi did not hide how hard the choice was. "It was a decision that hurt and hurts in a soul, but I understand that this is the moment," he wrote. He said he had "nothing left to give the national [[squad]]," and that a [[talented]] younger [[generation]] [[deserved]] the chance to play. For him, it is time to {{hand over}} the team and {{move on}}.

verbs.correct: To give control to another person
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to decide
verbs.why: A retiring manager hands over the store to her deputy, and a club treasurer hands over the accounts to the next volunteer. Messi believes it is time to hand over the team to a talented younger generation.

verbs.correct: To accept a change and continue with life
verbs.wrong: To make a big decision in a hurry
verbs.why: After a hard breakup, most people slowly move on. When a project ends, the team moves on to new work. Messi says he understands that this is the moment to move on.

chunks.text: When fans {{look back on}} his time with Argentina, the numbers tell the story. Messi {{racked up}} 207 [[appearances]] and 125 goals, and he retires as the country's [[all-time leader]] in both. He made his [[debut]] in 2005 and played in six World Cups. He won the 2021 Copa America, then {{went on}} to win the 2022 World Cup as [[captain]], ending Argentina's 36-year wait. He also won the 2024 Copa America.

verbs.correct: To think about a past time
verbs.wrong: To wait for a better chance
verbs.why: People look back on their school days with a smile, and a company looks back on its first year at a party. When fans look back on Messi's time with Argentina, the numbers alone tell the story.

verbs.correct: To collect a large total over time
verbs.wrong: To share credit with the whole team
verbs.why: A busy driver racks up a lot of miles every month. A good striker racks up goals all season. Messi racked up 207 appearances and 125 goals for Argentina.

verbs.correct: To continue and later achieve something
verbs.wrong: To leave a team before the season ends
verbs.why: Many top students go on to become doctors. Some small local bands go on to fill stadiums. Messi won the 2021 Copa America and then went on to win the 2022 World Cup as captain.

chunks.text: Even at his last [[tournament]], Messi {{stood out}}. Argentina {{fell short}} in the 2026 final, but he scored eight goals and finished second in the [[scoring race]]. The head of Argentina's soccer [[federation]] said it left the decision entirely up to Messi after the final. Argentina will now {{carry on}} without its captain, and the next generation has a big [[record]] to {{live up to}}.

verbs.correct: To be clearly better than the rest
verbs.wrong: To spend the game on the bench

lines.text: Did you see? Messi {{hung up}} his boots for the Argentina team. He announced it on Monday.
I saw. [[End of an era]]. Twenty years, six World Cups.
He wrote the letter back in July, right after the final against Spain. But he {{held off}} on publishing it.
Because of his father?

[[The timing says it all]]. He lost the final and his father in the same summer.
[[That's a lot for one summer]]. He said the decision hurt, but he understands this is the moment.
Still, what a record he leaves. 207 appearances, 125 goals.
He {{racked up}} more of both than anyone in Argentina's history. And after the 2021 Copa America, he {{went on}} to win the World Cup as captain.
[[You can't argue with those numbers]]. Even in his last tournament he {{stood out}}, didn't he?

They {{carry on}} without him. He said a younger generation deserved the chance, and it's time to {{hand over}} the team and {{move on}}.
[[Big shoes to fill]]. That's a lot to {{live up to}}.
