stories.headline: Rope bridges let monkeys cross Amazon roads safely

sources.title: Good Good Good: Rope canopy bridges lead to 15,000 safe wildlife crossings
DailyGood: Amazon Canopy Bridges Lead to 15K+ Safe Road Crossings
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute: How Brazil's Unique Canopy Bridges Are Saving Species
Brazilian monkeys cross highways using canopy bridges (video, CNN 10)

chunks.text: Monkeys in the Brazilian Amazon now {{cross over}} roads safely on rope bridges. The bridges are the work of a [[biologist]], the [[founder]] of a wildlife bridge project. In 2024, her team {{set up}} eight [[canopy]] bridges in the town of Alta Floresta. The project is [[in the news]] because it has reported more than 15,000 safe [[crossings]] in 15 months. Since the bridges went in, no animal has been killed on that [[stretch of road]].

verbs.correct: To go from one side to the other
verbs.wrong: To climb to the top of a tall tree
verbs.why: Hikers cross over a stream on a small wooden bridge, and children wait for the light before they cross over a busy street. Monkeys in the Brazilian Amazon now cross over roads safely on rope bridges strung between the trees.

verbs.correct: To install something in a place
verbs.wrong: To start a journey to a new place
verbs.why: Volunteers set up new bird boxes in a park, and a city sets up cameras at its busiest crossing. In 2024, the biologist's team set up eight canopy bridges over a road in Alta Floresta.

chunks.text: Roads {{cut through}} the forest, and animals of the [[treetops]] rarely {{come down}}. If the trees are too [[far apart]], a monkey crosses [[on foot]], and many get {{run over}}. The project estimates [[roughly]] 9 million [[mammals]] die on Brazilian roads each year. A canopy bridge lets monkeys {{keep away from}} traffic. Each has several [[layers]] of rope, since different [[species]] move differently: some [[leap]], some climb [[hand over hand]]. Two [[camera traps]] on each bridge {{pick up}} every crossing.

verbs.correct: To split a forest into two parts
verbs.wrong: To remove trees from an area
verbs.why: A new railway line can cut through a valley, and an old highway can cut through a wetland for miles. Roads cut through large areas of Amazon forest, leaving treetop animals with no safe way across.

verbs.correct: To move from a high place to the ground
verbs.wrong: To find something without looking for it
verbs.why: A cat finally comes down from the roof at dinner time, and squirrels come down to the ground to look for nuts. Many animals that live in the treetops rarely come down, so a road is a serious problem for them.

verbs.correct: To hit an animal with a car or truck
verbs.wrong: To use all of something until none is left
verbs.why: Drivers slow down so they do not run over the ducks, and a deer can get run over on a dark country road. Monkeys that try to cross on foot are the ones that get run over, and an estimated 9 million mammals die on Brazilian roads every year.

verbs.correct: To avoid going near something
verbs.wrong: To move at the same speed as something
verbs.why: Signs tell visitors to keep away from the edge of a cliff, and parents tell children to keep away from a hot stove. A canopy bridge gives the monkeys a way to keep away from the traffic below.

verbs.correct: To notice and record something
verbs.wrong: To choose one thing from a group
verbs.why: A sensor can pick up movement near a gate at 3 a.m., and night cameras pick up animals that people never see. Two camera traps on each bridge pick up every animal that crosses.

chunks.text: The cameras in Alta Floresta have recorded spider monkeys, howler monkeys, and tamarins. It also {{turned out}} that monkeys were not the only users. When the team {{looked through}} the [[footage]], they found opossums, sloths, and mouse opossums crossing as well. The project says its goal is simple: a canopy bridge reconnects forest that a road has separated, and it reduces [[roadkill]].

verbs.correct: To be discovered to be true later
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: A strange noise in the attic can turn out to be a bird, and odd tracks in the snow can turn out to belong to a fox. It turned out that monkeys were not the only animals using the bridges.

verbs.correct: To examine many things one by one
verbs.wrong: To take care of an animal
verbs.why: A student looks through old maps in a library, and a photographer looks through hundreds of pictures to find the right one. When the team looked through the footage, they found opossums, sloths, and mouse opossums crossing as well.

chunks.text: Since 2021, the team has installed 32 bridges on another Amazon [[highway]]. Cameras there have recorded [[primate]] crossings for five years, and the total {{adds up to}} about 1,250. The team has also {{taken on}} roads in other parts of Brazil. Eight more are planned for Alta Floresta's [[urban area]], and the project hopes to {{branch out}} to other South American countries. The researchers say the pattern is simple: give animals a safe way across, and they use it.

verbs.correct: To reach a total of a certain amount
verbs.wrong: To make something bigger than before
verbs.why: Small donations can add up to more than a thousand dollars, and many short trips add up to a lot of driving. On another major Amazon highway, five years of recorded primate crossings add up to about 1,250.

verbs.correct: To agree to do a new piece of work
verbs.wrong: To become successful very quickly
verbs.why: A cleanup group can take on two more beaches, and a busy builder cannot take on another house this year. The team has also taken on roads in other parts of Brazil.

verbs.correct: To extend work to new areas
verbs.wrong: To separate from a main road
verbs.why: A charity can start in one town and branch out across the whole region, and a company can branch out into three new countries. The project hopes to branch out to other countries in South America as well.

mainIdea.s: Rope bridges over an Amazon road have given monkeys and other animals more than 15,000 safe crossings. Researchers report no road deaths there and are building more bridges on other highways.
mainIdea.why: Cameras counted more than 15,000 safe crossings, no animal has been killed on that stretch of road, and more bridges are planned for other highways and other countries.

mainIdea.s: Brazil has cut roadkill across the whole country by hanging rope bridges above its highways. Researchers say the yearly total of 9 million road deaths has dropped sharply since 2024.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the zero-roadkill result is for one stretch of road in Alta Floresta. Nobody says the national figure of 9 million has fallen.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in the Brazilian Amazon have found a new species of titi monkey near a busy highway. They say the small animal lives only in a few small forest patches and is already at risk.
mainIdea.why: Spider monkeys, howler monkeys, and tamarins were all recorded on the bridges, but none of them is a new discovery. The news is about safe road crossings, not a new species.

tf.why: Monkeys were not the only users. The footage showed opossums, sloths, and mouse opossums crossing as well.

tf.why: The project estimates roughly 9 million mammals die on Brazilian roads each year.

tf.why: Eight bridges were installed there in 2024, and cameras have since recorded more than 15,000 safe crossings.

tf.why: The team has already taken on roads in other parts of Brazil, and the project hopes to branch out to other countries in South America as well.

tf.why: The researchers report that no animal has been run over on that stretch of road since the bridges were installed.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the monkeys in Brazil? They {{cross over}} roads on rope bridges now.
Rope bridges for monkeys? Who builds something like that?

A biologist and her team. They {{set up}} eight of them over a road in the Amazon back in 2024. Since then the cameras have {{picked up}} more than 15,000 crossings, and no animal has been killed on that stretch of road.
[[Not a single one]]? That's impressive. But why do monkeys need a bridge in the first place?

Roads {{cut through}} the forest, and those animals almost never {{come down}} to the ground. If the trees are too far apart, they try to cross on foot, and that's when they get {{run over}}. An estimated 9 million mammals a year on Brazilian roads.
Nine million. [[I can't wrap my head around]] a number like that. So the bridge lets them {{keep away from}} the traffic completely.
Exactly. And it {{turned out}} monkeys aren't the only ones using them. When the team {{looked through}} the footage, they found sloths and opossums too.
[[The more the merrier]]. Are they stopping at eight bridges?
[[Not even close]]. They've {{taken on}} highways in other parts of Brazil, and they want to {{branch out}} to other countries in South America next.
[[Hats off to them]]. It all {{adds up to}} one simple idea: give animals a safe way across, and they'll use it.

stories.headline: Hundreds feared trapped in Nepal flood tunnels

sources.title: Nepal tunnel traps hinder flood rescue: How many are dead or missing?
Search for hundreds in hydropower tunnels in Nepal
Hundreds trapped underground after Nepal flood disaster (DW News, video)

chunks.text: One week after Nepal's glacier flood, rescuers face a new [[emergency]]. Hundreds of workers are believed trapped inside tunnels at [[hydropower]] projects on the flooded rivers. When the [[flash flood]] hit on August 26, mud and debris {{piled up}} at the [[entrances]] and {{blocked them off}}, sealing the workers inside. About 900 workers were at sites in the [[flood zone]]. Those at about six tunnels are [[feared]] trapped, most at the Trishuli projects in Rasuwa district.

verbs.correct: To collect in a large heap
verbs.wrong: To wash slowly down a river
verbs.why: Dirty dishes pile up in the sink after a party, and unread emails pile up over a long weekend. Here mud and debris piled up at the tunnel entrances when the flood hit.

verbs.correct: To close a way so nothing can pass
verbs.wrong: To mark a route as safe to use
verbs.why: Police block off a street for a parade. A fallen tree sometimes blocks off a country road. The flood's mud blocked off the tunnel entrances and sealed the workers inside.

chunks.text: Rescue [[crews]] are working [[day and night]] to {{clear away}} the mud, by hand and with machines. A Nepal Army [[spokesperson]] said a large amount of debris had been [[deposited]] there, "posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels." Where crews have managed to {{break through}}, they have {{sent in}} oxygen through small openings. Nearly 300 workers have already been {{brought out}} alive, but a few bodies have also been [[recovered]] from the tunnels.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a place
verbs.wrong: To measure how deep the mud is
verbs.why: We clear away the plates after dinner, and crews clear away snow from a runway before a flight. Rescue crews are now clearing away the mud by hand and with heavy machines.

verbs.correct: To force a way past a barrier
verbs.wrong: To make a dark space brighter
verbs.why: A strong drill breaks through a concrete wall in minutes. Firefighters break through a locked door to reach people inside. Where crews have managed to break through, they have reached the workers inside.

verbs.correct: To pass something into a closed space
verbs.wrong: To count the people in a group
verbs.why: A mechanic sends in a small camera to see inside the engine, and a beekeeper sends in smoke to calm the bees inside the hive. Rescuers sent in oxygen through small openings to the trapped workers.

verbs.correct: To carry someone from inside a place
verbs.wrong: To treat an injury on the spot
verbs.why: Firefighters bring out people from a smoky building, and divers bring out sailors from a sunken boat. Nearly 300 workers have already been brought out of the tunnels alive.

chunks.text: Six days after the disaster, officials say they are in a [[race against time]]. The biggest fear is [[suffocation]]: the workers still trapped could {{run out of}} air, and they have little or no food and water. Nobody knows how long they can {{hold out}}. Outside the tunnels, [[relatives]] of the missing workers are waiting for news. Rescue teams have not {{given up}}, and the digging continues.

verbs.correct: To have no more of something
verbs.wrong: To share something with others
verbs.why: A car runs out of gas on a long trip, and a store runs out of bread before a storm. Officials fear the trapped workers could run out of air, food, and water.

verbs.correct: To stay alive in a hard situation
verbs.wrong: To call for help with a radio
verbs.why: Lost hikers often hold out for days on very little food. A small town without power holds out through a long, cold winter. Nobody knows how long the trapped workers can hold out underground.

verbs.correct: To stop trying or hoping
verbs.wrong: To wait quietly for news
verbs.why: A good runner never gives up before the finish line. Some students give up on math after one bad grade. Rescue teams have not given up, and the digging continues.

chunks.text: The tunnel rescue is part of a larger [[operation]]. The flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, and over a dozen in Tibet. Thousands are still missing, including hundreds of [[foreign nationals]]. Nearly 21,000 [[security personnel]] and [[volunteers]] have {{pitched in}}. China {{flew in}} more than 2,000 rescue workers and dropped [[equipment]] from the air, and India sent army officers trained in tunnel rescue. Crews now hope to {{step up}} the search. For the workers still [[underground]], every hour counts.

verbs.why: Neighbors pitch in to clean a park after a storm, and the whole family pitches in to cook a holiday dinner. Nearly 21,000 security personnel and volunteers have pitched in to help with the rescue.

verbs.correct: To bring people by airplane
verbs.wrong: To drop supplies from the sky
verbs.why: A couple flies in relatives from other states for their wedding, and a music festival flies in a band from Europe for one night. China flew in more than 2,000 rescue workers to help Nepal.

verbs.wrong: To leave a dangerous place
verbs.why: A school steps up security after a theft, and a city steps up cleaning during flu season. With more help arriving, crews hope to step up the search for the missing workers.

mainIdea.s: A week after Nepal's glacier flood, rescuers are trying to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in mud-blocked tunnels. Crews fear the workers could run out of air before help arrives.
mainIdea.why: Mud and debris blocked off the tunnel entrances, nearly 300 workers have been brought out, and suffocation is now the biggest fear for those still inside.

mainIdea.s: A new flood in Nepal's mountains has trapped hundreds of hydropower workers inside tunnels this week. Rescuers say the workers have enough air and food to wait safely for several more days.

mainIdea.s: A tunnel collapsed during construction of a new hydropower dam in northern India, trapping about forty workers. Rescue teams drilled through solid rock for two weeks before reaching them.
mainIdea.why: This describes a different event. The workers here are in Nepal, trapped by flood mud, and India sent officers to help with the rescue.

lines.text: Have you been following the Nepal flood news? There's a new problem now. Hundreds of workers are trapped inside tunnels.
Tunnels? I thought the flood was in the river valleys.
It was. But there were hydropower projects along those rivers, and the workers were inside the tunnels when the flood hit. Mud and debris {{piled up}} at the entrances and {{blocked them off}}.
So they've been in there since last week? [[What a nightmare]].
Six days. Crews are trying to {{clear away}} the mud by hand and with machines, but an army spokesperson said the amount of debris is a huge challenge.
Has anyone reached them?
In some places, yes. Where crews managed to {{break through}}, they {{sent in}} oxygen through small openings. And nearly 300 workers have already been {{brought out}} alive.
That's something, at least. But the rest are [[not out of the woods yet]].
No. Officials fear they could {{run out of}} air before the tunnels are open. Food and water too.
How long can a person {{hold out}} like that?
Nobody really knows. [[The clock is ticking]], and that's why nobody wants to {{give up}}.
What about the families? Do they know anything?
Mostly they're just waiting outside the tunnels, [[completely in the dark]]. [[That's the part that gets me]].
Is anyone helping Nepal with this?
Nearly 21,000 soldiers, police, and volunteers have {{pitched in}}. China {{flew in}} more than 2,000 rescue workers, and India sent army officers trained in tunnel rescue.
I hope all of that helps them {{step up}} the search before it's too late.
Every hour counts now.

chunks.text: Canada has announced new [[tariffs]] on American goods in a [[trade dispute]] with the United States. Trade talks {{broke down}} on August 22, and the US then {{put on}} a 50 percent tariff covering about 20 billion dollars' [[worth of]] Canadian goods, including [[dairy]] and hockey equipment. Those goods {{make up}} about 5.5 percent of Canada's [[exports]] to the US. On August 25, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney {{laid out}} Canada's answer: it is {{striking back}} with tariffs of its own.

verbs.correct: To fail or end without agreement
verbs.wrong: To make sudden progress after difficulty
verbs.why: Peace talks often break down over one small detail. Many deals between landlords and tenants break down over money. Trade talks between Canada and the United States broke down on August 22, three days before Canada's announcement.

verbs.correct: To make goods subject to a tax
verbs.wrong: To remove a tax from goods
verbs.why: Many cities put a tax on sugary drinks. Most states put a tax on gas at the pump. After the talks ended, the United States put a 50 percent tariff on about 20 billion dollars' worth of Canadian goods.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a total
verbs.wrong: To send goods to another country

verbs.correct: To explain a plan clearly
verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan at the last minute
verbs.why: A coach lays out the game plan before kickoff, and a teacher lays out the rules on the first day of class. Prime Minister Mark Carney laid out Canada's answer on August 25: tariffs of its own.

verbs.correct: To respond to an attack with your own
verbs.wrong: To cancel a law or rule in court
verbs.why: A boxer strikes back after taking a punch. A losing team often strikes back with a quick goal. Canada is now striking back at the American tariffs with tariffs of its own.

chunks.text: Carney said Canada would [[match]] the American tariffs "[[dollar for dollar]] in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses." Canada's tariffs {{add up to}} about 20 billion dollars, at rates of 15 to 50 percent. The new [[measures]] {{single out}} steel and aluminum for the largest share. The list includes cheese and other dairy, [[appliances]], farm equipment, seafood, [[cosmetics]], toilet paper, and electronics. Canadian tariffs on American auto parts [[remain in place]].

verbs.correct: To reach a total of
verbs.wrong: To include one more item
verbs.why: Small daily coffees add up to a big bill by the end of the month, and three short drives add up to a full tank of gas. Canada's new tariffs add up to about 20 billion dollars, the same amount as the American ones.

mainIdea.s: After talks with the United States failed, Canada announced tariffs on 20 billion dollars of American goods. The prime minister says the move matches the US tariffs and protects Canadian workers.

mainIdea.s: Canada acted first with tariffs on American goods, and the United States then answered with 50 percent tariffs. Canadian officials say the goal is to protect workers, farmers, and businesses.

mainIdea.s: The United States and Canada have signed a trade deal that removes most tariffs on steel and aluminum. Officials say it will take effect next year once lawmakers in both countries approve it.

lines.text: Did you see the news? Canada is {{striking back}} with tariffs on American goods.
[[So much for]] the trade talks. I thought both sides were still at the table.
Not anymore. The talks {{broke down}} on August 22. Then the US {{put a 50 percent tariff on}} Canadian goods, and now Canada is doing the same.
That's a lot of money. Twenty billion dollars, right?
Yes, dollar for dollar. Steel and aluminum are the biggest part, but the list {{adds up to}} way more than that. Cheese, furniture, even toilet paper.
Toilet paper, [[of all things]]? What else is on there?
Cosmetics, appliances, seafood, electronics. And all of it will probably {{push up}} prices on both sides of the border.
So [[where does that leave]] regular people?
[[Caught in the middle]]. The government {{set aside}} some money to help businesses, but small companies could still {{go under}} if this {{drags on}}.
Do you think either side will {{back down}}?
[[Somebody has to blink first]]. But a poll found most Canadians don't want their government to make more concessions.
I hope they {{work out}} something before September 8.
[[I wouldn't hold my breath]]. That's not much time.

stories.headline: TikTok users skip showers to attract partners

sources.title: Forbes: 'Pheromone Maxxing' TikTok Dating Trend Has People Not Showering
Vice: Introducing Pheromone Maxxing, TikTok's Latest Disgusting Dating Trend
MedBound Times: Teen Trend 'Pheromone Maxxing': Social Media & Health Risks Explained

chunks.text: A TikTok trend called "pheromone maxxing" has {{caught on}} this month. Forbes reported on it on August 16, and other [[news outlets]] followed. Followers {{give up}} daily showers and {{go without}} [[deodorant]]. A few even drink [[urine]]. They believe soap and water {{wash off}} a natural "musk" of sex pheromones that attracts [[potential partners]]. The trend {{grew out of}} "looksmaxxing," an older TikTok trend about improving your [[appearance]].

verbs.correct: To become popular quickly
verbs.wrong: To reach the same level as others
verbs.why: New slang words catch on fast among teenagers. A good song often catches on after one popular video. The pheromone maxxing trend caught on this month after Forbes first reported on it on August 16.

verbs.correct: To stop doing something
verbs.wrong: To release a smell into the air
verbs.why: Some people give up sugar for a month. Many smokers give up cigarettes in the new year. People who follow this trend give up daily showers in the hope of smelling more attractive.

verbs.correct: To not use something you normally use
verbs.wrong: To agree with what other people do
verbs.why: Campers often go without hot water for a week. Busy nurses sometimes go without lunch on a hard day. Followers of the trend go without deodorant because they think it hides a natural body musk.

verbs.correct: To remove something with water
verbs.wrong: To slowly lose its effect over time
verbs.why: Rain washes off the mud on a car, and a quick rinse washes off the soap in your hair. Trend followers believe soap and water wash off a natural musk that contains sex pheromones.

verbs.correct: To develop from something earlier
verbs.wrong: To change from a child into an adult
verbs.why: Many big companies grow out of small college projects. Some holidays grow out of old farm traditions. Pheromone maxxing grew out of looksmaxxing, an older TikTok trend about looking as attractive as possible.

chunks.text: The science does not {{hold up}}: in over 60 years of research, no human sex pheromone has been confirmed. A 2025 review called one chemical in male [[sweat]] "[[inconclusive]]." Experts {{point out}} that the organ other [[mammals]] use to detect pheromones is small and underdeveloped in humans. People also {{mix up}} the trend with the "sweaty T-shirt" studies, which found women prefer the [[body odor]] of men with different immune genes. That preference is real, but it does not attract partners, and hormonal [[birth control]] [[reverses]] it.

verbs.correct: To remain true when tested
verbs.wrong: To keep information secret
verbs.why: A weak excuse does not hold up when a parent asks questions, and a good theory holds up in experiment after experiment. Researchers say the science behind this trend does not hold up, since no human sex pheromone has ever been confirmed.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To measure something in a study
verbs.why: A teacher points out mistakes in an essay, and a friend points out that the deadline is tomorrow. Experts point out that the organ animals use to detect pheromones is small and probably underdeveloped in humans.

verbs.correct: To confuse two different things
verbs.wrong: To invent a story that is not true
verbs.why: People mix up the names of twins, and travelers mix up two cities with similar names. Part of the problem is that people mix up the trend with real research, like the sweaty T-shirt studies.

chunks.text: Doctors warn of real health risks. When people stop washing, bacteria and sweat {{build up}} on the skin, and some {{come down with}} [[skin infections]], including fungal ones, or respiratory infections. Others buy [[unregulated]] "pheromone" oils and sprays and {{end up}} with [[allergic reactions]]. Drinking urine is worse: it contains [[waste products]] and harmful microbes. No evidence shows that avoiding [[hygiene]] increases pheromone effects. Feeling more attractive, experts say, is a [[boost]] in confidence, not body chemistry.

verbs.correct: To slowly collect in one place
verbs.wrong: To suddenly appear on the skin
verbs.why: Dust builds up on shelves nobody cleans, and ice builds up on a plane's wings in cold weather. When people stop washing, bacteria and sweat build up on the skin and can lead to infections.

verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.wrong: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Half a class often comes down with the flu in winter. Travelers sometimes come down with a cold after a long flight. Some people who stop washing come down with skin infections, including fungal infections.

verbs.correct: To reach a result you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To accept something unpleasant
verbs.why: Lost drivers sometimes end up in the wrong town. Many people who skip breakfast end up with a headache by noon. A few people who buy unregulated pheromone sprays end up with allergic reactions.

chunks.text: Many followers are teenagers, and researchers are not surprised. [[Adolescents]] are still {{figuring out}} who they are, and friends strongly influence them. A 2025 study on [[viral challenges]] described "[[social proof]]": when many people online seem to be doing something, it looks normal and safe. Teens then {{take up}} a challenge quickly and often {{buy into}} the idea behind it. Doctors' advice is simple: skipping showers will not help anyone find a partner. Hygiene still matters.

verbs.correct: To understand after some thought
verbs.wrong: To exercise to keep the body fit
verbs.why: Most new employees figure out the office printer in a day. Many students figure out what to study only in their second year. Researchers say adolescents are still figuring out who they are, so friends have a strong influence on what they do.

verbs.correct: To start doing an activity
verbs.wrong: To look or act like a parent
verbs.why: Many retired people take up painting. More kids take up chess every year. When something looks normal and safe online, teens take up a challenge quickly.

verbs.correct: To believe an idea completely
verbs.wrong: To bring a good result later
verbs.why: Not everyone buys into the idea that money brings happiness, and many fans buy into rumors about their favorite band. Thanks to social proof, teens often buy into the idea behind a challenge.

mainIdea.s: A viral TikTok trend tells people to skip showers so their natural scent will attract dates. Scientists say no human sex pheromone has been proven, and doctors warn the habit brings infections.
mainIdea.why: No human sex pheromone has been confirmed in more than 60 years of research, and doctors link the habit to skin, fungal, and respiratory infections.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that skipping showers really makes people smell more attractive, because sweat carries immune signals. Doctors still warn against the trend, since unwashed skin can cause infections.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the science does not hold up. The sweaty T-shirt studies show a real preference, not a scent that attracts partners, and any benefit is likely psychological.

mainIdea.s: A TikTok skincare trend has teenagers buying strong anti-aging creams made for adults. Dermatologists report more young patients with rashes and damaged skin, and some brands now add age warnings.
mainIdea.why: The trend is about skipping showers and deodorant to keep a natural scent. There are no anti-aging creams, dermatologists, or age warnings here.

lines.text: Did you see this pheromone maxxing thing? People are {{giving up}} showers to smell more attractive.
[[You can't make this stuff up]]. On purpose?
On purpose. They {{go without}} deodorant too, because they think soap {{washes off}} some natural musk that attracts partners.
And that actually {{caught on}}? Does the science {{hold up}} at all?
Not really. Researchers {{point out}} that nobody has confirmed a human sex pheromone in 60 years of studies.
So the whole idea [[doesn't pass the smell test]]. Where did it even come from?
It {{grew out of}} looksmaxxing. And people {{mix it up}} with those sweaty T-shirt studies, which were about something different.
Using a T-shirt study to justify skipping showers is [[a stretch]]. And doesn't all that sweat just {{build up}}?
It does. Some people {{come down with}} skin infections, and others {{end up}} with allergic reactions from cheap sprays.
So you could ruin your skin and still not find a date.
That's what doctors say. If you feel more attractive after a week without soap, it's [[all in your head]], not your body chemistry.

stories.headline: 2026 is the new 2016: the internet replays a decade

sources.title: It's 2016 Again, TikTok Users Have Declared, Using Decade-Old Songs And Filters (Forbes)
Fetty Wap, Zara Larsson & More: How 2016 Nostalgia Is Impacting Charts (Billboard)
'2026 Is the New 2016': Inside the Nostalgia Wave Taking Over Your Feed (Central Jersey)
Is it 2026 or 2016? Social media users turn back the clock in viral trend (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: Open a video app this year, and you may think your phone traveled back in time. Ten years have {{gone by}}, but millions of people are {{looking back}} at 2016 with warm smiles. In January, new videos under the [[hashtag]] 2016 {{blew up}}, growing by more than 450 percent, and [[searches]] for 2016 songs [[jumped]] 290 percent. The internet has decided that 2026 is the new 2016.

verbs.correct: To pass, as time does
verbs.wrong: To stop very suddenly
verbs.why: Years go by, summers go by, and sometimes a whole childhood goes by before you notice it. A full ten years have gone by since 2016, and this year the internet decided to notice.

verbs.correct: To think about the past
verbs.wrong: To plan for next year
verbs.why: People look back on their childhood, look back with regret, or just look back at old photos for fun. Here millions of fans look back at 2016 with nothing but warm smiles.

verbs.correct: To become hugely popular fast
verbs.wrong: To disappear from the internet
verbs.why: A photo can blow up online overnight, a new dance can blow up on video apps, and a small joke can blow up into a trend. Here the 2016 hashtag blew up in January, growing by more than 450 percent.

chunks.text: The [[nostalgia]] is easy to see on the street. Teens {{dress up}} in [[chokers]], [[skinny jeans]], and [[wired headphones]], filming videos in the flat, bright style of old phones. Photo apps {{brought back}} [[beloved]] tricks like the famous dog-ears [[filter]], and the [[mannequin challenge]], where whole rooms freeze like [[statues]], {{came back}} [[from the dead]]. For one video, at least, it is 2016 again.

verbs.correct: To wear special or fancy clothes
verbs.wrong: To buy clothes you do not need
verbs.why: People dress up for parties, dress up for costume contests, and sometimes just dress up for no reason at all. This year teens dress up in chokers and skinny jeans to enjoy the whole look of 2016 all over again.

verbs.correct: To return something from the past
verbs.wrong: To make something disappear
verbs.why: Stores bring back old recipes, radio stations bring back forgotten songs, and apps now bring back old photo filters too. Here photo apps brought back the famous dog-ears filter that everyone used a decade ago.

verbs.correct: To become popular again
verbs.wrong: To lose value over time
verbs.why: Old trends come back, forgotten songs come back, and sometimes a whole decade comes back all at once. Here the mannequin challenge has come back, with whole rooms freezing like statues again.

chunks.text: The clearest sign is the music. Thanks to a viral dance, Swedish singer Zara Larsson's 2016 hit Lush Life re-entered the British [[charts]] at number eight and returned to the American list, a full [[decade]] after its [[release]]. Fans say the bright, simple pop of that year still {{holds up}} today, and old songs by other 2016 [[stars]] are climbing again too. What was once just a [[playlist]] has {{turned into}} a giant online party.

verbs.correct: To stay good as time passes
verbs.wrong: To sound strange and old
verbs.why: A good joke can hold up for years, and an old song can hold up even better. Fans say Zara Larsson's 2016 hit still holds up today, a full decade after its release.

verbs.correct: To become something different
verbs.wrong: To stay exactly the same
verbs.why: A hobby can turn into a career, and a small argument can turn into a big fight. Here a private playlist of old songs turned into a giant online party that everyone wanted to join.

chunks.text: Why 2016? Psychologists point to [[timing]]. Many fans call it the last year before the world got complicated, and the trend is strongest among tired people who wish life would {{slow down}} a little. There is also a younger crowd: today's teenagers were small children in 2016, so they {{missed out on}} the fun the first time. Experts add one [[warning]] about the nostalgia [[cycle]]: it is {{speeding up}}, with each [[revival]] arriving sooner than the last. And the [[rerun]] always looks better than the [[original]], because the videos {{leave out}} the bad days. That year had them too.

verbs.correct: To move at a calmer speed
verbs.wrong: To become more exciting
verbs.why: Traffic slows down before a red light, a runner slows down near the finish line, and life slows down once summer ends. Many tired fans just wish life would slow down a little, the way it feels in old memories.

verbs.correct: To lose the chance to enjoy something
verbs.wrong: To remember something perfectly
verbs.why: Shoppers miss out on a sale, latecomers miss out on the best seats, and quiet kids sometimes miss out on the fun. Today's teenagers missed out on 2016 the first time around, since they were only small children then.

verbs.correct: To happen faster than before
verbs.wrong: To repeat without changing
verbs.why: A heartbeat can speed up during a scary movie, and a slow project can speed up once more people help. Experts say the nostalgia cycle itself is speeding up, with each new trend arriving sooner than the one before it.

verbs.correct: To not include something
verbs.wrong: To describe something fully
verbs.why: A story can leave out the hard parts, a recipe can leave out one key ingredient, and a memory can leave out the bad days entirely. These 2016 videos leave out the difficult moments, so the whole year looks better than it really was.

stories.headline: AI slop is flooding your feed, and it pays

sources.title: What is AI slop? Why you are seeing more fake photos and videos in your feeds (The Conversation)
AI slop's meteoric rise and the impact of synthetic content in 2026 (Digital Watch Observatory)
AI Slop won in 2025 - fingerprinting real content might be the answer in 2026 (TechRadar)
AI news videos blur line between real and fake reports (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: A bear doing a [[backflip]] on a trampoline. A baby made of spaghetti. A famous actor celebrating his 1800th birthday. None of it is real, but it is everywhere. [[Critics]] call it [[AI slop]]: cheap, strange [[content]] created by [[artificial intelligence]] in seconds. New AI tools can {{pump out}} this [[material]] faster than any human could type, and the fake posts now {{clog up}} feeds on every major app.

verbs.correct: To produce quickly in large amounts
verbs.wrong: To check slowly for mistakes
verbs.why: A factory can pump out a thousand toys an hour, and a busy kitchen can pump out fresh bread all morning. New AI tools now pump out fake photos and videos faster than any person could type.

verbs.correct: To block something so it cannot flow
verbs.wrong: To clean something completely
verbs.why: Fallen leaves clog up a drain after a storm, and holiday traffic clogs up the highway every year. Now these fake posts clog up feeds on every major app, leaving little room for anything real.

chunks.text: Why does the internet [[drown]] in slop? Because it pays. Millions of people {{fall for}} the fake photos and share them, and every click means [[advertising]] money. Big [[platforms]] reward popular posts with real payments, so slop [[factories]] treat fake content like a business: it costs almost nothing to make, and one viral [[hit]] can {{rake in}} more than a month of honest work. One writer described slop as [[clickbait]] with a brain. The [[algorithm]] cannot tell the difference, and often it does not care.

verbs.correct: To believe a trick is real
verbs.wrong: To pay too much for something
verbs.why: Grandparents sometimes fall for a phone scam. Shoppers can fall for an ad that promises free money. Millions of people fall for fake AI photos and share them online.

verbs.correct: To earn a lot of money quickly
verbs.wrong: To spend money without thinking
verbs.why: A hit movie can rake in millions in one weekend, and an ice cream shop can rake in cash during a heat wave. Here one viral fake post can rake in more money than a month of honest work.

chunks.text: The good news: most slop still makes mistakes, and those mistakes {{give away}} the fakes. Look closely and you may find hands with six fingers, [[shadows]] pointing in different directions, or [[background]] details that simply do not {{add up}}. Experts say readers should {{look out for}} strange hands, [[melted]] letters, and too-perfect faces, and always check the original [[sources]] before believing a photo.

verbs.correct: To show the hidden truth about something
verbs.wrong: To make something look expensive
verbs.why: Shaking hands can give away a person's fear, and a small smile can give away a hidden secret. Here strange shadows and extra fingers give away a photo that was never real.

verbs.correct: To make sense as a whole
verbs.wrong: To happen at the same time
verbs.why: The two answers he gave me do not add up, and a price that low for a new car does not add up at all. In a fake photo, background details often do not add up, and that is how careful readers spot them.

verbs.correct: To watch carefully for something
verbs.wrong: To fix something before it breaks
verbs.why: Drivers look out for deer at night, and shoppers look out for fake price tags on sale days. Experts want readers to look out for strange hands, melted letters, and faces that look too perfect.

chunks.text: Some [[accounts]] posting slop have millions of followers, and companies promise to {{crack down on}} the worst [[offenders]]. But as long as fake [[views]] earn real money, the [[flood]] will not {{die down}} soon. Until then, the best defense costs nothing: when a video looks too strange to be true, just {{scroll past}} without a second look. Every [[ignored]] fake makes slop a little less [[profitable]].

verbs.correct: To start punishing rule-breakers
verbs.wrong: To quietly ignore a problem
verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding drivers near schools, and cities crack down on illegal parking downtown. Big platforms now promise to crack down on the accounts that post the worst fake content.

verbs.correct: To become weaker or quieter
verbs.wrong: To spread to new places
verbs.why: Strong wind usually dies down by morning, and loud laughter dies down after a few minutes. As long as fake views earn real money, this flood of AI content will not die down soon.

verbs.correct: To skip something on a screen
verbs.wrong: To share something with friends
verbs.why: On the bus she scrolls past ad after ad, stopping only when a friend's photo appears. The simplest defense against a fake video is to scroll past it, since every ignored fake earns less money for its maker.

tf.why: That speed, plus a cost near zero, is why slop factories treat fakes like a business.

tf.s: Making AI slop is expensive, so only big companies produce it.
tf.why: It costs almost nothing to make, and one viral hit can rake in more than a month of honest work.

tf.s: Hands with six fingers can give away a fake image.
tf.why: Experts say to look out for strange hands, melted letters, and details that do not add up.

tf.s: The article says the flood of slop will die down within weeks.
tf.why: As long as fake views earn real money, the flood will not die down soon.

tf.s: The best defense against slop costs a lot of money.
tf.why: It costs nothing. Just scroll past strange videos without a second look.

tf.s: Every click on a fake post can mean advertising money for its creator.
tf.why: Millions fall for the images and share them, and platforms reward popular posts with payments.

lines.text: Did you see that video of a bear doing a backflip on a trampoline? [[No way]] that was real.
Yeah, it's fake. Somebody made it with AI in about ten seconds.
[[Honestly]], I almost shared it. And my cousin {{fell for}} one last week, some baby made of spaghetti.
That's the problem. These accounts are {{pumping out}} hundreds of these a day, and they {{clog up}} everybody's feed.
But why? Who has time to make all that junk?
It pays. Every click is ad money, so one viral fake can {{rake in}} more than most people make in a month.
[[You're kidding]]. So it's basically a business.
[[Pretty much]]. And the algorithm can't tell what's real, so it just pushes whatever gets clicks.
Some of them are hard to spot, though. That actor with the 1800th birthday almost got me.
Usually something {{gives away}} the fake. Weird hands, six fingers, shadows that don't {{add up}}.
Six fingers. That [[creeps me out]] every time.
Melted letters too. Experts say to {{look out for}} faces that are a little too perfect.
Aren't the platforms supposed to {{crack down on}} this stuff?
They say they will. But as long as fake views earn real money, [[I guess]] it won't {{die down}} anytime soon.
So what do we do? Report every single one?
Simpler than that. If it looks too weird to be real, just {{scroll past}}. No like, no share, no money for them.
[[Fair enough]]. Every fake that nobody clicks earns them a little less.
Exactly. Starve the spaghetti baby.

stories.headline: Deadly floods hit the mountains of Nepal

sources.title: Nepal Flash Floods Leave Over 380 Dead and Hundreds More Missing (Time)
Floods kill more than 500 people in Nepal and Tibet (NPR)
2026 Nepal Debris Avalanche and Flash Flood (U.S. Geological Survey)
Recovery efforts underway for hundreds missing after Nepal flash flood (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: It began high in the mountains, where almost nobody was watching. On Wednesday, August 26, a huge mass of ice and rock {{broke off}} a [[mountainside]] in a national park near Nepal's [[border]] with China. Within minutes, the frozen wall {{came down}} into the [[valley]] below and {{set off}} a giant [[flood]] of mud, water, and stone. A wall of water nearly 30 feet high {{swept away}} houses, bridges, and roads along two rivers.

verbs.correct: To separate from a larger piece
verbs.wrong: To stop working suddenly
verbs.why: Icebergs break off glaciers, and branches break off trees in storms. Here a mass of ice and rock broke off a mountainside above the valley.

verbs.correct: To fall to the ground
verbs.wrong: To slide slowly for years
verbs.why: Old walls come down, heavy rain comes down, and power lines come down in storms. The frozen wall came down into the valley within minutes.

verbs.correct: To make something start happening
verbs.wrong: To measure the size of a quake
verbs.why: A spark can set off a fire, and one rumor can set off a panic. The falling ice set off a giant flood of mud, water, and stone.

verbs.correct: To take something with rushing water
verbs.wrong: To bury something under dry snow
verbs.why: Rivers sweep away cars, and big waves sweep away beach houses. The wall of water swept away homes, bridges, and roads along two rivers.

chunks.text: Scientists thousands of miles away {{picked up}} the shaking. The collapse [[released]] as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 [[earthquake]], according to the United States Geological Survey, and the flood then traveled about 62 miles [[downstream]]. Experts are still not sure exactly why the [[glacier]] failed, but warm weather and heavy rain both weaken mountain ice. The same region was hit by a [[deadly]] [[avalanche]] after the 2015 earthquake.

verbs.correct: To notice a sound or signal
verbs.wrong: To send a warning message
verbs.why: Radios pick up distant stations, and sensors pick up small movements in the ground. Scientists thousands of miles away picked up the shaking from the collapse.

chunks.text: The human cost is [[enormous]], and it is still growing. By Friday, [[officials]] had counted more than 540 deaths in Nepal, and about 1,500 people were still [[missing]], more than half of them foreigners. Among them were more than 100 Indian [[pilgrims]] traveling to a [[holy]] mountain, and dozens of Americans. Whole villages were {{cut off}} from the outside world when the flood destroyed the bridges and the [[main highway]] to China. Rescue helicopters {{pulled out}} more than 120 people, but many places were impossible to reach, and the [[death toll]] was expected to {{go up}}.

verbs.correct: To separate a place from outside help
verbs.wrong: To warn a place about danger
verbs.why: Heavy snow can cut off mountain towns, and floods cut off whole islands. Villages here were cut off when the water destroyed the bridges and the main highway.

verbs.correct: To take someone from a dangerous place
verbs.wrong: To search a building for people
verbs.why: Firefighters pull people out of burning houses, and lifeguards pull swimmers out of the sea. Helicopters pulled out more than 120 people from the flood zone.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher number
verbs.wrong: To stay the same for weeks
verbs.why: Prices go up, temperatures go up, and rents go up every year. Sadly, officials expected the death toll to go up as rescuers reached more villages.

chunks.text: More than 4,000 police officers joined the [[search]], and [[rescuers]] {{dug out}} [[survivors]] from the mud. The work is dangerous. Teams had to {{call off}} operations for a time when a new lake, formed by the [[debris]], began to [[overflow]]. Foreign governments have {{reached out}} to offer help, but [[aid]] cannot {{get through}} to villages without roads. For families waiting for news, every hour matters.

verbs.correct: To free someone from mud or snow
verbs.wrong: To carry food to a village
verbs.why: Rescue dogs help dig out skiers after an avalanche, and neighbors dig out cars after a snowstorm. Rescuers dug out survivors from the deep mud.

verbs.correct: To stop something that was planned
verbs.wrong: To shout to people far away
verbs.why: Schools call off classes in bad weather, and couples sometimes call off a wedding. Teams had to call off the search when a new lake began to overflow.

verbs.correct: To make contact to offer help
verbs.wrong: To fly over a flooded area
verbs.why: Charities reach out to homeless families, and old friends reach out after a disaster. Foreign governments reached out to Nepal with offers of aid.

verbs.correct: To reach a place despite problems
verbs.wrong: To build a bridge over a river
verbs.why: Supply trucks get through after storms, and letters get through even in wartime. With the roads gone, aid cannot get through to the cut villages.

mainIdea.s: Falling ice and rock started a huge flood in Nepal's mountains that killed hundreds and left many more missing. Rescuers struggle to reach villages that lost their roads and bridges.
mainIdea.why: The collapse set off a flood that killed over 540 people, and cut off villages are still waiting for help.

mainIdea.s: Weeks of heavy monsoon rain slowly raised Nepal's rivers until they finally flooded hundreds of villages. Officials say early warnings helped almost all of the foreign tourists escape.
mainIdea.why: Close, but this was a sudden collapse of ice and rock, not slow rain, and hundreds of foreigners are among the missing.

mainIdea.s: A strong earthquake in the mountains of Nepal destroyed roads and bridges near the border with China. Neighboring countries have sent rescue teams to search the fallen buildings there.
mainIdea.why: There was no earthquake this time. The collapse only released as much energy as one, which is how scientists noticed it.

tf.s: A mass of ice and rock broke off a mountainside and set off the flood.
tf.why: It fell in a national park near the border with China, and the flood followed within minutes.

tf.s: Scientists far away picked up the shaking from the collapse.
tf.why: The event released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to the USGS.

tf.s: All of the missing people are citizens of Nepal.
tf.why: More than half of the roughly 1,500 missing are foreigners, including Indian pilgrims and dozens of Americans.

tf.s: Some villages were cut off because bridges and the main highway were destroyed.
tf.why: That is why aid cannot get through to many places, even though helicopters pulled out more than 120 people.

tf.s: The rescue teams have never had to stop their work.
tf.why: They had to call off operations for a time when a lake formed by the debris began to overflow.

tf.s: Officials expected the death toll to go up.
tf.why: By Friday more than 540 deaths were counted in Nepal, with many areas still impossible to reach.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the floods in Nepal?
I did. [[That's awful]]. It started with a glacier, didn't it?
Yes. A huge piece of ice and rock {{broke off}} a mountain near the Chinese border. It {{came down}} into the valley in minutes and {{set off}} a flood of mud, water, and stone.
And the flood {{swept away}} whole villages. Houses, bridges, roads. [[I can't imagine]] being there.
[[Honestly]], neither can I. Scientists thousands of miles away {{picked up}} the shaking. It was like a small earthquake.
I read that. And the number of deaths is still {{going up}}?
Yes. More than 540 so far, and about 1,500 people are missing. Many of them were foreign visitors.
[[The worst part is]] the villages nobody can reach. The flood {{cut off}} the whole area when the bridges were destroyed.
Helicopters have {{pulled out}} more than a hundred people, but a lot of places are still impossible to reach.
And the rescuers on the ground are {{digging out}} survivors from the mud with their hands. That must be so dangerous.
It is. They had to {{call off}} the search for a while because a new lake started to overflow.
[[Makes sense]]. They can't risk losing the rescue teams too.
Other countries have {{reached out}} to offer help, but the aid can't {{get through}} to the villages without roads.
So the families just have to wait. Do you think more help will arrive in time?
[[I hope so]]. Every hour matters for those families.

stories.headline: Dolly Parton dies at age 80

sources.title: Dolly Parton, one of country music's most singular performers, has died at age 80 (NPR)
Dolly Parton dies after brief battle with cancer, according to publicist (WSMV Nashville)
Dolly Parton, country music icon, dead at 80 (Global News)
Dolly Parton dies at 80 | Special Report (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: Dolly Parton, the [[queen]] of American [[country music]], {{passed away}} on Tuesday, August 25, in Nashville, Tennessee. She was 80 years old. Her team said she died after a short [[battle]] with [[cancer]], surrounded by [[loved ones]]. Only days earlier, she had told a magazine that she had {{put off}} dealing with her own health while she {{looked after}} her husband, who died last year after nearly 60 years of [[marriage]].

verbs.correct: To die, said in a gentle way
verbs.wrong: To faint for a few moments
verbs.why: Many older people pass away peacefully in their sleep. Families often hold a small service when a grandparent passes away. Parton passed away in Nashville with her loved ones around her.

verbs.correct: To delay something until later
verbs.wrong: To finish work ahead of time
verbs.why: People put off homework, dentist visits, and hard conversations. Parton admitted she had put off dealing with her own health for too long.

verbs.correct: To care for a person who needs help
verbs.wrong: To search for a lost item
verbs.why: Grandparents look after the kids, and nurses look after patients through the night. Parton looked after her sick husband instead of watching her own health.

chunks.text: Her story sounded like one of her songs. Parton {{grew up}} poor in the mountains of Tennessee and {{started out}} singing as a young girl. She {{broke through}} to national fame in the late 1960s and never stopped, writing [[classics]] like "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," and "I Will Always Love You." She reached pop fans with "Here You Come Again" and the theme from the movie "9 to 5," and {{went on}} to act in films like "Steel Magnolias." She won 10 Grammy Awards, and her records sold more than 100 million copies around the world.

verbs.correct: To spend your childhood
verbs.wrong: To move to a new city
verbs.why: Many children grow up on farms in the countryside. Some kids grow up speaking two languages at home. Parton grew up poor in the mountains of Tennessee, and she sang about it forever.

verbs.correct: To begin a career or journey
verbs.wrong: To sing another singer's song
verbs.why: Many stars start out in tiny clubs, and some companies start out in a garage. Parton started out singing as a young girl long before the world knew her name.

verbs.correct: To reach success after a struggle
verbs.wrong: To take a break from music
verbs.why: A young singer often breaks through with one big hit. Some small bands break through after years of playing in clubs. Parton broke through in the late 1960s and stayed on top for decades.

verbs.correct: To continue with the next thing
verbs.wrong: To rest between two long tours
verbs.why: Many top students go on to medical school. Some college players go on to careers in professional sports. After she became famous for her music, Parton went on to act in movies like 'Steel Magnolias.'

chunks.text: Parton was more than a singer. She built the [[theme park]] Dollywood in the Smoky Mountains, which brings visitors from around the world to her [[home region]]. Through her Imagination Library, she {{gave away}} free books to children every month from birth to age five. She also {{stepped in}} during the pandemic, giving one million dollars to [[medical research]] that helped create a Covid vaccine. Her [[charity]] work made her loved far beyond music. She often said she simply wanted to {{give back}}.

verbs.correct: To hand out things for free
verbs.wrong: To sell tickets at the door
verbs.why: Stores give away samples, and rich founders sometimes give away their fortunes. Through her library program, Parton gave away millions of children's books.

verbs.correct: To act when help is needed
verbs.wrong: To leave a difficult project
verbs.why: A referee steps in to stop a fight, and a neighbor steps in when a family struggles. Parton stepped in during the pandemic with a million dollars for research.

verbs.correct: To return help to your community
verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: Athletes give back by coaching kids, and graduates give back to their old schools. Parton said her books and gifts were her way to give back.

chunks.text: The [[tributes]] came quickly. The president ordered [[flags]] [[lowered]] and said there had never been anyone like her. Radio stations across Tennessee played her [[signature song]] at the same moment, and [[stars]] from country and pop remembered her as a [[legend]]. Fans around the world shared their [[grief]] online. There will be no big public [[funeral]]. [[At her request]], only close family will attend a small private [[service]]. Her music, her park, and her books will {{carry on}} without her, and her songs will still {{bring together}} fans of every kind.

verbs.correct: To continue after someone stops
verbs.wrong: To pack for a long journey
verbs.why: A family business often carries on for generations. Old traditions carry on long after their founders die. Her park, her books, and her music will carry on without her.

verbs.correct: To unite different people
verbs.wrong: To make people compete
verbs.why: Big games bring strangers together, and family recipes bring generations together. Her songs brought together country fans, pop fans, and everyone in between.

lines.text: The world lost Dolly Parton this week. She {{passed away}} in Nashville at 80, after a short battle with cancer.
I saw. Even people who never listen to country music are sad.
Because she was more than a singer. She {{grew up}} poor in the Tennessee mountains, {{started out}} singing as a young girl, and {{broke through}} to national fame in the late 1960s.
And never stopped.
Never. "Jolene," "I Will Always Love You," ten Grammys, more than 100 million records. She {{went on}} to act in films too.
Didn't she almost stop performing recently?
She had {{put off}} dealing with her own health while she {{looked after}} her husband. He died last year, after nearly 60 years of marriage.
[[That detail breaks my heart]].

Mine too. And the giving never stopped. Through her Imagination Library she {{gave away}} free books to children every month. During the pandemic she {{stepped in}} with a million dollars for vaccine research. She said she simply wanted to {{give back}}.
How is the world honoring her?
Flags lowered, and radio stations across Tennessee played her signature song at the same moment. But no big public funeral. At her request, only close family.
Quiet, after a life that loud. [[Somehow that fits]].
Her park, her books, and her songs will {{carry on}} without her. Music that will still {{bring together}} fans of every kind.
[[Legends don't really leave]].

stories.headline: America's top spy makes a quiet trip to Moscow

sources.title: CIA Director Arrives in Moscow for 'Meetings,' Reports Say (The Moscow Times)
CIA director Ratcliffe visits Moscow (Axios)
CIA director visits Putin's Russia in talks that Trump calls 'sort of semi-routine' (Fortune)
Here's why the CIA director traveled to Russia (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: The head of the CIA, America's main [[intelligence agency]], has made a [[surprise visit]] to Russia. The agency's director {{set off}} from Washington on Sunday, August 23, {{stopped over}} in Riga, Latvia, and {{touched down}} at a Moscow airport on Tuesday. He flew on a C-17, a military [[transport plane]] usually used to carry soldiers and [[equipment]]. The trip was [[unannounced]]. It was the first visit by a CIA [[chief]] to Russia since November 2021, a few months before the war in Ukraine began.

verbs.correct: To begin a trip
verbs.wrong: To cancel a plan
verbs.why: Hikers set off at dawn, and ships set off from port. The CIA chief set off from Washington on a Sunday and reached Moscow two days later.

verbs.correct: To stay somewhere during a long trip
verbs.wrong: To wait for a delayed airplane
verbs.why: Travelers stop over in big airport cities like Dubai or Amsterdam on long routes. The director's plane stopped over in Riga before the final flight into Russia.

verbs.wrong: To speed up before landing
verbs.why: Planes touch down on the runway, and travelers feel relieved when their plane touches down. The C-17 touched down in Moscow on Tuesday, August 25.

chunks.text: Secret flights rarely stay secret. [[Flight trackers]] followed the plane's path across Europe, and the public data {{gave away}} the story. Within hours, the news {{came out}} in American media. Russian officials first said they knew nothing. Later, a Kremlin [[spokesman]] [[confirmed]] the visit and called it "contacts between [[security services]]." The American spy chief did not meet President Putin. Instead, he {{sat down}} with the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service, who described the talks as "nothing special."

verbs.correct: To let a secret become known
verbs.wrong: To stop trying after difficulty
verbs.why: A nervous smile can give away a lie, and fingerprints give away a thief. Public flight data gave away a trip that was supposed to stay quiet.

verbs.correct: To become public
verbs.wrong: To seem a certain way
verbs.why: The truth comes out, test results come out, and big news comes out. This story came out within hours of the landing in Moscow.

verbs.correct: To meet for serious talks
verbs.wrong: To argue in an angry way
verbs.why: Rivals sit down for peace talks, and unions sit down with company bosses. The American spy chief sat down with Russia's foreign intelligence head, not with the president.

chunks.text: In Washington, President Trump {{played down}} the trip, calling it "sort of semi-routine." Experts disagreed. They {{pointed out}} that a CIA director almost never travels to Moscow, and that such visits usually mean something serious is [[on the agenda]], like a [[warning]] or a [[negotiation]]. What did the two sides discuss? Officially, nobody will say, and both governments are keeping the details [[under wraps]]. [[Analysts]] believe the topics may have included the war in Ukraine and Russia's growing [[partnership]] with Iran.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To repeat something many times
verbs.why: Politicians often play down bad polls. Companies sometimes play down their losses. The president played down the trip, but experts said a visit to Moscow by a CIA director was very unusual.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to think
verbs.why: Teachers point out mistakes in homework, and a coworker may point out that the meeting has moved. Experts pointed out that a CIA director almost never flies to Moscow.

chunks.text: One detail shows how unusual the moment was. Before the visit, Washington asked Ukraine to {{hold off}} on attacks against Moscow and St. Petersburg until the American [[delegation]] left, although [[strikes]] were {{carried out}} in other [[regions]]. Meanwhile, the war {{drags on}} into its fifth year, and [[peace talks]] have [[made no progress]] for months. Analysts do not expect a quick [[breakthrough]], and nobody knows if one quiet trip can help both sides {{work out}} a deal.

verbs.correct: To wait before doing something
verbs.wrong: To attack without any warning
verbs.why: Shoppers hold off on big purchases, and coaches hold off on naming the team. Washington asked Ukraine to hold off on strikes against two Russian cities.

verbs.correct: To do a planned action
verbs.wrong: To cancel at the last minute
verbs.why: Scientists carry out experiments, and armies carry out orders. Ukrainian strikes were still carried out in other parts of Russia that week.

verbs.wrong: To become more violent
verbs.why: Court cases can drag on for years. A boring meeting can drag on all afternoon. The war in Ukraine drags on into its fifth year, and peace talks have made no progress for months.

verbs.wrong: To write something down quickly
verbs.why: Friends work out their differences, and lawyers work out the fine details. Nobody knows if the two countries can work out a real peace deal.

lines.text: The head of the CIA made a surprise trip to Moscow. The first CIA chief to visit Russia since 2021.
How does a spy chief travel, exactly?
On a military transport plane. He {{set off}} from Washington on Sunday, {{stopped over}} in Riga, and {{touched down}} in Moscow on Tuesday. The trip was unannounced.
But it didn't stay secret.
Secret flights rarely do. Flight trackers followed the plane across Europe, and the public data {{gave away}} the story. The news {{came out}} [[within hours]].
Who did he meet? Putin?
No. He {{sat down}} with the head of Russia's foreign intelligence service, who called the talks "nothing special." The American president {{played down}} the trip too, calling it "semi-routine."
Is it routine?
Experts say no. They {{pointed out}} that a CIA director almost never travels to Moscow. Visits like this usually mean something serious: a warning or a negotiation.
What did they discuss?
[[Officially]], nobody will say. Analysts believe the topics may have included Ukraine and Russia's partnership with Iran.
Any detail that shows how unusual this was?
One. Washington asked Ukraine to {{hold off}} on attacks against Moscow until the delegation left, though strikes were {{carried out}} in other regions.
And the war itself?
It {{drags on}} into its fifth year, and peace talks have made no progress for months. Nobody knows if one quiet trip can help both sides {{work out}} a deal.
A plane full of secrets, tracked by everyone with an app. [[Times have changed]].

stories.headline: A robot runs 100 meters faster than any human

sources.title: Chinese humanoid robots smash records in 100m sprint and high jump at Beijing robot games (AP via ABC News)
China's humanoid robots put machines to the test in global competition (NBC)
Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at humanoid games (Al Jazeera)
Humanoid robots smash human records in 100m sprint at robot games (video, ABC7)

chunks.text: The runners {{lined up}} in Beijing, but these [[athletes]] were made of metal. At the second World Humanoid Robot Games in late August, a Chinese robot ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds. That is faster than the human [[world record]] of 9.58 seconds, set by Usain Bolt in 2009. The machine {{sped up}} [[smoothly]] down the [[track]], crossed the [[finish line]], and then {{ended up}} in a [[padded wall]] because it could not stop in time. Fans {{cheered on}} the machines anyway.

verbs.correct: To stand in a row before a start
verbs.wrong: To practice before a big race
verbs.why: Sprinters line up in their lanes, and kids line up before class. In Beijing, robot runners lined up just like human athletes.

verbs.wrong: To measure your own speed
verbs.why: Trains speed up after leaving the station, and swimmers speed up in the final lap. The robot sped up smoothly and beat the fastest human time in history.

verbs.wrong: To win by a small distance
verbs.why: A lost tourist can end up at the wrong hotel, and a bad throw can end up in the crowd. The winning robot ended up in a padded wall because it could not stop.

verbs.wrong: To laugh at someone's mistake
verbs.why: Parents cheer on their kids at games, and whole cities cheer on their teams. The fans in Beijing cheered on the machines like real athletes.

chunks.text: More than 2,000 [[humanoid robots]] from 16 countries, including Germany, Japan, and the United States, {{took on}} the world's best records and each other in 51 events, from soccer and table tennis to [[weightlifting]] and [[tug of war]]. Another machine jumped 2.88 meters in the standing [[high jump]], higher than any human has ever jumped. There were plenty of [[failures]], too. Robots {{fell over}}, crashed, and sent [[sparks]] flying. Some {{got up}} by themselves and kept going, and that [[impressed]] the crowd most of all.

verbs.correct: To compete against someone strong
verbs.wrong: To watch a rival carefully
verbs.why: A small team can take on the champions, and a new phone can take on the market leader. These robots took on the best human records ever set.

verbs.correct: To drop to the ground from standing
verbs.wrong: To jump higher than before
verbs.why: Toddlers fall over when they learn to walk, and bikes fall over in strong wind. Plenty of robots fell over on the track in Beijing.

verbs.correct: To stand again after falling
verbs.wrong: To leave a race early
verbs.why: Boxers get up before the count of ten, and skaters get up after every fall. Some robots got up by themselves, and the crowd loved it.

chunks.text: Between events, teams {{plugged in}} their machines to charge batteries and replace [[spare parts]]. For China, the games are about much more than sport. The country's robot [[industry]] has {{taken off}}, with [[government support]] and hundreds of companies building machines for factories, hospitals, and homes. China now produces about 82 percent of the world's humanoid robots, and other countries are racing to {{catch up}}. The United States recently [[restricted]] [[imports]] of foreign humanoid robots, calling them a [[national security]] question.

verbs.correct: To connect to electric power
verbs.wrong: To repair a broken wheel
verbs.why: You plug in a phone at night and plug in a lamp by the couch. Between events, teams plugged in their robots to charge the batteries.

verbs.correct: To grow quickly and successfully
verbs.wrong: To copy another company's idea
verbs.why: A small app can take off overnight, and sales take off before the holidays. China's robot industry has taken off with strong government support.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as others
verbs.wrong: To start before the others
verbs.why: Students catch up after missing class, and slow starters catch up by the finish. Other countries are now racing to catch up with China's robot industry.

chunks.text: So how close are robot workers, really? Experts say the technology has {{come along}} fast, but most humanoid robots are still used for shows, [[research]], and [[demonstrations]], not for daily jobs. A machine that runs like a [[champion]] can still fail to [[pour]] a cup of coffee. The games {{showed off}} both sides of that story: amazing speed, and a long distance still to go.

verbs.correct: To improve over time
verbs.wrong: To cost more each year
verbs.why: A student's English comes along with practice, and a garden comes along by summer. Experts say robot technology has come along amazingly fast.

lines.text: A robot just ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds. Faster than Usain Bolt's world record.
A robot beat Bolt?!

At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. The machines {{lined up}} like real athletes. The winner {{sped up}} smoothly, crossed the line, and then {{ended up}} in a padded wall because it couldn't stop in time.
[[I'm laughing and impressed at the same time]].
The crowd {{cheered on}} the machines anyway. More than 2,000 robots from 16 countries {{took on}} the world's best records in 51 events: soccer, table tennis, weightlifting, tug of war.
Any other records?

One machine jumped 2.88 meters in the standing high jump, higher than any human ever. There were failures too: robots {{fell over}}, crashed, sent sparks flying. Some {{got up}} by themselves and continued.
Honestly, [[that's the impressive part]].
The crowd agreed. Between events, teams {{plugged in}} their machines to charge batteries and replace parts.
Why does China host this?
The country's robot industry has {{taken off}}. China produces about 82 percent of the world's humanoid robots, and other countries are racing to {{catch up}}.
So are robot workers close?
The technology has {{come along}} fast, but most humanoids still do shows and research, not daily jobs. A machine that runs like a champion can still fail to pour a cup of coffee.
So the games {{showed off}} both sides.
Amazing speed, and a long distance still to go.
9.39 seconds and no brakes. [[Story of our times]].

stories.headline: Electronic skin gives robots a sense of touch

sources.title: Electronic skin gives robots and prosthetics human-like touch sensing (Robotics and Automation News)
Electronic skin enables tunable touch and proximity sensing (TechXplore)
Hanyang University researchers develop electronic skin with human-like touch (PR Newswire)

chunks.text: Your skin can feel a [[raindrop]], a [[handshake]], or a hot cup before you even think about it. Robots cannot. Now [[researchers]] at Hanyang University in South Korea have built an electronic skin that can {{pick up}} even a very light touch. The results {{came out}} this year in the science [[journal]] Nano Energy. One day, the [[technology]] could {{give back}} a real [[sense of touch]] to people who use [[artificial]] hands.

verbs.correct: To notice or detect something
verbs.wrong: To hold something with force
verbs.why: A microphone can pick up the softest whisper, and a security camera can pick up motion in the dark. This new electronic skin can pick up even a very light touch, almost like real human skin.

verbs.correct: To be published for the public
verbs.wrong: To be tested in a hidden lab
verbs.why: A new study comes out in a science journal every month, and a popular book sometimes comes out years after the research began. The results of this project came out this year in the journal Nano Energy.

verbs.correct: To return something that was lost
verbs.wrong: To copy something exactly
verbs.why: A kind stranger might give back a lost wallet, and a doctor can give back movement to an injured arm. One day, this skin could give back a real sense of touch to people who use artificial hands.

chunks.text: The skin is a thin, soft [[layer]] with tiny electronic [[sensors]] inside. It feels [[pressure]], and it can even notice a finger that only [[comes near]] the [[surface]], before any [[contact]] happens. The clever part is that [[engineers]] can {{turn up}} its [[sensitivity]] with a small electric [[signal]], the way you raise the [[volume]] on a speaker. A soft version could be {{built into}} a robot hand, so the hand knows the difference between an egg and a rock.

verbs.correct: To make something stronger
verbs.wrong: To repair something quickly
verbs.why: You turn up the volume on a speaker, and you turn up the heat on a stove to cook faster. Engineers can turn up this skin's sensitivity with a small electric signal, the same way you raise a volume knob.

verbs.correct: To make something part of a machine
verbs.wrong: To place something on a shelf
verbs.why: Car makers build airbags into every new vehicle, and phone makers build a camera into the back of each phone. A soft version of this electronic skin could be built into a robot hand within a few years.

chunks.text: The team also tested how long the skin lasts. It {{went through}} more than one thousand touch tests and kept working without {{wearing out}}. It [[reacts]] in about one tenth of a second, almost as fast as human skin. The researchers {{hooked up}} a small square of one hundred sensors to a computer, and it could tell exactly where each touch [[landed]].

verbs.correct: To complete a whole process
verbs.wrong: To fail an important check
verbs.why: New cars go through crash testing before they reach a showroom, and new medicine goes through years of trials. This electronic skin went through more than one thousand touch tests and kept working the whole time.

verbs.correct: To stop working from long use
verbs.wrong: To become hot and unsafe
verbs.why: Old shoes wear out after months of daily walking, and a phone battery wears out after a few years of charging. In the tests, this electronic skin kept working for over a thousand touches without wearing out.

verbs.correct: To connect to a machine
verbs.wrong: To glue onto a surface
verbs.why: A technician might hook up new speakers to a stereo, and a nurse might hook up a monitor to a patient. Researchers in this study hooked up a small square of one hundred sensors to a computer.

chunks.text: There is still work to do. The scientists are {{figuring out}} how to cover a whole robot arm instead of one small [[patch]], and how to keep the skin cheap. But the [[direction]] is clear. If the technology {{takes off}}, future robots could help [[nurses]] lift [[patients]] gently, and an artificial hand could feel a child's [[grip]]. For machines, touch is no longer [[science fiction]].

verbs.correct: To find the answer to a problem
verbs.wrong: To write the results of a test
verbs.why: A driver might figure out a shortcut after a few wrong turns, and an engineer might figure out why a machine keeps failing. Scientists are still figuring out how to cover a whole robot arm instead of just one small patch.

verbs.correct: To become successful quickly
verbs.wrong: To become cheap to produce
verbs.why: A small business can take off after one good review, and a new song can take off on social media in a week. If this technology takes off, future robots could help nurses lift patients gently and safely.

lines.text: Researchers in South Korea built an electronic skin that can feel a touch lighter than a raindrop.
Skin? For robots?

For robots, and maybe for people. It's a thin, soft layer with tiny sensors that {{pick up}} even the lightest pressure. It can even notice a finger that only comes near the surface, before any contact.
[[Before you even touch it?]] How?
That's the clever part: engineers can {{turn up}} its sensitivity with a small electric signal, like raising the volume on a speaker.
Is it strong enough for real use?

It {{went through}} more than a thousand touch tests without {{wearing out}}, and it reacts in about a tenth of a second, almost as fast as human skin. The team {{hooked up}} a hundred sensors to a computer, and it could tell exactly where each touch landed.
What would robots do with it?
A soft version could be {{built into}} a robot hand, so it knows the difference between an egg and a rock. Future robots could help nurses lift patients gently.
And for people?
[[That's the part that gets me]]. The technology could {{give back}} a real sense of touch to people who use artificial hands. Imagine feeling a child's grip again.
Where did this appear?
The results {{came out}} in the journal Nano Energy this year. The team is still {{figuring out}} how to cover a whole arm and keep it cheap.
And if it {{takes off}}?
Then touch stops being science fiction for machines.
Machines that feel. [[What a time to be alive]].
