stories.headline: A personalized cancer vaccine passes its biggest test

sources.title: Moderna and Merck say mRNA cancer vaccine succeeded in late-stage melanoma trial (STAT News)
Moderna, Merck unveil mRNA-based cancer vaccine that cuts spread (Al Jazeera)
Cancer breakthrough as personalised mRNA vaccine stops melanoma returning (Gavi VaccinesWork)
Moderna reaches 'landmark moment' in melanoma vaccine trial (video, CBS News)

chunks.text: For years, scientists have dreamed of a [[vaccine]] against cancer. This week, that dream took a giant step forward. Drug companies Moderna and Merck, which {{teamed up}} years ago, announced that their [[personalized]] [[melanoma]] vaccine passed its biggest test yet. The news {{came out}} on August 19, and doctors around the world are calling it a possible [[turning point]]. It is the first time a vaccine of this kind has succeeded in a large, final-stage [[trial]].

verbs.correct: To join forces with someone
verbs.wrong: To compete against a rival
verbs.why: Companies, students, and police departments all team up. Moderna teamed up with Merck years ago, and that partnership just passed its biggest test.

verbs.correct: To be published for the public
verbs.wrong: To be kept secret for years
verbs.why: News, results, movies, and albums come out. These results came out on August 19, the way a new phone comes out every fall.

chunks.text: Here is how it works. First, [[surgeons]] {{cut out}} the patient's [[tumor]] and send a piece to a [[laboratory]]. Scientists read the cancer's [[genetic code]] and {{pick out}} up to 34 tiny changes, called [[mutations]], that are most likely to alert the body's defenses. Next, a personal [[dose]] is {{put together}} piece by piece for that one patient and nobody else. The shot trains the [[immune system]] to {{hunt down}} escaped cancer cells the way police chase a runaway prisoner.

verbs.correct: To remove something by cutting
verbs.wrong: To measure something exactly
verbs.why: Surgeons cut out tumors during an operation, and kids cut out paper shapes with scissors. In this treatment, surgeons first cut out the patient's tumor and send a piece to a lab.

verbs.correct: To choose from a larger group
verbs.wrong: To count every single item
verbs.why: You pick out a shirt, a ring, or a name from a list. Here scientists pick out the 34 mutations most likely to wake the immune system.

verbs.correct: To build from separate parts
verbs.wrong: To divide into small pieces
verbs.why: You put together furniture, a team, or a plan. Each dose is put together for one patient, like a recipe written for a single person.

verbs.correct: To search for until found
verbs.wrong: To frighten from far away
verbs.why: Police hunt down escaped prisoners, and editors hunt down every last error. Here immune cells hunt down cancer cells hiding in the body.

chunks.text: The numbers behind the announcement are strong. More than 1,000 patients with serious melanoma joined the [[Phase 3]] trial after surgery. Patients who received the vaccine together with Keytruda, a famous cancer [[drug]], stayed [[cancer-free]] longer than patients who got the drug alone. For many of them, the melanoma has not {{come back}} at all. The [[combination]] also {{slowed down}} the disease's spread to other [[organs]]. An earlier, smaller study had already cut the risk of return in half. [[Investors]] noticed too: Moderna's [[stock price]] {{shot up}} within hours of the announcement.

verbs.correct: To return after being away
verbs.wrong: To disappear forever
verbs.why: Headaches, old fashions, and cancer can all come back. For most patients in this trial, the melanoma has not come back at all.

verbs.correct: To make something less fast
verbs.wrong: To stop something completely
verbs.why: You can slow down a car, a disease, or your spending. The vaccine combination slowed down the cancer's spread to other organs.

verbs.correct: To rise very fast
verbs.wrong: To fall little by little
verbs.why: Prices, fevers, and stocks shoot up. Moderna's stock shot up within hours, the way gas prices sometimes jump overnight.

chunks.text: What happens next? The companies are already talking with [[regulators]], and independent [[experts]] will {{go over}} the full numbers line by line at a coming medical meeting. Nobody knows yet how long the [[protection]] lasts. But if everything holds, the companies hope to {{roll out}} the treatment to thousands of patients as early as next year. And researchers are ready to {{take on}} the next challenge: using the same method against lung, kidney, and [[pancreatic]] cancer. One cancer expert said it best: this is where things begin.

verbs.correct: To examine something carefully
verbs.wrong: To forget to check something
verbs.why: You go over homework, contracts, and bills. Independent experts will go over these numbers line by line before anyone celebrates.

verbs.correct: To make available to many people
verbs.wrong: To test on a small group first
verbs.why: Companies roll out new products, apps, and programs to reach more customers. If the results hold, the companies hope to roll out this vaccine to thousands of patients as early as next year.

verbs.wrong: To avoid a hard task politely
verbs.why: A student takes on a hard class, and a worker takes on a job nobody else wants. Researchers now want to take on lung, kidney, and pancreatic cancer.

lines.text: Big medical news: a personalized cancer vaccine passed its biggest test. A large final-stage trial, the first success of its kind.
Personalized how?

Each dose is made for one patient and nobody else. Surgeons {{cut out}} the tumor and send a piece to a lab. Scientists read the cancer's genetic code and {{pick out}} up to 34 mutations most likely to alert the body's defenses. Then a personal dose is {{put together}} piece by piece.
And what does the shot actually do?
It trains the immune system to {{hunt down}} escaped cancer cells, like police chasing a runaway prisoner.
What were the results?

More than 1,000 melanoma patients joined after surgery. Those who got the vaccine with a famous cancer drug stayed cancer-free longer, and for many the melanoma hasn't {{come back}} at all. The combination also {{slowed down}} the spread to other organs.
[[This sounds almost too good]]. [[What's the catch?]]
[[Fair caution]]. Nobody knows yet how long the protection lasts, and independent experts still need to {{go over}} the full numbers line by line.
When could patients get it?

The companies that {{teamed up}} on it are talking with regulators and hope to {{roll out}} the treatment as early as next year. Researchers are ready to {{take on}} lung, kidney, and pancreatic cancer next.
How did the world react?
The news {{came out}} on August 19, and doctors call it a possible turning point. Moderna's stock {{shot up}} within hours.
A vaccine built for one person at a time.
One expert said it best: [[this is where things begin]].

stories.headline: Rage bait: the trick that turns your anger into money

sources.title: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait (Oxford University Press)
Don't get angry, but the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year is 'rage bait' (NPR)
Oxford University Press picks 'rage bait' as its word of the year (CBS News)
Why 'Rage Bait' is Oxford's Word of the Year (video, Firstpost)

chunks.text: You see a post so wrong that your face gets hot. A cooking video that [[ruins]] a famous [[dish]] on purpose. An opinion nobody could truly believe. Before you type your [[furious]] reply, stop: it may be [[rage bait]], content made [[deliberately]] to {{stir up}} anger. The trick works because rage bait {{relies on}} one simple fact: angry people click, comment, and share more than happy ones.

verbs.correct: To cause strong feelings or trouble
verbs.wrong: To calm a group of people
verbs.why: A rumor stirs up worry in the office, and one loud complaint can stir up a whole crowd. Rage bait stirs up your feelings on purpose, because angry people click.

verbs.correct: To need something to work or succeed
verbs.wrong: To copy something step by step
verbs.why: You rely on your phone, your friends, or your paycheck. This whole business relies on one fact: anger gets more clicks than joy.

chunks.text: Here is how the game works. A creator posts something designed to feel [[unfair]] or completely wrong. Readers {{give in}} to the [[temptation]] to [[correct]] it, and soon hundreds of [[strangers]] {{pile on}} in the comments. Every reply pushes the post higher, so the crowd {{winds up}} paying the creator with the one thing he wanted: [[attention]]. The [[outrage]] is real, but the [[opinion]] often is not. Some rage baiters [[admit]] they do not believe a word of their own posts.

verbs.correct: To stop fighting a feeling or demand
verbs.wrong: To make a promise to yourself
verbs.why: People give in to temptation, pressure, and cravings. You promise not to reply, you read the post again, and you give in.

verbs.correct: To join many others in attacking
verbs.wrong: To leave a group one by one
verbs.why: When hundreds attack the same post or person, they pile on. It feels safe to pile on because everyone else is already doing it.

verbs.correct: To reach an end you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To start something with energy
verbs.why: You wind up lost, awake at 3 a.m., or deep in an argument with a stranger. Nobody plans it, they just wind up there.

chunks.text: The word had a big year. In December 2025, dictionary experts at Oxford picked rage bait as their [[word of the year]], beating aura farming and biohack. More than 30,000 people voted, and use of the term [[tripled]] in just twelve months. The phrase {{caught on}} quickly, but the idea is older: it first appeared in an online [[forum]] back in 2002. The [[editors]] define rage bait as content built to cause anger and raise a site's [[traffic]] and [[engagement]]. Angry readers who {{call out}} the trick in the comments often just make it stronger.

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To confuse almost everyone
verbs.why: Songs, slang, and trends catch on. This phrase caught on so fast it went from internet forums to the dictionary.

verbs.correct: To publicly say something is wrong
verbs.wrong: To whisper a secret to a friend
verbs.why: People call out lies, cheating, and fake stories. Creators who use rage bait are now called out by name, publicly.

chunks.text: So what should you do when a post [[makes your blood boil]]? Experts say the hardest step is to {{pass up}} the chance to tell a stranger he is wrong. Try to {{hold back}} your first hot reply until the anger cools, and ask a simple question: who [[profits]] from my anger? The [[storm]] around a rage bait post usually {{blows over}} in a day, but the views remain forever. If a post exists only to make you angry, the smartest answer is quiet: do not [[take the bait]], and just {{log off}}.

verbs.correct: To choose not to take a chance
verbs.wrong: To grab an offer with both hands
verbs.why: You pass up job offers, desserts, and chances. The hardest thing online is passing up the chance to correct a stranger.

verbs.correct: To keep a strong feeling inside
verbs.wrong: To express a feeling loudly
verbs.why: You hold back tears when you say goodbye, and you hold back a smile during a serious meeting. The advice here: hold your first comment back until the anger cools.

verbs.correct: To pass and be forgotten soon
verbs.wrong: To grow bigger every hour
verbs.why: Office gossip blows over, and an argument between friends blows over in a few days. The outrage blows over in a day, but the creator keeps the views forever.

verbs.correct: To stop using an app or website
verbs.wrong: To create a new online account
verbs.why: You log off a website, an app, or a work computer. Sometimes the smartest reply to the internet is logging off.

lines.text: You know that post that made you furious last week? The terrible cooking video?
The one where he put ketchup in the carbonara? I typed three replies!
Did you send them?
...One.

Then the trick worked on you. That was probably rage bait, content made deliberately to {{stir up}} anger. It {{relies on}} one simple fact: angry people click, comment, and share more than happy ones.
So my furious comment helped him?

Every reply pushes the post higher. Readers {{give in}} to the temptation to correct it, hundreds of strangers {{pile on}}, and the crowd {{winds up}} paying the creator with attention. Some rage baiters admit they don't believe a word of their own posts.
[[That's diabolical]]. Is this new?

The idea appeared in an online forum back in 2002, but the word had a big year. Oxford's dictionary experts picked "rage bait" as word of the year, and use of the term tripled in twelve months. It really {{caught on}}.
What about calling the trick out in the comments?
Angry readers who {{call out}} the trick usually just make the post stronger.
So what's the smart move?

{{Pass up}} the chance to tell a stranger he's wrong. {{Hold back}} the hot reply until the anger cools, and ask: who profits from my anger? The storm {{blows over}} in a day, but the views stay forever.
And if the post exists only to make me angry?
Then the smartest answer is quiet. Don't [[take the bait]]. Just {{log off}}.
Deleting my other two drafts now. [[Lesson learned]].

stories.headline: US debt passes 40 trillion dollars

sources.title: The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion (NPR)
U.S. government debt passes $40 trillion, more than doubling in a decade (CNBC)
US debt hits $40 trillion: Who does Washington owe? (Al Jazeera)
US debt hits 40 trillion dollars: the price per American (video, CNN)

chunks.text: The United States government has never [[owed]] this much money. Its [[debt]] has been {{piling up}} for [[decades]], and in August it passed 40 [[trillion]] dollars for the first time. Divide that by [[every man, woman, and child]] in the country, and it {{works out to}} more than 115,000 dollars each. The [[pace]] is {{speeding up}}, too: the last trillion arrived in only about five months.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted one more time
verbs.why: Debt, dishes, emails, and homework pile up. Forty trillion did not arrive at once, it piled up over decades.

verbs.correct: To equal after the math is done
verbs.wrong: To become a smaller number
verbs.why: Use it for the result of math. The debt works out to 115,000 dollars per person, and 40 hours at 15 dollars works out to 600.

verbs.correct: To happen faster than before
verbs.wrong: To become easier to stop
verbs.why: Cars, hearts, and bad habits speed up. The borrowing has sped up too: the last trillion took only five months.

chunks.text: How does a country build a debt like that? Every year, the government {{takes in}} far less in [[taxes]] than it spends, and the [[gap]] is now more than two trillion dollars a year. To [[cover]] it, the government [[borrows]], and borrowed money is never free. The government must now {{set aside}} more than one trillion dollars from its [[budget]] every year just to pay [[interest]] on the old debt.

verbs.correct: To receive as income
verbs.wrong: To spend on programs
verbs.why: Governments take in taxes, stores take in cash, movies take in millions. Washington spends far more than it takes in.

verbs.correct: To save for one special use
verbs.wrong: To borrow at a lower rate
verbs.why: You set aside savings, an hour for exercise, or part of a budget. Over a trillion a year is now set aside just for interest.

chunks.text: Why should [[ordinary]] people care? Because heavy government borrowing can {{drive up}} [[interest rates]] for everyone else. When the government needs to borrow so much, families who {{take out}} a [[loan]] for a house or a car feel it too. The [[average]] rate on a 30-year US home loan is now near 6.7 percent, and [[long-term]] borrowing costs recently reached their highest level in almost twenty years.

verbs.correct: To force something higher
verbs.wrong: To spread something evenly
verbs.why: Wars, shortages, and heavy borrowing drive up prices and rates. A debt this size can drive up the cost of your own car loan.

verbs.correct: To arrange to borrow money
verbs.wrong: To pay a debt very slowly
verbs.why: You take out a loan, a mortgage, or a credit card. Families taking out a house loan feel it when government borrowing grows.

chunks.text: Experts from both political parties call the [[path]] [[unsustainable]], and, so far, the country's leaders keep {{putting off}} the [[hard choices]]. But the problem will not {{go away}} on its own, and the longer the country waits, the more expensive the [[fix]] becomes. In the end, the [[options]] {{boil down to}} spending less, collecting more in taxes, or both. [[One way or another]], someone will have to {{pick up}} the [[bill]], and it may be today's students.

verbs.correct: To delay until later
verbs.wrong: To argue about loudly
verbs.why: People put off homework, dentist visits, and hard conversations. Leaders have put off this decision for thirty years.

verbs.correct: To stop existing
verbs.wrong: To become smaller
verbs.why: Headaches, storms, and problems go away, or we hope so. Every expert agrees this debt will not go away by itself.

verbs.correct: To reduce to the main choices
verbs.wrong: To grow more complicated
verbs.why: Long debates boil down to something simple. This one boils down to three options: spend less, tax more, or both.

verbs.correct: To pay for something yourself
verbs.wrong: To split a cost with others
verbs.why: You pick up the bill at a restaurant or the cost of a friend's ticket. Someone always pays in the end, and here it may be today's students.

It's been {{piling up}} for decades. Every year the government {{takes in}} far less in taxes than it spends. The gap is over two trillion a year, and borrowed money is never free.
How much is the interest?
The government must {{set aside}} more than one trillion dollars every year just for interest on the old debt. And the pace is {{speeding up}}: the last trillion arrived in about five months.
Why should regular people care?
Because heavy government borrowing can {{drive up}} interest rates for everyone. Families who {{take out}} a loan for a house or a car feel it. The average 30-year home loan is near 6.7 percent.
Is anyone doing something about it?
Experts from both parties call the path unsustainable, but leaders keep {{putting off}} the hard choices.
And the problem won't just disappear.
No, it won't {{go away}} on its own. The options {{boil down to}} spending less, collecting more in taxes, or both.
So someone has to {{pick up}} the bill.
And it may be today's students. [[The longer you wait, the more it costs]].

chunks.text: Were [[likes]], [[endless]] feeds, and [[constant]] notifications designed [[on purpose]] to [[hook]] children? That is the question [[at the heart of]] a huge [[trial]] that began in mid-August in a [[federal court]] in California. Four US states have {{teamed up}} to {{take on}} Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, in one of the biggest tech cases in American history.

chunks.text: The case is about app features everyone knows. [[Notifications]] {{pop up}} on the screen [[at all hours]], so young users return [[again and again]]. The [[feed]] never ends, so there is no natural place to stop. Likes and other small rewards {{draw in}} teenagers and keep them [[scrolling]]. Many teens say they cannot {{put down}} the phone, even at dinner or late at night. The states [[argue]] that these [[designs]] were built to hold children's [[attention]], [[whatever the cost]].

verbs.wrong: To sound louder at night

verbs.wrong: To push people away

chunks.text: The states want big changes. They ask the court to make Meta {{do away with}} some of these features for young users, and they demand up to 1.4 trillion dollars, one of the largest amounts ever requested in a US court. Meta {{pushes back}} hard against the [[claims]]. The company {{stands by}} its [[record]], saying it has built strong [[protections]] for teens and that the [[demands]] are [[unfair]].

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To improve something slowly
verbs.why: Cities do away with old rules, schools with exams, companies with fees. The states want Meta to do away with these features for minors.

verbs.correct: To resist and disagree strongly
verbs.wrong: To ignore every question

chunks.text: The trial is expected to {{go on}} for about six weeks, and the whole tech world is watching. A loss could change how social media looks and feels for everyone. An entire [[generation]] has {{grown up}} with likes, notifications, and endless feeds, and courts are only now deciding what that means. chunks.text: Just after [[dawn]] on August 10, the ground in western Colombia began to shake. The earthquake, with a [[magnitude]] of 7.4, was one of the strongest in the country's modern history. People {{rushed out}} of their homes in cities as far away as Bogota and Medellin, and the [[shaking]] was felt in Ecuador and Panama. In several cities, buildings {{came down}}, and more than 290 people [[lost their lives]].

verbs.correct: To fall to the ground
verbs.wrong: To shake from side to side
verbs.why: A tree branch can come down in a strong wind, and an old chimney might come down during a storm. Several buildings in western Colombia came down when the magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck.

chunks.text: The worst problems are in Choco, a [[region]] of mountains and deep forest near the [[epicenter]]. The quake {{set off}} [[landslides]] that [[buried]] the roads, and some villages were completely {{cut off}}: no cars, no trucks, no help. [[Rescue teams]] are trying to {{get through}} to them, but with the roads gone, even reaching the smallest towns can take days. Helicopters may be the only [[way in]].

verbs.wrong: To predict something early
verbs.why: A dropped match can set off a grass fire, and heavy rain can set off a flood warning downtown. The earthquake set off landslides that buried the mountain roads leading into Choco.

verbs.wrong: To leave without any lights
verbs.why: Deep snow can cut off a mountain town for days, and a flood can cut off the only bridge to a farm. Several villages near the epicenter were completely cut off, with no cars, no trucks, and no way to reach them.

verbs.wrong: To request extra helpers
verbs.why: Snowplows work all night so trucks can get through after a blizzard, and climbers sometimes cannot get through in a storm. Rescue teams are trying to get through to villages the landslides left blocked.

chunks.text: Closer to the cities, the rescue work never stops. Neighbors and [[firefighters]] {{dug out}} [[survivors]] from under fallen walls with [[bare hands]] and [[shovels]]. Rescuers work [[day and night]] and refuse to {{give up}} while people are still missing. Every person pulled from the [[rubble]] brings new energy to the teams.

verbs.wrong: To carry someone to a doctor

More than 140 people are still [[missing]], so [[officials]] fear the number of dead may {{go up}}. Many families lost everything and must now {{start over}} and slowly [[rebuild]] their lives. chunks.text: It started as a normal workday in Dendermonde, a town in the Belgian region of East Flanders. A construction [[crew]] was digging under an old building, once home to a [[brewery]], to lay new [[sewer pipes]]. Then a worker's [[drill]] {{broke through}} an old [[cellar]] wall, and something yellow appeared in the dust. While doing one of the least [[glamorous]] jobs in construction, the crew had {{come across}} it [[by pure chance]]: a [[fortune]] in gold.

chunks.text: In three big US cities, a taxi with no driver just became normal. Waymo's newest robotaxi, a [[roomy]] electric [[minivan]] called the Ojai, is now open to everyone in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco. The vans have been {{showing up}} in [[traffic]] next to regular cars all summer, but riders could not choose one until now. Today, anyone with the app can {{hop in}} when their car arrives, with no one [[behind the wheel]].

verbs.wrong: To make a loud noise
verbs.why: Guests, buses, and taxis show up, or they do not. Here the car shows up by itself, with nobody behind the wheel.

verbs.wrong: To wait beside the road
verbs.why: Hop in the car, hop in a taxi: quick, casual entering. Riders just hop in when their van arrives.

chunks.text: The Ojai is built to cost less. The base van comes from China, but it arrives without its Chinese internet [[software]]: Waymo {{takes out}} that system and {{puts in}} its own [[self-driving]] brain at a [[factory]] in Arizona. Each van is cheaper to build and run than the Jaguar cars the company used before. There is one problem: [[import taxes]] {{push up}} the price of every van that crosses the ocean.

verbs.correct: To remove something from inside
verbs.wrong: To test something one more time

verbs.correct: To make a price higher

verbs.why: Taxes, demand, and shortages push up prices. Import taxes push up the cost of every van that crosses the ocean.

chunks.text: Riding in one feels simple. [[Passengers]] sit down, {{buckle up}}, and press a button. The van joins traffic [[on its own]]. A talking [[assistant]] answers questions during the ride. For now, the app [[decides]] which car you get, so riders {{end up}} with either the new van or an older Jaguar. Soon, riders will be able to {{pick out}} the [[model]] they want right in the app.

verbs.wrong: To choose the safest seat
verbs.why: Buckle up in a car, a plane, or a rollercoaster. Passengers sit, buckle up, press a button, and the van drives.

chunks.text: Waymo is [[moving fast]]. About 300 of the new vans are [[on the road]] today, and one [[analyst]] expects the [[fleet]] to reach 5,000 [[by the end of the year]]. The company also plans to {{roll out}} the service in Denver, Las Vegas, and San Diego later this year. [[Driverless]] rides are [[no longer]] a science [[experiment]]. The question now is price: will cheaper vans mean cheaper rides, and will lower prices {{win over}} people who still {{hold back}}?

chunks.text: What does a [[hurricane]] eat? Warm ocean water. Big storms {{feed on}} heat near the sea [[surface]], and a [[patch]] of unusually warm water can {{set off}} rapid growth in a passing storm. To [[predict]] that growth, [[forecasters]] need to know how warm the ocean is, and not just at the top. The problem: the open sea is huge, and much of it is never measured.

lines.text: [[Guess what]] hurricanes and sharks now have in common.
[[I have no idea where this is going]].
Forecasting. Hurricanes {{feed on}} warm ocean water, and a patch of unusually warm sea can {{set off}} rapid growth in a passing storm. The problem is that most of the open ocean is never measured.
So where do sharks fit?

Scientists {{went over}} 20 years of shark-tracking records and {{settled on}} two species that often swim near the surface: makos and blue sharks. Small sensors on their fins measure temperature, depth, and saltiness.
And how does the data reach anyone?
Whenever a shark {{comes up}} to the surface, the tag {{sends back}} the measurements by satellite. Makos {{turned out}} to be perfect, they visit the surface about twice a day.
Why not just use robots and buoys?
Machines have limits. A robot can {{break down}}, and a buoy stays in one place. Sharks never stop swimming, and they move up and down through the water all day.
How many sharks are tagged?

The project is {{starting out}} small, a handful so far, and the engineers are still improving the tags. But [[every measurement counts]]. More sharks could {{fill in}} the empty spots on the ocean heat map.
And better maps mean better forecasts?
Which gives coastal towns more time to prepare or {{get out}} before a storm arrives.
Sharks saving beach towns. [[Who would have thought]].

stories.headline: Dogs can read the feelings on your face

sources.title: Brain scans show that dogs can distinguish emotions in human faces (University of Vienna)
Dogs can tell fear from sadness (ScienceDaily)

chunks.text: Does your dog know when you are sad? Many [[owners]] feel that their pets can [[sense]] their [[moods]], and new [[brain scans]] point to an answer: yes, more than we thought. Scientists at the University of Vienna {{set out}} to test what really happens inside a dog's head when it looks at a human face.

verbs.correct: To begin a job with a plan
verbs.wrong: To finish a long project
verbs.why: A young company might set out to change an entire industry, and a researcher might set out to answer one hard question. Scientists at the University of Vienna set out to test what happens inside a dog's brain when it sees a human face.

chunks.text: The team {{signed up}} 12 friendly family dogs whose owners wanted to help. Each dog {{went through}} careful [[training]] so it could [[lie still]] and [[stay awake]] inside the [[scanner]]. [[Treats]] and soft words helped the dogs {{settle down}} in the [[noisy]] machine. The researchers then {{put together}} sets of photos showing four feelings on human faces: happiness, anger, fear, and sadness.

verbs.wrong: To pay someone for their work
verbs.why: A gym signs up new members every January, and a coach signs up kids for the summer soccer camp. For this study, researchers signed up 12 friendly family dogs whose owners wanted to take part.

verbs.correct: To complete a whole process
verbs.wrong: To skip an important part
verbs.why: New employees go through a week of training, and pilots go through a strict safety checklist before takeoff. Each dog in the study went through careful training so it could lie still inside the brain scanner.

verbs.correct: To become calm and quiet
verbs.wrong: To fall into a deep sleep
verbs.why: A crying baby can settle down with a soft song, and a noisy classroom can settle down once the teacher speaks. Treats and gentle words helped the dogs settle down inside the loud scanning machine.

verbs.correct: To prepare a set of things
verbs.wrong: To choose one favorite thing
verbs.why: A chef might put together a meal from a few simple ingredients, and a manager might put together a team for a new project. The researchers put together sets of photos showing four human feelings for the dogs to view.

chunks.text: When the dogs saw a happy face, a [[reward]] area deep in the brain {{lit up}} like a Christmas tree: the same area that becomes active for food and play. Smiles clearly matter to dogs. With help from a [[computer program]], the scans also showed that dogs could {{pick up on}} the [[difference]] between fear and sadness, two feelings that even people sometimes [[confuse]]. The brain [[pattern]] for fear {{stood out}} from the patterns for anger and sadness.

verbs.correct: To become active and bright
verbs.wrong: To slowly stop working
verbs.why: A child's face can light up at the sight of a birthday cake, and a dark room can light up when lightning flashes. In the scans, a reward area deep in the brain lit up whenever a dog saw a happy face.

verbs.correct: To notice something not obvious
verbs.wrong: To guess without any proof
verbs.why: A good friend can pick up on a small change in your mood, and a teacher can pick up on a quiet, worried student. The scans showed dogs pick up on the difference between a fearful face and a sad one.

verbs.correct: To be clearly different
verbs.wrong: To disappear from view
verbs.why: A bright red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one wrong answer stands out on an otherwise perfect test. In the scans, the brain pattern for fear stood out clearly from the patterns for anger and sadness.

chunks.text: The study came out this month in a science [[journal]], and it is the first clear [[evidence]] that dogs can read several human feelings in a face. Still, the scientists are careful. All the dogs were [[well-loved]] pets, and real life gives dogs much more than [[still photos]]: dogs also read [[body language]], voices, and [[smell]]. The team wants to {{follow up}} with tests closer to daily life. One thing is sure: the [[friendship]] between people and dogs {{goes back}} thousands of years, and dogs may understand us better than we knew.

verbs.correct: To continue with more work
verbs.wrong: To argue against a result
verbs.why: A doctor might follow up with a phone call after surgery, and a reporter might follow up on a story with new questions. The research team wants to follow up with tests that feel closer to a dog's daily life.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a time
verbs.wrong: To improve year after year
verbs.why: A family recipe can go back several generations, and an old friendship can go back to grade school. The bond between people and dogs goes back thousands of years, and this study shows how deep it runs.

lines.text: Science finally answered a big question: your dog really can read your face.
[[I knew it!]] My dog always knows when I'm sad.
Now there are brain scans to prove it. Researchers in Vienna {{set out}} to test what happens inside a dog's head when it looks at a human face.
How do you scan a dog's brain? They never sit still.

Training. The team {{signed up}} 12 family dogs, and each one {{went through}} careful training to lie still and stay awake in the scanner. Treats and soft words helped them {{settle down}} in the noisy machine.
[[I would watch a whole documentary about that]]. What did they show the dogs?
The researchers {{put together}} photo sets of four feelings: happiness, anger, fear, and sadness.
And?
When a dog saw a happy face, a reward area deep in its brain {{lit up}} like a Christmas tree. The same area that reacts to food and play.
So smiles matter to dogs.

Clearly. And with a computer's help, the scans showed dogs could {{pick up on}} the difference between fear and sadness, two feelings even people confuse. The fear pattern {{stood out}} from anger and sadness.
So they know more than we thought.
The scientists stay careful. These were well-loved pets, and real life gives dogs voices, body language, and smell, not just photos. The team wants to {{follow up}} with tests closer to daily life.
Still. Thousands of years of friendship, and they've been reading us [[the whole time]].
The bond {{goes back}} that far, yes. Maybe that's why it works. [[Dogs really are something else]].

chunks.text: How far can you walk from your [[front door]]? In some [[neighborhoods]], people can {{get around}} on foot all day: the school, the store, and the park are just minutes away. In others, every little [[errand]] means a car trip that {{eats up}} time. This month, the National Institutes of Health {{put out}} its regular health [[newsletter]] with a big question: can the [[design]] of your street make you healthier?

verbs.correct: To move from place to place
verbs.wrong: To travel a very long way
verbs.why: Without a car, some people get around by bike and bus, and tourists often get around an old town easily on foot. In walkable neighborhoods, people can get around on foot for the school, the store, and the park.

chunks.text: The answer seems to be yes. One large study found that people who moved to more [[walkable]] cities {{ended up}} walking about 1,100 extra steps every day. Those steps {{add up}} to almost one extra hour of [[movement]] every week. lines.text: [[Quick question]]: how far can you walk from your front door? School, store, park?
[[Ha]]. In my neighborhood, every errand is a car trip.

Then this is about you. A newsletter the National Institutes of Health just {{put out}} asks: can the design of your street make you healthier? In some places people {{get around}} on foot all day. In others, the car {{eats up}} all the time.
How big is the effect?
One large study found that people who moved to more walkable cities {{ended up}} walking about 1,100 extra steps a day. Those steps {{add up}} to almost an extra hour of movement a week.
An hour a week from street design alone. [[Not bad!]]
Over the years it lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, and depression.
But I can't rebuild my street.

Residents can push, though. In one Stanford project, neighbors {{team up}}, walk their own streets, and {{point out}} problems to local leaders: missing crosswalks, dark corners. They {{send in}} photos to city planners through an app.
Does that actually change anything?
It has spread to more than 30 states and 30 countries, and many fixes are cheap: paint a crosswalk, add a bench, fix the lighting.
And until my city acts?
Small moves. Park farther away, take the stairs, walk to the store. Doctors suggest you {{map out}} a short walking route near home and {{stick to}} it even on busy days.
Does it really {{pay off}}?
A stronger heart and a better mood. [[Hard to argue with that]].

stories.headline: A short video game may spot depression

sources.title: Depression screening using video games (NIH Research Matters)
3-Minute Video Game Identifies Patients Who Have Depression (NYU Langone)
This 3-Minute Video Game Is Surprisingly Good at Spotting Depression (Gizmodo)

chunks.text: A short video game on a phone may help doctors spot [[depression]] in about three minutes. The illness is hard to [[measure]], so a team at New York University had to {{come up with}} a [[fresh]] way to test for it: two simple games. The team {{carried out}} a study where 120 people played the games, 50 with the illness and 70 without. The results were published in May in a major science [[journal]], and this month the National Institutes of Health [[featured]] the study in its health news for the public. One day, doctors could use short games like these [[instead of]] long [[questionnaires]].

verbs.correct: To invent a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To copy an older way of testing
verbs.why: A team can come up with a clever name for a new product, and engineers sometimes come up with a cheaper way to build something. A team at New York University came up with two short games to test for depression in just minutes.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of planned work
verbs.wrong: To pay for a piece of research
verbs.why: A hospital carries out safety checks every month, and a scientist carries out an experiment step by step. The NYU team carried out a study where 120 people played the games, 50 of them living with depression.

chunks.text: The first game asks players to pick apples from a tree on the screen. Every pick gives fewer apples, so each tree slowly {{runs low}} on fruit, and the player must decide when to {{move on}} to a fresh tree. [[On average]], healthy players {{held out}} until a tree was almost empty. Players with depression {{walked away from}} their trees much sooner, and the worse their illness was, the earlier they left. The game measures the moment when picking apples stops feeling [[rewarding]]. About 70 percent of people with depression lose [[pleasure]] in things they [[used to]] enjoy.

verbs.correct: To have less and less left
verbs.wrong: To become full again slowly
verbs.why: A printer can run low on ink in the middle of a big job, and water sometimes runs low on the third day of a hike. In the game's first task, each apple tree slowly runs low on fruit the longer a player keeps picking.

verbs.correct: To leave and go to the next thing
verbs.wrong: To rest before starting again
verbs.why: After years in one job, a person might feel ready to move on, and a meeting moves on to the next topic once everyone has spoken. In the apple game, the player must decide the exact moment to move on to a fresh tree.

verbs.correct: To continue for as long as possible
verbs.wrong: To count the apples one by one
verbs.why: A phone battery can hold out until the end of a long flight, and packed food might hold out for a whole camping trip. In the study, healthy players on average held out picking apples until a tree was almost empty.

verbs.correct: To leave something without finishing it
verbs.wrong: To shake something to get more fruit
verbs.why: Some people walk away from a well paid job to try something new, and you cannot always walk away from a project halfway through. In the study, players with depression walked away from their apple trees much sooner than healthy players did.

chunks.text: In the second game, players looked at 30 [[snacks]] and said what each one should cost. Then the game showed some players only the cheapest items, [[over and over]]. Healthy players changed their minds: seeing cheap snacks {{brought down}} the price they expected to pay, [[little by little]]. Players with depression mostly {{stuck with}} their first numbers. The scientists say their [[expectations]] did not [[adjust]] to the new situation, and that this stuck feeling may be an important part of the illness.

verbs.correct: To make something lower
verbs.wrong: To make something fair
verbs.why: A new factory can bring down the price of batteries over time, and fresh competition often brings down airline fares. In the snack game, seeing cheap items again and again slowly brought down the price healthy players expected to pay.

verbs.correct: To keep using the same thing
verbs.wrong: To forget something quickly
verbs.why: Some people stick with the same hairdresser for twenty years, and a runner might stick with water instead of anything sweet during a race. In the snack game, players with depression mostly stuck with their first price guesses, even after seeing new information.

chunks.text: The team hopes to {{roll out}} the game to [[clinics]] one day and plans to ask US [[regulators]] for official [[approval]] as a medical [[device]]. Patients could also play at home once a week, so doctors can {{keep track of}} how well a [[treatment]] is working [[within]] two or three weeks instead of months. The researchers are careful about the [[limits]]. Not everyone with depression plays the same way, and a game cannot {{rule out}} that a player is simply tired or stressed. [[For now]], the game's job is to {{back up}} a doctor's opinion with extra information, not to [[replace]] the doctor.

verbs.correct: To make something widely available
verbs.wrong: To keep something secret for a time
verbs.why: A bank might roll out a new app in the spring, and a city can roll out electric buses one route at a time. The NYU team hopes to roll out its short game to clinics once it earns official approval.

verbs.correct: To follow and record changes
verbs.wrong: To make something change faster
verbs.why: Some people keep track of their spending in a small notebook, and a running app can keep track of how far you go each day. With this game, doctors could keep track of a patient's progress in a few weeks instead of months.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To treat something with medicine
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a broken bone with a quick scan, and police sometimes cannot rule out any suspects early in a case. This game cannot rule out that a low score simply means a player is tired or stressed that day.

verbs.correct: To support with more evidence
verbs.wrong: To watch someone very closely
verbs.why: Two witnesses might back up a friend's story, and solid data can back up a coach's tough decision. For now, this game's job is to back up a doctor's opinion with extra information, not to replace the doctor.

lines.text: Doctors may soon spot depression with a three-minute video game.
A video game? How would that work?
Depression is hard to measure, so a team in New York {{came up with}} two simple games and {{carried out}} a study with 120 people.
What do the games look like?
The first one is about picking apples from trees. Every pick gives fewer apples, so each tree slowly {{runs low}}, and you decide when to {{move on}} to a fresh tree.
And people play differently?

Very. Healthy players {{held out}} until a tree was almost empty. Players with depression {{walked away from}} their trees much sooner. The game measures the moment when picking stops feeling rewarding.
[[That's clever, and a little sad]].

It matches the illness: about 70 percent of people with depression lose pleasure in things they used to enjoy. The second game is about expectations. Players guessed what 30 snacks should cost. Then the game showed them only the cheapest snacks, again and again. Healthy players [[got the message]]: snacks are cheap here. Little by little, that {{brought down}} the price they expected to pay for the next snack. Players with depression didn't update. They {{stuck with}} their original prices.
Meaning their expectations didn't adjust?
Exactly. The world changed, and their guesses didn't move with it. That stuck feeling may be an important part of the illness.
What's the plan for it?

The team hopes to {{roll out}} the game to clinics and ask regulators to approve it as a medical device. Patients could play at home weekly, so doctors {{keep track of}} whether a treatment is working in weeks instead of months.
Can a game really diagnose someone, though?
No, and the researchers say so themselves. A game can't {{rule out}} that a player is just tired or stressed. Its job is to {{back up}} a doctor's opinion, not replace the doctor.
[[Fair enough]]. [[A tool, not a judge]].
[[Exactly that]]. And three minutes instead of a long questionnaire.

stories.headline: Three midlife risks are linked to dementia

sources.title: Avoiding These 3 Things in Midlife Is Linked to 13 More Dementia-Free Years
3 things to avoid in middle age could mean 13 more years without dementia, study finds
Avoiding 3 risk factors in midlife could add 13 dementia-free years

chunks.text: A long American study {{took in}} 12,409 adults who {{started off}} with [[no sign of]] [[dementia]]. Researchers {{kept track of}} them for about 26 years, and the results were published in the journal Neurology on August 5. The work asked a simple question: how much does health in [[midlife]] change what happens later? It looked at three [[risk factors]]: [[high blood pressure]], [[diabetes]] and [[smoking]].

verbs.correct: To include people in a study
verbs.wrong: To follow a patient for one year
verbs.why: A study can take in thousands of volunteers, and a survey might take in people from many countries. A long American study took in more than 12,000 adults who showed no sign of dementia at the start.

verbs.correct: To be in a state at the beginning
verbs.wrong: To leave a study before it ends
verbs.why: A meeting can start off with introductions, a road trip can start off badly in traffic, and a new job can start off stressful. Every adult in this study started off with no sign of dementia at all.

verbs.correct: To follow something over a long time
verbs.wrong: To treat an illness with medicine
verbs.why: People keep track of their spending, coaches keep track of a player's progress, and parents keep track of a child's growth. Researchers kept track of this group of adults for about 26 years to see what happened to their health.

chunks.text: Adults who had none of the three in middle age {{went on}} to live about 30 years without dementia after the study began. Adults who had all three [[managed]] about 17. The [[gap]] {{adds up to}} roughly 13 years. People with all three were also about 2.7 [[times more likely]] to [[develop]] dementia [[at some point]]. The same [[pattern]] {{came through}} for men and women, with only small differences.

verbs.correct: To continue living for a period
verbs.wrong: To join a different research study
verbs.why: Students go on to college, an injured athlete can go on to have a great career, and a small shop can go on for generations. Adults with none of the three risks went on to live about 30 more years without dementia.

verbs.correct: To reach a total of a certain amount
verbs.wrong: To count the years without dementia
verbs.why: Small tips add up to real money by the end of a shift, and daily coffees add up to hundreds of dollars a year. The gap between these two groups adds up to roughly 13 extra years of healthy life.

verbs.correct: To show clearly in the results
verbs.wrong: To appear in men but not in women
verbs.why: Hard work comes through in a final score, and nervousness often comes through in an interview. In this study, the same pattern of lower risk with fewer conditions came through for both men and women.

chunks.text: The three factors were measured together, so the study cannot {{single out}} which one matters most. It also cannot {{tell apart}} a real [[cause]] from a [[coincidence]]. This is [[observational]] work: it watched what happened to people who already smoked or already had [[raised]] blood pressure. Money, education and [[genes]] shape health [[as well]], and they may {{make up}} part of the gap.

verbs.correct: To choose one thing out of a group
verbs.wrong: To measure two things at once
verbs.why: Teachers single out one student for special praise, and judges single out one dish as the best of the night. Because the three risks were measured together, this study cannot single out which one matters most.

verbs.correct: To see the difference between two things
verbs.wrong: To explain a result to the public
verbs.why: Even close friends sometimes cannot tell twins apart, and new drivers may not tell two similar cars apart. This study also cannot tell apart a real cause from simple coincidence, since it only watched people over time.

verbs.correct: To form one part of a whole
verbs.wrong: To disprove an earlier finding
verbs.why: Women make up half of the company's staff, and fruit makes up most of a healthy diet. Money, education, and genes may also make up part of the 13-year gap between these two groups.

chunks.text: The numbers are real, but they are not a promise. Nobody can say that if you {{steer clear of}} cigarettes today, or {{cut out}} sugar, or {{get into}} walking, your own dementia will be {{pushed back}} [[by]] 13 years. What the study does show is that doctors already treat these three conditions in [[middle age]], and the same conditions are linked to dementia [[decades]] later. The [[funders]] were the National Institutes of Health.

verbs.correct: To avoid something harmful
verbs.wrong: To improve your health very slowly
verbs.why: Drivers steer clear of icy roads, and many people steer clear of fried food during the week. The study does not promise that steering clear of cigarettes today will delay your own dementia by exactly 13 years.

verbs.correct: To stop eating a type of food
verbs.wrong: To measure blood sugar every day
verbs.why: Many people cut out sugar to lose weight, and some cut out red meat for their heart. The study cannot promise that if you cut out sugar today, dementia will arrive exactly 13 years later.

verbs.correct: To begin doing an activity often
verbs.wrong: To reach an older age in good health
verbs.why: People get into running after a health scare, and others get into cooking during a long winter. The study cannot promise that if you get into walking now, your own dementia risk will change by an exact amount.

verbs.correct: To make something happen later
verbs.wrong: To lower the risk of an illness
verbs.why: Airlines push back flights during storms, and offices push back meetings when someone arrives late. The study cannot promise that your own dementia risk will be pushed back by exactly 13 years.

mainIdea.s: A 26-year study found that adults with no high blood pressure, diabetes or smoking lived about 13 more years without dementia. It only watched people, so the gap may not be a direct cause.
mainIdea.why: Adults with none of the three risks lived about 30 years without dementia, and those with all three lived about 17. The study calls this gap observational, not a proven cause.

mainIdea.s: Doctors say quitting smoking or treating blood pressure today will push back a person's dementia risk by 13 years. The study proves these three habits directly cause the illness later in life.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article says nobody can promise that one person's own risk will be pushed back by 13 years. This is observational work, not proof of a direct cause.

mainIdea.s: A separate study this year found older adults who followed a Mediterranean diet showed slower memory loss over five years. Researchers say the diet may also lower the risk of heart disease.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a different study on diet and memory loss, not about the midlife risks and dementia study.

lines.text: A 26-year study found that three midlife health risks are linked to 13 fewer years without dementia.
Which three?
High blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking. The study {{took in}} more than 12,000 adults who {{started off}} with no sign of dementia, and researchers {{kept track of}} them for about 26 years.
And the difference was 13 years?

Adults with none of the three {{went on}} to live about 30 years without dementia. Adults with all three managed about 17. The gap {{adds up to}} roughly 13 years, and the pattern {{came through}} for both men and women.
Which of the three is the worst?
[[Good question]], and the honest answer is nobody knows. The factors were measured together, so the study can't {{single out}} one. It also can't {{tell apart}} a real cause from a coincidence.
Meaning?
It's observational. It watched people who already smoked or had high blood pressure. Money, education, and genes may {{make up}} part of the gap too.
So I can't just quit sugar and buy 13 years?
No. Nobody can promise that if you {{steer clear of}} cigarettes, {{cut out}} sugar, or {{get into}} walking, your dementia will be {{pushed back}} by 13 years.
Then what's [[the takeaway]]?
Doctors already treat these three conditions in middle age, and the same conditions are linked to dementia decades later. Taking them seriously now is [[a bet worth making]].
Midlife me, protecting old me.
[[That's one way to put it]]. And a good one.

stories.headline: An ad about love upsets the internet

sources.title: 'You literally can't': AI startup Orchid sparks backlash over its 'second brain' assistant
Orchid AI assistant launches, gets backlash for relationship ad
'Tech people need to stop': Startup faces backlash after suggesting its AI can save bad relationships

chunks.text: An argument {{kicked off}} on July 28, when a short [[advertisement]] for an AI [[assistant]] called Orchid appeared online. The app works [[by text message]] and {{sorts out}} small jobs: [[bookings]], [[reminders]], files. In the [[clip]], a man forgets his [[anniversary]] while he is playing a video game. His partner messages the assistant instead of him, and the assistant {{stands in for}} him by handling the conversation. It books a restaurant and sends lilies, because it remembers that she likes them better than roses.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly and noisily
verbs.wrong: To end a video with a joke
verbs.why: A loud argument can kick off after just one careless comment, and a new sports season kicks off every fall with high hopes. An online argument kicked off on July 28 when a short ad for the AI assistant Orchid appeared.

verbs.correct: To handle small tasks
verbs.wrong: To reply to a message very fast
verbs.why: An assistant might sort out your schedule before a busy week, and a good manager sorts out small problems before they grow. The Orchid app sorts out small jobs like bookings, reminders, and files through text messages.

verbs.correct: To do something in place of someone
verbs.wrong: To send flowers to a partner
verbs.why: A backup actor stands in for the main actor when she gets sick, and a backup singer sometimes stands in for the star at the last minute. In the ad, the assistant stands in for the man by handling all of his partner's messages.

chunks.text: The video {{blew up}}. It reached 3.2 million [[views]] and more than 600 [[replies]] [[in a few days]]. Many people who had been [[ready to]] {{sign up}} {{turned on}} the company instead. The line that made people angriest was the assistant's own: "You literally can't. [[That's why]] I'm here." Its [[critics]] said the app was selling a way to look [[thoughtful]] without doing any of the caring.

verbs.correct: To suddenly get a lot of attention
verbs.wrong: To delete a post after an argument
verbs.why: A funny video can blow up online within hours, and one lucky post might blow up overnight after a celebrity shares it. This ad blew up fast, reaching 3.2 million views and more than 600 replies in just a few days.

verbs.correct: To join a service as a member
verbs.wrong: To book a table at a restaurant
verbs.why: Students sign up for a free workshop within minutes of it opening, and a new member can sign up for the gym online in seconds. Many people who had planned to sign up for Orchid criticized the company instead after seeing the ad.

verbs.correct: To suddenly attack someone
verbs.wrong: To share a video with a friend
verbs.why: Fans quickly turn on a coach after the team loses many games in a row, and a crowd can turn on a referee after one unfair decision. Many people who once liked Orchid turned on the company after this advertisement appeared online.

chunks.text: A [[licensed therapist]] {{spoke out}} too. She warned that texting a machine instead of your partner is [[a form of]] [[triangulation]]: a third person {{cuts in}} on a conversation that should happen only between the two partners. Some readers said [[the whole thing]] {{put off}} people who had planned to try the app. Others called it [[ragebait]], made to be shared in anger.

verbs.correct: To say publicly what you think
verbs.wrong: To answer a message in private
verbs.why: Employees sometimes speak out against a rule they think is unfair, and worried parents speak out at a school board meeting. A licensed therapist spoke out too, warning that texting an assistant instead of a partner can hurt real communication.

verbs.correct: To interrupt and take a place
verbs.wrong: To lower the price of an app
verbs.why: A stranger sometimes cuts in during a private conversation at a party, and a rude driver might cut in front of others on the highway. The therapist warned that a machine can cut in on a conversation that should stay strictly between two partners.

verbs.correct: To make someone lose interest
verbs.wrong: To remind someone of a date
verbs.why: Bad reviews put off many potential buyers before they even visit a store, and rude service can put off even loyal customers forever. Some readers said the whole argument put off people who had once planned to try the Orchid app.

chunks.text: The company has not {{backed down}}. It said it wanted a story built around a real situation [[rather than]] a normal product video, and it {{brushed off}} the criticism by leaving the clip online. A second advertisement, which claimed the app could check food for [[allergens]], was quietly deleted. The fight {{sums up}} a question the [[tech industry]] keeps [[running into]]: people will let software book a table, but they do not want it to do the caring for them.

verbs.correct: To stop defending your position
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim more loudly
verbs.why: A union refuses to back down during a long, difficult strike, and some companies back down fast once bad news stories about them start to spread. Orchid has not backed down, and it left the anniversary ad online rather than removing it.

verbs.correct: To treat something as unimportant
verbs.wrong: To delete a video from the internet
verbs.why: A driver might brush off a warning light and keep driving anyway, and some workers brush off small rumors around the office. Orchid brushed off the criticism and simply left the ad online for anyone to see.

verbs.correct: To capture the whole of something
verbs.wrong: To start a new argument online
verbs.why: One photo can sum up an entire vacation better than any story, and a single quote sometimes sums up a whole argument. This fight sums up a real tension in tech: people accept an app booking a table but not doing their emotional work.

lines.text: An ad for an AI assistant made the whole internet angry this week.
What did it show?

A man forgets his anniversary while playing a video game. His partner messages his AI assistant instead of him, and the assistant {{stands in for}} him: books a restaurant, sends her favorite flowers, handles the whole conversation.
[[Oof]]. And people saw this as a good thing?

The company did. The internet didn't. The video {{blew up}}: 3.2 million views and hundreds of angry replies. The argument {{kicked off}} over one line from the assistant itself: "You literally can't. That's why I'm here."
Meaning the man literally can't care?
[[That's how people read it]]. Critics said the app was selling a way to look thoughtful without doing any of the caring. People who had been ready to {{sign up}} {{turned on}} the company instead.
What do therapists say?
One {{spoke out}} and called it triangulation: a third party {{cuts in}} on a conversation that should happen only between partners.
Did the company apologize?
No, it hasn't {{backed down}}. It said it wanted a story around a real situation, and it {{brushed off}} the criticism by leaving the clip online. A second ad was quietly deleted, though.
What does the app even do normally?
Ordinary useful things. It works by text and {{sorts out}} small jobs: bookings, reminders, files. Some readers said the ad {{put off}} exactly the people who wanted that.
So the ad {{sums up}} a bigger question.
[[Perfectly]]. People will let software book a table, but they don't want it to do the caring for them.
The restaurant, yes. The flowers... [[that's a line you don't cross]].

chunks.text: A long [[heatwave]] in northern Italy is {{cutting into}} the country's most famous cheese. When the air goes above 40 degrees Celsius, which is 104 Fahrenheit, [[dairy cows]] eat less and give [[up to]] ten [[percent]] less milk. Parmigiano Reggiano is made from that milk. The [[producers]] who {{stand behind}} the name sell about four [[billion]] euros of cheese a year, and a farmer cannot {{make up}} the milk that a hot summer {{takes away}}.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.wrong: To move milk from farm to dairy

verbs.wrong: To store cheese for a longer time

chunks.text: The cheese also [[takes a long time]] to make. A [[wheel]] must [[sit]] for [[at least]] twelve months, and most are kept for two or three years. About four million wheels a year come from around 300 [[dairies]]. While a wheel waits in [[storage]], money has already {{gone out}} for [[feed]], work and power. No money {{comes in}} for years, so the costs {{pile up}}.

verbs.correct: To be spent and leave the farm
verbs.wrong: To be sold in another country
verbs.why: Rent money goes out on the first of every month no matter what, and cash goes out fast whenever the car needs repairs. Money for feed, labor, and power all goes out long before a wheel of cheese is ready to sell.

verbs.correct: To arrive as money that is earned
verbs.wrong: To join a group of producers
verbs.why: Extra cash comes in every summer from tourists renting rooms near the coast, and steady rent money comes in on the first of each month. No money comes in from a wheel of Parmesan for years while it slowly ages in storage.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted at the end of a year
verbs.why: Unpaid bills pile up fast once payments are missed, and emails pile up in an inbox during a long vacation. With no income for years while a wheel ages, a farmer's costs pile up quickly.

chunks.text: Italian banks {{thought up}} an answer to this [[a long time ago]]. One bank has accepted cheese as [[security]] for a loan since 1953. The farmer gives the bank his wheels, the bank {{puts away}} the cheese in a [[vault]], and the farmer {{takes out}} a [[loan]] [[worth]] 60 to 80 percent of what it is worth. One vault holds more than 500,000 wheels.

verbs.correct: To invent a clever answer to a problem
verbs.wrong: To copy an idea from another country
verbs.why: A good manager thinks up a smart fix for a tricky parking problem. Bored kids often think up new games. Italian banks thought up a clever system decades ago: farmers could borrow against wheels of aging cheese.

verbs.correct: To store something in a safe place
verbs.wrong: To sell cheese before it is ready
verbs.why: A careful saver puts away a little money every single month, and a librarian puts away returned books at the end of each day. The bank puts away each farmer's wheels of cheese inside a locked, cool vault.

verbs.correct: To arrange a loan from a bank
verbs.wrong: To repay money that is owed
verbs.why: A young couple often takes out a loan for their first home. Many students take out loans for college costs. In this system, a farmer takes out a loan worth 60 to 80 percent of what the cheese is worth.

chunks.text: So the extreme heat is now affecting the banks that lend money against cheese. Less milk means fewer wheels, and fewer wheels mean the banks are holding less. Keeping those vaults cool costs about 30 percent more [[electricity]] in the hottest weeks, and the Po River has {{dried up}} to under a third of its normal [[level]]. Farmers can still {{fall back on}} the loans and {{get by}}, but there is less money left [[at the end of the year]].

verbs.correct: To lose most of its water
verbs.wrong: To be measured twice each summer
verbs.why: A backyard well dries up during a long drought. Small ponds often dry up in extreme summer heat. The Po River has dried up to under a third of its normal level this year.

verbs.why: A family falls back on its savings when work is slow. A nervous speaker falls back on old notes when memory fails. Farmers can still fall back on these cheese loans when a bad, hot summer cuts their income.

verbs.why: A young family often gets by on a tight monthly budget. Many students get by on a small part-time salary. Farmers can still get by on these cheese loans, even though less money is left at the end of the year.

lines.text: Here's a story that connects a heatwave, cheese, and banks. Italy's Parmesan is in trouble.
Cheese and banks? [[Go slowly]].

Start with the cows. When the air goes above 40 degrees, they eat less and give up to ten percent less milk. Parmigiano Reggiano is made from that milk, and a farmer can't {{make up}} what a hot summer {{takes away}}.
And the cheese [[takes ages]], right?

At least twelve months per wheel, usually two or three years. While a wheel waits in storage, money has already {{gone out}} for feed, work, and power. Nothing {{comes in}} for years, so the costs {{pile up}}.
So where do banks enter the story?

[[This is my favorite part]]. Since 1953, one Italian bank has accepted cheese as security for loans. The farmer gives his wheels to the bank, the bank {{puts away}} the cheese in a vault, and the farmer {{takes out}} a loan worth 60 to 80 percent of its value.
A vault full of cheese.
One vault holds more than 500,000 wheels. Whoever {{thought up}} that system [[deserves a statue]].
So how does the heat reach the banks?

Less milk means fewer wheels, and fewer wheels mean the banks hold less security. Cooling the vaults costs 30 percent more electricity, and the Po River has {{dried up}} to under a third of its normal level.
Can the farmers survive this?
They can {{fall back on}} the loans and {{get by}}, but there's less money left at the end of the year. The heat is {{cutting into}} a four-billion-euro business.
And the quality?
The producers who {{stand behind}} the name won't lower standards. That's the whole point of Parmigiano.
A cheese so trusted a bank will hold it. [[Only in Italy]].

chunks.text: A new word has {{caught on}} online [[among]] teenage boys and young men. Looksmaxxing means improving your [[appearance]] [[as much as possible]]. The soft version is [[grooming]] and a [[daily routine]] of sleep and exercise. The hard version is [[surgery]] on the nose or the [[jawline]]. Many who follow it are still {{growing up}}, and they {{look up to}} influencers who give a face a [[rating]] [[out of ten]].

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To be noticed by only a few people
verbs.why: A new slang word catches on fast online, and a new trend catches on among teenagers within weeks. This word, looksmaxxing, has caught on among teenage boys and young men.

verbs.correct: To change from a child into an adult
verbs.wrong: To raise a child inside a family
verbs.why: Kids grow up fast these days, and many now grow up online, surrounded by social media. Many of the young men following looksmaxxing trends are still growing up themselves.

verbs.correct: To admire someone you want to copy
verbs.wrong: To study a problem very carefully
verbs.why: Kids look up to athletes, and teenagers often look up to older siblings or coaches. Many boys who try looksmaxxing look up to online influencers who rate a face out of ten.

chunks.text: A social worker at the University of Michigan wrote in July 2026 that these behaviors [[look like]] the [[signs]] of an [[eating disorder]] or [[body dysmorphia]]. Some young men {{cut out}} [[whole food groups]] or {{give up}} meals for days. A few hit their own face with a [[hammer]]. She says the [[trend]] is not [[harmless]], and that a boy who starts small can {{end up}} in danger.

verbs.wrong: To spend less money than before
verbs.why: Some people cut out sugar from their diet, and others cut out carbs to lose weight fast. A social worker said some young men following looksmaxxing trends cut out whole food groups for weeks.

verbs.correct: To stop having something you want
verbs.wrong: To gain weight in a short time
verbs.why: People give up sweets for a diet, and some give up meat entirely for their health. A social worker found that some young men give up meals for days while chasing a certain look.

verbs.correct: To reach a situation you did not plan
verbs.wrong: To close an online account for good
verbs.why: A small habit can end up as a serious problem, and a light diet can end up as something dangerous. A social worker warns that a boy who starts small with looksmaxxing can end up in real danger.

chunks.text: Looksmaxxing spreads because it [[pays to]] {{show off}}. A researcher at Northeastern University says the most [[extreme]] [[stunts]] get the most clicks, so the advice keeps getting harder. He also says the [[ideal]] face in these videos copies old European [[beauty standards]]. A [[psychologist]] there says men are a new market for beauty companies. For some boys, looksmaxxing stops being a hobby and can {{take over}} the whole day. Then the wish to {{stand out}} [[turns into]] a fear of being [[judged]].

verbs.correct: To try to impress other people
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place as planned
verbs.why: Teenagers show off a new haircut online, and some show off their workout results for likes. Looksmaxxing spreads partly because it pays for young men to show off online.

verbs.correct: To fill all of a person's time
verbs.wrong: To hire a person for a new job
verbs.why: A hobby can take over your weekends, and stress can take over your whole day. For some boys, looksmaxxing stops being a hobby and starts to take over the entire day.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice in a crowd
verbs.wrong: To copy someone else's style exactly
verbs.why: A bright red coat makes you stand out in a crowd, and a strong resume helps you stand out at an interview. For some boys, the wish to stand out becomes a fear of being judged instead.

chunks.text: Doctors {{point out}} that the problem is easy to [[miss]] in boys. Most tests ask about a fear of being fat, so a boy who trains hard to look [[lean]] can pass them. Researchers estimate that [[one in three]] people with an eating disorder is male. The [[warning signs]] include [[obsessive]] mirror checks and secret rules about food. Experts say it is healthy to {{work out}}. But they also advise parents to help a son {{open up}} and to [[seek help]] early, since [[self-esteem]] problems can have [[long-term]] effects.

verbs.correct: To tell people about an important fact
verbs.wrong: To argue against a popular opinion
verbs.why: Doctors point out warning signs early, and teachers point out mistakes before a test. Doctors point out that eating disorders are easy to miss in boys who look physically fit.

verbs.why: People work out at the gym to build strength, and others work out at home with simple equipment. Experts say it is healthy to work out, but they worry when it becomes too extreme.

lines.text: Doctors are warning about something called looksmaxxing. Have you heard the word?
No. What is it?
A trend that has {{caught on}} among teenage boys: improving your appearance as much as possible. The soft version is grooming, sleep, exercise. The hard version is surgery.
Surgery? For boys who are still {{growing up}}?
[[That's the worry]]. Many of them {{look up to}} influencers who rate faces out of ten. A social worker wrote that the behaviors look like signs of an eating disorder or body dysmorphia.
[[Like what, exactly?]]
Some boys {{cut out}} whole food groups or {{give up}} meals for days. In extreme cases, worse. She says a boy who starts small can {{end up}} in danger.
Why does it spread so fast?
Because online, [[it pays to]] {{show off}}. The most extreme stunts get the most clicks, so the advice keeps getting harder. For some boys the routine can {{take over}} the whole day.
And then it isn't a hobby anymore.
Right. The wish to {{stand out}} turns into a fear of being judged.
Why is this hard for parents and doctors to catch?
Most eating disorder tests ask about a fear of being fat, so a boy training to look lean can pass them. Researchers estimate one in three people with an eating disorder is male.
What should parents actually do?
Watch for warning signs like obsessive mirror checks and secret food rules. It's healthy to {{work out}}, but experts say help a son {{open up}}, and seek help early.
So the message isn't "don't exercise." It's "watch how it feels."
[[Well put]]. Self-esteem problems can have long-term effects, and early support makes the difference.

chunks.text: The United States has [[confirmed]] 2,371 cases of measles in 2026, the worst year since 1991. [[Figures]] that [[health officials]] {{put out}} [[at the end of]] July show 53 new cases in a single week, and the total has already {{gone past}} last year's 2,288, which was itself a [[record]]. Thirty-seven separate [[outbreaks]] have {{cropped up}} in 45 states and [[territories]]. No one has died of measles this year. Three people died in 2025, two of them children.

verbs.wrong: To delay something until later

verbs.wrong: To grow larger every year

chunks.text: Measles spreads more easily than almost any other disease. If one person has it, [[up to]] [[nine out of ten]] [[unprotected]] people close to them will {{come down with}} it, and the virus can stay in the air of a room for two hours after the patient has left. About 7 percent of this year's patients have {{ended up}} needing [[hospital care]]. Children aged 5 to 19 [[account for]] half of all cases, and children under 5 {{make up}} another [[fifth]].

verbs.correct: To become ill with a disease
verbs.wrong: To fall to a lower level

verbs.correct: To be somewhere in the end
verbs.wrong: To leave before the end
verbs.why: After a wrong turn you might end up in a different town, and a small mistake at work can end up costing extra time. About 7 percent of this year's measles patients have ended up needing hospital care.

verbs.wrong: To divide into equal parts
verbs.why: Tourists make up nearly a third of visitors to the city, and nurses make up half of the hospital staff. Children under 5 make up about a fifth of this year's measles cases, and kids 5 to 19 make up half.

chunks.text: Ninety-three percent of this year's patients had either never been [[vaccinated]] or could not [[prove]] that they had been. Two [[doses]] of the measles vaccine stop the disease 97 percent of the time, but fewer children are getting them. The [[coverage]] rate among [[kindergarten]] children has {{dropped off}}, from 95.2 percent in the 2019 to 2020 school year to 92.5 percent in 2024 to 2025. That now {{falls short of}} the 95 percent that doctors say a community needs to {{hold back}} an outbreak.

verbs.correct: To become lower over time
verbs.wrong: To rise higher than before

verbs.correct: To be less than what is needed

verbs.correct: To stop something from spreading
verbs.wrong: To measure a disease every year
verbs.why: Clean water can hold back many diseases, and a good firewall can hold back most computer viruses. Doctors say a community needs a 95 percent vaccination rate to hold back a measles outbreak once it starts.

chunks.text: The United States {{wiped out}} measles in 2000. That does not mean nobody has caught it since. It means health experts could show that the virus had stopped spreading inside the country [[all year round]], and they call that [[elimination]]. A country keeps that status only as long as the status stays true, and the country loses the status if a single [[chain of infection]] {{carries on}} for more than 12 months. Researchers writing in The Lancet say it is [[highly likely]] the United States will lose its status when a Pan American Health Organization [[committee]] meets in November 2026. Health officials say the way to {{turn around}} the numbers has not changed: two doses of the vaccine, [[on time]], for every child. Without that, a disease the country beat 26 years ago will have {{come back}} to stay.

verbs.correct: To remove something completely
verbs.wrong: To require a vaccine by law
verbs.why: A hard frost can wipe out a whole garden overnight, and a bad storm can wipe out an entire harvest. The United States wiped out measles in 2000, meaning the virus no longer spread inside the country.

verbs.why: A new coach can turn around a team's losing streak, and a company can turn around its losses in just a year. Health officials say the way to turn around the falling vaccination numbers has not changed: two doses on time for every child.

verbs.why: Sunshine often comes back quickly after a storm. Birds come back to the same lake every spring. The country stopped measles in 2000, but without two vaccine doses for every child, the disease will come back and stay.
