lines.text: Measles just hit a 35-year high in the US. Over 2,300 confirmed cases this year.
Measles? Wasn't that gone?

The country {{wiped out}} measles in 2000. Elimination means the virus stopped spreading inside the country year-round. But 37 separate outbreaks have {{cropped up}} in 45 states and territories this year.
How contagious is it exactly?
Extremely. If one person has it, up to nine of ten unprotected people close to them will {{come down with}} it, and the virus can stay in a room's air for two hours after the patient leaves.
Two hours? [[That's frightening]].
About 7 percent of patients have {{ended up}} needing hospital care. Half the cases are children between 5 and 19, and kids under 5 {{make up}} another fifth.
Why is it spreading now?

Vaccination. 93 percent of this year's patients were never vaccinated or couldn't prove it. Kindergarten coverage has {{dropped off}} to 92.5 percent, which {{falls short of}} the 95 percent needed to {{hold back}} an outbreak.
What do the new numbers mean for the total?
The figures officials {{put out}} in July show the total has already {{gone past}} last year's record.
Could the US lose its elimination status?
[[Very likely]]. If a single chain of infection {{carries on}} for more than 12 months, the status is gone. Researchers expect a decision in November.
And the fix?
The same as always: two vaccine doses, [[on time]], for every child. Doctors say that's the only way to {{turn around}} the numbers.
Otherwise a disease the country beat 26 years ago will have {{come back}} to stay.
[[Sadly, yes]].

chunks.text: An Ebola [[outbreak]] in central Africa has killed more than 1,500 people since May, and this time doctors have no vaccine to {{fall back on}}. The disease {{broke out}} in Ituri, a province in the northeast of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the World Health Organization declared a global health [[emergency]] on May 17, 2026. By 30 July the number of [[confirmed cases]] had {{gone up}} to 3,626, and 1,589 people had died. The [[death rate]] is 44 percent, so [[close to]] half of the patients do not [[survive]].

verbs.correct: To use when nothing else works
verbs.wrong: To leave a dangerous place
verbs.why: A family might fall back on savings during a hard month, and a cook might fall back on a simple backup recipe when something goes wrong. Doctors fighting this Ebola outbreak have no vaccine to fall back on this time.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly
verbs.wrong: To stop working properly
verbs.why: A fight can break out in a crowded stadium, and a fire can break out from a single spark. This Ebola outbreak broke out in Ituri, a province in the northeast of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

verbs.correct: To rise to a higher number
verbs.wrong: To continue for a long time
verbs.why: Hospital bills can go up fast after a long stay, and case numbers go up during a bad flu season. By July 30, confirmed Ebola cases had gone up to 3,626, with 1,589 deaths recorded.

chunks.text: Most Ebola outbreaks come from the Zaire [[species]] of the virus, and a vaccine for that one has been [[approved]] since 2019. This outbreak is different. It comes from a species called Bundibugyo, and the vaccine that health teams {{rolled out}} in past outbreaks does nothing against it. There is no proven [[treatment]] [[either]]. Scientists are {{carrying out}} tests on possible new vaccines, but none of them is ready. Until one arrives, teams have to {{make do with}} older methods: find patients early, keep them apart from others, and {{track down}} every person they met.

verbs.correct: To start using something new
verbs.wrong: To send workers to an area
verbs.why: A company might roll out a new phone model each fall, and health agencies roll out flu shots every autumn. The vaccine that health teams rolled out during past Ebola outbreaks does nothing against this new strain.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To approve a vaccine for public use
verbs.why: A lab carries out tests before releasing new medicine, and inspectors carry out checks on every new building. Scientists are now carrying out tests on possible new vaccines, though none of them is ready yet.

verbs.correct: To manage with what you have
verbs.wrong: To wait for a cure to arrive
verbs.why: A cook without the right spice might make do with what is in the cabinet, and a traveler might make do with a small hotel room. Health teams fighting this outbreak have to make do with older methods like finding patients early.

verbs.correct: To find after a long search
verbs.wrong: To warn a whole village at once
verbs.why: A detective might track down a missing witness for weeks, and a family might track down a lost relative after many years. Health teams in this outbreak have to track down every single person that an infected patient met.

chunks.text: The virus has now [[spread]] to five provinces, and Ituri is a busy trading region where people cross [[borders]] every day. Twenty cases {{turned up}} in [[neighboring]] Uganda, where two people died, and a single case was recorded in France. [[Health workers]] have [[paid a heavy price]]: 151 of them have caught the virus and 44 have died. Teams have [[identified]] 17,863 [[contacts]] and are {{checking up on}} more than 13,000 of them.

verbs.correct: To appear in a place
verbs.wrong: To get worse over time
verbs.why: New symptoms sometimes turn up days after a first infection, and a lost passport can turn up in an unexpected place. Twenty cases of this Ebola strain turned up in neighboring Uganda, where two patients died.

verbs.correct: To watch someone's health
verbs.wrong: To arrive and report your name
verbs.why: A nurse checks up on a patient every few hours, and a family member checks up on an elderly relative each day. Health teams in this outbreak are checking up on more than 13,000 people who may have been exposed.

chunks.text: Uganda has not reported a new case since June 21, which [[suggests]] the [[chain of infection]] there has been broken. In the Congo the work continues. European health experts say the risk to people in Europe is very low, because Ebola only {{passes on}} through [[close contact]] with blood and other [[body fluids]], not through the air. Aid teams have {{set up}} [[isolation units]] and are training [[local staff]], and health agencies say the outbreak will only {{die out}} when [[every last]] chain is found.

verbs.correct: To give a disease to someone
verbs.wrong: To travel between two towns
verbs.why: A sick coworker might pass on a cold in a crowded office, and children often pass on stomach illnesses at school. This form of Ebola only passes on through close contact with blood and other body fluids, not through the air.

verbs.correct: To build and start something
verbs.wrong: To begin a long journey
verbs.why: A new business might set up a store in a busy downtown area, and campers set up a tent before dark. Aid teams in this outbreak have set up isolation units and are training local health workers to help.

verbs.correct: To stop existing completely

mainIdea.s: More than 1,500 people have died in this Ebola outbreak in Central Africa, and there is no vaccine. Health experts say the disease spreads through the air between people nearby.

mainIdea.s: Health teams in West Africa ended a separate Ebola outbreak last year using an approved vaccine. That outbreak affected far fewer people and never spread beyond a single country.

lines.text: There's a serious Ebola outbreak in central Africa. More than 1,500 deaths since May, and this time there's no vaccine.
No vaccine? I thought Ebola had one.

For the usual species, yes, approved since 2019. But this outbreak {{broke out}} from a different species called Bundibugyo, and the vaccine teams {{rolled out}} in past outbreaks does nothing against it.
So what can doctors do?
With no vaccine to {{fall back on}}, they {{make do with}} older methods: find patients early, isolate them, and {{track down}} every person they met.
How big is it now?
Confirmed cases have {{gone up}} to more than 3,600 across five provinces, and the death rate is 44 percent. Twenty cases {{turned up}} in Uganda, and one in France.
What about the health workers?
[[They've paid a heavy price]]. 151 caught the virus and 44 have died. Teams have identified almost 18,000 contacts and are {{checking up on}} more than 13,000 of them.
Is any of it working?
[[There's one hopeful sign]]. Uganda hasn't reported a new case since June 21, which suggests the chain of infection there has been broken.
Should people in Europe worry?
Experts say the risk is very low. Ebola only {{passes on}} through close contact with blood and body fluids, not through the air.
And the long-term plan?

Scientists are {{carrying out}} tests on new vaccines, but none is ready. Aid teams have {{set up}} isolation units and are training local staff. The outbreak will only {{die out}} when every last chain is found.
Those health workers are [[the real story]] here.
[[They always are]].

stories.headline: A boat maker turned down 400 million dollars

sources.title: He worked 100-hour weeks to save a nearly bankrupt boat company. At 83, he's just turned down $400 million for it
Grady-White's Owner Is Giving Away His Legendary Boat Company
Grady-White's Owner Turned Down $400 Million to Give the Company Away Instead
Instead of selling his luxury boat company for millions, he invested in his employees (video, CBS Evening News)

chunks.text: An 83-year-old American has {{turned down}} more than 400 million dollars for the company he built. Eddie Smith Jr. owns Grady-White Boats in Greenville, North Carolina, and buyers have spent years trying to get him to sell. In July 2026 he refused [[for the last time]]. [[Rather than]] {{hold on to}} the money himself, he has [[arranged]] things so that the company's [[profits]] will {{end up}} with [[charities]] instead.

verbs.correct: To refuse an offer
verbs.wrong: To sign a contract
verbs.why: A worker can turn down a big promotion to stay close to family, and a company can turn down a huge offer to protect its values. Here Eddie Smith turned down more than 400 million dollars for the company he spent his life building.

verbs.correct: To keep something you own
verbs.wrong: To sell part of a company
verbs.why: A grandson might hold on to his grandfather's old watch for years, and a family might hold on to a house instead of selling it. Smith could have held on to the company's profits himself, but he chose to send them elsewhere instead.

verbs.correct: To be somewhere in the end
verbs.wrong: To finish a job early
verbs.why: Leftovers can end up forgotten in the back of the fridge, and a small argument can end up somewhere nobody ever expected. Here the company's future profits will end up with charities instead of staying in Smith's own pocket.

chunks.text: Smith bought Grady-White in 1968, when he was 26 and the business was [[close to]] {{going under}}. He {{put in}} 80 to 100 hour weeks in those early years and stopped playing golf for [[decades]]. Over 58 years he {{built up}} a company that now earns hundreds of millions of dollars a year. He never sold shares to the public, never accepted [[outside investors]] and never {{took on}} any [[debt]]. During the [[boom]] of the 1970s he refused to grow the company by 300 or 400 percent, because he believed the boats would get worse.

verbs.correct: To fail as a business
verbs.wrong: To move to a bigger factory
verbs.why: A small bookshop can go under during a slow year, and a family bakery can go under once a new highway changes where customers shop. Grady-White itself was close to going under when Smith bought it in 1968, at just 26 years old.

verbs.correct: To give time and effort
verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: Volunteers put in extra hours before a big festival opens, and new employees often put in overtime during their first year. Smith put in 80 to 100 hour weeks in the company's early struggling years.

verbs.correct: To make something grow slowly
verbs.wrong: To design a new kind of boat
verbs.why: A worker can build up savings a little at a time, and a shop can build up a loyal following over many years. Smith built up Grady-White over 58 years into a company earning hundreds of millions a year.

verbs.correct: To agree to owe money
verbs.wrong: To repay a loan early
verbs.why: A couple can take on a loan to remodel their kitchen, and a small firm can take on debt to grow faster. Smith never took on any debt at all, choosing to grow the company only with its own earnings.

chunks.text: What he has {{set up}} is unusual. The [[voting shares]] now sit in a [[trust]] that makes selling the company [[impossible]], so Grady-White should {{live on}} as an [[independent]] business. The other shares went to a charity that will {{give away}} tens of millions of dollars every year to education, [[healthcare]], [[conservation]] and [[local causes]]. Smith copied the idea from Yvon Chouinard, who handed the [[clothing company]] Patagonia to a similar trust in 2022.

verbs.correct: To create something new
verbs.wrong: To close a business for good
verbs.why: Neighbors set up a small community garden behind an old school, and a retired teacher might set up a scholarship fund for local kids. Smith set up a trust structure that makes it impossible for anyone to ever sell the company.

verbs.correct: To continue to exist
verbs.wrong: To move to another town
verbs.why: An old tradition can live on for generations in a small town, and a grandmother's recipes can live on in her daughter's kitchen. Thanks to the trust, Grady-White should live on as an independent company long after Smith himself is gone.

verbs.correct: To give with no payment
verbs.wrong: To rent something for a year
verbs.why: A neighborhood bakery gives away free bread near closing time, and a store sometimes gives away samples on a busy Saturday. Here a charity linked to the company will give away tens of millions of dollars every year to health and education causes.

chunks.text: About 350 people work at the single factory in Greenville. The company shares its profits with them, spends 350,000 to 400,000 dollars a year so that staff can read books, and employs a [[chaplain]]. Smith has {{stepped down}} to an [[honorary role]]. He did not {{pass down}} the company to his family, and he has had [[hard years]]: his wife Jo died in 2021 and his son Chris died of a [[nerve disease]] in 2022. He says a trust will {{look after}} the business better than any owner could. [[In his words]], by not selling, Grady-White will always be Grady-White.

verbs.correct: To leave an important job
verbs.wrong: To take a longer vacation
verbs.why: A tired mayor might step down after years in office, and a coach often steps down once a favorite player retires. After 58 years running the business, Smith has now stepped down to a purely honorary role.

verbs.correct: To give to your children
verbs.wrong: To divide money between workers
verbs.why: A grandmother can pass down her best recipes to her daughters, and a farmer often passes down land to the next generation. Smith chose not to pass down Grady-White to his own family, sending it to a trust instead.

verbs.correct: To keep someone safe and well
verbs.wrong: To watch a person from far away
verbs.why: A nurse looks after a patient through a long recovery, and a good manager looks after the whole team, not just the top earners. Smith believes a trust will look after the business better than any single owner ever could.

lines.text: An 83-year-old boat maker just {{turned down}} more than 400 million dollars for his company. For the last time, he says.
Who says no to 400 million?
Eddie Smith, the owner of Grady-White Boats. Buyers chased him for years. Instead of selling, he arranged things so the profits {{end up}} with charities.
[[Wait, all of it?]] What's the story there?
He bought the company in 1968, when he was 26 and it was close to {{going under}}. He {{put in}} 80-to-100-hour weeks and {{built up}} a business that now earns hundreds of millions a year.
And he never sold any part of it?
Never. No public shares, no outside investors, and he never {{took on}} debt. In the boom years he even refused to triple the company's size because he believed the boats would get worse.
[[A man of principle]]. So what happens to the company now?
He {{set up}} a trust that makes selling impossible, so the business should {{live on}} independently. The other shares went to a charity that will {{give away}} tens of millions every year.
Where did he get the idea?
From the founder of Patagonia, who did the same in 2022. Smith has {{stepped down}} to an honorary role, and he didn't {{pass down}} the company to his family.
Why not keep the money, or {{hold on to}} the company for his kids?

He's had hard years. His wife died in 2021 and his son in 2022. He says a trust will {{look after}} the business better than any owner could. [[In his words]], by not selling, Grady-White will always be Grady-White.
The employees must love him.
The company shares profits with all 350 of them, pays for their books, even employs a chaplain. [[They don't make many like him]].

stories.headline: Nuclear plants slow down as the Danube drops

sources.title: Record low Danube levels push some countries in Eastern Europe to the brink of energy emergency
Record low Danube levels prompt central European governments to take emergency action
Romania seeks to divert Danube water to keep Cernavoda nuclear power plant online
Hungary: Prime minister flags 'critical' days ahead as country's nuclear power plant goes offline (video, DW News)

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen to its lowest level [[on record]], and the countries along it are [[short of]] electricity. In Budapest the river measured about 10 centimeters on Monday, August 3, 2026, [[well under]] the old record of 33 centimeters, set in 2018. Hungary's only nuclear plant stands beside the town of Paks, about 90 kilometers south of the [[capital]], and normally {{makes up}} about half of the country's electricity production. On Monday its four Soviet-built reactors had been {{cut back}} to 240 megawatts, [[compared with]] a normal 2,000. The Danube has been low before. What is new is that it has almost {{shut down}} a nuclear plant [[for the first time in]] 44 years.

verbs.correct: To form a part of something
verbs.wrong: To measure the level of a river
verbs.why: Immigrants make up a large share of the workforce in some cities, and tourists make up most of a small town's income each summer. Hungary's Paks nuclear plant normally makes up about half of the country's electricity.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount produced
verbs.wrong: To send power to another country
verbs.why: A family might cut back on spending during a hard month, and a factory might cut back its hours when demand falls. Hungary's four reactors were cut back to 240 megawatts, far below their normal 2,000.

verbs.correct: To make a plant stop working
verbs.wrong: To fill a plant with river water
verbs.why: A storm can shut down a factory for days, and low staff can shut down a small shop early. This summer low water almost shut down Hungary's nuclear plant for the first time in 44 years.

chunks.text: The Paks plant uses Danube water to cool its reactors, so a low river means less power. To {{keep up with}} [[demand]], Hungary has asked everyone to use less. On Saturday the government {{brought in}} [[mandatory]] limits for large factories and shops, and asked families to save electricity between 5 and 10 in the evening, the hours of [[peak]] use. Electric freight trains cannot run in those hours, a step expected to save 70 to 90 megawatt hours a day. Prime Minister Péter Magyar said [[voluntary]] savings on Sunday cut demand by 700 megawatts, and that a full shutdown could still be {{put off}}, [[at least for now]].

chunks.text: Romania is [[in the same position]]. The [[flow]] of the Danube there has fallen to about 1,500 cubic meters a second, less than a third of the July [[average]]. One of the two 680 megawatt reactors at the Cernavoda plant has already stopped, and the other is running at about half [[capacity]]. Together they normally [[supply]] [[roughly]] a fifth of Romania's electricity. More than 100 soldiers {{set off}} 180 kilograms of [[explosives]] at a rock formation on Monday. The blast will {{hold back}} the water that escapes down a side channel called the Bala arm and {{send it past}} the plant instead. The navy also plans to sink four barges carrying about 500 tons of stone across the same channel. Acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan declared a nationwide energy [[alert]] for August and {{turned to}} Ukraine for extra nuclear power. The carmakers Dacia and Ford have stopped production until August 19.

verbs.correct: To stop water from flowing
verbs.wrong: To collect water in a lake
verbs.why: A dam can hold back a whole river, and a small wall can hold back floodwater during a storm. In Romania, the planned blast will hold back water that now escapes down the Bala side channel.

verbs.correct: To make water reach the plant
verbs.wrong: To pump water into a tank
verbs.why: Engineers send water past a blocked pipe to a nearby town, and workers send trucks past a closed road to finish a delivery on time. In Romania, the planned blast will send the Danube water past the Bala side channel to the power plant instead.

verbs.correct: To make something explode
verbs.wrong: To take rocks from a riverbed

verbs.correct: To ask another country to help

verbs.why: A country low on supplies might turn to its neighbors for help, and a small business might turn to a bank for a loan. Romania's acting prime minister turned to Ukraine for extra nuclear power during the crisis.

chunks.text: Serbia is feeling the same [[squeeze]]. Its two hydroelectric plants on the Danube, Djerdap I and Djerdap II, are running at 20 and 30 percent of capacity, and together they normally provide about 18 percent of the country's power. Prime Minister Djuro Macut held an emergency meeting and asked people to use air conditioning [[as little as possible]]. Slovakia's prime minister, Robert Fico, said his country was watching closely and was ready to {{step in}}. Daytime temperatures have {{gone up}} past 38 degrees Celsius, and the heat has not {{let up}} since May. Romania's energy ministry expects the hardest [[stretch]] to last until about August 15, but no real rain is [[forecast]] for weeks.

verbs.correct: To get involved and help

verbs.why: A manager steps in when a deal turns risky, and a coach steps in when a player gets hurt. Slovakia's prime minister said his country was watching the crisis closely and was ready to step in if needed.

mainIdea.s: Record low water on the Danube has cut power at nuclear and hydro plants in three countries. Hungary, Romania and Serbia have all had to ask people to use less electricity this summer.
mainIdea.why: The article says low river levels have cut output at Paks, Cernavoda and Serbia's Djerdap plants, forcing limits on use.

mainIdea.s: Hungary's only nuclear plant needed emergency repairs after a fire broke out at the site this month. The government has also brought in mandatory power limits for large factories and shops.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article does not mention a fire at the plant. The Paks reactors were cut back because of low river levels, not a fire.

mainIdea.s: Falling water levels on the Danube have also exposed dozens of sunken German warships from World War Two. Crews near Prahovo, Serbia are now removing the wrecks to widen the shipping channel.
mainIdea.why: This story is about the energy crisis along the Danube, not about the sunken warships being removed near Prahovo.

lines.text: The Danube just hit its lowest level ever recorded, and now whole countries are short of electricity.
A river causes a power shortage?

Nuclear plants use river water for cooling. Hungary's only nuclear plant normally {{makes up}} about half of the country's electricity. Its reactors have been {{cut back}} from 2,000 megawatts to 240.
[[That's a huge drop]]. How low is the river?
In Budapest it measured 10 centimeters. The old record was 33.
Ten centimeters?! What is Hungary doing?

The government {{brought in}} mandatory limits for factories and shops, and asked families to save power in the evening. Electric freight trains can't run in peak hours. [[So far]], a full shutdown has been {{put off}}.
What about the other countries on the river?

Romania stopped one reactor, and the other runs at half capacity. Soldiers even {{set off}} 180 kilograms of explosives at a rock formation to {{hold back}} water escaping down a side channel and {{send it past}} the plant instead.
Explosives to steer a river. [[Now I've heard everything]].
They'll also sink four barges of stone across the same channel. Romania declared an energy alert and {{turned to}} Ukraine for extra power. Two carmakers stopped production entirely.
Serbia too?
Its two hydro plants run at 20 and 30 percent. The government is asking people to use less air conditioning, while Slovakia says it's ready to {{step in}}.
And the heat?
Temperatures {{went up}} past 38 degrees and haven't {{let up}} since May. Demand is hard to {{keep up with}} when every fan and AC is running.
When does it end?
The hardest stretch should last until mid-August, but no real rain is coming. [[Not a drop]].

stories.headline: Low water on the Danube uncovers sunken warships

sources.title: Low water levels: EU clears old Nazi warships from the Danube
WWII German Warships Reappear as Danube Drought Exposes Wrecks in Serbia
Danube WWII wrecks cleanup boosts Serbia economy, environment
Sunken WWII ships emerge from Danube as river levels go down amid drought. #BBCNews (video, BBC News)

chunks.text: The Danube has fallen so low this summer that a sunken German [[fleet]] has {{shown up}} again near Prahovo, a town in eastern Serbia. Photographs published in late July 2026 show rusted [[hulls]] {{sticking out}} of the water along a [[stretch]] that boats normally {{pass over}} without seeing anything. The ships have been down there since 1944. What is different this year is that [[crews]] are finally {{pulling them out}}.

verbs.correct: To appear after being hidden
verbs.wrong: To move slowly down the river
verbs.why: An old letter can show up in a forgotten box, and a hidden problem can show up years later during an inspection. This summer the sunken German fleet has shown up again near the town of Prahovo.

verbs.correct: To rise above the water
verbs.wrong: To lie on the river bottom
verbs.why: A rusty nail can stick out of an old board, and a rock can stick out of the sand at low tide. Photos from July show the rusted hulls of the sunken ships sticking out of the shallow Danube water.

verbs.correct: To travel above something
verbs.wrong: To stop and dock at a port
verbs.why: A plane passes over a city on its way to another airport, and clouds pass over the mountains before a storm. Boats normally pass over this stretch of the Danube without noticing anything below the surface.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a place
verbs.wrong: To cover something with sand
verbs.why: A dentist pulls out a bad tooth, and a gardener pulls out weeds by the root. Crews on the Danube are now slowly pulling the sunken World War Two ships out of the riverbed.

chunks.text: In late 1944, the German navy was {{pulling back}} along the Danube as Soviet forces {{closed in}}. Rather than {{hand the ships over}} to the enemy, the crews sank about 200 of their own [[vessels]] near Prahovo, hoping the [[wrecks]] would block the river and {{hold up}} the Soviet [[advance]]. The plan lasted far longer than they [[intended]]. Eight [[decades]] later the hulls are still on the riverbed, and they have narrowed the safe [[channel]] from 180 meters to about 80.

verbs.correct: To leave when the enemy is near
verbs.wrong: To send more soldiers to a battle
verbs.why: An army pulls back when the enemy grows too strong, and a team sometimes pulls back from a losing position. In late 1944 the German navy was pulling back along the Danube as Soviet forces advanced.

verbs.correct: To get nearer on all sides
verbs.wrong: To stop and wait for orders
verbs.why: Police can close in on a suspect from every side, and darkness can close in fast on a winter afternoon. In 1944, Soviet forces were closing in on the German navy as it escaped along the river.

verbs.correct: To give something to someone else
verbs.wrong: To hide something from the enemy
verbs.why: A manager hands over the keys to a new owner, and a losing team hands over the trophy to the winner. Rather than hand their ships over to the enemy, German crews chose to sink them instead.

verbs.correct: To make something happen later
verbs.wrong: To send a warning to the army
verbs.why: Heavy traffic can hold up a delivery truck, and bad weather can hold up a flight for hours. The German crews hoped the sunken wrecks would block the river and hold up the advancing Soviet army.

chunks.text: That narrow channel costs Serbia about 5 million euros a year, because ships have to [[wait their turn]] to [[get through]]. Two boats passing each other can take [[anywhere from]] 40 minutes to four hours. [[Surveys]] with sonar and divers in 2021 {{turned up}} 38 wrecks in the worst section, and 21 of them are now being removed. The European Union {{put up}} a [[grant]] of 16.5 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, part of a project worth about 30 million. Divers {{clear away}} sand and silt with pumps before lifting gear takes each hull off the bottom. Some wrecks are too big or too [[fragile]] to move, so they are buried deeper instead, and others may still have [[ammunition]] on board.

verbs.correct: To find something after a search
verbs.wrong: To measure the depth of water
verbs.why: A lost ring can turn up months later in a coat pocket, and new evidence can turn up during a police search. Sonar surveys in 2021 turned up 38 wrecks in the worst section of the river.

verbs.correct: To give money for something
verbs.wrong: To ask other countries for help
verbs.why: An investor puts up the cash to start a business, and a sponsor puts up funding for a local festival. The European Union put up a grant of 16.5 million euros to help clear the wrecks.

verbs.correct: To clean dirt or sand from a place
verbs.wrong: To mark a safe path for ships
verbs.why: Workers clear away snow after a storm, and a family clears away leaves and dirt from the yard each fall. On the Danube, divers clear away sand and mud with pumps before crews raise each ship from the riverbed.

chunks.text: The work is due to {{carry on}} until 2028. Serbia expects [[cargo]] on this part of the river to rise from 12.7 million tons a year in 2019 to 25 million by 2040, and one river ship can move as much grain as 120 trucks. Alessandro Bragonzi, who [[heads]] the European Investment Bank's office for the Western Balkans, said the project is an example of the kind of clean transport the bank wants to keep funding. In Prahovo, low water is [[an old story]]. The new part is that the ships people there {{grew up}} with may soon be gone [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.wrong: To change the plan for a project
verbs.why: A family might carry on an old holiday tradition, and a team might carry on with a project after its leader leaves. The wreck removal work on the Danube is set to carry on until 2028.

verbs.correct: To become an adult
verbs.wrong: To move to another town
verbs.why: Many people grow up in a small town, and some grow up speaking two languages at home. In Prahovo, generations of families grew up with these sunken ships as a familiar part of the river.

Exactly. They've narrowed the safe channel from 180 meters to about 80. Boats normally {{pass over}} them without seeing anything, but two ships passing each other can take up to four hours. It costs Serbia about 5 million euros a year.
So what's happening now?
Crews are finally {{pulling them out}}. Surveys {{turned up}} 38 wrecks in the worst section, and 21 are being removed. The EU {{put up}} a grant of 16.5 million euros.
How do you lift an 80-year-old warship?
[[Carefully]]. Divers {{clear away}} sand and silt with pumps first, then lifting gear takes each hull off the bottom. Some are too fragile to move, and some may still have ammunition on board.
Still with ammunition on board? [[No thank you]].
That's why the careful part matters. The work will {{carry on}} until 2028.
Strange feeling for the local people, probably.
The rusted hulls {{sticking out}} of the water are the ships they {{grew up}} with. Soon they may be gone [[for good]].

stories.headline: A wildfire destroys 640 buildings in one afternoon

sources.title: Old Trails fire in northwest Spokane destroys 640 structures
The Wildfire Disaster Unfolding In Spokane, Washington
Fires on more than 250,000 acres of Washington state prompt evacuations
600+ structures lost, thousands of people are evacuated | Spokane County Wildfires: 10 a.m. Update (video, KREM 2 News)

chunks.text: A [[wildfire]] {{broke out}} on Saturday, August 1, on open ground west of Spokane, in the eastern half of Washington state. Within hours it had {{torn through}} whole streets on the edge of the city. By Sunday the fire chief for the district said 640 [[structures]] had {{burned down}}, most of them houses, and many of them inside the Spokane city [[limits]]. No deaths have been reported.

verbs.correct: To start suddenly
verbs.wrong: To spread from tree to tree
verbs.why: A fight can break out in a crowded bar, and a fever can break out overnight. The wildfire broke out on open ground west of Spokane before the wind carried it into the city.

verbs.correct: To move through a place fast and destroy it

verbs.correct: To be destroyed completely by fire
verbs.wrong: To be damaged by heat but still stand
verbs.why: An old barn can burn down in minutes, and a candle slowly burns down to nothing. About 640 structures burned down in one afternoon near Spokane, most of them family homes.

chunks.text: The wind was the biggest factor in what happened that day. [[Gusts]] {{picked up}} to between 35 and 45 miles an hour and held there for hours, pushing the flames northeast into a state park. From there the fire [[jumped]] a river, climbed the [[bluffs]] on the [[far side]] and reached the first houses. [[Crews]] could not {{hold back}} a [[front]] moving that fast, and they could not {{put out}} what was already burning, so they worked instead on getting people away from it.

verbs.correct: To become stronger
verbs.wrong: To change direction suddenly
verbs.why: Wind picks up before a big storm, and traffic picks up after a busy game ends. Gusts picked up to 45 miles an hour and pushed the flames northeast into a state park.

verbs.correct: To stop something from advancing
verbs.wrong: To make a fire spread even faster
verbs.why: A dam holds back a flooding river, and security holds back an excited crowd. Firefighters could not hold back a wind driven fire moving that fast.

verbs.correct: To stop a fire from burning
verbs.wrong: To carry water to the fire line
verbs.why: Firefighters put out house fires, and campers put out a fire before leaving a campsite. Crews could not put out flames that were already spreading through entire neighborhoods.

chunks.text: Thousands of people were {{moved out}} of their homes across Spokane County, some with a few minutes' [[notice]]. The city {{set up}} its main [[shelter]] in the [[convention center]] downtown. The mayor declared a city [[emergency]]. The governor declared one for the whole state, {{called in}} the [[National Guard]] and {{brought in}} a [[burn ban]] that [[covers]] every county. The cause of the fire is still under [[investigation]].

verbs.correct: To make people leave a place
verbs.wrong: To start living in a new home
verbs.why: Officials move out residents before a flood, and workers move out families during a gas leak. Thousands of people were moved out of their homes across Spokane County with only a few minutes notice.

verbs.correct: To create and organize something
verbs.wrong: To pay the cost of something
verbs.why: Campers set up a tent before dark, and cities set up shelters after a disaster. Spokane set up its main shelter inside the downtown convention center.

verbs.correct: To ask for official help
verbs.wrong: To send workers back home
verbs.why: Coaches call in a substitute player during a tough game, and mayors call in extra police for a large event. The governor called in the National Guard once wildfires spread across the state.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule
verbs.wrong: To explain a rule to the public
verbs.why: Schools bring in guest speakers, and cities sometimes bring in new rules during an emergency. The governor brought in a burn ban that covers every county in the state.

chunks.text: Spokane [[is not alone]]. Fires across Washington now {{add up}} to more than 250,000 [[acres]], and smoke has {{built up}} over seven counties [[badly enough for]] [[air quality]] warnings. Eastern Washington has spent the summer in record [[drought]], and [[forecasters]] expect dry air and more wind [[rather than]] rain. A separate fire north of the city started from a single [[ember]] and took three more houses. What made Saturday different was not that a fire started, but that the wind carried it into a place where people live.

verbs.wrong: To be counted by satellite
verbs.why: Small daily expenses add up over a year, and little mistakes can add up fast. Fires across Washington now add up to more than 250,000 burned acres.

verbs.wrong: To leave toward the coast
verbs.why: Dust builds up on a shelf, and pressure builds up before a big exam. Smoke built up over seven counties until air quality warnings were needed.

lines.text: A wildfire destroyed 640 buildings near Spokane in one afternoon. Most of them houses.
One afternoon? [[How is that even possible?]]
Wind. The fire {{broke out}} on open ground west of the city, then gusts {{picked up}} to 45 miles an hour and held there for hours. The flames {{tore through}} whole streets on the edge of the city.
Couldn't firefighters stop it?
Not a front moving that fast. Crews couldn't {{hold back}} the fire or {{put out}} what was already burning, so they focused on getting people away from it.
Did everyone escape?
[[Thankfully]], no deaths have been reported. But thousands were {{moved out}} of their homes, some [[with minutes of notice]]. The city {{set up}} a shelter in the convention center.
How did the fire even reach the houses?
It jumped a river. Pushed into a state park, over the water, up the bluffs, and into the first streets. 640 structures had {{burned down}} by Sunday.
What are officials doing?
The governor declared a state emergency, {{called in}} the National Guard, and {{brought in}} a burn ban for every county.
Is Spokane the only place burning?
No. Fires across Washington {{add up}} to more than 250,000 acres, and smoke has {{built up}} over seven counties. The region has spent the summer in record drought.
And rain?
[[Not in the forecast]]. Dry air and more wind instead. [[Fingers crossed]] for those crews.

stories.headline: A bomb kills three outside a Moscow restaurant

sources.title: Female Bomber Kills at Least 3, Injures 21 Near Moscow Restaurant
Moscow mayor calls Saturday's deadly bomb attack on a restaurant a 'terrorist act'
Three dead including female bomber in Moscow restaurant attack
Three people killed, at least 21 wounded in Moscow restaurant bombing, Russian officials say (video, AP Archive)

chunks.text: A [[homemade]] bomb {{went off}} outside an Italian restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, August 1. A woman carrying the [[device]] tried to walk in through the front door. A [[security guard]] {{stepped in}} and {{turned her away}}, and the bomb exploded on the street [[a moment later]]. Three people were killed, the woman herself, the guard and one customer. Twenty-one others were [[wounded]], six of them [[seriously]].

verbs.correct: To explode suddenly
verbs.wrong: To be carried into a building
verbs.why: A firework can go off with a loud crack, and a firecracker can go off without warning if someone drops it. In Moscow, a homemade bomb went off outside a restaurant just seconds after a guard stopped a woman at the door.

verbs.correct: To get involved in order to stop something
verbs.wrong: To hold the door open for a customer
verbs.why: A teacher can step in before a fight turns physical, and a manager sometimes has to step in during a crisis. A security guard stepped in just before the woman reached the restaurant door, moments before the bomb exploded outside.

verbs.correct: To refuse to let someone enter
verbs.wrong: To search a person at the door
verbs.why: A full restaurant sometimes has to turn away customers at the door, and a clinic may turn away patients without an appointment. A security guard turned the woman away just before the bomb exploded on the street outside.

chunks.text: The restaurant [[sits on]] Kudrinskaya Square, under one of the seven tall [[Stalin-era]] towers that stand around the city. It had been closed that evening for a [[private event]]. Russia's national [[anti-terrorism committee]] is {{looking into}} the attack but has {{put out}} very little. It has not named the woman, the [[victims]] or any [[suspect]], and it has not {{ruled out}} [[the possibility that]] she did not know what she was carrying.

verbs.correct: To investigate something carefully
verbs.wrong: To watch a place from outside
verbs.why: Police often look into complaints before deciding whether to open a full case, and journalists look into a story before publishing it. Russia's anti-terrorism committee is looking into the bombing but has shared very few details so far.

verbs.correct: To release information to the public
verbs.wrong: To send officers to a crime scene
verbs.why: Companies put out statements after a crisis, and weather agencies put out warnings before a storm. Investigators have put out very little so far, not even the name of the woman who carried the bomb.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To question a witness about something
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a serious illness after running tests, and police sometimes rule out early guesses in a case. The police have not ruled out the chance that the woman herself did not know what she was carrying.

chunks.text: Nobody has {{come forward}} to say they organized it. The mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, called the [[blast]] a brutal [[terrorist act]] and said those [[behind it]] would be found. [[Beyond that]], almost nothing [[official]] has been said, and the space has filled with [[guesswork]]. Some Russian [[war bloggers]] blamed Ukraine without offering [[proof]], and Kyiv did not answer them. One Russian newspaper suggested the bomb may have been detonated [[from a distance]] by somebody else. So far nothing public {{points to}} any single answer. Russians have {{looked back}} to a café bombing in the same city in 2023, when a woman who carried a hidden bomb to a public event was later [[sentenced to]] 27 years in prison.

verbs.correct: To make yourself known in public
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place before others
verbs.why: A witness sometimes comes forward months after a crime, and a person with new information may come forward once they feel safe. Nobody has come forward yet to say they organized the Moscow bombing.

verbs.correct: To suggest that something is true
verbs.wrong: To name a person in an official list
verbs.why: Small clues sometimes point to who is responsible for a crime, and test results can point to an answer before doctors confirm it. So far, nothing public points to any single answer about who planted the bomb.

verbs.correct: To think about something in the past
verbs.wrong: To repeat an earlier mistake
verbs.why: People often look back on their school years with a smile, and historians look back at earlier events to find patterns. Russians have looked back to a similar 2023 cafe bombing that also used a hidden device.

chunks.text: What is left is a short list of things nobody can {{clear up}} yet. Investigators must {{track down}} whoever built the device and whoever chose the place and the hour. They are {{holding back}} most of what they know, which is normal early in a case like this but [[leaves everyone else guessing]]. The [[square]] is open again, the tower still stands above it, and a restaurant that was closed for a quiet evening has become the address of the worst attack in the [[capital]] this year.

verbs.correct: To explain something that is confusing
verbs.wrong: To close a street to traffic
verbs.why: A short phone call can clear up a misunderstanding fast, and one clear test can clear up a doctor's doubt. Investigators still cannot clear up who built the bomb or why that restaurant was chosen.

verbs.correct: To find someone after searching
verbs.wrong: To follow a person without being seen
verbs.why: Detectives track down missing people after a long search, and collectors sometimes track down a rare item for years. Investigators must track down whoever built the device and whoever chose the time and place.

verbs.correct: To refuse to share information
verbs.wrong: To close a case without an answer
verbs.why: A company sometimes holds back the true cost of a repair, and a witness may hold back details out of fear. Investigators are holding back most of what they know, which is normal early in a serious case.

mainIdea.s: Outside a Moscow restaurant, a bomb killed three people after a guard stopped a woman at the entrance. Russian authorities have officially confirmed that a foreign government ordered the attack.

lines.text: There was a bombing in central Moscow on Saturday. A homemade bomb {{went off}} outside an Italian restaurant. Three people were killed.
[[That's terrible]]. What happened exactly?

A woman carrying the device tried to enter through the front door. A security guard {{stepped in}} and {{turned her away}}. The bomb exploded on the street [[moments later]]. The woman, the guard, and one customer died, and 21 people were wounded.
The guard probably saved many lives.
Almost certainly. The restaurant was closed for a private event that evening.
Who did it?
Nobody knows. No one has {{come forward}} to claim it, and investigators have {{put out}} very little. They haven't named the woman or any suspect.
No theories at all?

Guesses, not facts. Some war bloggers blamed Ukraine without proof. One newspaper suggested the bomb was detonated from a distance, and officials haven't {{ruled out}} that the woman didn't know what she was carrying.
She might not have known? [[That's chilling]].
It has happened before. People {{looked back}} to a 2023 cafe bombing in the same city, where a woman carried a hidden bomb to a public event.
What happens now?
The anti-terrorism committee is {{looking into}} it. Investigators must {{track down}} whoever built the device and chose the place. So far, nothing public {{points to}} a single answer.
Why so quiet about the details?
They're {{holding back}} most of what they know, which is normal [[early on]], but it leaves everyone guessing. There's a long list of things nobody can {{clear up}} yet.
A quiet evening that became the worst attack in the capital this year.

stories.headline: A traveler gave his passcode and his phone erased itself

sources.title: US accuses American of allegedly wiping his phone using a 'duress' password during border search
Border agents can lie to search your phone, but wiping your own data could land you in prison
Traveler Gave CBP A Passcode That Wiped His Phone At Atlanta Airport. Now He Faces Five Years In Prison
Man Prosecuted in First-Ever Phone Duress Password Case (video, FOX 35 Orlando)

chunks.text: Samuel Tunick landed in Atlanta in January 2025 on a [[flight]] from the Dominican Republic. [[Customs]] officers {{pulled him aside}} for a second check and asked him to {{hand over}} the [[passcode]] to his phone. He gave them a code. The screen [[went dark]], [[flashed]] a few times, and the phone [[appeared to]] restart. The code he had typed was a [[duress]] code, and it {{wiped out}} everything on the device.

verbs.correct: To stop someone for extra questioning
verbs.wrong: To check a bag before it boards a plane
verbs.why: Security guards pull aside travelers for a random bag check, and teachers sometimes pull a student aside after class. Customs officers pulled Tunick aside at the Atlanta airport for a second check of his phone.

verbs.correct: To give something to a person in authority
verbs.wrong: To read something out loud to an officer
verbs.why: Drivers hand over their license at a traffic stop, and travelers hand over passports at customs. Tunick handed over his passcode when Customs officers asked for it at the airport.

verbs.correct: To erase everything stored on a device
verbs.wrong: To lock a device until it is unlocked again
verbs.why: A virus can wipe out a hard drive, and a factory reset wipes out every photo and app. Tunick's duress code wiped out his whole phone in seconds, erasing everything he owned.

chunks.text: A duress code is a second passcode that the owner {{sets up}} in advance. When it is typed, it looks exactly like the real one, but [[instead of]] opening the phone it orders a [[factory reset]] and destroys the [[encryption]] keys, so the phone {{starts up}} clean and the old files cannot be read. The feature exists to {{keep out}} anyone who forces the owner to unlock a phone. It is built into GrapheneOS, an [[operating system]] that some people install to replace the software that came with their phone.

verbs.correct: To arrange something in advance
verbs.wrong: To type a code very quickly
verbs.why: People set up a spare key with a neighbor, a backup email, or an emergency contact just in case. The phone's owner had set up his duress code long before any officer ever asked for his passcode.

verbs.correct: To begin working from the beginning
verbs.wrong: To send a copy of files to a server
verbs.why: An old car can be slow to start up on a cold morning, and a new laptop starts up in seconds. After the duress code ran, Tunick's phone started up clean, with nothing left on it.

verbs.correct: To prevent someone from entering
verbs.wrong: To warn the owner about a search
verbs.why: A locked door keeps out strangers, and a strong password keeps out hackers. This duress feature exists to keep out anyone who forces the owner to unlock the phone.

chunks.text: The stop happened in January 2025, but the case only became public in July 2026, and it is being fought in court now. [[Prosecutors]] have charged Tunick with destroying property to stop it being [[seized]], a rarely used law that carries [[up to]] five years in prison. He has pleaded not [[guilty]]. The officers said they were looking for illegal images, but they gave no reason for that [[suspicion]], and Tunick's [[lawyers]] say they had [[nothing to go on]]. They want a [[judge]] to {{throw out}} the [[evidence]] the officers gathered that day, and they argue that the stop would never {{stand up in court}} if the same thing had happened on a street [[rather than]] at an airport.

verbs.correct: To officially reject something
verbs.wrong: To return property to its owner
verbs.why: A referee can throw out a goal after watching the video, and a judge can throw out evidence collected the wrong way. Tunick's lawyers want the judge to throw out everything the officers found on his phone.

verbs.correct: To be accepted as valid by a judge
verbs.wrong: To be argued by a lawyer in person
verbs.why: A weak excuse rarely stands up in court, and neither does evidence gathered without good reason. Tunick's lawyers argue the airport stop would never stand up in court if it had happened on an ordinary street.

chunks.text: The case {{comes down to}} an old question with a new object [[at the center of it]]. Courts have long allowed officers at a border to search a bag without a [[warrant]], and the government says a phone is [[no different]]. Lawyers who work on [[privacy]] say a phone holds a person's whole life, so {{going through}} one is not like opening a suitcase. [[Congress]] has never {{stepped in}} to write a clear rule, and no court has {{sorted out}} the question [[for good]]. Until one does, every traveler who is asked for a passcode is standing in the same [[gray area]] Tunick stood in.

verbs.correct: To depend on one main question
verbs.wrong: To reach a court after many years
verbs.why: A tough decision often comes down to money, and an argument can come down to who spoke first. This case comes down to one question: does a phone deserve the same privacy as a home?

verbs.correct: To examine things one after another
verbs.wrong: To copy every file onto a disk
verbs.why: A detective goes through old case files, and a nurse goes through a patient's chart page by page. Searching a phone means going through years of someone's messages, photos, and private life.

verbs.correct: To get involved in order to act
verbs.wrong: To vote against a proposed law
verbs.why: A manager steps in when a meeting becomes an argument, and a referee steps in to stop a fight. Congress has never stepped in to write a clear rule about phone searches at the border.

verbs.correct: To settle a question completely
verbs.wrong: To pass a brand new law quickly
verbs.why: Neighbors sort out a fence dispute, and a manager sorts out a scheduling conflict before it grows. No court has sorted out whether border agents can demand a passcode from every traveler.

lines.text: A traveler landed in Atlanta, and customs officers {{pulled him aside}} for a second check. They asked him to {{hand over}} his phone passcode. He typed a code, the screen flashed, and the phone erased itself.
Erased itself? [[On purpose]]?

On purpose. It was a duress code, a second passcode the owner {{sets up}} in advance. It looks like the real one, but it {{wipes out}} everything and destroys the encryption keys. The phone {{starts up}} clean.
[[Wait, that exists?]] Why would phones have that?
The feature exists to {{keep out}} anyone who forces you to unlock your phone. It's built into a special operating system some people install.
What happened to him?
Prosecutors charged him with destroying property to stop it being seized, a rarely used law with up to five years in prison. He pleaded not guilty.
What were the officers even looking for?
They said illegal images, but they gave no reason for the suspicion. His lawyers say there was no real evidence, and they want a judge to {{throw out}} what the officers gathered that day.
Can officers really demand your passcode at the border?

[[That's the gray area]]. Courts allow bag searches at borders without a warrant, and the government says a phone is no different. Privacy lawyers say a phone holds your whole life, so {{going through}} one is not like opening a suitcase.
Hasn't anyone settled this?
No. Congress never {{stepped in}}, and no court has {{sorted out}} the question [[for good]]. His lawyers argue the stop would never {{stand up in court}} if it had happened on a street.
So the whole case {{comes down to}} one question: is a phone a suitcase?
That's the question a court now has to answer.

stories.headline: Sixty thousand people cross into Ceuta in one day

sources.title: Migrant deaths in Ceuta rise to 72 after border surge from Morocco
Situation in Ceuta 'almost entirely reversed' as death toll climbs to 67, Spain says
Why Thousands of Moroccan Migrants Crossed Into the Spanish Exclave Ceuta
Ceuta: Spain says over 60,000 migrants have entered from Morocco (video, ITV News)

chunks.text: About 60,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on Thursday, July 30. Ceuta is a small Spanish [[enclave]] on the north coast of Africa, with about 83,000 [[residents]]. Most of those who came {{set out}} from beaches near the Moroccan town of Fnideq and swam around the end of a stone [[breakwater]] that stretches into the sea. No city that size can {{take in}} that many people [[in a single day]]. At least 72 of them died, most of them [[drowned]] or were [[crushed]] against the rocks, and officials say the number may still {{go up}}.

verbs.correct: To begin a journey
verbs.wrong: To travel in a large group
verbs.why: Hikers set out at dawn to reach a summit, and sailors set out from port before a storm arrives. Most of the migrants set out from beaches near the Moroccan town of Fnideq before swimming toward Ceuta.

verbs.correct: To provide shelter for people
verbs.wrong: To count people as they arrive
verbs.why: A shelter takes in families after a fire, and a small town can take in visitors during a festival. Ceuta, a city of only 83,000 residents, could never take in 60,000 people arriving in a single day.

verbs.correct: To become higher in number
verbs.wrong: To be announced by officials
verbs.why: Grocery prices go up every summer, and a fever can go up quickly overnight. Spanish officials warned that the number of deaths from the crossing could still go up in the days that followed.

chunks.text: The reason [[lies partly in]] a court case. In June, Spain's Supreme Court {{handed down}} a [[ruling]] that stopped the government from returning people who arrive by sea without first hearing their case. Word {{got around}} on Moroccan social media that anyone who reached Ceuta by water could no longer be {{sent back}} the same day. That was [[not quite]] what the court had said, but thousands believed it. For years Moroccan police had {{held back}} crowds at the border fences, and [[youth unemployment]] in Morocco sits near 37 percent.

verbs.correct: To officially give a decision
verbs.wrong: To send a case to a lower court
verbs.why: A judge hands down a decision in court, and a company can hand down a new rule to its workers. In June, Spain's Supreme Court handed down a decision that stopped the government from returning people who arrive by sea without first hearing their case.

verbs.correct: To become known by many people
verbs.wrong: To be posted by a government office
verbs.why: A rumor gets around a small office within a day, and gossip gets around a school before lunch. Word got around on Moroccan social media that people who reached Ceuta by water could no longer be forced to leave the same day.

verbs.correct: To make someone return to their own country
verbs.wrong: To record someone's name at the border
verbs.why: Airlines send back passengers without a valid visa, and a country can send back people who cross the border illegally. The rumor claimed that arriving in Ceuta by water would stop officials from sending migrants back the same day.

verbs.correct: To stop people from moving forward
verbs.wrong: To keep a road closed at night
verbs.why: Security holds back fans until a stadium gate opens, and a thin line of officers can hold back a large crowd. For years, Moroccan police held back crowds at the border fences near Ceuta.

chunks.text: Spain's answer came quickly. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez flew to Ceuta on Friday and called the crossing a [[violation of]] Spanish [[sovereignty]]. His government {{ruled out}} declaring a national [[emergency]], but it sent extra police, and on Saturday workers {{put up}} a floating [[barrier]] 500 meters long across the sea border. On the other side, Moroccan [[riot police]] used [[tear gas]] and [[water cannon]] to clear people from the gates. Twenty-two European countries {{called for}} emergency talks, Italy suspended passport-free travel with Spain, and France [[tightened]] its own border.

verbs.correct: To decide against something
verbs.wrong: To announce something officially
verbs.why: A company can rule out layoffs before a hard quarter, and a coach might rule out a risky play. Spain's government ruled out declaring a national emergency, though it still sent extra police to Ceuta.

verbs.correct: To build something as a barrier
verbs.wrong: To repair a damaged fence
verbs.why: Workers put up a fence around a construction site, and a city puts up flood walls before a storm. Spanish workers put up a floating barrier 500 meters long across the sea border in just one day.

verbs.correct: To publicly ask for something
verbs.wrong: To agree to a plan without a vote
verbs.why: Doctors call for stricter safety rules, and a mayor can call for calm after a difficult week. Twenty-two European countries called for emergency talks once news of the mass crossing spread.

chunks.text: By Saturday morning the [[flow]] had [[reversed]]. More than 48,000 people were back in Morocco within two days, and Spain's interior minister described Morocco as a partner [[rather than]] a threat. The crossings {{died down}} almost as fast as they had begun. The questions they {{brought up}} are much harder to settle. The Civil Guard is still {{going through}} [[fingerprints]] and DNA to [[identify]] the dead, more than a thousand people needed [[medical treatment]], and the city [[morgue]] has received 88 bodies, some of them from earlier attempts in the same two weeks. The new barrier covers 500 meters of the only [[land border]] between the European Union and Africa.

verbs.correct: To become less strong
verbs.wrong: To stop for one night only
verbs.why: Loud applause dies down after a few minutes, and anger between old friends can die down in a week. The crossings into Ceuta died down almost as fast as they had begun.

verbs.correct: To mention a subject
verbs.wrong: To settle an old argument
verbs.why: A child brings up an old promise at dinner, and a coworker can bring up a topic nobody wants to discuss. The mass crossing brought up hard questions about the border that will take much longer to answer.

verbs.correct: To examine things one after another
verbs.wrong: To send evidence to another country
verbs.why: A detective goes through old case files, and a clerk goes through the mail every morning. The Civil Guard is still going through fingerprints and DNA to identify each of the dead.

lines.text: Did you follow what happened in Ceuta? Sixty thousand people crossed from Morocco into the small Spanish enclave in a single day.
Sixty thousand? Into a city of 83,000?

[[Exactly the problem]]. No city that size can {{take in}} that many people at once. Most {{set out}} from nearby beaches and swam around the breakwater. At least 72 people died, most drowned or crushed against the rocks.
[[That's horrific]]. Why did so many go at the same time?

Partly a court ruling. Spain's Supreme Court had {{handed down}} a decision that stopped same-day returns for people arriving by sea. Word {{got around}} on social media that nobody could be {{sent back}} anymore.
Was that true?
[[Not quite]], but thousands believed it. And [[behind it all]], youth unemployment in Morocco is near 37 percent. For years police had {{held back}} crowds at the fences.
What did Spain do?

The prime minister flew to Ceuta, called it a violation of sovereignty, but {{ruled out}} a national emergency. Workers {{put up}} a 500-meter floating barrier across the sea border, and 22 European countries {{called for}} emergency talks.
Did the crossings continue?
No, they {{died down}} almost as fast as they began. Within two days, more than 48,000 people were back in Morocco.
And the people who died?
Investigators are still {{going through}} fingerprints and DNA to identify them. The morgue has received 88 bodies, some from earlier attempts.
The questions this {{brings up}} won't disappear with the barrier.
No. It covers 500 meters of the only land border between the European Union and Africa. And officials say the number of dead may still {{go up}}.

mainIdea.s: At a health conference in Rio de Janeiro, the US displayed a map with African countries placed wrongly. A watermark suggested the map came from an AI tool, right as HIV funding fell sharply.
mainIdea.why: The map placed several African countries in the wrong spot and seemed to come from an AI tool. It appeared just as international HIV funding fell sharply.

mainIdea.s: The map shown at the Rio conference was an old graphic that had not been updated in years. Officials said the error had nothing to do with artificial intelligence or last minute preparation.

mainIdea.s: A separate UN report this month called for better satellite mapping of African countries' borders. The report said outdated maps have caused border disputes between neighboring governments.
mainIdea.why: This is about a UN report on satellite mapping of borders, not the mislabeled map shown at the health conference.

tf.why: Nigeria had been placed in the Sahara desert, Mozambique had shifted across to the Horn of Africa, and Ivory Coast was on the wrong side of the continent.

tf.why: The audience picked up on it at once. The room was full of doctors, researchers and health officials from across Africa.

lines.text: Have you seen the map story? The US State Department {{put up}} a slide at a big health conference showing Africa, with the countries in the wrong places.
Wrong how?
Nigeria was in the Sahara. Mozambique had {{shifted across to}} the Horn of Africa. Ivory Coast was on the wrong side of the continent.
[[You're joking]]. Who was in the room?
[[That's the worst part]]. Doctors and health officials from all over Africa, many from the exact countries that had been {{shuffled around}}.
Did anyone notice [[right away]]?
Immediately. The audience {{picked up on}} it at once, and a watermark suggested an AI tool made the map. It looked like the slide had been {{thrown together}} minutes before the session.
So the AI drew the map and nobody checked?

Exactly the habit people criticized: {{handing over}} a job to software and then {{signing off on}} the result without reading it. If nobody could {{make out}} their own country, someone should have checked before the slide ever {{went up}}.
Did they apologize?

Yes, the slide was quickly {{taken down}} and they called it an unfortunate error. But the story {{caught on}} because of the timing. The same conference heard that HIV funding has {{dropped off}} sharply, the steepest fall in about twenty years.
So a careless map [[on top of]] deep funding cuts.
That's what delegates kept {{coming back to}}. Carelessness carries a message, [[whether anyone intends it or not]].

stories.headline: The daughter of a jailed president leads Peru

Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president after narrow election win (video, Al Jazeera English)

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori became president of Peru on July 28, [[at the age of]] 51 and at her fourth [[attempt]]. She had lost three earlier elections. She won this one by [[fewer than]] 50,000 votes in a [[second round]] in June. She now {{takes over}} a country that has {{gone through}} eight presidents in ten years, in a system where governments rarely {{last out}} a full [[term]].

verbs.correct: To become the person in charge
verbs.wrong: To win a close election
verbs.why: A new coach takes over a losing team and hopes to start winning, and a daughter sometimes takes over her family's small shop. Keiko Fujimori now takes over a country that has had eight presidents in just ten years.

verbs.correct: To experience many things in turn
verbs.wrong: To keep the same leader for years
verbs.why: A struggling team can go through three different coaches in one season, and a person might go through several jobs before finding the right one. Peru itself has gone through eight presidents in just ten years of near-constant change.

verbs.correct: To continue to the end
verbs.wrong: To be removed before the end
verbs.why: Cheap batteries rarely last out a long camping trip, and a weak umbrella will not last out a real storm. Few Peruvian leaders manage to last out a complete term before being forced from power.

chunks.text: Her [[surname]] is the reason many Peruvians voted for her and the reason many others voted against. Her father, Alberto Fujimori, ruled Peru in the 1990s. During those years the state {{put down}} a violent [[rebellion]] and the economy became [[stable]]. Those same years ended with him leaving office in [[disgrace]], and he was later [[sentenced]] to 16 years in prison for [[corruption]] and for [[crimes against humanity]]. [[Supporters]] say he {{brought back}} order to a country [[close to]] [[collapse]]. [[Opponents]] say he {{did away with}} democratic limits and that people died because of it. Both of those things are [[in the record]].

verbs.correct: To stop a revolt by force
verbs.wrong: To begin an armed attack
verbs.why: An army once put down a peasant revolt within a few short weeks, and troops were sent to put down an armed uprising in the north. Alberto Fujimori is remembered for putting down a violent rebellion during his years in power.

verbs.correct: To make something exist again
verbs.wrong: To promise something in a speech
verbs.why: A bakery might bring back a popular bread after customer requests, and a new manager could bring back an old rule that had been dropped. His supporters believe Alberto Fujimori brought back much needed order during a very unstable time.

verbs.correct: To end something completely
verbs.wrong: To ignore a rule but keep it
verbs.why: A company might do away with its strict dress code after employees complain, and a school could do away with letter grades entirely. Opponents say Alberto Fujimori did away with democratic limits on his own power while he was president.

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori has {{taken up}} crime as her main issue. It is the topic that worries most Peruvians, according to [[pollsters]]. She has promised what she calls [[an iron fist]]. That means a very large new prison, more police on the streets, and judges whose names are not published so that criminals cannot [[threaten]] them. Human rights groups have already {{spoken out}} about those [[anonymous]] judges. Their argument is that a [[defendant]] cannot [[properly]] {{stand up for}} himself in a court when he does not know who is judging him.

verbs.correct: To start doing something new
verbs.wrong: To choose a new political party
verbs.why: An activist might take up a new cause after seeing something unfair, and a retiree could take up painting to fill her free time. Keiko Fujimori has taken up crime as her main issue, since it worries so many Peruvians.

verbs.correct: To state opinions publicly
verbs.wrong: To be asked to give an opinion
verbs.why: Human rights groups often speak out when a new law threatens someone's basic rights, and workers may speak out about unsafe conditions at a factory. Human rights groups have already spoken out about judges whose names are kept secret from the public.

verbs.correct: To defend or support
verbs.wrong: To appear before a judge
verbs.why: A good friend always stands up for you when others are unfair, and a brave employee might stand up for a coworker being treated badly. Critics argue a defendant cannot properly stand up for himself in court without knowing who the judge is.

chunks.text: Whether she can {{hold on to}} power [[long enough to]] do any of it is the open question. Peru's [[Congress]] has {{pushed out}} several recent presidents, and her party does not control it. She has {{called on}} other parties to work [[alongside]] her. In a country that has changed leader almost every year, simply reaching the end of a full term would be unusual.

verbs.correct: To keep possession of
verbs.wrong: To share power with others
verbs.why: A leader must work hard to hold on to power. A worker tries to hold on to a steady job. Nobody knows yet if Fujimori can hold on to power for long, because Peru's Congress has removed several recent presidents.

verbs.correct: To force someone to leave
verbs.wrong: To block a new law from passing
verbs.why: Rising rents can push out small family shops from a neighborhood, and a new owner sometimes pushes out the old staff right away. Peru's Congress has pushed out several recent presidents before they finished a full term.

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone
verbs.wrong: To offer someone a position
verbs.why: Protesters often call on the government to act faster after a disaster, and a teacher may call on a quiet student to answer a question. Since her party lacks a majority in Congress, Fujimori has called on rival parties for support.

mainIdea.s: A former president's daughter won Peru's presidency by a wide margin in the June election. Her party now firmly controls Congress, so lawmakers are expected to support her easily.
mainIdea.why: Close, but she won by fewer than 50,000 votes, not by a wide margin. Her party also does not control Congress, so she cannot count on easy support there.

lines.text: Peru has a new president: the daughter of a former president who is in prison.
That sounds complicated already.
Very. She won on her fourth attempt, by fewer than 50,000 votes, and {{takes over}} a country that has {{gone through}} eight presidents in ten years.
Why is her father in prison?

He ruled in the 1990s. Supporters say he {{brought back}} order and a stable economy. Opponents say he {{did away with}} democratic limits, and he was sentenced for corruption and crimes against humanity.
Both can be true, I suppose.
[[It's all in the record]]. The state {{put down}} a violent rebellion in those years, and people died.
What is she promising?
She has {{taken up}} crime as her main issue, an "iron fist": a huge new prison, more police, and judges whose names stay secret so criminals can't threaten them.
Secret judges? Is that legal?
Human rights groups have {{spoken out}} about it. Their argument: a defendant can't properly {{stand up for}} himself if he doesn't know who is judging him.
Can she actually govern?
[[That's the open question]]. Congress has {{pushed out}} several recent presidents, and her party doesn't control it. She has {{called on}} other parties to work with her.
So just finishing her term would be an achievement.
In Peru right now, a president who can {{last out}} a full term and {{hold on to}} power would be unusual all by itself.

chunks.text: Google said on July 24 that its Pixel phones will cost more, and gave a reason people did not expect. The company is not paying more for design or for [[labor]]. It is paying more for [[memory]]. Memory is the set of [[chips]] that hold information while a phone is actually working, and it is separate from the [[storage]] where photos and apps sit. A [[senior]] Google [[manager]] said the company had {{held off}} on raising prices for [[as long as]] it could, but that the [[economics]] underneath had changed.

verbs.correct: To delay doing something
verbs.wrong: To refuse something completely
verbs.why: Companies hold off on hiring, hold off on big purchases, or hold off on a decision until the timing feels right. Google held off on raising phone prices for as long as it could, until rising memory costs left it no choice.

chunks.text: The numbers are [[steep]]. According to figures from one [[investment bank]], a [[gigabyte]] of this memory cost about 2.80 dollars in 2025 and costs about 12 dollars in 2026. That is [[roughly]] six times more in a single year. The Google manager said there had never been a rise in memory prices like the one the world is {{going through}} now. Reports suggest the next Pixel may {{cut back on}} memory [[compared with]] the [[model]] before it, with extra storage offered instead.

verbs.correct: To experience something
verbs.wrong: To cause something to happen
verbs.why: People go through hard times, go through a divorce, or go through big changes at work. Right now the entire tech industry is going through a jump in memory prices unlike anything seen before.

verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of
verbs.wrong: To buy from a different maker
verbs.why: People cut back on sugar, cut back on spending, or cut back on coffee to save money or stay healthy. The next Pixel model may cut back on memory chips and offer more storage space instead.

chunks.text: The cause has nothing to do with phones. Companies building [[data centers]] for artificial intelligence have been {{buying up}} memory chips in [[enormous]] [[quantities]], and the factories cannot {{churn out}} enough to serve everyone. lines.text: Your next phone will probably cost more, and the reason is AI.
What does AI have to do with my phone?
Memory chips. Companies building AI data centers have been {{buying up}} memory in enormous quantities, and factories can't {{churn out}} enough for everyone.
How bad is it?
A gigabyte of this memory cost about $2.80 last year. Now it's about $12. Six times more in one year.
[[Ouch]]. Who said this?
Google, about its Pixel phones. They said they {{held off}} on raising prices as long as they could. The next model may even {{cut back on}} memory and offer extra storage instead.
So a few giant buyers {{soak up}} the supply, and everyone else pays more.
Exactly. Phone makers, laptop makers, console makers, all standing in the same line. The world is {{going through}} a memory price rise like never before.
And regular people?
Someone replacing a broken phone in Manila or Warsaw will {{pay out}} more this year, and the reason {{traces back}} to warehouses of computers on another continent.
Will other phone companies raise prices too?
That's the question. Rivals may {{put up}} their prices as well, or {{hold out}} a little longer.
Suddenly my cracked screen doesn't look so bad. [[I can live with it]].

stories.headline: The Louvre reopens its jewel room empty

sources.title: Louvre Reopens Apollo Gallery Nine Months After Jewel Heist
Louvre's Apollo Gallery Reopens With No Jewelry on Display After Heist
Louvre reopens Apollo Gallery after brazen heist, with no jewels on display
