lines.text: Cuba's power grid has {{broken down}} again. The whole island lost electricity, about 10 million people {{cut off}} at once.
Again? Didn't that just happen?
Third major blackout in about two weeks. The system completely {{shut down}} in the middle of the day.
What keeps causing it?

Two things. The island is {{running out of}} fuel for its plants, partly because of new US sanctions. And the power stations are ancient, some built in the 1960s. One unit failed in the east and {{set off}} the wider collapse.
How do you even repair a whole country's grid?

Piece by piece. Engineers {{turned on}} small islands of electricity and joined them into a bigger network. Hospitals and food factories came first, workers {{dealt with}} them before anything else. Then teams started to {{bring back}} power in Havana.
What's daily life like in a blackout?
Hard. No cooking, no water pumps, no way to {{log on}} to the internet. Hospitals even {{called off}} surgeries.
[[I don't know how they do it]].
People are tired of it. Families have {{put up with}} one outage after another, and anger is growing.
[[Any end in sight?]]
Not soon. Fuel is still short, so few Cubans expect a [[quick fix]].

chunks.text: In China, a new [[regulation]] has {{shut down}} [[one of the most]] personal uses of AI. Millions of people had been chatting with [[virtual]] "[[companion]]" apps that could [[act like]] a close friend or even a [[romantic]] partner. Now the government wants technology companies to {{turn off}} these [[features]]. Officials say the apps were [[built to]] {{reel in}} [[lonely]] users and [[keep them coming back]].

chunks.text: Several big companies quickly {{gave in}} to the new law. ByteDance, which runs the popular app Doubao, {{took away}} its romantic-companion feature on July 15. Alibaba and Tencent removed similar tools even earlier in the year. The rules also {{keep out}} anyone under 18, so [[minors]] can [[no longer]] form these [[bonds]].

verbs.correct: To finally agree to something you were resisting
verbs.wrong: To stop trying and abandon something completely

chunks.text: For many users, the change was hard to {{deal with}}. Some had {{grown attached to}} their [[chatbots]] over months or even years. One person wrote that their AI companion [[felt like]] family, and that saying goodbye left their heart feeling [[hollow]]. Others {{broke down}} online, sharing long [[farewell]] messages before the apps closed [[for good]].

verbs.correct: To handle or cope with a difficult situation
verbs.wrong: To fully solve a problem so it never returns
verbs.why: A new employee deals with a heavy workload in the first month, and a family deals with a hard loss. For many users in China, losing their AI companion was hard to deal with.

verbs.correct: To develop a strong emotional bond with someone or something

verbs.correct: To lose control of your emotions and start crying

chunks.text: The government says the rules will {{look after}} people's [[mental health]] and stop apps from {{taking advantage of}} [[loneliness]]. Doubao will let users save their chat history until October. [[Still]], many people [[wonder whether]] a machine can ever {{make up for}} real [[human connection]].

chunks.text: Archaeologists in Egypt have {{dug up}} an [[ancient]] [[tomb]] near the city of Luxor. A Dutch team from Leiden University {{teamed up with}} Egypt's [[antiquities]] authority to [[explore]] the west bank of the Nile. The tomb is about 3,000 years old, and it [[belonged to]] an [[official]] named Paser. Experts believe it {{dates back}} to the Ramesside period, a great age of Egyptian [[pharaohs]].

lines.text: Archaeologists near Luxor have {{dug up}} a painted tomb that's 3,000 years old.
Painted? After all that time?
That's the amazing part. Time hasn't {{worn away}} the colors. The walls still {{show off}} bright scenes of an official named Paser worshiping the gods.
[[Imagine that]]. Three thousand years and the paint survives.
There's even a scene of him beside his wife, with a table of offerings. Researchers say the art really {{leaps out}} at you.
Who found it?
A Dutch team from Leiden University. They {{teamed up with}} Egypt's antiquities authority and have worked at the site since 2018.
So they didn't just {{come across}} it by luck?
Not at all. Years of careful digging finally {{paid off}}. As they {{cleared away}} sand and fallen stone, a courtyard, a chapel, and burial chambers appeared.
How old exactly?
It {{dates back}} to the Ramesside period, the great age of the pharaohs.
What happens next?
Experts will {{pore over}} the writing on the walls. They hope it will {{shed light on}} Paser's life and his role in Egyptian society.
[[Who knows]] what else is still under those sands.

chunks.text: The US House of Representatives wants to {{do away with}} the twice-a-year clock changes. On Tuesday, [[lawmakers]] {{voted for}} a [[bill]] called the Sunshine Protection Act by 308 votes to 117. The plan would {{lock in}} [[permanent]] [[daylight saving time]] all across the country. Many [[supporters]] say the change is [[long overdue]].

chunks.text: So what does 'changing the clocks' [[actually]] mean? In many countries, people turn their clocks forward by one hour in spring and back again in fall. This [[custom]] is called daylight saving time, and it helps people {{make use of}} the extra evening light in summer. The original goal was also to save energy. But twice each year, millions of people must {{get used to}} a new [[schedule]], and [[the switch]] can {{throw off}} their sleep for several days.

lines.text: New York just became the first state to {{put off}} building giant AI data centers. Governor Hochul {{signed off on}} a one-year pause.
A whole state said no to data centers? [[Bold move]].
A pause, not a full no. These hyperscale centers {{use up}} enormous amounts of electricity and water, and residents have {{spoken out}} about it.
What are they afraid of?
That the centers will {{drive up}} their utility bills, and that the power grid can't handle the extra load.
So what happens during the pause?

State agencies will {{look into}} the effects on energy, water, and air quality. Experts will {{press ahead with}} a full environmental study, and the state wants to {{set up}} rules so local communities actually benefit.
Are the tech companies angry?
Some have {{pushed back}}. They say jobs and investment could go to other states. But the governor won't {{back down}}.
Has any other state done this?
Cities and counties have blocked projects, but no state had {{weighed in}} until now.
And after the year ends?
If the study goes well, building may {{go ahead}} again under stricter standards.
[[Watch this space]]. Everyone will copy whatever New York does.

chunks.text: Every year on July 14, France celebrates Bastille Day, the country's national day. This year, France {{put on}} its yearly military [[parade]] down the famous Champs-Élysées [[avenue]] in Paris. [[Soldiers]], [[tanks]], and planes moved slowly along the wide street while huge [[crowds]] {{turned up}} to watch. The holiday {{looks back}} at [[a key moment]] in French history and gives the whole nation [[a chance to]] feel [[proud]].

chunks.text: This year's parade was different from all the others. [[For the first time]], [[troops]] from other European countries {{joined in}} and marched together with the French army. The event was planned to {{stand up for}} Ukraine, which has been fighting a war against Russia for years. Through the parade, these nations wanted to {{show off}} their [[unity]] and [[prove]] to Ukraine that it is [[not alone]].

Around 30 world leaders {{showed up}} to [[stand beside]] him. A heat wave was so strong that many towns had to {{call off}} their [[fireworks]], but the [[mood]] in Paris stayed proud and strong.

lines.text: Did you see the pictures from Bastille Day? France {{put on}} its big parade in Paris, but this year was special.

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} a new medicine that may bring [[relief]] to people with [[late-stage]] dementia. The medicine [[carefully]] mixes two [[compounds]] from the cannabis plant, known as THC and CBD. Doctors tested it on patients who often [[deal with]] [[agitation]], a state of restlessness and [[distress]]. In early results that just {{came out}}, the treatment {{calmed down}} many patients.

verbs.wrong: To completely cure a person's long-term illness
verbs.why: A soft voice can calm down a scared child, and quiet music calms down a nervous dog before a storm. In the trial, the new medicine calmed down many patients who had been restless for months.

chunks.text: The researchers {{went about}} the LiBBY [[trial]] [[with great care]], testing about 120 people whose dementia was very [[advanced]]. Their [[average]] age was 80, and most were [[eligible]] for [[hospice]] care. Nurses {{handed out}} the medicine as a [[fast-acting]] oil that patients could swallow. For 12 weeks, the team {{kept track of}} how each person's behavior and mood changed.

verbs.why: A careful cook goes about a recipe step by step, and a good manager goes about a project with a clear plan. The research team went about the dementia trial with great care, testing about 120 patients.

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very strong. Close to 90 percent of the patients on the medicine got better, while [[far fewer]] improved on a [[placebo]]. That large [[gap]] made the study {{jump out}} at other researchers. One lead doctor said it is [[rare]] to see so many patients respond so well to a new drug.

The medicine was made in a lab and given under close [[supervision]]. [[Side effects]] were [[mild]], and doctors could not {{rule out}} that some were caused by the illness itself. As they {{look ahead}}, the team hopes larger trials will [[confirm]] these [[hopeful]] results.

lines.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} a cannabis-based medicine for people with late-stage dementia. Early results just {{came out}}.
Cannabis for dementia patients? [[Really?]]
For agitation, the restlessness and distress many patients feel. In the trial, the treatment {{calmed down}} most of them.
How did they test it?

Very carefully. The team {{went about}} the trial with 120 patients, average age 80. Nurses {{handed out}} the medicine as an oil, and for 12 weeks doctors {{kept track of}} every change in mood and behavior.
And the results?
They {{turned out}} to be strong. Almost 90 percent of patients got better. That gap made the study {{jump out}} at other researchers.
Wait, is this the same [[stuff]] people buy in stores?

Any side effects?
Mild ones, though doctors couldn't {{rule out}} that some came from the illness itself. As they {{look ahead}}, they want larger trials.
My grandmother had those restless days. [[This one hits close to home]].

chunks.text: The United States has lost one of its most [[familiar]] politicians. Lindsey Graham, a [[Republican]] [[senator]] from South Carolina, {{passed away}} on Saturday evening at the age of 71. In the days before, he had {{come down with}} a [[sudden]] illness, and his health {{went downhill}} very quickly. His family shared the news late that night and asked people to [[respect]] their [[privacy]].

chunks.text: [[At first]], doctors were not sure what had happened. chunks.text: Graham had {{taken up}} politics many years earlier and had {{stayed on}} in public office [[ever since]]. He was first {{voted in}} to the [[Senate]] in 2002. Around the world, he was [[known for]] his strong views on war, peace, and [[foreign affairs]].

chunks.text: Scientists in the United Kingdom have {{come across}} something [[surprising]] about exercise. A team at the University of Bristol {{found out}} that regular [[aerobic]] exercise does more than make the heart muscle stronger. It also reshapes the [[tiny]] [[nerves]] that {{take care of}} the heart's [[rhythm]]. The [[discovery]] could [[lead to]] better care for people with dangerous heartbeat problems.

verbs.correct: To find or discover something by chance
verbs.wrong: To search hard for something over a long time
verbs.why: You come across an old photo while cleaning a closet, or come across a great recipe while scrolling online. Scientists in Bristol came across a surprising fact: exercise reshapes the tiny nerves that control the heart's rhythm.

verbs.correct: To learn something after study or investigation
verbs.wrong: To share news with the public for the first time
verbs.why: Detectives find out the truth after weeks of work, and students find out their grades online. A team at the University of Bristol found out that exercise reshapes the heart's nerves, not just its muscle.

verbs.correct: To be responsible for something and control it
verbs.wrong: To develop brand new cells to replace old ones
verbs.why: Parents take care of young children, and a good manager takes care of a busy team. In this study, tiny nerves take care of the heart's rhythm, keeping every beat steady.

chunks.text: To find these changes, the team {{set up}} a study on rats. The animals {{worked out}} on a regular plan for ten weeks, [[a bit like]] a person going to the gym. Using powerful 3D [[imaging]], the scientists could {{zoom in}} on small clusters of nerve cells near the heart. These cells [[act like]] a [[dimmer switch]] that turns the heartbeat up or down.

verbs.correct: To start or organize something new
verbs.wrong: To trick someone into taking the blame
verbs.why: You set up a tent before camping, or set up a new phone before using it. Scientists set up a ten week exercise study on rats to see how their hearts would change.

verbs.correct: To do physical exercise to get fit
verbs.wrong: To follow a special diet to lose weight
verbs.why: People work out at the gym before work, or work out at home with simple equipment. In this study, the rats worked out on a set plan for ten weeks, much like someone training for a race.

verbs.correct: To focus closely on one small area to study it
verbs.wrong: To take a photograph from a long distance away
verbs.why: A camera can zoom in on a small detail, and a map app lets you zoom in on one street. Powerful 3D imaging let the scientists zoom in on tiny clusters of nerve cells near the heart.

chunks.text: The results {{turned out}} to be very [[unusual]]. On the right side of the heart, the trained rats {{wound up with}} about four times more [[neurons]], the special cells that carry nerve [[signals]]. On the left side, the number of cells [[stayed the same]], but each one nearly [[doubled]] in size. Exercise did not shape the two sides in the same way, and that difference intrigued the scientists.

verbs.correct: To happen or be shown to be true in the end
verbs.wrong: To go exactly as the scientists had predicted
verbs.why: A rainy forecast can turn out sunny, and a stranger can turn out to be a good friend. In this study, the results turned out to be very unusual, since the two sides of the heart changed in different ways.

verbs.correct: To finally have something as a result
verbs.wrong: To slowly relax after a busy time
verbs.why: You can wind up with extra tickets when friends cancel, or wind up with a messy kitchen after a big dinner. The trained rats wound up with about four times more nerve cells on one side of the heart.

chunks.text: The team hopes these [[findings]] will {{open up}} new ways to [[treat]] heart problems. Doctors already work on these nerves to calm a racing heart, and knowing which side to focus on could make the treatment [[far better]]. This could help people with [[arrhythmias]], chest pain, and other conditions. [[For now]] the work is [[at an early stage]], so scientists must {{follow up}} with studies in humans before any [[therapy]] is ready.

verbs.wrong: To make an existing treatment work faster
verbs.why: A good certificate can open up new job options, and travel can open up new friendships. The team hopes these findings will open up new ways to treat heart problems.

verbs.wrong: To repeat the exact same test with no changes
verbs.why: A doctor might follow up after surgery, and a company can follow up on an email that went unanswered. Scientists must follow up with studies in humans before any new heart therapy is ready.

lines.text: Scientists in the UK {{came across}} something surprising about exercise. It changes the nerves around your heart, not just the muscle.
The nerves? [[What do you mean]]?
A team in Bristol {{found out}} that aerobic exercise reshapes the tiny nerve cells that {{take care of}} the heart's rhythm.
How do you even study that?

They {{set up}} a ten-week study with rats. The animals {{worked out}} on a regular plan, a bit like going to the gym. Then powerful 3D imaging let the scientists {{zoom in}} on nerve clusters near the heart.
And what did they see?
The results {{turned out}} to be strange. On the right side of the heart, trained rats {{wound up with}} four times more neurons. On the left side, the cells doubled in size instead.
Different changes on each side? [[Weird]].
Very. But useful. Doctors already treat these nerves to calm a racing heart, so knowing which side to target could {{open up}} better treatments.
For people with rhythm problems?
Exactly, arrhythmias and similar conditions. It's early, though. The team still has to {{follow up}} with human studies.
Another reason to exercise, I guess. My heart [[will thank me]].

chunks.text: Doctors have long wondered how people can keep their minds [[sharp]] as they grow older. Now, a large study across Latin America has {{set out}} to answer that question. Scientists {{teamed up}} with older adults in 11 countries and {{rolled out}} a two year program to protect memory and slow mental [[decline]]. The results were shared at a major [[dementia]] conference in July 2026.

lines.text: Engineers in Chile just {{pulled off}} a beautiful test. The world's biggest telescope turned for the first time.
The one in the Atacama Desert?
That's it, the Extremely Large Telescope. A small team pushed the structure by hand, centimeters at a time, while the others {{looked on}}. Then the motors {{took over}} and completed a full turn.
They moved a giant telescope by hand? [[How is that possible]]?
The whole thing is {{held up}} by a layer of oil only 80 microns thin, so it slides almost without effort.
[[That's genius]]. How big is it exactly?
The metal parts {{add up to}} about 3,500 tons now, and the weight will {{go up}} past 4,600 once the mirrors are installed.
Mirrors, plural?
The main mirror will be {{made up of}} 798 glass segments that {{carry out}} the work of one giant mirror, 39 meters wide.
When can astronomers actually use it?
Builders hope to {{wrap up}} around 2028. It will {{stand out}} as the largest optical telescope in the world.

stories.headline: Speaking more languages may keep the brain younger

sources.title: Speaking multiple languages may slow brain aging by years, study finds
Multilingualism Subtracts Up to 13 Years from Brain Age
Speaking another language could slow aging in the brain
Study shows learning another language appears to slow brain aging (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{come up with}} [[a new way to]] measure how quickly the human brain grows older. At a large science [[conference]] in Europe, a research team from the Basque region of Spain {{pointed out}} that people who speak several languages often have younger brains than their [[chronological]] age would suggest. The team {{set out}} to test [[whether]] knowing more than one language can [[slow]] this kind of [[aging]]. Their [[early results]] suggest that it can.

verbs.correct: To think of or create a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem you did not expect
verbs.why: Teams come up with new plans when the old one fails, and kids come up with clever excuses for being late. Scientists came up with a new way to measure how quickly a person's brain is aging.

verbs.correct: To tell people a fact they may not have noticed
verbs.wrong: To prove that something is completely true
verbs.why: A good editor points out small mistakes before a piece is published, and a friend might point out a detail you missed completely. Researchers pointed out that people who speak several languages often have younger looking brains.

verbs.correct: To begin doing something with a clear goal in mind
verbs.wrong: To hope strongly for a particular result
verbs.why: A runner sets out to break a personal record, and a young company sets out to change how people shop. This research team set out to test whether speaking more languages could slow brain aging.

chunks.text: The researchers used [[a form of]] artificial intelligence to {{work out}} each person's 'brain age' from [[patterns]] of brain [[connectivity]]. They looked at 144 people in the Basque region who spoke between one and four languages, such as Spanish, Basque, French, and English. As the number of languages grew, the brains [[appeared]] younger and younger. People who spoke two languages had brains that seemed about six years younger, while those who spoke four {{ended up}} with brains that looked around thirteen years younger.

verbs.correct: To calculate or figure something out
verbs.wrong: To guess an answer without any real evidence
verbs.why: Friends work out a fair way to split a bill, and a student might work out the answer in her head before checking it. Researchers used artificial intelligence to work out each person's brain age from patterns in the brain.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain result or state
verbs.wrong: To improve step by step over many years
verbs.why: You end up lost on a new street sometimes, or you end up with the last slice of pizza nobody else wanted. People who spoke four languages in this study ended up with brains that looked about thirteen years younger.

chunks.text: The scientists say the number of languages is not the only thing that {{stands out}}. People who {{picked up}} a second language early in life, and who reached [[a high level of]] [[proficiency]], seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly. Being truly [[fluent]] appeared to matter [[just as much as]] speaking many languages. Constantly [[switching between]] languages may give the brain a kind of daily workout that keeps it healthy.

verbs.correct: To be clearly noticed as important
verbs.wrong: To be the main cause of a result
verbs.why: One answer can stand out as clearly the best in an interview, and good manners often stand out in a crowded room. In this research, the number of languages a person speaks is not the only factor that stands out.

verbs.correct: To learn a skill or language informally
verbs.wrong: To formally study a subject in a class
verbs.why: Children pick up new words just by listening, and travelers often pick up a bit of the local language after a few weeks abroad. People in this study who picked up a second language early in life kept more of the brain benefit.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose or give it up
verbs.wrong: To gain even more of something over time
verbs.why: People hold on to old photos for years, and a worker might hold on to a steady job through hard times. Early, fluent language speakers in this study seemed to hold on to the brain benefit more strongly than others.

chunks.text: These [[findings]] match a much larger project that {{looked into}} the health of 86,149 older people across 27 European countries. In that [[survey]], people who spoke several languages were about [[half as likely]] to show fast, unhealthy aging. Experts say the two studies {{back up}} a simple message: it is [[never too late]] to start. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow some of the mental [[decline]] that often [[comes with age]].

verbs.correct: To examine or investigate something carefully
verbs.wrong: To protect and be responsible for something
verbs.why: Doctors look into the cause of an illness, and a shopper might look into cheaper flights before booking a trip. A separate, much larger project looked into the health of more than 86,000 older adults across Europe.

verbs.correct: To support something and show that it is true
verbs.wrong: To give a short summary of the main points
verbs.why: New evidence can back up an old theory, and test results sometimes back up exactly what a doctor already suspected. Experts say these two language studies back up a simple message: it is never too late to start.

verbs.correct: To start doing a new activity, hobby, or study
verbs.wrong: To fill or use a large amount of time or space
verbs.why: Adults take up gardening after retirement, and some people take up running to relieve stress. Adults who take up a new language later in life may still slow some of the mental decline that often happens with age.

lines.text: [[Good news for you]]. Scientists say speaking more languages may keep your brain younger.
Really? So my three languages are good for something?
Very good. Researchers in Spain {{came up with}} a way to measure "brain age" and {{set out}} to test whether languages slow aging.
How do you measure a brain's age?
With AI. It can {{work out}} your brain age from connection patterns. They tested 144 people who spoke one to four languages.
And?
The more languages, the younger the brain. Two languages looked about six years younger. People with four {{ended up}} with brains around thirteen years younger.
Thirteen years younger? [[Not bad!]]
The scientists {{pointed out}} that fluency matters too. People who {{picked up}} a second language early and reached a high level seemed to {{hold on to}} the benefit more strongly.
What {{stands out}} most to you?
A bigger project {{looked into}} the health of 86,000 older people across Europe, and it {{backs up}} the same message. Multilinguals were half as likely to show fast aging.
So it's never too late?
Never. Adults who {{take up}} a new language may slow the decline that comes with age.
Okay. French classes, [[here I come]].

chunks.text: A [[growing number of]] governments are trying to {{clamp down}} on children's use of social media. The trend {{kicked off}} in Australia, which {{rolled out}} a [[ban]] on the apps for anyone under 16. Now the European Union is thinking about a similar [[policy]] for the young people in its [[member countries]]. Leaders say the plan is [[meant to]] protect [[minors]] from [[harm]].

verbs.correct: To take strong action to stop or control something
verbs.wrong: To punish people who have already broken an existing rule

verbs.correct: To start or begin an event or activity

chunks.text: Under the new idea, children under 13 would not be able to {{sign up}} for social media at all. After that age, teenagers would [[gradually]] be allowed to join, but only [[once]] the [[platforms]] {{carry out}} stronger safety checks. Ursula von der Leyen, who {{heads up}} the European Commission, said the plan is not about stopping children from using the apps. She said it is really about deciding when the apps can [[reach into]] children's lives.

chunks.text: People who support the rules [[point to]] studies that connect [[heavy]] app use with worse [[mental health]] [[among]] teenagers. They [[argue]] that the apps are built to {{draw in}} young users and keep them scrolling for hours. To deal with this, the EU may make companies {{turn off}} features like [[autoplay]] and [[endless]] scrolling. Others say a ban might {{shut out}} young people from useful advice, support groups, and online friends. The EU [[is expected to]] {{put forward}} a formal [[proposal]] after the summer break, and countries around the world are watching to see [[what happens next]].

lines.text: Europe may keep young children off social media completely.
Like the Australian ban?

How would it work?
Children under 13 couldn't {{sign up}} at all. Teenagers would join gradually, but only after the platforms {{carry out}} stronger safety checks.
Whose plan is this?

[[I can see both sides]], honestly.

chunks.text: The Detroit Zoo is celebrating a very special [[new arrival]]. Late in the evening on July 12, 2026, a baby girl gorilla was born to a [[first-time]] mother named Tulivu. lines.text: Big tech drama. Apple and OpenAI have completely {{fallen out}}.

chunks.text: China has {{pulled off}} [[a major step]] in space travel. lines.text: China just {{pulled off}} something only SpaceX had done before. They recovered a rocket booster after launch.
Really? How did they do it?
Their new rocket {{took off}} from Hainan, carried a satellite into orbit, and then the booster {{came down}} toward the sea. A giant net on a floating platform caught it.
A net? [[That's wild]].
Engineers {{set up}} the whole capture system themselves, and they had never {{tried out}} the design in a real flight before.

chunks.text: The European Union has {{spoken out}} against two of the world's most popular apps. Officials said that Instagram and Facebook, which are both [[owned by]] the company Meta, are [[designed]] to be too [[addictive]]. They believe the apps break a European law called the Digital Services Act, because their design can [[harm]] users' health and [[well-being]].

verbs.wrong: To start a legal case against someone
verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think

chunks.text: The [[regulators]] {{pointed out}} three [[features]] that keep people using the apps [[for hours]]. One feature, called infinite scroll, lets a feed load forever; videos {{start up}} [[on their own]] through [[autoplay]]; and the app keeps {{serving up}} posts it thinks you will like. Together, officials said, these [[tricks]] push the brain into "[[autopilot]]," so users {{end up}} [[scrolling]] without really deciding to.

verbs.wrong: To officially declare something illegal
verbs.correct: To tell someone about a fact or detail
verbs.why: A friend might point out a stain on your shirt, and a teacher can point out a mistake in an essay. European officials pointed out three features that keep people using Instagram and Facebook for hours.

verbs.wrong: To save something to watch later

verbs.wrong: To lose track of time completely
verbs.correct: To reach a final situation or place
verbs.why: You might end up with the last slice of pizza, or end up in an argument with a stranger. Here small design tricks push users to end up scrolling for hours without ever deciding to.

chunks.text: Europe now wants Meta to {{turn off}} infinite scroll and autoplay [[unless]] a user chooses them, and to {{cut down}} how much the app decides for each person. Meta does not agree. It says it has already {{brought in}} strong rules to protect [[teenagers]], and that the EU's review does not [[fairly]] show the steps it has taken.

verbs.wrong: To make a feature harder to find
verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working

verbs.wrong: To let users make every choice

verbs.wrong: To promise stronger rules for the future

chunks.text: If Meta cannot [[win the argument]], it may have to {{pay out}} a very large [[fine]], [[up to]] 6% of the money it makes around the world each year. The company can still respond before Europe {{hands down}} [[a final decision]] [[in the coming months]]. lines.text: Did you read about Ukraine's big drone campaign? It lasted three days.
The one against the oil sites?
Yes. Ukraine {{stepped up}} its attacks and {{carried out}} strikes on refineries and oil tankers. The drones {{set off}} fires at several energy sites.
How far can those drones even fly?
Far. One refinery in Siberia, Russia's largest, {{shut down}} some operations after it was hit. That's about 1,700 miles from Ukraine.
1,700 miles? [[You're kidding]].
The strikes {{knocked out}} part of the country's oil production. Long lines {{built up}} at gas stations, prices {{went up}}, and some stations completely {{ran out}} of gasoline.
How is Russia responding?
It {{hit back}} by cutting exports. Officials will {{hold back}} diesel exports to keep fuel [[at home]], and some regions {{brought in}} limits on how much fuel drivers can buy.
So the effects reach [[far beyond]] the war zone.
Right. To {{deal with}} the shortages, Russia even started importing gasoline from India. Analysts say global diesel prices could rise too.

chunks.text: Health officials say a tiny [[parasite]] called cyclospora has {{broken out}} across the United States. The CDC reported that this [[outbreak]] has made more than 1,000 people sick [[so far this year]]. The parasite is [[microscopic]], so people cannot see it on their food. chunks.text: Cyclospora usually [[spreads]] through contaminated fresh [[produce]], [[such as]] fruits and vegetables. When people {{come down with}} the [[illness]], they often have [[long-lasting]] [[diarrhea]] and stomach pain. The [[infection]], which doctors call cyclosporiasis, is not usually dangerous. Still, some patients {{end up}} needing [[medical care]] to {{deal with}} their [[symptoms]].

lines.text: [[Quick warning]] before dinner. Wash your vegetables really well.
Why, what happened?
A tiny parasite has {{broken out}} across the US. Over 1,000 people have gotten sick this year.
A parasite? [[Gross]]. Where does it come from?
Mostly fresh fruits and vegetables. Officials are still trying to {{find out}} which foods are contaminated. The problem is you can't see it, it's microscopic.
What happens if you {{come down with}} it?

chunks.text: A dangerous [[heat wave]] {{heated up}} much of the United States over the July 4 holiday weekend. A large [[heat dome]] [[settled]] over the country, and the [[extreme]] heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast. lines.text: Remember that heat wave over the July 4 weekend? The numbers are [[unbelievable]].
I heard it was bad. How bad?
The whole country {{heated up}} at once. The extreme heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast, and 40 million people were under a heat alert.
Forty million? [[Seriously?]]
Temperatures {{shot up}} past 100 degrees in many cities. Washington hit 103, a new record.
What about the nights? It usually gets better [[after dark]].
Not this time. The air didn't {{cool down}} overnight, so people couldn't {{cool off}} at all. It stayed near 80.
That's the dangerous part, right?
Exactly. At least 24 people died. Officials {{pointed out}} that extreme heat is one of the deadliest kinds of weather.
What did they tell people to do?
To {{carry on}} drinking water, rest indoors, and {{look out for}} older neighbors. Cities opened cooling centers to help people {{deal with}} it, and some outdoor events were {{called off}}.
Did it ever end?
[[Thankfully]], yes. The heat finally {{let up}} when cooler air arrived.

stories.headline: New cells bring back sight in mice

sources.title: Blind People Offered Hope of Seeing Again After Stem Cell Breakthrough Remakes Retinal Blood Vessels (Good News Network)
Researchers Grow Rare Eye Vessel Cells to Halt Vision Loss (Neuroscience News)
Lab-Grown Retinal Cells Show Promise for New Eye Therapies (Duke Pratt School of Engineering)

chunks.text: Scientists at Duke University said they had {{carried out}} an [[exciting]] experiment. A team led by Professor Sharon Gerecht {{set out}} to grow tiny blood vessels for the [[retina]] using [[stem cells]]. These special cells are very hard to make, but the scientists {{came up with}} a [[clever]] way to grow them in the lab. Their [[goal]] was to help people who are slowly [[losing their sight]].

verbs.wrong: To repeat an experiment to check the results
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task or experiment
verbs.why: Scientists carry out experiments, and companies carry out surveys before launching a product. The Duke University team carried out a study on growing new blood vessel cells for the eye.

verbs.wrong: To promise to finish something important
verbs.correct: To begin a task with a clear goal
verbs.why: Explorers set out on long journeys, and researchers set out to answer a hard question. The Duke team set out to grow the delicate blood vessels found in the retina.

verbs.wrong: To copy a method from another team
verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Inventors come up with new gadgets, and cooks come up with recipes using leftovers. The scientists came up with a clever way to grow cells that are normally very hard to produce.

chunks.text: The researchers used stem cells that can [[turn into]] almost any cell in the body. In the lab, these cells slowly grew into the [[tissue]] that [[lines]] the blood vessels in the eye. To copy eye disease, the team put the tissue [[under stress]], and it started to {{break down}} [[in the same way]] it does in sick patients. These blood vessel tissue cells normally come only from inside the body, so growing them outside the body in the lab was a real [[breakthrough]].

verbs.wrong: To grow larger and stronger
verbs.correct: To stop working or collapse
verbs.why: Old cars break down on the highway, and a diet plan can break down after a few weeks. Under stress, the lab grown eye tissue broke down the same way it does in sick patients.

chunks.text: Next, the team tested the new cells in mice, not in people. They [[injected]] the cells into mice with weak, [[damaged]] eyes. The cells joined the tissue and {{built up}} strong, healthy blood vessels. This slowly {{brought the animals' sight back}}, and their [[vision]] got better. Mice that were treated early did not {{end up}} completely [[blind]].

verbs.wrong: To replace old cells with donor tissue
verbs.correct: To make something grow stronger
verbs.why: Regular training builds up muscle, and steady saving builds up a bank account over time. Inside the treated mice, the new cells built up strong, healthy blood vessels.

verbs.wrong: To start talking about a topic
verbs.correct: To make something return
verbs.why: A good night's sleep can bring back energy, and physical therapy can bring back lost movement. In the treated mice, the new cells slowly brought back some of their lost vision.

verbs.wrong: To stay the same without any change
verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation or place
verbs.why: Travelers end up lost without a map, and careless spenders end up with no money by the end of the month. Mice that were treated early did not end up completely blind.

chunks.text: Professor Gerecht said the results [[point to]] a [[hopeful]] future, but she was [[careful]]. [[So far]] the [[method]] has only been tested in mice, so scientists cannot say yet that it will work in humans. They still need to work on safety before any tests in people. Doctors do not {{rule out}} problems, and they say a real [[treatment]] for [[diabetic retinopathy]], [[a leading cause]] of [[blindness]], may still be many [[years away]].

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: Doctors rule out serious illness with tests, and mechanics rule out engine trouble first. Researchers do not rule out safety problems before any human trials can begin.

mainIdea.why: The scientists grew the blood vessel cells from stem cells and tested them in mice with damaged eyes. The mice slowly got some of their vision back.

mainIdea.s: Doctors are running new trials of a laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy in older adult patients. Early results show the therapy slows vision loss without any surgery.

lines.text: [[Here's some good news]] from science. Researchers {{brought back}} sight in blind mice.
[[No way]]. How did they do that?
With stem cells. A team at Duke {{set out}} to grow tiny blood vessels for the eye, and they {{carried out}} the whole experiment in their lab.
I thought cells like that were impossible to grow outside the body.
Almost impossible. But the scientists {{came up with}} a clever way to do it.
And it worked?
First they copied eye disease in the lab, and the tissue began to {{break down}} just like in sick patients. Then they injected healthy new cells into mice with damaged eyes.
[[Poor mice]]. What happened?
The cells {{built up}} strong new blood vessels, and the animals' sight slowly returned. Mice treated early didn't {{end up}} blind at all.
[[That actually gives me hope]]. Could it help people one day?
Maybe, but the scientists are careful. They don't {{rule out}} problems, and a real treatment could still be [[years away]].

chunks.text: News reports said Italy may become the next country to {{roll out}} a solar railway. The idea comes from Sun-Ways, a Swiss [[start-up]] that {{came up with}} [[a way to]] place solar [[panels]] between train tracks. After a Swiss [[pilot project]] passed its [[one-year mark]] with strong results, [[supporters]] say Italy could {{end up}} building its own line that turns unused rail space into clean energy.

chunks.text: The Swiss company first {{set up}} the test track in Buttes, in the canton of Neuchatel, in April 2025. Workers [[laid]] 48 special panels between the [[rails]] on the wooden [[sleepers]]. mainIdea.s: Rescuers pulled a security guard out of a collapsed parking lot alive after eight days. A strong concrete booth had protected him, and teams from seven countries dug for 70 hours.
mainIdea.why: The booth held up and made a safe pocket around him. Rescuers from seven countries needed more than 70 hours of careful work to reach it.

mainIdea.s: Eight days after the earthquakes, workers reached a security guard who was still alive. He had food and water passed down to him, and doctors say he will need months to recover.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he had no food and very little water for those eight days. Doctors say he is in good condition and is already getting over the ordeal.

mainIdea.s: Two powerful earthquakes have killed more than 2,500 people in Venezuela, and the government is asking other countries for help. Thousands of damaged homes must now be rebuilt.
mainIdea.why: The earthquakes are only the background here. This story is about one man being pulled out alive after eight days.

tf.s: For eight long days, the concrete booth held on and formed a protective pocket around him.
tf.why: A structure cannot actively endure the way a person does, so calling it held on instead of held up is unambiguous.

tf.s: In the end, the rescuers' effort paid off and they saved the man alive.
tf.why: The workers refused to give up, and in the end their effort paid off (brought a good result).

tf.s: After more than 70 hours of digging, the rescue teams gave up before finding the man.
tf.why: The rescue workers refused to give up. Their effort paid off after more than 70 hours and they found the man alive.

tf.s: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up to save the trapped man.
tf.why: Rescue teams from seven countries teamed up (joined together) to save him.

tf.s: Doctors say Gil is slowly getting over his terrible ordeal.
tf.why: At the hospital, doctors say he is slowly getting over (recovering from) the ordeal and is now in good condition.

tf.s: Gil brought about his own terrible ordeal under the rubble.
tf.why: Gil did not cause what happened to him. Bring about means to cause something to happen, but it was the earthquake that trapped him. Doctors say he is getting over the ordeal.

lines.text: Did you hear about the man in Venezuela? The one they {{pulled out}} of a collapsed building?
The security guard? Eight days under the rubble, right?
Eight days. The whole parking lot {{came down}} on him, but he {{ended up}} inside a small concrete booth. [[Somehow]] it {{held up}} and protected him.
No food, almost no water. [[I can't imagine]] how he {{held on}} that long.
[[Me neither]]. Rescue teams from seven countries {{teamed up}} to find him. It took them 70 hours just to {{dig out}} the booth.
[[Wow]]. Most rescues stop after three days, don't they?
Usually, yes. But they refused to {{give up}}, and it {{paid off}}.
How is he now?
In good condition, they say. He'll need time to {{get over}} it, but he's alive.
After everything that's happened there, that country needed some good news.
[[That's what everyone's saying]]. One rescue {{brought about}} a little bit of hope.

stories.headline: Giraffes can do simple math

sources.title: Study finds giraffes may be capable of rudimentary math - UPI
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - University of Barcelona
Giraffes combine quantities similarly to addition - Phys.org
9@9: Giraffes can do math (video, WGN Living)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{found out}} that giraffes can do simple math. [[Researchers]] at the University of Barcelona {{carried out}} a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain. They wanted to see [[whether]] the animals could {{work out}} which [[amount]] of food was bigger. The results [[surprised]] many people.

verbs.wrong: To share a fact with the public
verbs.correct: To learn or discover something
verbs.why: You check the mail to find out if a package arrived, and a quick search can find out a restaurant's hours. Scientists at the University of Barcelona found out that giraffes can do simple math.

verbs.wrong: To plan something in detail
verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Doctors carry out tests before a surgery, and a company can carry out a survey to learn what customers want. Researchers at the University of Barcelona carried out a study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.

verbs.wrong: To smell the difference in food type
verbs.correct: To find the answer to something
verbs.why: You work out a fair price for a used car, and kids work out how to split candy evenly between friends. The scientists wanted to see if the giraffes could work out which pile of food was bigger.

chunks.text: In the test, the scientists {{set up}} [[clear]] [[containers]] with different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces. Sometimes they added more pieces, and sometimes they {{took away}} a few. Each time, the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the container with more food. To get the [[reward]], the animals used their long [[tongues]] to reach it.

verbs.wrong: To hide something from view
verbs.correct: To prepare or arrange something
verbs.why: You set up chairs before a party, and a photographer might set up lights before taking pictures. The scientists set up clear containers holding different numbers of carrot and vegetable pieces.

verbs.wrong: To put things in a row
verbs.correct: To remove something
verbs.why: A waiter takes away empty plates at the end of a meal, and a nurse might take away an old bandage. Sometimes the scientists added pieces of food, and sometimes they took away a few.

verbs.wrong: To point at something you want
verbs.correct: To choose one thing from several
verbs.why: You pick out a birthday card at the store, and a shopper can pick out the ripest fruit from a pile. Each time, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food to earn a reward.

chunks.text: When the scientists added pieces, the giraffes did [[far better]] than [[luck]] [[alone]] would explain. [[According to the study]], they chose the larger amount about 68 percent of the time. This helped the team {{rule out}} the idea that the animals were only [[guessing]]. The results [[suggest]] giraffes can {{keep track of}} small numbers and can {{tell apart}} large and small amounts of food. However, the animals could not [[solve]] harder tasks, [[such as]] [[subtraction]].

verbs.wrong: To show that an idea is only partly true
verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.why: A mechanic can rule out a battery problem after a quick test, and a doctor might rule out a serious illness with one scan. The strong results helped the team rule out the idea that the giraffes were only guessing.

verbs.wrong: To multiply two numbers together quickly
verbs.correct: To follow the number or progress of something
verbs.why: You keep track of your spending in a small notebook, and a coach keeps track of the score during a close game. The results suggest giraffes can keep track of small numbers of carrots and vegetables too.

verbs.wrong: To choose the thing that you like best
verbs.correct: To see the difference between things
verbs.why: Twins can be hard to tell apart at first glance, and a new driver might struggle to tell apart the brake and the gas pedal. The study suggests giraffes can tell apart large and small amounts of food.

chunks.text: [[For a long time]], people thought that only humans and a few [[clever]] animals, such as [[primates]] and crows, had [[a sense of]] numbers. This new study adds to [[a growing list]] of animals that can count [[in some way]]. The researchers now want to {{carry on}} their work with other zoo animals. They hope it will help us {{figure out}} more about how animal minds work.

verbs.wrong: To repeat the same test one more time
verbs.correct: To continue doing something
verbs.why: A band can carry on playing even after the lights dim, and a runner might carry on despite heavy rain. The researchers now want to carry on their work by testing other zoo animals too.

verbs.wrong: To watch something very closely
verbs.correct: To understand or solve something
verbs.why: You figure out a tricky math problem after some thought, and a mechanic can figure out a strange noise in an engine. Scientists hope this research will help figure out more about how animal minds work.

mainIdea.s: Four giraffes usually chose the container with more food, so it seems they can tell small numbers apart. They could not do harder math, such as subtraction.
mainIdea.why: They picked the larger amount about 68 percent of the time, which is better than guessing. But the study says they could not solve harder tasks such as subtraction.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Spain tested four zoo giraffes and found they can add and subtract small amounts of food. They say the animals are now as clever as primates.
mainIdea.why: Close, but subtraction was too hard for the giraffes. The study only shows they can tell a larger amount of food from a smaller one.

mainIdea.s: Zoos in Spain have started giving giraffes puzzle feeders to keep their minds busy. Keepers say the animals now eat more slowly and seem much calmer.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a test of whether giraffes can compare amounts of food. It is not about how zoos feed them.

tf.s: Researchers carried on a new study with four giraffes at a zoo in Spain.
tf.why: The researchers carried out (performed) a new study. Carry on means to continue something that is already happening.

tf.s: In the test, the giraffes had to pick out the container that held more food.
tf.why: Each time, the giraffes had to pick out (choose) the container with more food to get the reward.

tf.s: Sometimes the scientists picked out a few pieces of food from the containers.
tf.why: Sometimes the scientists took away (removed) a few pieces. Pick out means to choose one thing from several, not to remove one.

tf.s: Scientists found out that giraffes can do simple math.
tf.why: Researchers at the University of Barcelona found out (discovered) that giraffes can do simple math.

tf.s: The researchers want to carry on their work with other zoo animals.
tf.why: The team wants to carry on (continue) their research to learn more about how animal minds work.

tf.s: This new study shows that giraffes cannot count in any way at all.
tf.why: The study suggests giraffes can keep track of small numbers, adding them to the growing list of counting animals.

lines.text: Okay, [[weird question]]. Do you think a giraffe can count?
...What?
I just read about it. Scientists in Barcelona {{found out}} giraffes can do simple math. They {{carried out}} a whole study at a zoo.
[[Come on]]. How do you even test a giraffe?
They {{set up}} containers with carrot pieces, and the giraffes had to {{pick out}} the one with more food. They got it right 68 percent of the time.
Maybe they [[just got lucky]].
[[That's what I said]]! But the numbers were too good, so the scientists {{ruled out}} guessing. They think giraffes can {{keep track of}} small amounts.
Huh. So [[what's next]], giraffes doing my taxes?
They failed at subtraction, so no. But the team wants to {{carry on}} with other animals and {{figure out}} how their minds work.
[[Honestly]]? Smarter than some people I know.
